In Amar Akbar Anthony (1977) Kapoor played Akbar, the qawwali singer, alongside Amitabh Bachchan's Anthony and Vinod Khanna's Amar; the film was a phenomenon, and Kapoor's share of it was the music and the courtship. Naseeb (1981) and Coolie (1983) followed the same design. Working for Desai gave Kapoor hits he could not have had alone, at the cost of never being the only centre of them — the structural fact that distinguishes his career from Bachchan's in exactly these years.

name: Rahul Rawail
career_background: Rahul Rawail is an Indian film director and editor, the son of the director H. S. Rawail. He began as an assistant to Raj Kapoor — an apprenticeship he later documented in his book Raj Kapoor: The Master at Work — and directed from 1980 to 2007.
debut: Directorial debut Gunehgaar (1980), starring Parveen Babi, Rishi Kapoor, Rajendra Kumar and Asha Parekh. His first two films failed; his third, Love Story (1981), was a hit.
major_works: With Kapoor: Gunahgaar (1980), Biwi-O-Biwi (1981), Deedar-E-Yaar (1982), Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001). Elsewhere, Love Story, Betaab (1983), Arjun (1985), Dacait, Anjaam and Aur Pyaar Ho Gaya.
recurring_themes: Youth romance against parental opposition, and the action drama of the angry young man of the 1980s.
creative_style: A launcher of new actors — Kumar Gaurav and Vijayeta Pandit in Love Story, Sunny Deol and Amrita Singh in Betaab, Kajol in Bekhudi, Aishwarya Rai in Aur Pyaar Ho Gaya — working in mainstream romance and action.
major_awards: Filmfare nominations for Best Director for Betaab (1983) and Arjun (1985).
historical_importance: A significant commercial director of the 1980s and one of Hindi cinema's most prolific star-launchers.
relationship_with_actor: Four films across twenty-one years, and the only collaborator whose directorial debut was a Kapoor film: his article names Gunehgaar (1980), with Kapoor, Parveen Babi, Rajendra Kumar and Asha Parekh, as his first film, which is how this workbook recovers the director credit for a film that has no Wikipedia article of its own. He then directed the R. K. production Biwi-O-Biwi (1981), co-wrote his father's Deedar-E-Yaar (1982) with Kapoor in the lead, and directed him again in Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001) after an eighteen-year gap.
biography: Rahul Rawail began his directing career with a Rishi Kapoor film and returned to him twice more. The son of the director H. S. Rawail, he trained as Raj Kapoor's assistant — the subject of his later book Raj Kapoor: The Master at Work — before making his debut with Gunehgaar in 1980, a film starring Kapoor, Parveen Babi, Rajendra Kumar and Asha Parekh that failed commercially and left so little trace that this workbook has to recover its director credit from Rawail's own article. Love Story the following year made him, and through the 1980s he launched a succession of new stars — Sunny Deol and Amrita Singh in Betaab, later Kajol and Aishwarya Rai — while earning Filmfare nominations for Betaab and Arjun. His other Kapoor films are the R. K. comedy Biwi-O-Biwi, his father's Deedar-E-Yaar, which he co-wrote, and Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi in 2001.

name: Rakesh Roshan
career_background: Rakesh Roshan Nagrath (born 6 September 1949) is an Indian actor turned director and producer, a son of the composer Roshan and brother of the composer Rajesh Roshan. He appeared in 84 films in the 1970s and 1980s, founded the production company Filmkraft in 1980, and from 1987 directed a series of films with titles beginning with K. He is the father of Hrithik Roshan.
debut: Acting from 1970; Filmkraft's first production was Aap Ke Deewane (1980), a box-office failure; his directing breakthrough was Khudgarz (1987).
major_works: With Kapoor: Aap Ke Deewane (1980), Khudgarz (1987), Kaun Sachcha Kaun Jhootha (1997), Karobaar (2000). Elsewhere, Khoon Bhari Maang, Karan Arjun, Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai and the Krrish series.
recurring_themes: Revenge and rebirth, family honour, and from 2000 the superhero and science-fiction franchise.
creative_style: Tightly formulaic commercial direction with a strong musical identity, usually scored by his brother, and a habit of launching or relaunching stars.
major_awards: Filmfare Awards for Best Film and Best Director for Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai and Koi... Mil Gaya.
historical_importance: A successful second-generation filmmaker who built one of Hindi cinema's enduring production houses and launched Hrithik Roshan's career.
relationship_with_actor: Four films as director or producer, plus a prior connection as a fellow actor — his article records him playing a supporting role in Khel Khel Mein, with Kapoor in the lead. His Filmkraft debut Aap Ke Deewane (1980) was a flop, but Khudgarz (1987) was among the few solid successes of Kapoor's weakest decade, and Kaun Sachcha Kaun Jhootha and Karobaar continued the association into the 1990s and 2000s. Three of the four are scored by his brother Rajesh Roshan.
biography: Rakesh Roshan moved from acting beside Rishi Kapoor to directing him, and gave him one of the few hits of his thinnest decade. The son of the composer Roshan, he appeared in 84 films through the 1970s and 1980s, including a supporting role in Khel Khel Mein opposite Kapoor's lead, before founding Filmkraft in 1980; its first production, Aap Ke Deewane, with Kapoor, failed. Khudgarz (1987), his breakthrough as a director, was different: a revenge melodrama that worked commercially and reminded the industry that Kapoor could still open a film. Kaun Sachcha Kaun Jhootha (1997) and Karobaar (2000) followed, by which time Roshan's attention was turning to launching his son Hrithik in Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai, which won him Filmfare Awards for Best Film and Best Director. Nearly all of his films with Kapoor are scored by his brother Rajesh Roshan, making this a two-family collaboration.

name: Ramesh Talwar
industry: Hindi cinema; Indian theatre and television
career_background: Ramesh Talwar is an Indian film, theatre and television director, co-producer and actor, and a nephew of the writer Sagar Sarhadi. He appeared as a child artist in Dhool Ka Phool (1959) and Love in Simla (1960), was Yash Chopra's assistant director from 1969 to 1979, and has directed extensively for the stage.
debut: Directorial debut Doosra Aadmi (1977), starring Raakhee, Rishi Kapoor and Neetu Singh.
major_works: With Kapoor: Doosra Aadmi (1977), Duniya (1984), Zamana (1985), Sahibaan (1993). Elsewhere, Baseraa (1981), which brought him a Filmfare nomination for Best Director.
recurring_themes: Adult romantic melodrama in the Yash Chopra manner: triangles, second chances and the pull of the past.
creative_style: A Chopra-trained director of restrained melodrama, more interested in performance and dialogue than in spectacle, and with a parallel career in theatre.
major_awards: Filmfare nomination for Best Director for Baseraa (1981).
historical_importance: A significant graduate of the Yash Chopra school and a long-serving figure in Hindi theatre and television.
relationship_with_actor: Four films, the first of them one of the most interesting in the filmography. Doosra Aadmi (1977), Talwar's debut, cast Kapoor as a young man drawn into an affair with an older woman played by Raakhee, who sees her dead lover in him — a deliberate inversion of the boyish romantic persona Bobby had created. Duniya (1984), Zamana (1985) and Sahibaan (1993) followed. His article names Kapoor and Neetu Singh among Doosra Aadmi's cast and records that only two of his seven films succeeded.
biography: Ramesh Talwar directed four Rishi Kapoor films, beginning with the one that most sharply questioned Kapoor's image. A nephew of the writer Sagar Sarhadi and a child actor in Dhool Ka Phool, Talwar spent a decade as Yash Chopra's assistant before making Doosra Aadmi in 1977, in which Kapoor's young advertising executive is pursued by an older woman, Raakhee, who is trying to recover a dead lover through him. Released four years after Bobby, it used his youth against him. Talwar went on to direct Duniya, Zamana and Sahibaan with Kapoor, and earned a Filmfare nomination for Baseraa in 1981, though by his article's own account only two of his seven features succeeded commercially. He has worked continuously in theatre and television since, and is one of the clearest examples in this filmography of a Chopra-trained director taking the romantic hero seriously enough to complicate him.

name: Ravi Malhotra
career_background: A Hindi-film producer active from the mid-1970s to the mid-1990s, with no Wikipedia article of his own. Three of his four Kapoor films were directed by Ravi Tandon, which suggests a standing producer-director partnership rather than four unrelated ventures.
major_works: With Kapoor: Khel Khel Mein (1975), Jhoota Kahin Ka (1979), Rahi Badal Gaye (1985), Hum Dono (1995).
recurring_themes: Youth comedy and light romance in the 1970s, moving to family drama in the 1980s and 1990s.
creative_style: Not documented; his output is identified with Ravi Tandon's direction and R. D. Burman's music.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Four films across twenty years, beginning with Khel Khel Mein (1975), the college musical that was among the defining successes of Kapoor's early career, and continuing through Jhoota Kahin Ka, Rahi Badal Gaye and Hum Dono. Three of the four pair him with the director Ravi Tandon and two with R. D. Burman's music, making this one of the stable production units of Kapoor's youth phase.
biography: Ravi Malhotra produced four Rishi Kapoor films and has no documented biography. What the credits show is a working unit rather than a series of one-off investments: three of his four films with Kapoor were directed by Ravi Tandon, and two were scored by R. D. Burman, the same combination that produced Khel Khel Mein in 1975. That film — a campus comedy of pranks and mistaken death, with Kapoor and Neetu Singh at its centre and a soundtrack that outlasted it — is among the handful that established his youthful persona in the years immediately after Bobby. Jhoota Kahin Ka (1979) and Rahi Badal Gaye (1985) continued the partnership in diminishing form, and Hum Dono followed in 1995. The row is built from film credits alone, and its confidence grade reflects that.

name: Ravi Tandon
career_background: Ravi Tandon (17 February 1935 – 11 February 2022) was an Indian film director and producer, born in Agra, who also worked as an assistant director and story writer. He was the father of the actress Raveena Tandon, and died of respiratory failure in Mumbai at the age of 86.
debut: Working from 1960; his best-known films include Khel Khel Mein, Anhonee, Majboor, Khud-daar and Nazrana.
major_works: With Kapoor: Khel Khel Mein (1975), Jhoota Kahin Ka (1979), Aan Aur Shaan (1984), Rahi Badal Gaye (1985). Elsewhere, Majboor, Khud-daar and Nazrana (1987), the fifth highest grosser of its year.
recurring_themes: Campus comedy and urban youth romance alongside star-vehicle action drama.
creative_style: Light, briskly paced commercial direction with a strong feel for song placement, and a preference for ensembles of young players.
historical_importance: A dependable commercial director of the 1970s and 1980s whose Khel Khel Mein helped establish the Hindi campus musical.
relationship_with_actor: Four films, and the director most responsible for the carefree comic register of Kapoor's youth. Khel Khel Mein (1975) is the key one: a campus comedy with Kapoor, Neetu Singh and Rakesh Roshan, a hit R. D. Burman soundtrack, and a plot driven by a prank that goes wrong. Jhoota Kahin Ka, Aan Aur Shaan and Rahi Badal Gaye followed over the next decade, three of the four produced by Ravi Malhotra. His article lists Khel Khel Mein first among his hits.
biography: Ravi Tandon directed four Rishi Kapoor films, and the first of them is one of the foundations of his early persona. Born in Agra in 1935 and the father of the actress Raveena Tandon, Tandon worked as an assistant director and story writer before building a career of dependable commercial hits — Anhonee, Majboor, Khud-daar, Nazrana — and his own article names Khel Khel Mein (1975) first among them. That film cast Kapoor, Neetu Singh and Rakesh Roshan as students whose prank spirals into a murder plot, and its R. D. Burman songs did as much as Bobby to fix Kapoor as the singing, flirting college hero. Jhoota Kahin Ka, Aan Aur Shaan and Rahi Badal Gaye followed, three of them produced by Ravi Malhotra, the same unit working repeatedly. Tandon directed until 1987 and died in February 2022.

name: Sagar Sarhadi
industry: Hindi cinema; Urdu literature and theatre
career_background: Sagar Sarhadi (11 May 1933 – 22 March 2021) was an Indian Urdu short-story writer and playwright who became a film writer, director and producer. Born in Baffa in what is now Pakistan, he was the uncle of the director Ramesh Talwar, and directed the parallel-cinema film Bazaar.
debut: Became known in films with Yash Chopra's Kabhi Kabhie (1976).
major_works: With Kapoor: Kabhie Kabhie (1976), Doosra Aadmi (1977), Deewana (1992), Karobaar (2000). Elsewhere, Noorie, Silsila, Bazaar and Faasle; his article also lists Chandni (1989) among his credits.
recurring_themes: Adult longing and renunciation; marriages shadowed by earlier loves; the Urdu literary sensibility inside the commercial romance.
creative_style: A literary writer of restrained, dialogue-driven romance, working mainly for Yash Chopra and in parallel cinema as a director.
major_awards: Lifetime Achievement Award at the International Cultural Artifact Film Festival in 2019.
historical_importance: One of the writers who gave the 1970s and 1980s Hindi romance its adult register, and a notable Urdu playwright in his own right.
relationship_with_actor: Four films across twenty-four years, three of them central. He wrote Kabhie Kabhie (1976), the Yash Chopra ensemble about a marriage haunted by a first love, and Doosra Aadmi (1977), in which Kapoor is loved as a dead man's substitute — two films that complicated his new stardom rather than confirming it. Deewana (1992) marked the end of his lead career and Karobaar (2000) came after it. His article records Chandni (1989) among his credits as well, though this workbook's Films row for that film does not list him.
biography: Sagar Sarhadi wrote the films in which Rishi Kapoor's romanticism was treated as a problem rather than a given. An Urdu short-story writer and playwright born in Baffa in 1933, Sarhadi entered cinema with Yash Chopra's Kabhi Kabhie in 1976 and went on to write Noorie, Silsila and Faasle while directing the parallel-cinema film Bazaar. His two most important films with Kapoor came in consecutive years: Kabhie Kabhie, where the young couple's romance is set against an older marriage's buried history, and Doosra Aadmi, where Kapoor's character is desired as the image of a dead man. Both are about love as repetition and substitution, and both were made at the moment when Kapoor's boyishness was most marketable. He wrote Deewana in 1992, the film that closed Kapoor's leading career, and Karobaar in 2000. Sarhadi received a lifetime achievement award in 2019 and died in March 2021.

name: Shankar–Ehsaan–Loy
industry: Hindi cinema; Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Marathi cinema
career_background: An Indian composing trio of Shankar Mahadevan, Ehsaan Noorani and Loy Mendonsa, formed in the mid-1990s, who have composed more than fifty soundtracks across six languages. Shankar Mahadevan received the Padma Shri in 2019.
debut: Composing together from 1997; their breakthrough soundtrack was Dil Chahta Hai (2001).
major_works: With Kapoor: Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic (2008), Luck by Chance (2009), Patiala House (2011), D-Day (2013). Elsewhere, Dil Chahta Hai, Kal Ho Naa Ho, Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna, My Name Is Khan and Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara.
recurring_themes: Urban friendship and self-discovery; the ensemble film; fusion of Indian classical and Western popular forms.
creative_style: Layered, arrangement-conscious composition that treats a soundtrack as an album, with Mahadevan's classical training audible inside pop structures.
major_awards: National Film Awards, Filmfare Awards and IIFA Awards, including the National Film Award for Best Music Direction and a Filmfare Award for Best Music Director.
historical_importance: The leading composers of the post-2000 urban Hindi film, and the sound of its shift from song-and-dance to soundtrack.
relationship_with_actor: Four films, all in Kapoor's character-actor phase and all in the new urban cinema that had replaced his own. Their soundtracks accompany him as the eccentric in Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic, the ageing producer in Luck by Chance — a film explicitly about the film industry's generations — the father in Patiala House and the elder in D-Day. Their article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Shankar–Ehsaan–Loy scored four Rishi Kapoor films, all of them after 2008, and their presence marks how completely the industry around him had changed. The trio of Shankar Mahadevan, Ehsaan Noorani and Loy Mendonsa became the defining composers of post-2000 urban Hindi cinema with Dil Chahta Hai, Kal Ho Naa Ho and Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara, winning National and Filmfare awards and working across six languages. Kapoor appears in their films as a character actor: the oddity in Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic, the father in Patiala House, the elder statesman in D-Day, and — most pointedly — the washed-up producer Rommy Rolly in Zoya Akhtar's Luck by Chance, a film about how Hindi cinema uses and discards its people. That a 1970s romantic lead should be scored by this trio in such a role is a neat summary of his second career.

name: A. R. Rahman
career_background: A. R. Rahman, born A. S. Dileep Kumar, is an Indian composer whose film career began with the Tamil film Roja in the early 1990s and who works from his own studio, Panchathan Record Inn. He received the Padma Bhushan in 2010 and an honorary doctorate from Berklee College of Music in 2014.
debut: Roja (1992), followed by Gentleman, Kaadhalan, Thiruda Thiruda and Bombay.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tehzeeb (2003), Delhi-6 (2009), Jab Tak Hai Jaan (2012). Elsewhere, Roja, Bombay, Lagaan, Slumdog Millionaire and Rang De Basanti.
recurring_themes: Fusion of Indian classical and devotional forms with electronica and world music; the soundtrack as a standalone album.
creative_style: Studio-centred composition built on layered arrangement and unconventional voices, often recorded over long periods and treated as an album rather than a set of cues.
major_awards: Two Academy Awards for Slumdog Millionaire (Best Original Score and Best Original Song for 'Jai Ho') at the 81st ceremony, two Grammy Awards in 2010, the BMI Award for Couples Retreat, the Padma Bhushan in 2010, and numerous National Film Awards.
historical_importance: The most internationally recognised Indian film composer, and the figure who changed how Hindi and Tamil soundtracks are recorded and sold.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, all in Kapoor's character-actor phase and all for directors of a newer generation: Khalid Mohamed's Tehzeeb (2003), Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra's Delhi-6 (2009), and Yash Chopra's final film Jab Tak Hai Jaan (2012). None is a Kapoor vehicle; in each he is a supporting presence inside an ensemble. His article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: A. R. Rahman scored three films in which Rishi Kapoor appears, all of them after 2003 and none of them his. Born A. S. Dileep Kumar, Rahman transformed Indian film music from Roja onwards, working out of his own Chennai studio and treating the soundtrack as an album; he won two Academy Awards and two Grammys for Slumdog Millionaire, received the Padma Bhushan in 2010 and an honorary Berklee doctorate in 2014. His Kapoor films are Tehzeeb, in which Kapoor plays a dying patriarch; Delhi-6, where he is a neighbourhood elder in Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra's Chandni Chowk ensemble; and Jab Tak Hai Jaan, Yash Chopra's last film. The pairing is a marker of era rather than of partnership: the composer who defined Indian film music after 1992 encountered Kapoor only once the actor had become a character player.

name: Amaal Mallik
career_background: Amaal Mallik (born 16 June 1990) is an Indian music director, composer and singer working primarily in Hindi cinema. He is a grandson of the composer Sardar Malik, a nephew of Anu Malik and a brother of the singer Armaan Malik.
debut: Jai Ho (2014); wider recognition came with 'Sooraj Dooba Hain' in 2015.
major_works: With Kapoor: All Is Well (2015), Sanam Re (2016), Kapoor & Sons (2016). Elsewhere, Airlift, Badrinath Ki Dulhania, Golmaal Again and Kabir Singh.
recurring_themes: Contemporary romantic pop for the urban Hindi film, and the non-film single.
creative_style: Melodic pop composition with heavy use of guest singers, written as much for streaming and radio as for a film's narrative.
major_awards: Several Mirchi Music and IIFA awards, and a Filmfare nomination for Best Music Director shared with Tanishk Bagchi and Akhil Sachdeva.
historical_importance: One of the principal composers of the 2010s Hindi film song, a period in which soundtracks were increasingly assembled from several composers.
relationship_with_actor: Three films in two years at the very end of the career, all of them ensembles in which Kapoor plays an elder: All Is Well (2015), Sanam Re (2016) and Kapoor & Sons (2016), the last his most admired late performance. His article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Amaal Mallik is the youngest composer in this filmography, and his three credits all come in Rishi Kapoor's final decade. Born in 1990 into the Malik family of composers — grandson of Sardar Malik, nephew of Anu Malik, brother of Armaan Malik — he debuted with Jai Ho in 2014 and became one of the busiest composers of the following years, working in the fragmented manner of 2010s Hindi soundtracks where several composers share one film. He wrote songs for All Is Well and Sanam Re, both mediocre vehicles in which Kapoor plays a father, and for Kapoor & Sons, where Kapoor's ninety-year-old patriarch under heavy prosthetics drew the best reviews of his late career. That a composer born after Kapoor's lead career ended should score his last substantial ensemble is a measure of how long that second career ran.

name: Bhushan Kumar
career_background: Bhushan Kumar Dua (born 27 November 1977) is an Indian film and music producer, chairman and managing director of Super Cassettes Industries Limited, better known as T-Series. He is the son of the company's founder Gulshan Kumar.
debut: Took over T-Series after his father's murder in 1997 and built it into a dominant film producer as well as a music label.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patiala House (2011), All Is Well (2015), Sanam Re (2016). Elsewhere, a large slate of T-Series productions across the 2010s.
recurring_themes: Music-led production: films commissioned partly to generate soundtrack catalogue.
creative_style: A volume producer whose film and music businesses reinforce each other, with soundtracks typically split among several composers.
historical_importance: Head of the company that became both India's largest music label and one of its most prolific film producers.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, all late supporting roles and all T-Series productions scored by multiple composers — Patiala House (2011), All Is Well (2015) and Sanam Re (2016). The pattern shows how Kapoor's final decade was spent partly inside a music-industry production model rather than with individual filmmakers. His article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Bhushan Kumar produced three of Rishi Kapoor's late films. The son of Gulshan Kumar, the founder of T-Series who was murdered in 1997, he took over Super Cassettes Industries and turned it into both India's largest music company and one of Hindi cinema's most prolific film producers, with a slate built around soundtrack catalogue as much as story. Kapoor appears in Patiala House as the domineering London patriarch opposing his son's cricket career — one of his better late parts — and in All Is Well and Sanam Re as a father in weaker films. The association is institutional rather than personal: all three were cast and scored through the same production machinery, each soundtrack divided among several composers, which is characteristic of the system Kapoor worked in after 2010 and quite unlike the composer-and-director partnerships of his youth.

name: Himesh Reshammiya
career_background: Himesh Reshammiya (born 23 July 1973) is an Indian composer, playback singer, songwriter, producer and actor with over 1,300 credited songs. He began as a composer with Pyaar Kiya To Darna Kya (1998) and made his acting debut with Aap Kaa Surroor (2007).
debut: Composing from Pyaar Kiya To Darna Kya (1998); his singing breakthrough was 'Aashiq Banaya Aapne' (2005).
major_works: With Kapoor: Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002), Namastey London (2007), All Is Well (2015). Elsewhere, Tere Naam, Aashiq Banaya Aapne and Namastey London.
recurring_themes: Nasal-voiced romantic pop, the title-song hook, and the composer as performer.
creative_style: Immediately identifiable melodic pop, usually sung by himself, built around a single repeated hook.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Male Playback Singer in 2006 for 'Aashiq Banaya Aapne', with a Filmfare nomination for Best Music Direction.
historical_importance: One of the defining and most imitated popular voices of mid-2000s Hindi film music.
relationship_with_actor: Three films across thirteen years, each with Kapoor in a supporting role: the David Dhawan comedy Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002), the diaspora romance Namastey London (2007), in which he plays the Punjabi father, and All Is Well (2015). His article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Himesh Reshammiya scored three films in which Rishi Kapoor plays a father. A composer from 1998 and later one of the most recognisable singers in India, with more than 1,300 credited songs and a Filmfare Award for 'Aashiq Banaya Aapne', Reshammiya belongs to the period when a soundtrack's commercial identity could rest on a composer's own voice. His films with Kapoor are Yeh Hai Jalwa, a David Dhawan comedy in which Kapoor is the older generation; Namastey London, where his Punjabi father insisting on an Indian marriage for his British daughter is one of the most widely seen performances of his late career; and All Is Well. The relationship is characteristic of Kapoor's second act — employed as the paternal figure in films whose music, marketing and youth appeal belonged entirely to other people.

name: Hiroo Yash Johar
career_background: An Indian film producer and the co-head of Dharma Productions, who has no Wikipedia article of her own. The articles on her husband Yash Johar and her son Karan Johar record that she married Yash Johar in 1971, that she is a sister of the filmmaker Yash Chopra, and that Karan Johar — who named his daughter after her — was born in 1972.
major_works: With Kapoor: Agneepath (2012), Student of the Year (2012), Kapoor & Sons (2016). Elsewhere, she is credited as producer on the Dharma Productions slate from the 2000s onward.
recurring_themes: The Dharma house style: family, friendship and glossy urban romance.
creative_style: A producer working alongside her son on the company her husband founded, with credits across its entire modern output.
historical_importance: Co-head of one of the two dominant family studios of contemporary Hindi cinema, and a connecting figure between the Johar and Chopra families.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, all Dharma productions of Kapoor's late period, and all among its strongest: Agneepath (2012), where he plays Rauf Lala, Student of the Year (2012), where he is the dean, and Kapoor & Sons (2016), where he plays the ninety-year-old grandfather. Her family connections place her at the centre of this filmography's institutions — sister to Yash Chopra, whose banner employed Kapoor eleven times, and co-producer of the Dharma films that remade his late career.
biography: Hiroo Yash Johar co-produced the three Dharma Productions films that gave Rishi Kapoor his best late roles, and she has no Wikipedia article of her own. What is documented, through the articles on her husband and son, is that she married Yash Johar in 1971, that she is the sister of Yash Chopra, and that her son Karan Johar was born the following year and later named his daughter after her. Her credits with Kapoor are Agneepath, in which he plays the brothel-keeper Rauf Lala; Student of the Year, where he is the college dean; and Kapoor & Sons, where he plays a mischievous ninety-year-old under prosthetics. Her family position is worth stating plainly: the two production houses that account for most of Kapoor's work across fifty years, Yash Raj Films and Dharma Productions, were run by her brother and by her husband and son.

name: Honey Irani
career_background: Honey Irani is an Indian actress and screenwriter who began as a child actor in films including Pyar Ki Pyas, Chirag Kahan Roshni Kahan and Bombay Ka Chor, and turned to screenwriting as an adult. She was married to Javed Akhtar; their children are the filmmakers Farhan Akhtar and Zoya Akhtar. Her sister is the actress Daisy Irani.
debut: Child actor from the late 1950s; established as a screenwriter from the early 1990s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Anmol (1993), Pehla Pehla Pyar (1994), Prem Yog (1994). Elsewhere, Lamhe, Aaina, Kya Kehna and Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai.
recurring_themes: Women's choices inside family constraint; the romantic melodrama written from the woman's side.
creative_style: A screenwriter of emotionally driven mainstream drama, frequently centred on a female protagonist's decision.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Story, won again for Kya Kehna, and the Filmfare Award for Best Screenplay shared with Ravi Kapoor for Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai.
historical_importance: One of the few women writing mainstream Hindi screenplays in the 1990s, and the matriarch of the Akhtar filmmaking family.
relationship_with_actor: Three films in two years, 1993–94, at the close of Kapoor's lead career: Anmol, Pehla Pehla Pyar and Prem Yog, all romances written to a persona that was no longer selling. Her connection to this filmography is wider than the credits: her sister Daisy Irani was married to K. K. Shukla, one of Kapoor's most frequent writers, and the Ravi Kapoor with whom she shared a Filmfare Award is probably the writer of five other Kapoor films.
biography: Honey Irani wrote three Rishi Kapoor films at the point when his romantic lead was ending. A child actress of the late 1950s and 1960s who became one of the few women writing mainstream Hindi screenplays, she won the Filmfare Award for Best Story twice and shared the Best Screenplay award with Ravi Kapoor for Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai. Her Kapoor credits — Anmol, Pehla Pehla Pyar and Prem Yog, all from 1993 and 1994 — are romances built on his established image, made when audiences had moved to younger actors. Her family threads through this filmography more widely than her three credits suggest: she was married to Javed Akhtar, who has four credits of his own here; her children are Farhan and Zoya Akhtar, both of whom later employed Kapoor; and her sister Daisy was the wife of the screenwriter K. K. Shukla.

name: Javed Siddiqui
industry: Hindi and Urdu cinema; Urdu theatre and literature
career_background: Javed Siddiqui (born 13 January 1942) is a Hindi and Urdu screenwriter, dialogue writer and playwright who has written more than fifty storylines, screenplays and dialogue scripts. He has worked with directors from Satyajit Ray and Shyam Benegal to Yash Chopra and Subhash Ghai, and writes for Urdu theatre.
debut: Writing for films from 1977, beginning with Satyajit Ray's Shatranj Ke Khilari.
major_works: With Kapoor: Allah Rakha (1986), Tehzeeb (2003), Sadiyaan (2010). Elsewhere, Umrao Jaan, Mammo, Fiza, Zubeidaa, Baazigar and Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge.
recurring_themes: Muslim social milieu and Urdu idiom; the woman's story inside a conservative setting; and, in parallel, commercial masala dialogue.
creative_style: A writer equally employable in art and commercial cinema, valued for Urdu dialogue of unusual literary quality.
major_awards: Two Filmfare Awards, two Star Screen Awards and a BFJA Award.
historical_importance: One of the last major Urdu-trained dialogue writers of Hindi cinema, working across parallel and mainstream film for four decades.
relationship_with_actor: Three films across twenty-four years, in three different registers: the masala multi-starrer Allah Rakha (1986), Khalid Mohamed's Tehzeeb (2003), where Kapoor plays a dying patriarch in a Muslim-social setting that is Siddiqui's own territory, and the partition romance Sadiyaan (2010). His article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Javed Siddiqui wrote three Rishi Kapoor films, and they are unusually far apart in time and kind. Born in 1942, Siddiqui is among the last of Hindi cinema's Urdu-trained dialogue writers, with more than fifty films to his name and a career that ran simultaneously through parallel cinema — Satyajit Ray's Shatranj Ke Khilari, Umrao Jaan, Mammo, Zubeidaa — and the commercial mainstream, including Baazigar and Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge. He won two Filmfare Awards and continues to write for Urdu theatre. For Kapoor he wrote the masala ensemble Allah Rakha in 1986; then, seventeen years later, Tehzeeb, in which Kapoor plays the ailing father in a family drama set in precisely the Muslim-social world Siddiqui knows best; and finally the partition-era romance Sadiyaan in 2010.

name: K. Ravi Shankar
career_background: K. Ravi Shankar, born Krishnamoorthy Ravi Shankar, is an Indian film director best known for his Hindi films of the late 1980s and early 1990s. He also produced several films, including Swarag Se Sunder (1986) and Gharana (1989), and launched Govinda in Dariya Dil (1988) and Shilpa Shetty in Aag (1994).
debut: Directing from the mid-1980s; his films with Kapoor begin with Sindoor (1987).
major_works: With Kapoor: Sindoor (1987), Gharana (1989), Sadhna (1993). Elsewhere, Dariya Dil, Benaam Badsha, Apradhi, Meherbaan and Aag.
recurring_themes: Family melodrama of honour, sacrifice and restored respectability, usually with a large star cast.
creative_style: Mid-budget melodrama assembled around songs and confrontation scenes, and a habit of casting newcomers alongside established stars.
historical_importance: A dependable commercial director of the late 1980s, notable for launching Govinda and Shilpa Shetty.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, and one of them is among the more interesting of the period: Gharana (1989), in which Kapoor's character appears mercenary — renouncing one woman and marrying another for dowry money — precisely because he is sacrificing himself, an inversion of the lover-boy pattern. Sindoor (1987) preceded it and Sadhna (1993) followed. The Sadhna credit comes from this director's own article, since the film has none of its own.
biography: K. Ravi Shankar directed three Rishi Kapoor films in the stretch when Kapoor's vehicles had become mid-budget melodramas. Born Krishnamoorthy Ravi Shankar, he was a reliable commercial director of the late 1980s and early 1990s who also produced, and who launched Govinda in Dariya Dil and Shilpa Shetty in Aag. Sindoor (1987) and Gharana (1989) both gave Kapoor roles built on renunciation rather than courtship; in Gharana he plays a man who abandons the woman he loves and marries for dowry money, and whose apparent mercenariness is revealed as sacrifice — a deliberate inversion of the persona Bobby had established. Sadhna (1993) is the third, and is one of six films in this filmography with no Wikipedia article of its own; its director credit is recovered from Shankar's article, whose filmography list is unlabelled, so the attribution is recorded at Medium confidence.

name: Karan Johar
career_background: Karan Johar, born Rahul Kumar Johar on 25 May 1972, is an Indian filmmaker, producer and television personality, the son of the producer Yash Johar and of Hiroo Yash Johar. He has run Dharma Productions since 2004 and has launched the careers of numerous actors and directors.
debut: Directorial debut Kuch Kuch Hota Hai (1998), which won the National Film Award for Best Popular Film and the Filmfare Awards for Best Director and Best Screenplay.
major_works: With Kapoor: Agneepath (2012), Student of the Year (2012), Kapoor & Sons (2016). Elsewhere, Kuch Kuch Hota Hai, Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham, My Name Is Khan, Raazi and Shershaah.
recurring_themes: Family reconciliation, friendship and the diaspora; glamour as a moral setting; and, latterly, the youth ensemble.
creative_style: High-gloss studio filmmaking with an emphasis on star image, music and emotional set pieces, and an unusually active role in casting new actors.
major_awards: Four National Film Awards and eight Filmfare Awards; the Padma Shri in 2020.
historical_importance: The most visible producer-director of contemporary Hindi cinema and the architect of Dharma's second life as a star-making studio.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, as director of Student of the Year (2012), in which Kapoor plays the college dean, and as producer of Agneepath (2012) and Kapoor & Sons (2016), the two strongest performances of his late career. Johar's own article records that he launched three debutant actors in Student of the Year, and the use of Kapoor as its senior presence is part of the same calculation: a veteran to anchor a cast of newcomers.
biography: Karan Johar gave Rishi Kapoor three of his last significant roles, one as director and two as producer. Born in 1972 to Yash and Hiroo Johar, Johar took over Dharma Productions after his father's death in 2004 and became the most conspicuous producer-director in Hindi cinema, a four-time National Film Award and eight-time Filmfare Award winner honoured with the Padma Shri in 2020. He directed Kapoor as the dean in Student of the Year, a film cast with three debutants who needed a familiar older face beside them, and produced Agneepath, in which Kapoor's Rauf Lala is a genuinely frightening villain, and Kapoor & Sons, in which his ninety-year-old grandfather is comic and tender at once. For an actor whose own lead career had ended in anonymity, these were the films that re-established him with a young audience.

name: Keshav Rathod
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active in the late 1980s and 1990s, working on family melodrama. He has no Wikipedia article of his own, and his credits here are all shared.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani (1988), Saajan Ka Ghar (1994), Ghar Ki Izzat (1994).
recurring_themes: The household melodrama of duty and mistreatment; two of his three titles name the home directly.
creative_style: Not documented; he is credited alongside Kader Khan on two of the three films.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, two of them directed by Kalpataru and written with Kader Khan — Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani and Ghar Ki Izzat — plus Saajan Ka Ghar. All three belong to the dense run of domestic melodramas Kapoor made between 1988 and 1994, in which he plays sons and husbands rather than lovers.
biography: Keshav Rathod wrote three Rishi Kapoor films and has no documented biography. All three are family melodramas from the stretch between 1988 and 1994 when Kapoor's work had settled into domestic subjects: Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani, a remake of a Telugu film whose real subject is a mother-in-law's cruelty to her daughters-in-law; Ghar Ki Izzat, again for the director Kalpataru and again co-written with Kader Khan; and Saajan Ka Ghar. The grouping is more informative than the individual credits — the same small team of writers and directors, working to the same template of household duty, supplied a large share of Kapoor's output in those years, and almost none of them left a biographical record. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Krishan Kumar
career_background: Krishan Kumar Dua is an Indian actor and film producer, a younger brother of the T-Series founder Gulshan Kumar and an owner of the company. He is best known as an actor for Bewafa Sanam (1995).
debut: Acting from 1982; subsequently a producer within T-Series.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patiala House (2011), All Is Well (2015), Sanam Re (2016). Elsewhere, the T-Series production slate.
recurring_themes: Music-led production in partnership with his nephew Bhushan Kumar.
creative_style: A family producer inside the T-Series system rather than a filmmaker with a distinct signature.
historical_importance: A principal of India's largest music company and a producer on much of its film output.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, the same three T-Series productions as Bhushan Kumar — Patiala House, All Is Well and Sanam Re — in which Kapoor plays fathers. His article is chiefly concerned with his acting career and does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Krishan Kumar co-produced the same three late Rishi Kapoor films as his nephew Bhushan Kumar. A younger brother of Gulshan Kumar, who founded T-Series and was murdered in 1997, he began as an actor in the 1980s and is still best known in that capacity for Bewafa Sanam, while holding an ownership role in what became India's largest music company. His producing credits with Kapoor — Patiala House, All Is Well and Sanam Re — are family-firm productions in which Kapoor was cast as the patriarch, most effectively in Patiala House as the London Punjabi father who forbids his son's cricket career. The row is a reminder that in the 2010s Kapoor's employers were as often music-company proprietors as directors.

name: Kunal Kohli
career_background: Kunal Kohli is an Indian film director, producer, writer and actor, and a nephew of David Dhawan. He directed for Yash Raj Films before founding his own company, Kunal Kohli Productions.
debut: Directing from the early 2000s; his breakthrough was Hum Tum (2004).
major_works: With Kapoor: Hum Tum (2004), Fanaa (2006), Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic (2008). Elsewhere, Break Ke Baad, Teri Meri Kahaani and Phir Se...
recurring_themes: The modern romantic comedy of bickering equals; the romance that spans years and cities.
creative_style: Light, dialogue-driven romance in the Yash Raj register, with a strong reliance on star chemistry.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Director for Hum Tum (2004), won against Yash Chopra's Veer-Zaara.
historical_importance: One of the directors Yash Raj Films developed in-house during its studio phase, and the maker of a defining 2000s romantic comedy.
relationship_with_actor: Three consecutive films, 2004–2008, which together open Kapoor's character-actor phase: Hum Tum, where he plays the hero's father; Fanaa, where he is the Kashmiri father of Kajol's blind heroine; and Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic, produced by his own company. Hum Tum is the film that restarted Kapoor's mainstream employment after a quiet stretch, which makes Kohli more consequential to the late career than his three credits suggest.
biography: Kunal Kohli directed the film that began Rishi Kapoor's second career. A nephew of David Dhawan who came up inside Yash Raj Films, Kohli won the Filmfare Award for Best Director for Hum Tum in 2004 — beating his mentor Yash Chopra — with a romantic comedy about two people who meet and quarrel across years and continents. Kapoor plays the hero's father in it, his first prominent supporting role in a major studio film, and followed Kohli to Fanaa (2006) as the Kashmiri father of Kajol's blind heroine and to Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic (2008), produced by Kohli's own company. Three films in five years re-established Kapoor as a bankable senior presence in exactly the studio that had employed him as a young lead thirty years earlier.

name: MKD Films Combine
career_background: The production banner of the Desai family, named for Manmohan K. Desai, under which his son Ketan Desai made films from the mid-1980s. It has no Wikipedia article of its own, and its name appears in credits variously as MKD Films Combine, M.K.D Films Combines and MKD Films, consolidated here.
major_works: With Kapoor: Allah Rakha (1986), Anmol (1993), Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002).
recurring_themes: The masala multi-starrer inherited from Manmohan Desai: disguise, reunion and comic bravado.
creative_style: A family banner continuing the Desai formula after its originator stopped directing.
historical_importance: Not independently documented; of interest as the vehicle through which the Desai masala style persisted into the 1990s and 2000s.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, all directed by Ketan Desai and all attempts to sustain the multi-star entertainment that had given Kapoor his biggest hits under Manmohan Desai. Allah Rakha (1986) is the most ambitious; Anmol (1993) and Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002) are later and progressively further from the form's heyday.
biography: MKD Films Combine is the Desai family banner, and its three Rishi Kapoor films trace the long decline of the masala multi-starrer. Named for Manmohan K. Desai, whose Amar Akbar Anthony, Naseeb and Coolie had given Kapoor his largest commercial successes, the company was the vehicle through which his son Ketan Desai continued the family trade: Allah Rakha in 1986, with Kapoor in a cast assembled on the old pattern; Anmol in 1993; and Yeh Hai Jalwa in 2002, by which time Kapoor was playing the older generation in a David Dhawan comedy. The banner has no Wikipedia article and its name is spelled three different ways across these credits, which this workbook consolidates. Its real significance is as evidence of a formula outliving the audience that had made it.

name: Madan Joshi
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active from the late 1970s to the mid-1980s, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Badaltey Rishtey (1978), Aap Ke Deewane (1980), Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986).
recurring_themes: Melodrama of obligation and changed circumstance; the love triangle resolved by duty.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Three films spanning Kapoor's late youth and middle period: Badaltey Rishtey (1978), the Filmkraft debut Aap Ke Deewane (1980), and Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986), an adaptation of Rajinder Singh Bedi's novel and the most serious film of the three. The group covers the transition from Kapoor as young romantic lead to Kapoor as the man in a difficult marriage.
biography: Madan Joshi wrote three Rishi Kapoor films and left no biographical record. The three are more varied than most of the undocumented writers' groupings in this filmography: Badaltey Rishtey in 1978, a triangle from the end of his first flush of stardom; Aap Ke Deewane in 1980, the first production of Rakesh Roshan's Filmkraft and a commercial failure; and Ek Chadar Maili Si in 1986, adapted from Rajinder Singh Bedi's Urdu novel about a widow married to her dead husband's younger brother, which is among the few genuinely literary projects Kapoor took in that decade. That a writer with a credit on that film should have no article is characteristic of how thinly the Hindi film workforce of the period is documented. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Sajid–Wajid
career_background: An Indian composing duo of the brothers Sajid Khan and Wajid Khan, sons of the tabla player Sharafat Ali Khan and grandsons of the Padma Shri awardee Ustad Faiyyaz Ahmed Khan, from Saharanpur. They composed together from 1998 until Wajid Khan's death on 1 June 2020.
debut: Composing from 1998, closely associated with Salman Khan's films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009), Housefull 2 (2012), Chashme Buddoor (2013). Elsewhere, Dabangg, Partner and Wanted.
recurring_themes: Mass-market dance and romance songs, Sufi-inflected melody, and the star entrance number.
creative_style: Percussive, hook-led commercial composition built for star choreography.
historical_importance: Among the principal composers of the Salman Khan-led mass entertainer of the 2000s and 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, all late comedies or ensembles in which Kapoor plays a senior figure: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009), Housefull 2 (2012) and Chashme Buddoor (2013). Their article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Sajid–Wajid scored three of Rishi Kapoor's late comedies. The brothers Sajid and Wajid Khan came from a Saharanpur musical family — their father a tabla player, their maternal grandfather a Padma Shri-awarded classical musician — and from 1998 became among the most commercially dependable composers in Hindi cinema, closely tied to Salman Khan's run of mass entertainers. Their Kapoor films are Kal Kissne Dekha, Housefull 2, in which he is one of two feuding brothers in a large farce, and Chashme Buddoor, David Dhawan's remake, where he appears in support. The duo ended when Wajid Khan died in June 2020, six weeks after Kapoor's own death. None of these films is substantial, but together they show what kind of work was available to him at the very end: ensemble comedy, in which an ageing star is one attraction among many.

name: Sandeep Chowta
career_background: Sandeep Chowta, born in 1967 or 1968 in Buduburam, Ghana, is an Indian music director working mainly in Hindi and Telugu cinema, and has headed Columbia Records in India. He produced the anti-substance-abuse documentary Dead End in 2003 and is a core member of the world-music group AO Music.
debut: Composing from 1996.
major_works: With Kapoor: Daraar (1996), Om Shanti Om (2007), Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic (2008). Elsewhere, Satya and Kaante.
recurring_themes: Background score for the urban thriller; cross-genre work between film music and world music.
creative_style: An atmosphere-first score composer, usually hired for background music rather than songs, with a parallel career in non-film recording.
historical_importance: One of the first Hindi film composers to specialise in background score as a distinct craft from song composition.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, all as background-score composer rather than songwriter, and spread across the two halves of Kapoor's career: Daraar (1996), one of his last leads, and then the ensembles Om Shanti Om (2007), in which he appears as himself, and Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic (2008). His article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Sandeep Chowta wrote the background score for three films in this filmography, and his presence marks a structural change in how Hindi films were scored. Born in Ghana in the late 1960s, Chowta became one of the first composers in Hindi cinema to specialise in background music rather than songs — the division of labour that would later let Salim–Sulaiman score four Kapoor films whose songs were written by others — while also heading Columbia Records in India and recording with the world-music group AO Music. His Kapoor credits are Daraar in 1996, a thriller from the very end of Kapoor's leading career; Om Shanti Om in 2007, in which Kapoor appears briefly as himself among a crowd of stars; and Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic in 2008. Three films, three decades, and no songs between them.

name: Shiv–Hari
career_background: The composing duo of the santoor player Shivkumar Sharma and the flautist Hariprasad Chaurasia, both leading Hindustani classical soloists, who scored Hindi films together while maintaining concert careers. Their film work was done mainly for Yash Chopra.
debut: Active from 1967; their film scores are concentrated in the 1980s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Vijay (1988), Chandni (1989), Sahibaan (1993). Elsewhere, Silsila, Faasle, Lamhe and Darr.
recurring_themes: Classical instrumentation inside the popular love song; the Chopra romance.
creative_style: Two classical soloists composing film songs around santoor and bansuri, producing a sound more austere and raga-inflected than their contemporaries'.
historical_importance: The most prominent case of front-rank Hindustani classical musicians composing mainstream Hindi film soundtracks.
relationship_with_actor: Three films in six years, two of them for Yash Chopra, and one of them central: Chandni (1989), whose soundtrack carried Kapoor's return to romantic leading man opposite Sridevi. Vijay (1988) preceded it and Sahibaan (1993) followed. Their article does not mention Kapoor, and records that they worked mainly for Chopra.
biography: Shiv–Hari wrote the music for Rishi Kapoor's late romantic revival. The duo were not film composers by trade: Shivkumar Sharma, the santoor player who brought that instrument into classical concert music, and Hariprasad Chaurasia, the leading bansuri soloist of his generation, composed a small number of Hindi soundtracks almost exclusively for Yash Chopra, beginning with Silsila. Their work is audible as classical musicianship inside a popular form, and in Chandni (1989) it produced the songs that returned Kapoor to romantic leading man after a decade of melodrama, opposite Sridevi and in a film built around music more than plot. Vijay (1988) and Sahibaan (1993) complete their work with him. The pairing stands out in a filmography otherwise scored by career film composers.

name: Surendra Mohan
career_background: A Hindi-film director and producer active from the late 1970s to the early 1990s, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He is credited on Aap Ke Deewane as Surendera Mohan, a spelling this workbook consolidates.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aap Ke Deewane (1980), Hawalaat (1987), Honeymoon (1992).
recurring_themes: The triangle and the multi-star melodrama of the 1980s.
creative_style: Not documented; on two of the three films he is both director and producer.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Three films across twelve years. Aap Ke Deewane (1980) is a triangle whose ending the surviving account does not resolve, made as the first production of Rakesh Roshan's Filmkraft; Hawalaat (1987) is a multi-starrer with Mithun Chakraborty; Honeymoon (1992) comes at the close of Kapoor's lead career. On the latter two he produced as well as directed.
biography: Surendra Mohan directed three Rishi Kapoor films and has no documented biography. The first, Aap Ke Deewane (1980), is the better known: the debut production of Rakesh Roshan's Filmkraft, scored by Rajesh Roshan, with Kapoor in a triangle whose resolution the film's surviving summary does not record. He directed and produced Hawalaat in 1987, a multi-starrer with Mithun Chakraborty, and Honeymoon in 1992, as Kapoor's leading career was closing. His name is spelled Surendera Mohan on the first of the three, one of many small inconsistencies in the credits of this period that this workbook has had to reconcile. The row is built from film credits alone, and its confidence grade reflects that.

name: Umesh Shukla
career_background: Umesh Shukla is an Indian director, writer and actor who works in Hindi cinema and Gujarati theatre. He acted before directing — notably as a villain in Yaar Gaddar — made his directorial debut with Dhoondte Reh Jaaoge, and is best known for the comedy-drama Oh My God. He has directed many Gujarati plays, including Kanjee Viruddha Kanjee, the source of Oh My God.
debut: Working from 1994; directorial debut Dhoondte Reh Jaaoge.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kucch To Hai (2003), All Is Well (2015), 102 Not Out (2018). Elsewhere, Oh My God (2012).
recurring_themes: Adapted stage comedy; the argument between generations within a family.
creative_style: A theatre director's cinema: two or three characters, a confined setting, and dialogue carrying the comedy and the argument.
historical_importance: The director of Oh My God, one of the most successful Hindi adaptations of a Gujarati play, and of the two-hander that gave Kapoor his last lead.
relationship_with_actor: Three films across fifteen years, ending with the most important: 102 Not Out (2018), in which the 65-year-old Kapoor plays the 75-year-old son of Amitabh Bachchan's 102-year-old father, his last leading role and his ninth film with Bachchan. All Is Well (2015) preceded it and Kucch To Hai (2003) opened the association.
biography: Umesh Shukla directed Rishi Kapoor's last lead role. A Gujarati theatre director who moved into Hindi cinema, Shukla had his biggest success with Oh My God, adapted from his own stage play Kanjee Viruddha Kanjee, and his method stayed theatrical: small casts, enclosed settings, argument as structure. He first directed Kapoor in Kucch To Hai (2003), then in All Is Well (2015), and finally in 102 Not Out (2018), a two-hander in which Kapoor plays the morose seventy-five-year-old son of Amitabh Bachchan's irrepressible centenarian father. It was the ninth film the two men made together across forty-one years — they had first appeared together in Amar Akbar Anthony — and the only one in which Kapoor played the younger generation to Bachchan's elder. It was also his last lead before his death in 2020.

name: V. P. Sathe
career_background: A Hindi-film story and screenplay writer associated with Raj Kapoor's R. K. Films, where he worked alongside Khwaja Ahmad Abbas. He has no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Shree 420 (1955), Bobby (1973), Henna (1991).
recurring_themes: The R. K. Films subject: love across class or nation, the innocent tested by the city, and reconciliation through sacrifice.
creative_style: A collaborative story writer, credited with Abbas on all three of these films.
historical_importance: Not independently documented; notable as a long-serving member of the R. K. Films writing team across thirty-six years.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, and the same remarkable span as Khwaja Ahmad Abbas: Shree 420 (1955), in which Kapoor appears as a toddler, Bobby (1973), his first leading role, and Henna (1991), near the end of it. He is credited with Abbas on all three, which makes the pair the only writing partnership to touch both ends of this filmography.
biography: V. P. Sathe wrote three Rishi Kapoor films thirty-six years apart, and nothing about him is documented beyond those credits. He was part of the R. K. Films writing team, working with Khwaja Ahmad Abbas on Shree 420 in 1955 — the film in which a three-year-old Kapoor walks through 'Pyar Hua Iqrar Hua' — on Bobby in 1973, the romance that made him a star at twenty-one, and on Henna in 1991, the cross-border love story Randhir Kapoor completed after their father's death. The pairing with Abbas on all three is the notable fact: the same two writers framed the beginning, the making and the late recapitulation of Kapoor's romantic persona, and only one of them has an article. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Viacom18 Motion Pictures
career_background: Viacom18 Studios, credited on these films as Viacom18 Motion Pictures, was an Indian film production and distribution company based in Mumbai, among the first studio-model film businesses in India, covering acquisition, production, syndication, marketing and worldwide distribution. It distributed Paramount Pictures films in India from 2011 and was later merged into Star Studio18.
debut: Operating under the Viacom18 name from the late 2000s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chashme Buddoor (2013), Manto (2018), The Body (2019).
recurring_themes: A broad studio slate from mass comedy to festival-facing biography.
creative_style: A corporate studio acquiring and producing across genres rather than a banner with an authorial signature.
historical_importance: One of the first corporate studios in Indian cinema, and a model for the acquisition-and-distribution business that displaced the independent producer.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, and the three are unusually unalike: David Dhawan's remake Chashme Buddoor (2013), Nandita Das's Manto (2018), in which Kapoor has a small part in a serious biographical film, and The Body (2019), the last film released in his lifetime. The spread is characteristic of a corporate studio's slate rather than of a working relationship.
biography: Viacom18 Motion Pictures produced or distributed the last three Rishi Kapoor films in this filmography, including the final one released while he was alive. The company was among the first corporate studios in India, running acquisition, production, marketing and worldwide distribution on an integrated model and handling Paramount's Indian releases from 2011; it was later folded into Star Studio18. Its Kapoor films show the range such a studio carried: Chashme Buddoor, a David Dhawan comedy remake; Manto, Nandita Das's biographical film about the Urdu writer, in which Kapoor takes a small role in a festival-facing production quite unlike anything in his lead career; and The Body, a thriller released in December 2019, five months before his death. The studio is less a collaborator than the shape the industry had taken by the end.

name: Aadesh Shrivastava
career_background: Aadesh Shrivastava (4 September 1964 – 5 September 2015) was an Indian composer and playback singer from Jabalpur who worked as a drummer for composers including R. D. Burman and Rajesh Roshan before composing independently. He composed for over 100 Hindi films and was married to the singer Vijayta Pandit.
debut: Began as a session drummer; composing independently from 1990.
major_works: With Kapoor: Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002), Love at Times Square (2003).
recurring_themes: Percussion-forward commercial songs and qawwali-inflected numbers for the 1990s and 2000s mainstream.
creative_style: A drummer's composition, rhythm-led and built for large arrangements, often sung by himself.
historical_importance: A prolific composer of the 1990s and 2000s whose career began inside the orchestras of the composers he later succeeded.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both from 2002–03, in which Kapoor had moved to supporting and elder parts: the David Dhawan comedy Yeh Hai Jalwa and Love at Times Square. His article does not mention Kapoor. The connection worth noting is indirect: he played drums for R. D. Burman and Rajesh Roshan, the two composers with the largest share of Kapoor's own 1970s and 1980s soundtracks.
biography: Aadesh Shrivastava scored two late Rishi Kapoor films, and his career traces the generational handover in Hindi film music. A drummer from Jabalpur who played in the orchestras of R. D. Burman and Rajesh Roshan — the two composers most responsible for Kapoor's own hits — he began composing in 1990 and worked on more than a hundred films, usually in a percussive, large-ensemble idiom and often singing his own songs. His Kapoor credits are the comedy Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002) and Love at Times Square (2003), both films in which Kapoor plays the older generation. Shrivastava died of cancer in September 2015, one day after his fifty-first birthday.

name: Abrar Alvi
career_background: Abrar Alvi (1 July 1927 – 18 November 2009) was an Indian film writer, director and actor whose most celebrated work was done with Guru Dutt in the 1950s and 1960s. He wrote Pyaasa (1957), Kaagaz Ke Phool (1959) and Sahib Bibi Aur Ghulam (1962), for which he won the Filmfare Award for Best Director.
debut: Writing from 1954; his collaboration with Guru Dutt began in that decade.
major_works: With Kapoor: Laila Majnu (1976), Gharana (1989). Elsewhere, Pyaasa, Kaagaz Ke Phool and Sahib Bibi Aur Ghulam, which Time magazine's critics included among the All-Time 100 Movies in the case of Pyaasa.
recurring_themes: The doomed artist and the trapped woman; Urdu literary dialogue inside popular melodrama.
creative_style: Dialogue of unusual literary weight, written for performers rather than for plot, and a willingness to let a scene rest on silence.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Director for Sahib Bibi Aur Ghulam, a credit disputed in his lifetime but never contested by Guru Dutt himself.
historical_importance: One of the most respected writers in Indian cinema, central to the Guru Dutt films that are now its most internationally admired work.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both well after his Guru Dutt years and both unlike it: H. S. Rawail's Laila Majnu (1976), the classical tragic romance in which Kapoor played Qais, and the melodrama Gharana (1989). Laila Majnu is the significant one — a writer of Pyaasa supplying the text for Kapoor's first attempt at mythic, self-destroying love rather than teenage courtship.
biography: Abrar Alvi, the writer of Pyaasa and Sahib Bibi Aur Ghulam, wrote two Rishi Kapoor films. His reputation rests on his work with Guru Dutt in the 1950s and early 1960s, which produced some of the most admired films in Indian cinema — Time's critics later listed Pyaasa among the All-Time 100 Movies — and on Sahib Bibi Aur Ghulam, for which he received the Filmfare Award for Best Director amid a long dispute about how much of the film was his. His Kapoor credits came much later: Laila Majnu in 1976, where he supplied the dialogue for the classical tragedy of Qais and Laila, giving the twenty-four-year-old star a register of doomed love quite unlike Bobby's, and Gharana in 1989.

name: Achala Nagar
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active in the 1980s and 1990s, credited on both of these films with the honorific as Dr. Achala Nagar, which this workbook consolidates to the name. She has no Wikipedia article of her own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Nagina (1986), Amiri Garibi (1990).
recurring_themes: Melodrama of marriage and social obligation.
creative_style: Not documented; on both films she is credited alongside other writers.
historical_importance: Not independently documented. Her presence is worth noting for a different reason: women are very scarce among the 561 credited collaborators in this filmography, and she is one of only a handful of credited female writers.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both for the director Harmesh Malhotra, who accounts for five Kapoor films in six years: the fantasy hit Nagina (1986) and the melodrama Amiri Garibi (1990).
biography: Achala Nagar wrote two Rishi Kapoor films and has no documented biography. Both were directed by Harmesh Malhotra, who was Kapoor's most frequent director of the late 1980s: Nagina (1986), the snake-woman fantasy that became one of the year's biggest hits and briefly restored Kapoor's commercial standing, and Amiri Garibi (1990). She is credited on both as Dr. Achala Nagar. The row is built from film credits alone, but it records something the aggregate does not: of the 561 people and companies credited across this filmography, only a very small number of writers are women, and nearly all of them appear in the family melodramas of this period rather than in the romances on which Kapoor's reputation rests.

name: Aditya Raj Kapoor
career_background: Aditya Raj Kapoor (born 1 July 1956) is an Indian actor, filmmaker, author and retired businessman, the son of the actors Shammi Kapoor and Geeta Bali. After a career in business he returned to films as a writer-director in the 2000s.
debut: On screen from 1973; wrote and directed Don't Stop Dreaming and Sambar Salsa, both released in 2007.
major_works: With Kapoor: Don't Stop Dreaming (2007), Sambar Salsa (2007).
recurring_themes: Small-scale English-language Indian films aimed at an urban and diaspora audience.
creative_style: Independent, low-budget filmmaking outside the mainstream Hindi industry his family helped build.
historical_importance: Chiefly of interest as a member of the Kapoor family who worked at the margins of the industry rather than at its centre.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and they are the only two English-language films in this filmography: Don't Stop Dreaming and Sambar Salsa, both written and directed by him and both released in 2007. He is Rishi Kapoor's first cousin — the son of Shammi Kapoor, Raj Kapoor's brother — which makes these the clearest instance of the family network supplying work in the actor's quiet mid-2000s.
biography: Aditya Raj Kapoor directed the only two English-language films in this filmography, and he is Rishi Kapoor's first cousin. The son of Shammi Kapoor and Geeta Bali, he spent years in business before returning to cinema as a writer-director, making Don't Stop Dreaming and Sambar Salsa in 2007 — small independent films far from the scale of the family's studio productions, released in the stretch between Kapoor's Yash Raj supporting roles and his later Dharma successes. Both are among the least documented entries in the filmography. The pairing is a reminder of how much of Kapoor's work, early and late, came through family: his father directed him, his brothers produced and directed him, and his cousin cast him when little else was on offer.

name: Adnan Sami
industry: Hindi cinema; Indian and Pakistani popular music
career_background: Adnan Sami Khan (born 15 August 1971 in London) is an Indian singer, composer, pianist and actor of Pakistani origin who performs in Hindi, Urdu, English and several South Indian languages. His article credits him as the first musician to play the santoor and Indian classical music on the piano, and reports that he plays 32 instruments.
debut: Recording from 1986; a major figure in Indian popular music from the late 1990s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love at Times Square (2003), Sadiyaan (2010).
recurring_themes: The ghazal and the piano ballad brought into film and non-film popular music.
creative_style: A performer-composer whose film work is an extension of his concert and album career, built on his own voice and keyboard playing.
major_awards: Padma Shri, awarded in January 2020.
historical_importance: One of the most commercially successful non-film singers to cross into Hindi film music in the 2000s.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both marginal to his own career and to Kapoor's: Love at Times Square (2003) and the partition romance Sadiyaan (2010). Neither produced a notable song, and his article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Adnan Sami composed for two of Rishi Kapoor's later films. Born in London in 1971 to a Pakistani family and later an Indian citizen, Sami is better known as a singer and pianist than as a film composer — his article credits him with playing 32 instruments and with being the first to play the santoor and Indian classical music on the piano — and his popularity in India rested on non-film albums before he worked in cinema. He received the Padma Shri in January 2020. His Kapoor credits, Love at Times Square (2003) and Sadiyaan (2010), are minor in both careers. They belong to the period when Kapoor's films were often assembled around whichever popular musician was currently selling, rather than around a composer attached to the production.

name: Anand Raj Anand
career_background: Anand Raj Anand (born 14 November 1962 in Delhi) is an Indian composer, lyricist and playback singer in Hindi cinema. He is credited on one of these films as Anand Raaj Anand, a spelling this workbook consolidates.
debut: Composing from 1995; came to notice with Kaante (2002).
major_works: With Kapoor: Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002), Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006). Elsewhere, Kaante, Musafir, Shootout at Lokhandwala, Welcome and Shootout at Wadala.
recurring_themes: Hard-edged urban songs for crime and action films, and the Punjabi-inflected dance number.
creative_style: A composer-lyricist-singer who writes and performs his own hooks, usually for male-centred action cinema.
major_awards: Filmfare nomination for Best Music Director for Kaante (2003).
historical_importance: A dependable composer of the 2000s action film, writing songs designed to function as standalone singles.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both from Kapoor's weakest commercial stretch as a lead-turned-supporting player: Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002) and Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006), the latter one of the few outright unsympathetic parts of his career, in which he is top-billed but functionally the antagonist. His article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Anand Raj Anand wrote songs for two Rishi Kapoor films of the 2000s. A Delhi-born composer, lyricist and singer who came to notice with Kaante in 2002 and earned a Filmfare nomination for it, he specialised in the hard-edged urban soundtrack of the decade's crime and action films, usually writing and singing his own hooks. His Kapoor films are Yeh Hai Jalwa, a David Dhawan comedy in which Kapoor plays the older generation, and Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006), a variation on Indecent Proposal in which Kapoor is top-billed but is effectively the villain, coercing a younger couple — one of the very few unsympathetic roles he accepted. His name appears in these credits in two spellings, consolidated here to the one his article uses.

name: Anees Bazmee
career_background: Anees Bazmee, born in Modasa, Gujarat, is an Indian director, screenwriter and producer in Hindi cinema. He worked for years as a writer of commercial comedies and action films before becoming one of the industry's most successful comedy directors. He is credited on Bol Radha Bol as Aneez Bazmee for dialogue, a spelling this workbook consolidates.
debut: Writing from 1982; his directing successes begin with No Entry (2005).
major_works: With Kapoor: Bol Radha Bol (1992), Raju Chacha (2000). Elsewhere, as director, No Entry, Welcome, Singh is Kinng and the Bhool Bhulaiyaa sequels.
recurring_themes: Farce of mistaken identity and multiple deceptions; the large-ensemble comedy.
creative_style: Dialogue-driven comedy built on escalating confusion, written for star performers and later directed by himself.
historical_importance: One of the most commercially successful comedy writer-directors of post-2000 Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both as writer rather than director: the dialogue for David Dhawan's double-role comedy Bol Radha Bol (1992), one of Kapoor's last hits as a lead, and Raju Chacha (2000). His article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Anees Bazmee wrote dialogue for two Rishi Kapoor films before becoming a director in his own right. Born in Modasa, Gujarat, Bazmee spent the 1980s and 1990s writing commercial comedies and action pictures, then built one of the most consistently profitable directing careers in Hindi cinema with No Entry, Welcome, Singh is Kinng and the Bhool Bhulaiyaa sequels. His contribution here is the dialogue for Bol Radha Bol (1992), David Dhawan's double-role farce and one of the last unambiguous hits of Kapoor's leading career, and for Raju Chacha in 2000. The credits illustrate a pattern visible across this filmography: the writers and directors who would dominate the following two decades of popular Hindi cinema were, in Kapoor's last years as a lead, still working as his hired hands.

name: Arko
career_background: Arko Pravo Mukherjee, known by the mononym Arko, is an Indian composer, singer, lyricist and producer from Kolkata, and a qualified doctor. He has written and composed widely heard songs including 'Teri Mitti' (Kesari), 'Nazm Nazm' (Bareilly Ki Barfi), 'Tere Sang Yaara' (Rustom) and 'Saathi Rey' (Kapoor & Sons).
debut: Composing for Hindi films from 2012.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kapoor & Sons (2016), The Body (2019). Elsewhere, Kesari, Rustom, Bareilly Ki Barfi and Gold.
recurring_themes: The single-song commission: romantic ballads and patriotic numbers written for films scored by several composers.
creative_style: A composer-lyricist who writes and often sings one defining song per film rather than a whole soundtrack.
historical_importance: Representative of the 2010s model in which a film's songs are commissioned individually from several composers.
relationship_with_actor: Two films at the very end of the career: Kapoor & Sons (2016), for which he wrote 'Saathi Rey', and The Body (2019), the last film released in Kapoor's lifetime. Both are multi-composer soundtracks, which is the norm for the period and the opposite of the single-composer scores of his youth.
biography: Arko wrote songs for the last two Rishi Kapoor films released while he was alive. A Kolkata-born composer, lyricist and singer who is also a qualified doctor, Arko Pravo Mukherjee has worked in Hindi cinema since 2012 in the characteristic manner of the period: commissioned one song at a time, for films whose soundtracks are divided among several composers. Among his widely heard songs are 'Teri Mitti' from Kesari and 'Tere Sang Yaara' from Rustom. For Kapoor he wrote 'Saathi Rey' in Kapoor & Sons (2016), the family ensemble that gave the actor his most admired late performance, and a song for The Body (2019). The contrast with Laxmikant–Pyarelal's 32 films is the clearest measure of how the business of film music changed across this career.

name: Asrani
career_background: Govardhan Kumar Asrani, known professionally as Asrani (1 January 1941 – 20 October 2025), was an Indian actor and film director from Jaipur whose career spanned more than five decades and over 350 Hindi and Gujarati films. He is best remembered as the Hitler-caricaturing jailor in Sholay and for appearing in 25 films with Rajesh Khanna.
debut: Acting from 1967; he wrote, directed and starred in Chala Murari Hero Banne (1977).
major_works: With Kapoor: Chala Murari Hero Banne (1977), Salaam Memsaab (1979), both of which he directed and in both of which he played the lead. Elsewhere, Sholay, Aaj Ki Taaza Khabar and Balika Badhu.
recurring_themes: Satire of the film industry itself, and the comic everyman as protagonist.
creative_style: A comedian's direction: performance-led, self-deprecating, and built around his own screen persona rather than a star's.
major_awards: Two Filmfare Awards for Best Comedian, for Aaj Ki Taaza Khabar (1974) and Balika Badhu (1977).
historical_importance: One of the most prolific and best-loved comic actors in Hindi cinema, with a sideline as a director of films about the industry.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both of which Asrani directed and in both of which he, not Kapoor, played the lead — an unusual arrangement in this filmography. Chala Murari Hero Banne (1977) is a satire about a man trying to become a film hero, in which Kapoor appears as part of a large cast of stars playing within the joke; Salaam Memsaab (1979) followed. His article records that he took the lead in both.
biography: Asrani directed two films in this filmography, and in both he was the hero and Rishi Kapoor the guest. One of Hindi cinema's most prolific comic actors, with more than 350 films across five decades and two Filmfare Awards for Best Comedian, Asrani is remembered above all as the Hitler-aping jailor of Sholay. He also wrote and directed, and Chala Murari Hero Banne (1977) is his best-known work behind the camera: a satire about a hopeful trying to become a film star, in which the real stars appear as themselves or in cameo, Kapoor among them. Salaam Memsaab followed in 1979. The two films are useful markers of how quickly Kapoor's stardom became something other films could borrow and joke about. Asrani died in October 2025.

name: B. R. Chopra
career_background: Baldev Raj Chopra (22 April 1914 – 5 November 2008) was an Indian director and producer, a pioneer of both the Hindi social film and Indian television serials. He directed Afsana, Ek Hi Raasta, Naya Daur, Kanoon, Gumrah, Hamraaz, Dhund, Pati Patni Aur Woh and Nikaah, produced Dhool Ka Phool, Waqt, Ittefaq and The Burning Train, and made the television Mahabharat. He was the elder brother of Yash Chopra.
debut: Working from 1944; his breakthrough as a director came in the 1950s.
