major_works: With Kapoor: Pati Patni Aur Woh (1978), Tawaif (1985). Elsewhere, Naya Daur, Kanoon, Gumrah, Nikaah and the Mahabharat television series.
recurring_themes: The social problem film: adultery, law, communal division and the position of women, treated as argument rather than spectacle.
creative_style: Issue-driven mainstream cinema with a didactic structure, often built around a courtroom or a moral debate.
major_awards: Dadasaheb Phalke Award for 1998 and the Padma Bhushan in 2001.
historical_importance: One of the most important social filmmakers of Hindi cinema and the maker of its most widely watched television adaptation.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and both put Kapoor's romantic persona under pressure. Pati Patni Aur Woh (1978) is a comedy of adultery in which he is the husband who deceives both wife and mistress; Tawaif (1985), written by Rahi Masoom Raza, casts him as a man who takes in a courtesan and comes to love her. In a filmography dominated by courtship, these are two of the few films that treat marriage and its failures as the subject. His article names Pati Patni Aur Woh among his notable films.
biography: B. R. Chopra directed Rishi Kapoor twice, and both films stand apart from the courtships that define the rest of this filmography. The elder brother of Yash Chopra, Chopra was Hindi cinema's foremost maker of social problem films — Naya Daur, Kanoon, Gumrah, Nikaah — and later of the television Mahabharat, work for which he received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award and the Padma Bhushan. He cast Kapoor in Pati Patni Aur Woh (1978) as a husband conducting an affair and lying to both women, and in Tawaif (1985) as a man who gives shelter to a courtesan and falls in love with her, from a Rahi Masoom Raza script. Where most of Kapoor's directors asked him to be loveable, Chopra asked him to be compromised — a distinction that matters for reading the lover-boy pattern across the career.

name: B. S. Shaad
career_background: A Hindi-film producer active in the early 1990s, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pehla Pehla Pyar (1994), Prem Yog (1994).
recurring_themes: Romance built on the established Kapoor persona, produced at modest scale.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both released in 1994 and both written by Rumi Jaffery with Honey Irani also credited on one — romances made for a star whose romantic appeal was at that point no longer commercially current. They belong to the cluster of small productions that fills the last years of Kapoor's lead career.
biography: B. S. Shaad produced two Rishi Kapoor films, both released in 1994, and nothing about him is documented. Pehla Pehla Pyar and Prem Yog are romances written to the persona Kapoor had carried since Bobby, made at a point when audiences had moved to Shah Rukh Khan, Aamir Khan and Salman Khan; both were written by Rumi Jaffery, and Honey Irani is credited on them as well. The pairing is typical of this stretch of the filmography, in which a small producer, a comedy writer and an ageing romantic lead combined on films that received little attention then and have left almost no record since. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Bittu Anand
career_background: A Hindi-film producer active from the late 1970s to the mid-1980s, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The article on the writer Inder Raj Anand, who has two credits of his own in this filmography, names Bittu Anand as his son and a producer, and the actor-director Tinnu Anand as another son. He is credited on Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan as Bitu Anand, a spelling this workbook consolidates.
major_works: With Kapoor: Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan (1984).
recurring_themes: Romance and melodrama produced in partnership with Naresh Malhotra.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented; of interest as part of the Anand filmmaking family.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both co-produced with Naresh Malhotra and both starring Kapoor as a romantic lead: Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979) and Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan (1984). His father Inder Raj Anand wrote two other films in this filmography, so the family appears on four of Kapoor's films in different capacities.
biography: Bittu Anand produced two Rishi Kapoor films and has no article of his own; what is documented about him appears in his father's. Inder Raj Anand, the Urdu writer who scripted many Raj Kapoor films and has two credits in this filmography, is recorded as the father of both the actor-director Tinnu Anand and the producer Bittu Anand, with the director Siddharth Anand a grandson. Bittu Anand's own films with Kapoor — Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979) and Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan (1984) — were both co-produced with Naresh Malhotra and both cast Kapoor as a romantic lead in the years between Bobby's afterglow and the thin mid-1980s. The family's presence across four films in different functions is the more interesting fact; his own row rests on credits alone.

name: C. J. Pavri
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active in the 1980s, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He is credited on Bade Dilwala as C.J. Pavri, a spelling this workbook consolidates.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bade Dilwala (1983), Tawaif (1985).
recurring_themes: Melodrama of social respectability, written in collaboration.
creative_style: Not documented; on both films he is credited alongside Rahi Masoom Raza.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both shared with Rahi Masoom Raza, who wrote six Kapoor films in the 1980s: Bade Dilwala (1983) and B. R. Chopra's Tawaif (1985). The second is among the better films of Kapoor's middle period, which makes this undocumented writer a contributor to one of its more serious works.
biography: C. J. Pavri wrote two Rishi Kapoor films and left no record beyond the credits. Both were shared with Rahi Masoom Raza, the Urdu novelist and three-time Filmfare dialogue winner who was Kapoor's most literate collaborator of the 1980s: Bade Dilwala in 1983 and, more substantially, B. R. Chopra's Tawaif in 1985, the story of a courtesan taken into a man's home who becomes the object of his love. That a writer on a film of that standing should have no biography at all is characteristic of the lower tiers of this workbook's Collaborators sheet, where the credits of the period are often the only surviving evidence that a person worked in the industry.

name: Deepak Mukut
career_background: Deepak Mukut is an Indian film producer and distributor from Jaipur, the founder of Soham Rockstar Entertainment and Jhoom Jhoom Media. His productions include Sanam Teri Kasam, Mulk, Forensic, Thank God and Dhaakad.
debut: A distributor before becoming a producer; Soham Rockstar Entertainment is his own banner.
major_works: With Kapoor: Mulk (2018), Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
recurring_themes: Mid-budget films spanning issue-driven drama and broad comedy.
creative_style: A distributor-turned-producer backing modestly budgeted films across genres.
historical_importance: A significant independent producer of the late 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: Two films in Kapoor's final two years, and they could hardly be less alike: Anubhav Sinha's Mulk (2018), in which Kapoor plays a Muslim lawyer's patriarch defending his family against a terrorism charge — among the most substantial roles of his late career — and the farce Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019). His article names Mulk among the films that brought him awards.
biography: Deepak Mukut produced two of Rishi Kapoor's last films, one of them among the best things he did. A distributor from Jaipur who became a producer through his own Soham Rockstar Entertainment, Mukut backed mid-budget Hindi films across genres — Sanam Teri Kasam, Forensic, Thank God, Dhaakad — and, in 2018, Anubhav Sinha's Mulk, in which Kapoor plays Murad Ali Mohammed, the head of a Muslim family in Varanasi whose nephew is accused of terrorism. It gave him a late role of real weight and is one of the films that reframed his career as something more than romance. The following year Mukut produced Jhootha Kahin Ka, a broad comedy and one of Kapoor's last releases. The two together show the range available to him at the end.

name: Eastern Films
career_background: A Hindi-film production banner of the 1980s, with no Wikipedia article of its own. It is credited on Nigahen as Eastern films, a spelling this workbook consolidates.
major_works: With Kapoor: Nagina (1986), Nigahen (1989).
recurring_themes: The snake-woman fantasy: both of its films here are entries in that cycle.
creative_style: Not documented; both films were directed by Harmesh Malhotra.
historical_importance: Not independently documented; of interest as the banner behind one of the biggest commercial successes of Kapoor's middle period.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and they are a sequel pair: Nagina (1986), the hit in which Kapoor marries a shape-shifting serpent woman played by Sridevi, and Nigahen (1989), its follow-up. Both were directed by Harmesh Malhotra and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, making this a single production unit working twice on the same formula.
biography: Eastern Films produced the two snake-woman fantasies that gave Rishi Kapoor his biggest commercial success of the late 1980s. The banner has no article and no documented history; what the credits establish is a stable unit — Harmesh Malhotra directing, Laxmikant–Pyarelal scoring, Kapoor and Sridevi starring — that made Nagina in 1986 and its sequel Nigahen in 1989. Nagina was one of the year's largest hits and briefly restored Kapoor's standing as a star who could open a film, in a decade when most of his vehicles failed. That a company with no recorded existence produced one of the most commercially consequential films in this filmography is a fair illustration of how unevenly the Hindi industry of the period is documented.

name: Excel Entertainment
career_background: An Indian production company founded in Mumbai in 1999 by Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Akhtar. Its debut production, Dil Chahta Hai, was critically acclaimed, and it has won National Film Awards for that film and for Rock On!!. Its other productions include Don, Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara, Fukrey, Dil Dhadakne Do, Raees and Gully Boy, which was India's official entry to the 92nd Academy Awards.
debut: Dil Chahta Hai (2001).
major_works: With Kapoor: Luck by Chance (2009), Sharmaji Namkeen (2022). Elsewhere, Dil Chahta Hai, Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara and Gully Boy.
recurring_themes: Urban friendship and self-definition; the film industry examining itself; contemporary characters in a recognisable Bombay.
creative_style: Writer-director-led production with a contemporary idiom, built around the Akhtar family's own filmmakers.
major_awards: National Film Awards for Dil Chahta Hai and Rock On!!; Gully Boy was India's submission to the 92nd Academy Awards.
historical_importance: The company most associated with the turn to urban realism in mainstream Hindi cinema after 2001.
relationship_with_actor: Two films that bracket the end of the life. Luck by Chance (2009), Zoya Akhtar's debut, cast Kapoor as Rommy Rolly, a producer who uses and discards people — a role written knowingly against his own history in the industry. Sharmaji Namkeen (2022) was his last film, left unfinished at his death and completed with Paresh Rawal playing the same character in the remaining scenes, an unprecedented arrangement in Hindi cinema.
biography: Excel Entertainment produced Rishi Kapoor's most self-aware late role and his last film. Founded in 1999 by Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Akhtar, the company opened with Dil Chahta Hai and became the banner most identified with urban, contemporary Hindi cinema, winning National Film Awards and sending Gully Boy to the Academy Awards as India's official entry. It cast Kapoor as the producer Rommy Rolly in Zoya Akhtar's Luck by Chance (2009), a film about how the industry consumes its hopefuls, and then in Sharmaji Namkeen, which he was shooting when he died in April 2020; the film was completed with Paresh Rawal performing the remaining scenes as the same character and released posthumously in 2022. The two credits make this small company responsible for both the most reflexive and the most poignant entries in the filmography.

name: Farhan Akhtar
career_background: Farhan Akhtar (born 9 January 1974) is an Indian actor, filmmaker and singer, the son of the screenwriters Javed Akhtar and Honey Irani. He co-founded Excel Entertainment with Ritesh Sidhwani in 1999 and made his directorial debut with Dil Chahta Hai (2001).
debut: Dil Chahta Hai (2001), which won the National Film Award for Best Hindi Film and two Filmfare Awards for him.
major_works: With Kapoor: Luck by Chance (2009), Sharmaji Namkeen (2022). Elsewhere, Dil Chahta Hai, Lakshya, Don, Rock On!!, Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara and Bhaag Milkha Bhaag.
recurring_themes: Male friendship, self-discovery and the deliberate break from inherited expectation.
creative_style: A writer-director-actor working in a naturalistic contemporary register, with an unusual willingness to produce other people's films, including his sister's.
major_awards: National Film Awards for Dil Chahta Hai and Rock On!!, and Filmfare Awards including Best Male Debut and Best Actor for Bhaag Milkha Bhaag.
historical_importance: One of the central figures in the post-2001 turn of Hindi cinema towards urban realism.
relationship_with_actor: Two films as producer, both through Excel Entertainment, and both significant: his sister Zoya Akhtar's Luck by Chance (2009), in which Kapoor plays a film producer, and Sharmaji Namkeen (2022), Kapoor's last film, completed after his death with Paresh Rawal in the remaining scenes. Both of Akhtar's parents, Javed Akhtar and Honey Irani, also wrote films in this filmography, so the family appears across four decades of it.
biography: Farhan Akhtar produced the first and the last of Rishi Kapoor's late reflexive roles, and his family runs through this filmography across three generations. Born in 1974 to Javed Akhtar and Honey Irani, both of whom have writing credits here, Akhtar co-founded Excel Entertainment in 1999 and directed Dil Chahta Hai, a film that redirected mainstream Hindi cinema towards urban naturalism and won the National Film Award for Best Hindi Film. As a producer he backed his sister Zoya Akhtar's Luck by Chance (2009), casting Kapoor as a cynical producer, and Sharmaji Namkeen, the gentle comedy Kapoor was shooting when he died, which Excel completed by having Paresh Rawal play the remaining scenes as the same man and released in 2022.

name: Filmkraft
career_background: The production company founded by Rakesh Roshan in 1980, whose first production was Aap Ke Deewane (1980), a box-office failure. It has no Wikipedia article of its own; its founding and early history are recorded in Rakesh Roshan's article. The banner is credited on Aap Ke Deewane as Film Krafts, a spelling this workbook consolidates.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aap Ke Deewane (1980), Khudgarz (1987). Elsewhere, the Roshan family productions from Khoon Bhari Maang and Karan Arjun to Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai and the Krrish films.
recurring_themes: Revenge and rebirth melodrama, later science fiction and the superhero franchise; music by Rajesh Roshan throughout.
creative_style: A family company in which Rakesh Roshan directs and produces and his brother Rajesh Roshan scores, with a strong preference for formula tightly executed.
historical_importance: One of the most durable family production houses in Hindi cinema, and the launcher of Hrithik Roshan.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, which stand at opposite ends of the company's own fortunes. Aap Ke Deewane (1980) was Filmkraft's first production and failed; Khudgarz (1987) was Rakesh Roshan's breakthrough as a director and one of the few solid successes of Kapoor's weakest decade. Both were scored by Rajesh Roshan, who has nine credits of his own in this filmography.
biography: Filmkraft, Rakesh Roshan's production house, made two Rishi Kapoor films seven years apart, and the pair frames the company's rise. Its very first production, in 1980, was Aap Ke Deewane, a triangle with Kapoor that failed commercially — a fact recorded in Roshan's own article, since the banner has none of its own. By 1987 Roshan had moved behind the camera himself, and Khudgarz gave both the company and Kapoor a genuine hit, in a decade when almost nothing Kapoor led succeeded. Rajesh Roshan scored both films, as he did most of his brother's work. Filmkraft went on to become one of Hindi cinema's durable family firms, launching Hrithik Roshan in Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai and producing the Krrish series long after Kapoor's association with it ended.

name: Gauri Khan
career_background: Gauri Khan (born 8 October 1970) is an Indian film producer and interior designer who co-founded Red Chillies Entertainment with her husband, the actor Shah Rukh Khan, in 2001. She has produced Main Hoon Na, Om Shanti Om, Ra.One and Chennai Express, and launched the studio Gauri Khan Designs in 2013.
debut: Producing through Red Chillies Entertainment from the early 2000s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Om Shanti Om (2007), Student of the Year (2012).
recurring_themes: Star-led spectacle built around Shah Rukh Khan, and the industry's own mythology.
creative_style: A producer working within a star-owned company, with a parallel career in design.
historical_importance: Co-founder of one of the most powerful star-owned production houses in Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films. Om Shanti Om (2007) is a film about Hindi cinema's own history in which Kapoor appears as himself among dozens of stars; Student of the Year (2012) cast him as the college dean. Both are productions in which he is a recognisable fragment of the industry's past being used as such — a role his own career made available.
biography: Gauri Khan produced two films in which Rishi Kapoor appears as a piece of Hindi cinema's own history. With her husband Shah Rukh Khan — whose debut, Deewana, had been the film that marked the end of Kapoor's leading career — she co-founded Red Chillies Entertainment in 2001, producing Main Hoon Na, Om Shanti Om, Ra.One and Chennai Express, and later built a second career as an interior designer. Kapoor appears as himself in Om Shanti Om (2007), Farah Khan's pastiche of the 1970s industry, in a sequence crowded with stars, and as the dean in Student of the Year (2012). There is a symmetry worth noting: the actor displaced by Shah Rukh Khan in 1992 was, fifteen years later, being cast by his production company for exactly the stardom he had lost.

name: Gulshan Nanda
career_background: Gulshan Nanda (1919 – 16 November 1985), born in Rawalpindi, was an Indian novelist and screenwriter. Many of his novels were adapted into Hindi films in the 1960s and 1970s, including more than a dozen major hits, and he frequently worked with Rajesh Khanna.
debut: His novels were adapted from the 1960s; Kaajal (1965) was among the first major successes.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Premee (1980), Bade Dilwala (1983). Elsewhere, Kaajal, Khilona, Sharmeelee, Daag, Naya Zamana and Mehbooba.
recurring_themes: Melodrama of thwarted love, concealed identity and social disgrace, carried over from the popular Hindi novel.
creative_style: A bestselling novelist writing directly for the screen, with plots built on secrets and reversals.
major_awards: Six nominations for the Filmfare Award for Best Story — Kaajal (1965), Neel Kamal (1968), Khilona (1970), Naya Zamana (1971) and Mehbooba (1976) among them.
historical_importance: The most commercially successful popular novelist of his generation in Hindi, and the source of a long run of 1960s and 1970s hits.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both late in his own career and both modest: Do Premee (1980) and Bade Dilwala (1983). The interest is in the near-miss — Nanda supplied the plots for much of the melodrama of the 1960s and 1970s, including Daag and Khilona, but reached Kapoor only at the end of his life and in films neither of them is remembered for. His article does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Gulshan Nanda was the most widely read Hindi novelist of his generation and the source of a dozen major film hits, but he wrote only two Rishi Kapoor films, both minor. Born in Rawalpindi in 1919, Nanda saw his novels adapted into Kaajal, Khilona, Sharmeelee and Daag among others, worked repeatedly with Rajesh Khanna, and was nominated six times for the Filmfare Award for Best Story. His plots, built on concealed identity, disgrace and thwarted love, defined the melodrama of the era in which Kapoor grew up. By the time he wrote Do Premee (1980) and Bade Dilwala (1983) for him, both men were past their peak: Nanda died in 1985, and these two films are footnotes in a career that had shaped the form of Hindi romance Kapoor inherited.

name: Gyandev Agnihotri
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active in the late 1980s, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sindoor (1987), Gharana (1989).
recurring_themes: Melodrama of renunciation and family obligation.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside other writers on both films.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both directed by K. Ravi Shankar and both built on sacrifice rather than courtship: Sindoor (1987) and Gharana (1989), in which Kapoor's character renounces the woman he loves and marries another for dowry money, appearing mercenary precisely because he is sacrificing himself.
biography: Gyandev Agnihotri wrote two Rishi Kapoor films and has no documented biography. Both were directed by K. Ravi Shankar in the late 1980s, and both belong to the strain of Kapoor's middle period in which romance is structured around renunciation: Sindoor (1987) and Gharana (1989), where he plays a man who abandons one woman and marries another for money, the apparent mercenariness later revealed as self-sacrifice. These are among the films that complicate the lover-boy reading of the career, and the writer responsible for their structure is one of the many people in this workbook's lower tiers whose existence is attested only by the credits of the films themselves.

name: H. S. Rawail
career_background: Harnam Singh Rawail (21 August 1921 – 17 September 2004), credited as H. S. Rawail, was an Indian filmmaker born in Lyallpur. He debuted as a director with Dorangia Daku (1940) and became known for romantic films including Mere Mehboob (1963), Sunghursh (1968), Mehboob Ki Mehndi (1971) and Laila Majnu (1976). His son Rahul Rawail and grandson Rajat Rawail also became directors.
debut: Dorangia Daku (1940); his major success came with Mere Mehboob (1963).
major_works: With Kapoor: Laila Majnu (1976), Deedar-E-Yaar (1982). Elsewhere, Mere Mehboob, Sunghursh and Mehboob Ki Mehndi.
recurring_themes: The grand Muslim social romance, classical love legends, and tragic separation staged on a large scale.
creative_style: Lavish romantic melodrama with heavy emphasis on Urdu dialogue, qawwali and spectacle.
historical_importance: One of the principal directors of the Muslim social genre and of the classical romance in Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and both are attempts to place Kapoor inside a mythic rather than contemporary romance. Laila Majnu (1976) cast him as Qais opposite Ranjeeta Kaur in the classical Arabic love legend — his article records that the film was a success — and Deedar-E-Yaar (1982) was an expensive Muslim social that failed. His son Rahul Rawail co-wrote the second and directed three other Kapoor films, making the Rawails a two-generation presence here.
biography: H. S. Rawail directed the film in which Rishi Kapoor first played love as tragedy rather than courtship. Born in Lyallpur in 1921 and directing from 1940, Rawail became one of Hindi cinema's foremost makers of the Muslim social and the classical romance, with Mere Mehboob, Sunghursh and Mehboob Ki Mehndi behind him when he cast the twenty-four-year-old Kapoor as Qais in Laila Majnu (1976) opposite Ranjeeta Kaur. His article records the film as a success, and it remains the clearest early evidence that Kapoor could carry a role in which love destroys rather than rewards. Deedar-E-Yaar followed in 1982, an expensive failure co-written by his son Rahul Rawail, who directed Kapoor three times himself. Rawail stopped directing in 1982 and died in 2004.

name: Habib Faisal
career_background: Habib Faisal, from Bhopal, is an Indian filmmaker, screenwriter and lyricist who wrote Salaam Namaste (2005), Ta Ra Rum Pum (2007), Band Baaja Baaraat (2010), Ladies vs Ricky Bahl (2011), Ishaqzaade (2012) and Fan (2016), most of them for Yash Raj Films.
debut: Writing from 1992; directorial debut Do Dooni Chaar (2010), for which he won the Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Dooni Chaar (2010), Bewakoofiyaan (2014). Elsewhere, Band Baaja Baaraat, Ishaqzaade and Fan.
recurring_themes: The lower-middle-class household and its economics; aspiration measured in small sums; the marriage negotiated across class.
creative_style: Observational comedy-drama grounded in the specifics of money and milieu, with dialogue that carries the social detail.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue for Do Dooni Chaar.
historical_importance: One of the writers who gave the Yash Raj studio its modern middle-class register, away from the diaspora romance.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and the first is among the most important of the late career. Do Dooni Chaar (2010) cast Kapoor and his wife Neetu Singh — their first film together in decades — as a Delhi schoolteacher and his wife saving for a car, a performance that won Kapoor the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor and was widely treated as his reinvention as a character actor. Bewakoofiyaan (2014) followed, again with him as a father negotiating class and money.
biography: Habib Faisal wrote and directed the film that confirmed Rishi Kapoor's second career. A Bhopal-born writer who supplied Yash Raj Films with much of its modern middle-class material — Salaam Namaste, Band Baaja Baaraat, Ishaqzaade, Fan — Faisal made his directorial debut with Do Dooni Chaar in 2010, a small film about a Delhi schoolteacher, his wife and their ambition to replace a scooter with a car. Casting Kapoor opposite Neetu Singh, his wife and his co-star from the 1970s, gave the film its warmth and gave him the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor; Faisal won Best Dialogue for it. He directed Kapoor again in Bewakoofiyaan (2014) as a father whose objection to his daughter's suitor is frankly economic. Both films trade on exactly the ordinariness that Kapoor's lover-boy years had denied him.

name: Harish Shah
career_background: Harish Shah (7 October 1943 – 7 July 2020) was an Indian film producer, director and writer, known for Mere Jeevan Saathi with Rajesh Khanna, Kaala Sona with Feroz Khan, Ram Tere Kitne Naam with Sanjeev Kumar and Rekha, Zalzala, Ab Insaf Hoga and Jaal: The Trap. He died of throat cancer in July 2020.
debut: Working from 1968.
major_works: With Kapoor: Dhan Daulat (1980), Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985).
recurring_themes: Star-led melodrama and action, assembled around whoever was commercially current.
creative_style: A producer-director of mainstream vehicles across three decades, without a strong authorial signature.
historical_importance: A durable commercial producer whose films span Rajesh Khanna's peak to the 1990s.
relationship_with_actor: Two films in the early 1980s, both marginal: Dhan Daulat (1980), which he directed, and Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985). His own article lists the latter by its alternative spelling and names Sanjeev Kumar and Rekha rather than Kapoor among its cast, a useful reminder that Kapoor was not always the principal attraction of the films he led in this period.
biography: Harish Shah produced or directed two Rishi Kapoor films in the early 1980s. A producer-director working from 1968, Shah's better-known films were made with other stars — Mere Jeevan Saathi with Rajesh Khanna, Kaala Sona with Feroz Khan — and his own article names Sanjeev Kumar and Rekha, not Kapoor, when listing Ram Tere Kitne Naam. He directed Kapoor in Dhan Daulat (1980), with an R. D. Burman score and a Sachin Bhowmick story, and produced Ram Tere Kitne Nam in 1985. Both belong to the long middle stretch in which Kapoor worked steadily for producers whose interest was in assembling a saleable package rather than in him specifically. Shah died of throat cancer in July 2020, ten weeks after Kapoor.

name: Hitesh Sonik
career_background: An Indian composer and arranger working in Hindi cinema, mainly as a background-score composer. He has no Wikipedia article of his own: his name redirects to the article on his wife, the singer Sunidhi Chauhan, so no biographical detail is recorded here that could be verified about him rather than about her.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bewakoofiyaan (2014), Rajma Chawal (2018).
recurring_themes: Background score for contemporary urban comedy-drama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films from the last decade of the career, both contemporary urban stories in which Kapoor plays a father: Habib Faisal's Bewakoofiyaan (2014) and Leena Yadav's Rajma Chawal (2018), one of his last completed films.
biography: Hitesh Sonik scored two of Rishi Kapoor's late films, and almost nothing about him can be sourced. He is an established composer and arranger in Hindi cinema, best known for background scores, but Wikipedia has no article on him — his name redirects to his wife, the playback singer Sunidhi Chauhan, which is how an earlier pass of this research briefly attached her article to him. His two credits here are Bewakoofiyaan (2014), Habib Faisal's comedy about money and class in which Kapoor plays the frankly mercenary father, and Rajma Chawal (2018), Leena Yadav's film about a father who impersonates a young woman online to reach his estranged son. Both are quiet, contemporary films of the kind that occupied Kapoor's final years.

name: Humayun Mirza
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active in the mid-1980s, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rahi Badal Gaye (1985), Sitamgar (1985).
recurring_themes: Melodrama and romance of the mid-1980s commercial mainstream.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both released in 1985 and both from the weakest commercial stretch of the lead career: Ravi Tandon's Rahi Badal Gaye and Sitamgar, each with an R. D. Burman score.
biography: Humayun Mirza wrote two Rishi Kapoor films, both released in 1985, and has no documented biography. Rahi Badal Gaye, directed by Ravi Tandon and produced by Ravi Malhotra, and Sitamgar were both scored by R. D. Burman, whose association with Kapoor was by then almost over. The year is the low point of the filmography by any commercial measure: Kapoor appeared in five releases in 1985, none of which is remembered, while the films that defined that year in Hindi cinema belonged to other actors. The writers of those five films are, with one or two exceptions, as undocumented as this one. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Inder Raj Anand
career_background: Inder Raj Anand (died 6 March 1987), born in Sargodha in what is now Pakistan, was a dialogue and screenwriter in Hindi cinema who worked on many Raj Kapoor films from Aag (1948) onwards, including Aah (1953), Anari (1959) and Sangam (1964). Although credited as a Hindi film writer, he wrote in Urdu. He was the father of the actor-director Tinnu Anand and the producer Bittu Anand, and the grandfather of the director Siddharth Anand; the director Mukul Anand was his nephew.
debut: Writing from the 1940s, beginning with Raj Kapoor's Aag (1948).
major_works: With Kapoor: Raaja (1975), Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979). Elsewhere, Aag, Aah, Anari, Sangam and Shahenshah.
recurring_themes: The R. K. Films subject matter of class, innocence and sacrifice, written in Urdu for a Hindi screen.
creative_style: Urdu dialogue of a markedly literary cast, written for Raj Kapoor's generation of melodrama.
historical_importance: One of Raj Kapoor's principal writers across four decades and the patriarch of a filmmaking family that spans three generations of Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both in the early part of the career: Raaja (1975) and Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), the latter produced by his own son Bittu Anand and directed by his other son Tinnu Anand. The family's presence in this filmography is wider than his two credits — his sons account for four more — and his own connection runs through Raj Kapoor, for whom he wrote from 1948 and whose son he lived to write for.
biography: Inder Raj Anand wrote for Raj Kapoor from 1948 and, three decades later, for Raj Kapoor's son. An Urdu writer born in Sargodha who worked on Aag, Aah, Anari and Sangam, he was one of the writers who built the R. K. Films manner of class-crossing melodrama that Rishi Kapoor would inherit as a persona. His own two Kapoor credits are modest — Raaja in 1975 and Duniya Meri Jeb Mein in 1979 — but the second is a family production in the fullest sense: directed by his son Tinnu Anand and produced by his son Bittu Anand, with Kapoor as the romantic lead. The Anands appear on six films in this workbook across four functions. Inder Raj Anand died in March 1987; his grandson Siddharth Anand later became one of Hindi cinema's biggest commercial directors.

name: Iqbal Durrani
career_background: Iqbal Durrani, born in Banka, Bihar, is an Indian writer, director, actor and producer of Hindi films, and the author of several books.
debut: Working in Hindi cinema from the 1980s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sheshnaag (1990), Dhartiputra (1993).
recurring_themes: Mythological and folk material reworked as commercial melodrama; the snake-cult fantasy.
creative_style: A writer-director of mid-budget genre films drawing on folklore and religious narrative.
historical_importance: Not substantially documented beyond his filmography.
relationship_with_actor: Two films at the close of the lead career: Sheshnaag (1990), a snake-deity fantasy made in the wake of Nagina's success, and Dhartiputra (1993). Both are genre pictures in which Kapoor's romantic persona is secondary to the supernatural plot — the pattern that characterises much of his work between 1986 and 1993.
biography: Iqbal Durrani wrote and directed two Rishi Kapoor films at the end of his leading career. A writer-director from Banka in Bihar who also acts, produces and publishes books, Durrani worked in the folk-mythological register that Hindi cinema turned to in the late 1980s after Nagina made the snake-woman fantasy commercially viable. Sheshnaag (1990) is squarely in that cycle, with Kapoor in a story of serpent deities and curses, and Dhartiputra followed in 1993 with a Nadeem–Shravan score. Neither film treats him primarily as a lover: by this point the romance in a Kapoor vehicle was frequently subordinate to a supernatural or revenge plot, which is one reason his lover-boy scores drop through these years even as his billing stays high.

name: Jagmohan Kapoor
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active in the late 1980s, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He is not related to the Kapoor family of this filmography so far as the credits show.
major_works: With Kapoor: Nagina (1986), Nigahen (1989).
recurring_themes: The snake-woman fantasy, in both of its instalments.
creative_style: Not documented; credited with Achala Nagar and Ravi Kapoor on Nagina.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and they are the Nagina pair — the 1986 hit and its 1989 sequel Nigahen, both directed by Harmesh Malhotra for Eastern Films with Laxmikant–Pyarelal's music. Nagina was among the biggest commercial successes of Kapoor's career and the one that briefly arrested his decline, which gives its writers more weight in this filmography than their one-line records suggest.
biography: Jagmohan Kapoor co-wrote the two snake-woman films that gave Rishi Kapoor his biggest hit of the late 1980s, and nothing else about him is recorded. Nagina (1986), in which Kapoor marries a shape-shifting serpent played by Sridevi, was one of the year's largest successes; Nigahen (1989) was its sequel. Both were directed by Harmesh Malhotra, produced by Eastern Films and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, a unit that worked repeatedly on the same formula, and on Nagina he shares the writing credit with Achala Nagar and Ravi Kapoor. He has no Wikipedia article, and the surname is coincidental: there is no evidence in the credits of any relation to the Kapoor family. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Jeevanprabha M. Desai
career_background: A Hindi-film writer, born Jeevanprabha Gandhi, who was married to the director Manmohan Desai; his article records the marriage and names their son, the producer-director Ketan Desai. She has no Wikipedia article of her own, and is credited on Coolie with the honorific as Smt. Jeevanprabha M. Desai, which this workbook consolidates to the name.
major_works: With Kapoor: Amar Akbar Anthony (1977), Coolie (1983).
recurring_themes: The masala construction of her husband's cinema: separated families, coincidence and reunion.
creative_style: A collaborative writer inside the Desai unit, credited alongside Kader Khan, K. K. Shukla and Prayag Raj.
historical_importance: Not independently documented, though her two credits are on two of the largest hits in Hindi cinema of their decade.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and both are among the biggest commercial successes Kapoor ever appeared in: Amar Akbar Anthony (1977) and Coolie (1983), both directed by her husband Manmohan Desai. She is one of very few women credited as a writer anywhere in this filmography, and the only one credited on a Desai masala film.
biography: Jeevanprabha M. Desai is credited as a writer on two of the largest hits in this filmography and has no article of her own. Born Jeevanprabha Gandhi, she was the wife of Manmohan Desai — his article records the marriage and their son Ketan Desai, who also has four credits here — and she wrote with the collective team that produced his masala films, sharing credit with Kader Khan, K. K. Shukla and Prayag Raj on Amar Akbar Anthony (1977) and Coolie (1983). Both films are structured on the separations and coincidences that the Desai unit made its trademark, and both gave Kapoor his place inside an ensemble rather than at its centre. She is among the very few women credited as writers across the 561 collaborators in this workbook.

name: K. B. Pathak
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active around 1989–1990, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He is credited on Bade Ghar Ki Beti as K.B. Pathak, a spelling this workbook consolidates.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989), Amiri Garibi (1990).
recurring_themes: The household melodrama of class difference and family duty.
creative_style: Not documented; credited with Kader Khan and Mohanji Prasad on one film and Achala Nagar on the other.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films from consecutive years at the end of the 1980s, both domestic melodramas: Kalpataru's Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989), written with Kader Khan, and Harmesh Malhotra's Amiri Garibi (1990). Both cast Kapoor as a husband or son inside a family dispute rather than as a lover.
biography: K. B. Pathak wrote two Rishi Kapoor films at the turn of the 1990s and left no biographical record. Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989), directed by Kalpataru and co-written with Kader Khan, and Amiri Garibi (1990), for Harmesh Malhotra, are both household melodramas of the type that dominated Kapoor's output in those years: the titles name the family or its economic condition rather than a romance, and his role in each is the dutiful son or husband. The two films sit inside a dense cluster — nine releases between 1989 and 1991 — that is the least documented stretch of the filmography, and whose writers are known almost entirely from the credits.

name: K. C. Bokadia
career_background: Kistur Chand Bokadia, known as K. C. Bokadia, is an Indian film producer and director working from 1972. He produced Pyar Jhukta Nahin, Teri Meherbaniyan, Naseeb Apna Apna, Main Tera Dushman, Hum Tumhare Hain Sanam and Pyaar Zindagi Hai, and directed a long run of films from 1990 onwards.
debut: Producing from 1972 with Rivaaj; directing from 1990 with Aaj Ka Arjun.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naseeb Apna Apna (1986), Mohabbat Ki Arzoo (1994). Elsewhere, Pyar Jhukta Nahin, Teri Meherbaniyan and Lal Baadshah.
recurring_themes: Revenge melodrama and the rural-family action film, built for the single-screen market.
creative_style: A high-volume producer-director of formula melodrama, often working with stars past their commercial peak.
historical_importance: A prolific commercial producer of the 1980s and 1990s whose filmography table is the only record of the director credit for one film in this workbook.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, in different capacities. He produced T. Rama Rao's Naseeb Apna Apna (1986), and his own filmography table — whose columns separate Director from Producer — records him as the director of Mohabbat Ki Arzoo (1994), one of six films here with no Wikipedia article of its own, which is how this workbook recovers that credit.
biography: K. C. Bokadia produced one Rishi Kapoor film and directed another, and his article is the reason the second has a director at all. Born Kistur Chand Bokadia and working from 1972, he became one of the most prolific producer-directors of the 1980s and 1990s, with Pyar Jhukta Nahin and Teri Meherbaniyan among his successes and a long run of formula melodramas to his name. He produced Naseeb Apna Apna in 1986, directed by T. Rama Rao, with Kapoor opposite Farha and a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score. Mohabbat Ki Arzoo (1994) is one of the six films in this filmography with no Wikipedia article; Bokadia's own article carries a filmography table whose labelled Director column marks him for it, which is the basis of the credit recorded here.

name: K. K. Singh
career_background: K. K. Singh (died 2011) was an Indian screenwriter with director-producer credits for Veergati and an acting credit in Sham Ghansham. He entered Hindi films in 1982 as an assistant director on Raj Kapoor's Prem Rog and also worked in Bhojpuri cinema.
debut: Entered films in 1982 as an assistant director on Prem Rog.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ranbhoomi (1991), Gurudev (1993). Elsewhere, Krantiveer, Veergati and Sham Ghansham.
recurring_themes: Vigilante justice and the wronged common man; declamatory confrontation.
creative_style: A dialogue writer of the 1990s action melodrama, writing for the speech that stops a scene.
major_awards: Filmfare Awards for Best Dialogue and Best Story at the 40th Filmfare Awards in 1995, both for Krantiveer.
historical_importance: The writer of Krantiveer, one of the defining vigilante films of 1990s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and a notable circularity: his career began in 1982 as an assistant director on Prem Rog, which Raj Kapoor directed and in which Rishi Kapoor starred, and nine years later he was writing for the same actor on Ranbhoomi (1991) and Gurudev (1993). His article records the Prem Rog apprenticeship directly.
biography: K. K. Singh began his career on a Rishi Kapoor film and later wrote two. He entered Hindi cinema in 1982 as an assistant director on Prem Rog, Raj Kapoor's melodrama about widow remarriage starring his son, and a decade later was writing dialogue himself, winning both the Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue and the Filmfare Award for Best Story at the 40th ceremony for Krantiveer, the vigilante film that defined a certain register of 1990s Hindi cinema. His two Kapoor credits, Ranbhoomi (1991) and Gurudev (1993), come from the same years and are far less distinguished, both multi-star action melodramas made as Kapoor's lead career closed. He also directed and produced Veergati and acted in Sham Ghansham, and died in 2011.

name: Kamlesh Pandey
career_background: Kamlesh Pandey is an Indian screenwriter and dialogue writer from Ballia, Uttar Pradesh, resident in Mumbai. He wrote the television thriller Karamchand and the teleplays Kachchi Dhoop and Naqab for Amol Palekar, and in 1992 became head of programming at Zee TV.
debut: Writing for Hindi films and television through the 1980s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Shreemaan Aashique (1993), Delhi-6 (2009). Elsewhere, Tezaab, Saudagar and Rang De Basanti.
recurring_themes: Urban anger and institutional failure; the ensemble that stands in for a city or a nation.
creative_style: Dialogue-led writing with an ear for the political temperature of a moment, working in both film and television.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Tezaab, Star Screen Award for Saudagar, IIFA Award for Rang De Basanti, and Indian Television Academy and Indian Telly awards for Virrudh.
historical_importance: One of the significant commercial screenwriters of the late 1980s and of the 2000s socially engaged film.
relationship_with_actor: Two films sixteen years apart and in different registers: the romantic comedy Shreemaan Aashique (1993), one of the last films written to Kapoor's lover-boy persona, and Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra's Delhi-6 (2009), in which Kapoor is part of a Chandni Chowk ensemble. One other point of note: the teleplay Naqab that his article credits him with is a television work and is not the 1989 film Naqab in this filmography.
biography: Kamlesh Pandey wrote two Rishi Kapoor films at opposite ends of the actor's reinvention. A screenwriter from Ballia who won a Filmfare Award for Tezaab and later an IIFA Award for Rang De Basanti, Pandey worked across film and television, creating the thriller Karamchand and running programming at Zee TV in the 1990s. For Kapoor he wrote Shreemaan Aashique in 1993, a romantic comedy pitched at a persona that had stopped selling, and then Delhi-6 in 2009, Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra's film about a Chandni Chowk neighbourhood pulled apart by religious tension, in which Kapoor is one voice in an ensemble. The sixteen-year gap between the two credits covers almost exactly the period in which Kapoor ceased to be a leading man and became a character actor.

name: Kamna Chandra
career_background: Kamna Chandra is an Indian writer who wrote plays for All India Radio before writing stories and dialogue for the screen. Her credits include Prem Rog, Chandni and 1942: A Love Story, the last directed by her son-in-law Vidhu Vinod Chopra, as well as the television show Kashish.
debut: Radio plays for All India Radio; her first major film credit is Prem Rog (1982).
major_works: With Kapoor: Prem Rog (1982), Chandni (1989). Elsewhere, 1942: A Love Story.
recurring_themes: Romance organised around a woman's social position — widowhood, respectability, and the right to choose again.
creative_style: A writer from radio drama, strong on situation and on the moral predicament of a female protagonist.
historical_importance: One of the very few women writing story and dialogue for mainstream Hindi cinema in the 1980s, and the author of two of its best-known romances.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and both are central to this filmography. Prem Rog (1982), directed by Raj Kapoor, casts Kapoor as the man who loves and marries a young widow against his community; Chandni (1989), for Yash Chopra, restored him as a romantic lead opposite Sridevi. She is therefore the writer behind both his most serious role of the 1980s and his comeback as a lover, and one of a handful of women credited anywhere in this workbook.
biography: Kamna Chandra wrote the two films that mark the high points of Rishi Kapoor's romantic career after Bobby, and she is one of the few women credited in this filmography at all. A writer of radio plays for All India Radio before she wrote for the screen, Chandra supplied the story for Raj Kapoor's Prem Rog (1982), in which Kapoor's character loves a young widow and defies his community to marry her — the most morally serious part he played in that decade — and then for Yash Chopra's Chandni (1989), the hit that returned him to romantic leading man opposite Sridevi. She also wrote 1942: A Love Story for her son-in-law Vidhu Vinod Chopra. That both of Kapoor's most admired romances were written by the same woman is among the more striking findings of this phase.

name: Lalit Pandit
career_background: Lalit Pandit is an Indian composer, one half of the duo Jatin–Lalit with his brother Jatin Pandit. The duo worked together from 1991 until 2006 and both brothers have composed independently since. Wikipedia has no separate article on him; his name resolves to the duo's article, which carries a section on his solo filmography.
debut: With Jatin–Lalit from 1991; composing independently from 2006.
major_works: With Kapoor: Besharam (2013), Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017). Elsewhere, as half of Jatin–Lalit, Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge, Kuch Kuch Hota Hai and Mohabbatein; independently, Dabangg's 'Munni Badnaam Hui'.
recurring_themes: Melodic romance and, in his solo work, the item number and the Punjabi dance song.
creative_style: The more extrovert half of a duo known for melody, with a solo career tilted towards rhythm and spectacle.
historical_importance: Co-composer of the canonical 1990s Hindi romance soundtracks.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both solo credits and both late: Besharam (2013), in which Kapoor appeared with his wife Neetu Singh and their son Ranbir Kapoor — the only film with all three — and Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017). As half of Jatin–Lalit he also has four earlier Kapoor credits, recorded separately under the duo.
biography: Lalit Pandit scored two late Rishi Kapoor films on his own, having already worked on four as half of Jatin–Lalit. The Pandit brothers were the defining romantic composers of 1990s Hindi cinema; after their split in 2006 Lalit worked independently, with a harder, more rhythmic idiom best known from 'Munni Badnaam Hui'. His solo Kapoor credits are Besharam (2013), the Abhinav Kashyap comedy notable chiefly for being the only film in which Rishi Kapoor, his wife Neetu Singh and their son Ranbir Kapoor all appear, and Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017). He has no Wikipedia article of his own, so this row cites the duo's article, which includes a section on his solo filmography.

name: M. Balamurugan
career_background: A writer credited on two Hindi films of the mid-1980s, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He is credited on Dosti Dushmani simply as Balamurugan, a spelling this workbook consolidates; both films are connected to South Indian production units.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985), Dosti Dushmani (1986).
recurring_themes: Melodrama adapted for the Hindi market from southern formulas.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films from consecutive years, Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985) and T. Rama Rao's Dosti Dushmani (1986), both from the stretch when Kapoor was working frequently for South Indian directors and producers remaking southern material in Hindi.
biography: M. Balamurugan is credited as a writer on two Rishi Kapoor films of the mid-1980s and has no documented biography. Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985), where he shares credit with Jainendra Jain, and Dosti Dushmani (1986), directed by T. Rama Rao and written with Rahi Masoom Raza, both belong to the period in which a substantial share of Kapoor's films were made by South Indian filmmakers working in Hindi, often reworking Telugu or Tamil originals. The name appears in two spellings across the two credits. Like most of the writers in this tier of the workbook, he is attested only by the films themselves, and the row is graded accordingly.

name: Meet Bros Anjjan
career_background: An Indian musical duo from Gwalior consisting of the brothers Manmeet Singh and Harmeet Singh, who performed as Meet Bros Anjjan with their longtime collaborator Anjjan Bhattacharya before continuing as Meet Bros. They began as actors and turned to composing and singing after the success of their song 'Jogi Singh Barnala Singh'.
debut: Composing from Isi Life Mein and Do Dooni Chaar; wider recognition with Kyaa Super Kool Hain Hum and OMG – Oh My God!
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Dooni Chaar (2010), All Is Well (2015). Elsewhere, OMG – Oh My God! and the songs recorded with Kanika Kapoor that brought them a Filmfare Award for Best Music Director.
recurring_themes: Contemporary dance pop and the single-song commission.
creative_style: Hook-driven commercial songwriting for multi-composer soundtracks, frequently sung by the brothers themselves.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Music Director for a soundtrack featuring Kanika Kapoor's vocals.
historical_importance: Among the most employed composers of the 2010s Hindi film song.
relationship_with_actor: Two films. Do Dooni Chaar (2010) was one of their earliest scores and is the more significant — Habib Faisal's film in which Kapoor and Neetu Singh play a Delhi schoolteacher and his wife, and for which Kapoor won the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor. All Is Well (2015) followed, a multi-composer soundtrack of the kind typical of their work.
biography: Meet Bros Anjjan scored two Rishi Kapoor films, one of them at a pivotal moment. The brothers Manmeet and Harmeet Singh, from Gwalior, began as actors and became composers after a hit non-film song, working for several years under the name Meet Bros Anjjan with Anjjan Bhattacharya before continuing as a duo; they later won a Filmfare Award for Best Music Director. Do Dooni Chaar (2010) was among their first film assignments, and it is the film in which Kapoor, opposite his wife Neetu Singh, played the Delhi schoolteacher who wants a car — the performance that won him the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor and established his late career. All Is Well (2015) was their second, one of the fragmented multi-composer soundtracks characteristic of the decade.

name: Mithoon
career_background: Mithun Sharma, known as Mithoon, is an Indian composer, lyricist and playback singer working in Hindi films. He composed 'Tum Hi Ho' for Aashiqui 2, for which he received the Filmfare Award for Best Music Director, and wrote and composed 'Sanam Re', named Most Streamed Song of 2016 at the Global Indian Music Academy Awards.
debut: Composing from 2005.
major_works: With Kapoor: All Is Well (2015), Sanam Re (2016). Elsewhere, Aashiqui 2, Hamari Adhuri Kahani and Ek Villain.
recurring_themes: The slow romantic ballad, usually written and composed by himself and often the only memorable element of its film.
creative_style: Piano-and-voice balladry with a strong lyrical hand, written as a standalone song rather than as part of a score.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Music Director for Aashiqui 2 and a Filmfare nomination for Best Lyricist at the 59th awards.
historical_importance: One of the most commercially successful balladeers of 2010s Hindi film music.
relationship_with_actor: Two films at the end of the career: All Is Well (2015) and Sanam Re (2016), the latter taking its title from his own song, which became one of the most streamed Hindi recordings of its year. Kapoor plays a father in both.
biography: Mithoon wrote songs for two of Rishi Kapoor's last films. A composer, lyricist and singer working since 2005, Mithun Sharma became one of the most reliable hitmakers of 2010s Hindi cinema on the strength of slow romantic ballads — 'Tum Hi Ho' from Aashiqui 2, for which he won the Filmfare Award for Best Music Director, and 'Sanam Re', named the most streamed Hindi song of 2016. Both of his Kapoor films, All Is Well (2015) and Sanam Re (2016), are T-Series productions in which Kapoor plays the father and the soundtrack is divided among several composers. In each, the song outlived the film. It is a neat inversion of the actor's youth, when a Laxmikant–Pyarelal or R. D. Burman score and the film it belonged to succeeded or failed together.

name: Mohan Kaul
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active in the late 1980s and early 1990s, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The bare name resolves on Wikipedia to an unrelated organisation, so nothing beyond the credits can be established about him.
major_works: With Kapoor: Khudgarz (1987), Sheshnaag (1990).
recurring_themes: Revenge melodrama and folk-mythological fantasy.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films from the late 1980s, and the first matters: Rakesh Roshan's Khudgarz (1987) was one of the few unambiguous successes of Kapoor's weakest decade, a revenge drama that reminded the industry he could still open a film. Sheshnaag (1990), the snake-deity fantasy, followed.
biography: Mohan Kaul wrote two Rishi Kapoor films and has no documented biography; an earlier pass of this research briefly attached to his name the article of an unrelated organisation, which is the kind of collision that makes the lower tiers of this workbook laborious to verify. His credits are Khudgarz (1987), Rakesh Roshan's revenge melodrama and one of the few solid commercial successes Kapoor had between Nagina and Chandni, and Sheshnaag (1990), Iqbal Durrani's snake-deity fantasy. The pairing is characteristic of the period: a hit built on vengeance and a fantasy built on folklore, neither of them requiring the romantic persona on which Kapoor's reputation had been founded. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Mohanji Prasad
career_background: A Hindi-film director, producer and writer active around 1989–1991, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989), Ghar Parivar (1991).
recurring_themes: The joint-family melodrama of duty, property and domestic conflict.
creative_style: Not documented; on Bade Ghar Ki Beti he is credited as a writer alongside Kader Khan and K. B. Pathak.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films from the turn of the 1990s, both household melodramas: Kalpataru's Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989), on which he worked as a writer, and Ghar Parivar (1991). Both belong to the densest and least documented stretch of the filmography, when Kapoor was making three or four such films a year.
biography: Mohanji Prasad worked on two Rishi Kapoor family melodramas at the turn of the 1990s and has no documented biography. Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989), directed by Kalpataru from a script he shared with Kader Khan, and Ghar Parivar (1991), with a Kalyanji–Anandji score, are both domestic dramas of obligation and property in which Kapoor plays a son or husband rather than a lover. He is credited across direction, production and writing on these two films, which is itself characteristic of the tier of production involved: small units in which one person covered several functions. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Naresh Malhotra
career_background: A Hindi-film producer active from the late 1970s to the mid-1980s, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan (1984).
recurring_themes: Romance and melodrama produced in partnership with Bittu Anand.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both co-produced with Bittu Anand, son of the writer Inder Raj Anand: Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), directed by Tinnu Anand, and Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan (1984). Both cast Kapoor as a romantic lead in the years when that was still his principal function.
biography: Naresh Malhotra produced two Rishi Kapoor films and has no documented biography. Both were made with Bittu Anand — a son of the Raj Kapoor screenwriter Inder Raj Anand — as co-producer: Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), directed by Bittu's brother Tinnu Anand with a Rajesh Roshan score, and Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan (1984), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal film. The pairing suggests a standing partnership rather than two separate ventures, and places Malhotra inside the Anand family's production orbit, which accounts for six credits across this filmography. Nothing else about him is recorded, and the row is graded accordingly.

name: Nasir Hussain
career_background: Mohammad Nasir Hussain Khan (16 November 1926 – 13 March 2002), known as Nasir Hussain, was an Indian producer, director and screenwriter credited as a major trendsetter in Hindi cinema. He directed Yaadon Ki Baraat (1973), which his article credits with creating the masala genre that defined the 1970s and 1980s, and wrote and produced Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak (1988), which set the musical-romance template of the 1990s. His son is the director Mansoor Khan.
debut: Working from 1948; his run of musical hits begins with Jab Pyar Kisi Se Hota Hai (1961).
major_works: With Kapoor: Hum Kisise Kum Naheen (1977), Zamaane Ko Dikhana Hai (1982). Elsewhere, Teesri Manzil, Caravan, Yaadon Ki Baraat and Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak.
recurring_themes: Youth, music and masquerade: the lost-and-found plot, the talent-contest set piece, and courtship conducted through song.
creative_style: The musical as structure rather than decoration, built on R. D. Burman's scores and on young performers introduced by the film itself.
major_awards: A special Filmfare Award in 1996 for his contribution to Hindi cinema.
historical_importance: The filmmaker credited with establishing both the 1970s masala film and the 1990s musical romance — the two commercial templates that bracket Kapoor's leading career.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and they matter more than the number suggests. Hum Kisise Kum Naheen (1977) is the purest expression of Kapoor's youth persona: a musical of disguise and rivalry with an R. D. Burman score that his article names among the Burman collaborations, in which the hero sings his way through the plot. Zamaane Ko Dikhana Hai (1982) repeated the formula. Hussain's own later film Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak then launched the generation that displaced Kapoor.
biography: Nasir Hussain made only two Rishi Kapoor films, but they define one half of his screen identity. Hussain was Hindi cinema's great builder of musicals — Jab Pyar Kisi Se Hota Hai, Teesri Manzil, Caravan — and his Yaadon Ki Baraat is credited with inventing the masala form that dominated the 1970s. In Hum Kisise Kum Naheen (1977) he gave Kapoor the role his whole early persona rests on: a young man who sings, flirts, performs and competes, carried by an R. D. Burman soundtrack that outlived the film. Zamaane Ko Dikhana Hai followed in 1982. The irony is precise: Hussain also wrote and produced Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak in 1988, the film that launched Aamir Khan and set the romantic template of the 1990s — the decade in which Kapoor's own version of it stopped selling.

name: Nikkhil Advani
career_background: Nikkhil Advani, born Nikhil Suresh Advani on 28 April 1971, is an Indian director, producer and screenwriter in Hindi cinema. With his sister Monisha Advani and Madhu Bhojwani he co-founded the production company Emmay Entertainment.
debut: Working from 1996; his own company's first project was D-Day (2013).
major_works: With Kapoor: Patiala House (2011), D-Day (2013). Elsewhere, Kal Ho Naa Ho, Salaam-e-Ishq and Batla House.
recurring_themes: The diaspora family and its authority; the ensemble thriller; fathers who must be defied.
creative_style: Mainstream emotional drama with an ensemble structure, moving between family melodrama and the espionage thriller.
historical_importance: A Dharma-trained director who built his own production house, representative of the studio-to-independent path of 2010s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and the first is one of the better late roles. His article records that he wrote and directed Patiala House (2011) 'starring Rishi Kapoor, Dimple Kapadia, Akshay Kumar and Anushka Sharma' — naming Kapoor first — in which he plays the London Punjabi patriarch who forbids his son's cricket career, opposite Dimple Kapadia, his co-star from Bobby. D-Day (2013), Emmay Entertainment's first production, cast him as a fictionalised crime boss in Pakistan.
biography: Nikkhil Advani directed Rishi Kapoor in two very different late roles. A Dharma-trained filmmaker who made Kal Ho Naa Ho before founding Emmay Entertainment with his sister Monisha Advani and Madhu Bhojwani, Advani wrote and directed Patiala House in 2011 — his article lists Kapoor first among its stars — casting him as a Southall patriarch whose bitterness after a racist attack leads him to forbid his son's cricket career. The film reunited him with Dimple Kapadia, his Bobby co-star, for the fourth time, now as a long-married couple. Two years later Advani's own company produced D-Day, in which Kapoor plays a Dawood Ibrahim-like underworld figure hiding in Karachi — among the most unsympathetic parts of his career and evidence of how far his casting range had widened after 2010.

name: Nitin Manmohan
career_background: A Hindi-film producer active in the early 1990s, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bol Radha Bol (1992), Eena Meena Deeka (1994).
recurring_themes: The David Dhawan comedy vehicle.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both David Dhawan comedies from Kapoor's last years as a lead: Bol Radha Bol (1992), the double-role farce that was among his final hits, and Eena Meena Deeka (1994). Both were scored by Anand–Milind, making this another stable production unit of the period.
biography: Nitin Manmohan produced two Rishi Kapoor comedies and has no documented biography. Bol Radha Bol (1992) is the significant one: David Dhawan's farce in which Kapoor plays both a businessman and his lookalike opposite Juhi Chawla, released months after Deewana and one of the last films in which he carried a hit on his own. Eena Meena Deeka followed in 1994, again for Dhawan and again scored by Anand–Milind. The unit — this producer, that director, those composers — recurs across several of Kapoor's early-1990s films, which is the pattern of his final stretch as a lead: fewer distinguished directors, more reliable comedy teams. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Phani Majumdar
career_background: Phani Majumdar was a pioneering Indian film director and screenwriter who worked in both Bengali and Hindi cinema from 1938 to 1986. His Oonch Log was the actor Feroz Khan's first hit and won the National Film Award for Second Best Feature Film.
debut: Directing from 1938.
major_works: With Kapoor: Badaltey Rishtey (1978), Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986). Elsewhere, Oonch Log and a long career in Bengali and Hindi cinema.
recurring_themes: Social realism in a popular register; literary adaptation.
creative_style: An early-generation director of restrained, text-led cinema, working across two industries.
major_awards: National Film Award for Second Best Feature Film for Oonch Log.
historical_importance: A pioneer of Bengali and Hindi film direction whose career spanned nearly five decades.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, eight years apart and both as writer rather than director: Badaltey Rishtey (1978) and Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986), the adaptation of Rajinder Singh Bedi's novel about a widow married to her late husband's younger brother. The second, released at the end of his own career, is among the most serious literary projects in this filmography.
biography: Phani Majumdar, a director working from 1938, wrote two Rishi Kapoor films at the very end of a five-decade career. A pioneer in both Bengali and Hindi cinema whose Oonch Log won the National Film Award for Second Best Feature Film, Majumdar belonged to a generation two removed from Kapoor's. He is credited as a writer on Badaltey Rishtey in 1978 and, more notably, on Ek Chadar Maili Si in 1986 — the adaptation of Rajinder Singh Bedi's Urdu novel in which Kapoor plays a man made to marry his dead brother's widow. It is one of the few films of Kapoor's thin mid-1980s with literary standing, and the presence of a 1930s pioneer on its credits is a reminder of how long a working life Hindi cinema could accommodate.

name: Pritam
career_background: Pritam Chakraborty (born 14 June 1971), known as Pritam, is an Indian composer who graduated from the Film and Television Institute of India in sound engineering and worked on advertising jingles and television themes before entering films. He has composed for more than 125 Hindi films and won the National Film Award for Best Music Direction at the 70th ceremony.
debut: Co-composer on Tere Liye (2001) with Jeet Gannguli; solo debut Stumped (2003); breakthrough with Dhoom (2004).
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Aaj Kal (2009), Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011). Elsewhere, Dhoom, Jab We Met, Life in a... Metro, Barfi! and Ae Dil Hai Mushkil.
recurring_themes: Blending Indian classical and folk material with Western pop; the album-shaped soundtrack of the modern romance.
creative_style: A studio composer with a wide stylistic range and a reputation for identifying the one song a film needs, working repeatedly with Imtiaz Ali and Ayan Mukerji.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Music Direction at the 70th National Film Awards; numerous Filmfare nominations and awards.
historical_importance: The most commercially dominant Hindi film composer of the 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both small roles in his character-actor phase: Imtiaz Ali's Love Aaj Kal (2009), where Kapoor plays the older incarnation of the hero's counterpart in the period strand, and Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011). His article names Love Aaj Kal among the soundtracks of his rise but does not mention Kapoor.
biography: Pritam scored two films in which Rishi Kapoor appears, both after 2009. An FTII-trained sound engineer who moved from jingles and television themes to film, Pritam became the most commercially dominant composer of 2010s Hindi cinema, with more than 125 films and a National Film Award for Best Music Direction. His Kapoor credits are Imtiaz Ali's Love Aaj Kal (2009), in which Kapoor plays the elderly Veer Singh whose remembered courtship forms the film's period strand — a role that uses his own screen past as the content of the film's nostalgia — and Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011). The first is the more interesting: a 2009 soundtrack by the era's leading composer, attached to a story in which Kapoor embodies an older, slower idea of romance that the film treats as half-lost.

name: R. M. Films
career_background: A Hindi-film production banner active between the late 1970s and the mid-1990s, with no Wikipedia article of its own. It is credited on Hum Dono as R. M Films, a spelling this workbook consolidates.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhoota Kahin Ka (1979), Hum Dono (1995).
recurring_themes: Comedy and light romance in the 1970s; family drama by the 1990s.
creative_style: Not documented; both films were produced with Ravi Malhotra and the first was directed by Ravi Tandon.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films sixteen years apart, both involving the producer Ravi Malhotra: Ravi Tandon's comedy Jhoota Kahin Ka (1979), with an R. D. Burman score, and Hum Dono (1995), made as Kapoor's lead career was ending.
biography: R. M. Films produced two Rishi Kapoor films and has no documented history. Jhoota Kahin Ka (1979) belongs to the Ravi Tandon and Ravi Malhotra unit that also made Khel Khel Mein — a comedy of deception with an R. D. Burman soundtrack, from the period when Kapoor's youthful persona was at its most saleable. Hum Dono followed in 1995, in a quite different market, with Anand–Milind's music and Kapoor by then at the end of his run as a lead. The banner's name appears in two spellings across the two credits, consolidated here. Like most of the small production companies in this workbook's lower tiers, it survives only in the credits of the films it made.

name: Raj Kanwar
career_background: Raj Kanwar (28 June 1961 – 3 February 2012) was an Indian director, writer and producer of Hindi films, based in Mumbai and known for Deewana (1992), Jeet (1996) and Farz (2001). He died in Singapore. His brother is the filmmaker K. Pappu.
debut: Directorial debut Deewana (1992).
major_works: With Kapoor: Deewana (1992), Sadiyaan (2010). Elsewhere, Jeet, Judaai, Farz and Andaaz.
recurring_themes: Melodrama of love, loss and substitution; the romance built on a reversal of fortune.
creative_style: Efficient commercial melodrama with strong soundtrack placement, often launching or relaunching stars.
historical_importance: The director of Deewana, the film that introduced Shah Rukh Khan and is conventionally treated as a generational turning point in Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and the first is the pivot of this entire filmography. Deewana (1992), Kanwar's directorial debut, cast Kapoor as Ravi, the singer presumed dead, and the debuting Shah Rukh Khan as the younger man his widow marries; the film was a hit, and it is where Kapoor's leading career effectively hands over. Eighteen years later Kanwar directed him again in the partition romance Sadiyaan (2010), by then as a supporting player.
biography: Raj Kanwar directed the single most consequential film of Rishi Kapoor's later career. Deewana (1992) was Kanwar's own directorial debut: Kapoor plays a wealthy singer who marries Divya Bharti's character and is believed killed, after which she remarries the younger man played by a debuting Shah Rukh Khan. The film was a success, won Khan a Filmfare award for best debut, and is read — then and since — as the moment Hindi cinema's romantic lead passed from one generation to the next, with Kapoor himself performing the handover on screen. Kanwar went on to make Jeet, Judaai and Farz, and directed Kapoor once more in Sadiyaan (2010). He died in Singapore in February 2012 at fifty.

name: Rajiv Kapoor
career_background: Rajiv Kapoor (25 August 1962 – 9 February 2021) was an Indian actor, producer and director, the youngest son of Raj Kapoor and the younger brother of Randhir and Rishi Kapoor. He was best known as an actor for his lead role in Ram Teri Ganga Maili.
debut: Acting from 1983; produced Henna (1991) after his father's death and directed Prem Granth (1996).
major_works: With Kapoor: Henna (1991), Prem Granth (1996).
recurring_themes: The R. K. Films romance of prohibition and sacrifice, continued by the next generation.
creative_style: A brief career behind the camera maintaining the family studio's subject matter after Raj Kapoor's death.
historical_importance: Chiefly significant as the youngest of the three Kapoor brothers and as the director of R. K. Films' last production with his brother in the lead.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both family productions and both late R. K. Films. His article records that he took on the producer's role for Henna (1991) after their father's death, with Randhir directing, and he then directed Rishi Kapoor himself in Prem Granth (1996) — the last R. K. Films production in which his brother starred. The two films close the studio strand that had opened the career with Mera Naam Joker and Bobby.
biography: Rajiv Kapoor produced and directed the last two R. K. Films productions in which his brother starred. The youngest son of Raj Kapoor, best known as an actor for Ram Teri Ganga Maili, he stepped behind the camera after their father's death in 1988: his article records that he assumed the producer's role on Henna (1991), which Randhir Kapoor directed and in which Rishi Kapoor played the Indian engineer who loses his memory across the Pakistani border, and he then directed Prem Granth in 1996, a melodrama about a woman's rape and the man who marries her regardless. Both films restate the studio's long preoccupation with love across a prohibition. Rajiv Kapoor died in February 2021, ten months after his brother.

name: Rajkumar Santoshi
career_background: Rajkumar Santoshi (born 17 July 1956) is an Indian director, screenwriter and producer in Hindi cinema, the recipient of three National Film Awards and six Filmfare Awards. His directorial debut was Ghayal (1990), which was both a blockbuster and a critical success.
debut: Ghayal (1990), which won him the Filmfare Awards for Best Director and Best Story and the National Film Award for Best Popular Film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Damini (1993), Halla Bol (2008). Elsewhere, Ghayal, Andaz Apna Apna, Ghatak, China Gate and The Legend of Bhagat Singh.
recurring_themes: Justice denied and pursued: the courtroom, the vigilante, and the ordinary person against an institution.
creative_style: Forceful social melodrama with long confrontation scenes, alternating with broad comedy.
major_awards: Three National Film Awards and six Filmfare Awards, including consecutive Filmfare Awards for Best Director for Ghayal and Damini.
historical_importance: One of the defining commercial directors of the 1990s, and the only person to win consecutive Filmfare Best Director awards for his first two films.
relationship_with_actor: Two films. Damini (1993) is the significant one: a blockbuster about a woman who witnesses a rape and is disbelieved, in which Kapoor plays her husband opposite Meenakshi Seshadri and Sunny Deol, with the film's moral weight carried by others. Santoshi's article names Kapoor among its cast and records his second consecutive Filmfare Award for Best Director for it. Halla Bol (2008) followed fifteen years later with Kapoor in support.
biography: Rajkumar Santoshi directed Rishi Kapoor in Damini, the most critically substantial hit of his later career and a film in which he is deliberately not the hero. Santoshi, a three-time National Film Award and six-time Filmfare Award winner who made his debut with Ghayal in 1990 and became the only director to take consecutive Filmfare Best Director awards for his first two films, built Damini (1993) around Meenakshi Seshadri's character, who witnesses a servant's rape by her brother-in-law and is disbelieved, and Sunny Deol's alcoholic lawyer. Kapoor plays the husband whose family she is fighting — a weak, compromised figure, and a decisive break from the romantic lead. Santoshi used him again in Halla Bol (2008). The two films bracket Kapoor's transition from leading man to character actor.

name: Raju Saigal
career_background: A Hindi-film writer with credits in 1977 and 2001, and no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Doosra Aadmi (1977), Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001).
recurring_themes: Romantic melodrama and family comedy.
creative_style: Not documented; on Doosra Aadmi he is credited with Sagar Sarhadi.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films twenty-four years apart, and both for directors of the Yash Chopra school: Ramesh Talwar's Doosra Aadmi (1977), where he shares the writing credit with Sagar Sarhadi, and Rahul Rawail's Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001). The first is one of the most interesting films of Kapoor's youth, the second a late comedy with him as a father.
