biography: Raju Saigal wrote two Rishi Kapoor films nearly a quarter of a century apart and has no documented biography. The first, Ramesh Talwar's Doosra Aadmi (1977), is among the more unusual entries in the filmography: Kapoor's young advertising executive is pursued by an older woman, played by Raakhee, who is trying to recover a dead lover through him, and the film uses his boyishness against him only four years after Bobby. Saigal shares that credit with Sagar Sarhadi. The second, Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), is a Rahul Rawail comedy in which Kapoor plays the father of twins. Nothing further about him is recorded, and the row rests on the credits alone.

name: Raju Singh
career_background: Raju Singh, full name Rajinder Singh Panesar, is an Indian film score composer, session musician, singer and guitarist. He collaborated early with Malkit Singh and with Aadesh Shrivastava, and composed theme music for television series including Dekh Bhai Dekh, Aahat, Boogie Woogie and CID.
debut: Working from 1983, initially as a session musician and television composer.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chintu Ji (2009), Sanam Re (2016). Elsewhere, the background score for Raaz: The Mystery Continues and the themes for CID and Aahat.
recurring_themes: Television theme music and film background score rather than songs.
creative_style: A score and jingle specialist, working as arranger and session guitarist as well as composer.
major_awards: Mirchi Music Award for Best Background Score for Raaz: The Mystery Continues (2009); Indian Telly Awards for title music and background score.
historical_importance: One of Indian television's most recognisable theme composers, with a parallel career in film scoring.
relationship_with_actor: Two films as background-score composer: Chintu Ji (2009), in which Kapoor plays a fictionalised version of himself — 'Chintu' being his own lifelong nickname — and Sanam Re (2016). The first is among the most self-referential films of the career.
biography: Raju Singh wrote the background score for two late Rishi Kapoor films, one of them unusually personal. Born Rajinder Singh Panesar, Singh is better known in India for television than for film — his themes for Dekh Bhai Dekh, Aahat and CID are among the most recognisable on Indian television — and he won a Mirchi Music Award for the score of Raaz: The Mystery Continues. His first Kapoor film is Chintu Ji (2009), in which Kapoor plays a film star called Chintu Ji who returns to the village of his birth: Chintu was Kapoor's own nickname from childhood and the name by which the industry knew him, so the film is built directly on his public persona. Sanam Re followed in 2016, with Kapoor as a grandfather.

name: Randhir Kapoor
career_background: Randhir Raj Kapoor (born 15 February 1947) is a retired Indian actor, producer and director, the eldest son of Raj Kapoor, grandson of Prithviraj Kapoor and elder brother of Rishi and Rajiv Kapoor. He appeared as a child artist in Shree 420 (1955) and made his adult acting and directing debut in 1971. His daughters are the actresses Karisma and Kareena Kapoor.
debut: Child artist in Shree 420 (1955); directing from 1971.
major_works: With Kapoor: Henna (1991), Prem Granth (1996). Elsewhere, as an actor, Jeet, Hamrahi, Lafange and Ponga Pandit.
recurring_themes: The R. K. Films romance of separation and return.
creative_style: A family filmmaker completing and continuing his father's projects rather than pursuing a distinct style.
major_awards: Filmfare nomination for Best Director for Henna (1991).
historical_importance: The eldest of the three Kapoor brothers and the director who completed Raj Kapoor's final project.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both family productions. Henna (1991) was the film Raj Kapoor left unfinished at his death; Randhir Kapoor directed it with his brother Rishi in the lead and Rajiv producing, and earned a Filmfare nomination for Best Director. He also produced Prem Granth (1996), which Rajiv directed. The brothers appeared together as child artists in Shree 420 (1955) as well, the first film in this filmography.
biography: Randhir Kapoor directed his brother in the film their father did not live to finish. The eldest son of Raj Kapoor, he appeared as a child in Shree 420 in 1955 — the same film in which a three-year-old Rishi Kapoor walks through a song — and became an actor and director himself from 1971. After Raj Kapoor's death in 1988 he completed Henna, the cross-border romance in which Rishi Kapoor plays an Indian engineer who loses his memory in Pakistan and is cared for by the title character; the film was a success and brought Randhir a Filmfare nomination for Best Director. He then produced Prem Granth in 1996 under his brother Rajiv's direction. The two films close the R. K. Films strand of the career, thirty-six years after it opened.

name: Ravindra Jain
career_background: Ravindra Jain (28 February 1944 – 9 October 2015) was an Indian composer, lyricist and playback singer who worked from the early 1970s despite being blind from birth. His notable films include Chor Machaye Shor, Geet Gaata Chal, Chitchor, Ankhiyon Ke Jharokhon Se, Nadiya Ke Paar, Ram Teri Ganga Maili and Vivah, and he composed for Ramanand Sagar's television Ramayan (1987).
debut: Composing from 1972; his breakthrough came with Chor Machaye Shor (1974).
major_works: With Kapoor: Pati Patni Aur Woh (1978), Henna (1991). Elsewhere, Chitchor, Ram Teri Ganga Maili and the Ramayan television score.
recurring_themes: Devotional and folk-inflected melody; the rural romance; the bhajan as popular song.
creative_style: Simple, strongly melodic composition rooted in classical and devotional forms, frequently with his own lyrics.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Music Director for Ram Teri Ganga Maili (1985) and the Padma Shri in 2015.
historical_importance: The composer of the Ramayan television score, among the most widely heard pieces of music in India, and a central figure in the devotional strand of Hindi film music.
relationship_with_actor: Two films thirteen years apart, both significant in their way: B. R. Chopra's comedy of adultery Pati Patni Aur Woh (1978) and Henna (1991), the last R. K. Films production Raj Kapoor initiated, for which Jain wrote the songs. He had earlier scored Raj Kapoor's Ram Teri Ganga Maili, so the Henna commission continued a family association rather than a Rishi Kapoor one.
biography: Ravindra Jain wrote the music for Henna, the film Raj Kapoor left unfinished, and for one earlier Rishi Kapoor film. Blind from birth, Jain became one of the most distinctive composers of the 1970s and 1980s, working in a melodic, devotional idiom — Chitchor, Ankhiyon Ke Jharokhon Se, Nadiya Ke Paar — and winning the Filmfare Award for Best Music Director for Raj Kapoor's Ram Teri Ganga Maili in 1985. He received the Padma Shri in 2015, the year of his death. For Rishi Kapoor he scored B. R. Chopra's Pati Patni Aur Woh in 1978 and then Henna in 1991, a commission that came through the family rather than the actor. His score for Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan is probably the most widely heard music any collaborator in this workbook produced.

name: Red Chillies Entertainment
career_background: An Indian entertainment company established by Shah Rukh Khan and Gauri Khan, which evolved from their earlier company Dreamz Unlimited. Its own article gives the founding year as 2002 and Gauri Khan's gives 2001. Based in Mumbai, it spans production, marketing, distribution, licensing and a visual-effects division, Red Chillies VFX.
debut: Its early productions include Main Hoon Na; Om Shanti Om was its third film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Om Shanti Om (2007), Student of the Year (2012). Elsewhere, Main Hoon Na, Ra.One, Chennai Express and Jawan.
recurring_themes: Star vehicles built around Shah Rukh Khan, and Hindi cinema's own history as subject matter.
creative_style: A star-owned studio with heavy investment in visual effects and marketing.
historical_importance: One of the most powerful actor-owned production companies in Indian cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, in both of which Kapoor functions as a piece of the industry's past: Om Shanti Om (2007), Farah Khan's pastiche of 1970s Hindi cinema, where he appears as himself, and Student of the Year (2012), where he plays the dean. There is a pointed symmetry in the association — the company belongs to Shah Rukh Khan, whose debut in Deewana (1992) marked the end of Kapoor's run as a romantic lead.
biography: Red Chillies Entertainment, Shah Rukh Khan's company, employed Rishi Kapoor twice, both times for what he represented rather than what he could carry. Founded by Khan and his wife Gauri Khan out of their earlier Dreamz Unlimited — its own article dates this to 2002, hers to 2001 — the company became one of the most powerful star-owned studios in Indian cinema, with its own visual-effects division. Kapoor appears as himself in Om Shanti Om (2007), Farah Khan's affectionate pastiche of the 1970s industry in which he had been a leading man, and as the college dean in Student of the Year (2012). The relationship closes a circle: Khan's own debut, Deewana, was the film in which Kapoor handed over the romantic lead, and fifteen years later Khan's company was casting him as cinematic memory.

name: Rishi Kapoor
career_background: Rishi Raj Kapoor (4 September 1952 – 30 April 2020) is the subject of this workbook: an Indian actor and filmmaker, recipient of a National Film Award and four Filmfare Awards. He appears in the Collaborators sheet because he took a producer's credit on two of his own films, and he also directed one film in which he did not act, Aa Ab Laut Chalen (1999), which is outside this filmography's scope.
debut: National Film Award for Best Child Artist for Mera Naam Joker (1970); Filmfare Award for Best Actor for his first adult lead, Bobby (1973).
major_works: As producer: Prem Granth (1996), Pyaar Mein Twist (2005). As actor, the 160 films of this workbook.
recurring_themes: As producer, both credits are romances — one a family studio melodrama, the other a late-life love story.
creative_style: His production credits are family and personal projects rather than a business; his article records a lead romantic career of 92 films between 1973 and 2000.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Child Artist (Mera Naam Joker); Filmfare Award for Best Actor (Bobby); Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor (Do Dooni Chaar); Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor (Kapoor & Sons).
historical_importance: The defining romantic lead of 1970s and 1980s Hindi cinema and, after 2007, one of its most admired character actors.
relationship_with_actor: He is the selected actor. The two producer credits are revealing in different ways: Prem Granth (1996) is an R. K. Films production directed by his brother Rajiv, the last of the family studio's films with him in the lead, and Pyaar Mein Twist (2005) is a small film he produced himself in which he plays a widower courting a widow, with their adult children as the opposition — Bobby's structure inverted, with the lovers now old and the obstacle now filial rather than parental.
biography: Rishi Kapoor appears in this sheet as a producer of two of his own films, which is worth recording because of what he chose to produce. Prem Granth (1996) was an R. K. Films production, directed by his younger brother Rajiv, and the last film the family studio made with him as its lead — the end of the strand that had begun with Mera Naam Joker and Bobby. Pyaar Mein Twist (2005) is the more telling credit: a low-budget film he produced himself, in which he and Dimple Kapadia — his co-star from Bobby thirty-two years earlier — play a widower and widow whose late romance is opposed by their grown children. It is Bobby's situation with the generations reversed, and it is the only film in the filmography that he both produced and built around his own ageing persona.

name: Ritesh Sidhwani
career_background: Ritesh Sidhwani (born 1973) is an Indian film producer and the co-founder of Excel Entertainment with Farhan Akhtar. His first film as producer, Dil Chahta Hai, won National Awards in 2001, and the company later moved into streaming with Inside Edge, which was nominated for Best Drama Series at the 46th International Emmy Awards, followed by Mirzapur and Made in Heaven.
debut: Dil Chahta Hai (2001).
major_works: With Kapoor: Luck by Chance (2009), Sharmaji Namkeen (2022). Elsewhere, Dil Chahta Hai, Don, Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara, Dil Dhadakne Do, Fukrey and Gully Boy.
recurring_themes: Contemporary urban stories; the ensemble; and from 2017 long-form streaming drama.
creative_style: A producer who backs writer-directors and was among the first in Hindi cinema to build a streaming slate.
historical_importance: Co-founder of one of the production houses that defined post-2001 urban Hindi cinema and its move into streaming.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both through Excel Entertainment and both notable: Zoya Akhtar's Luck by Chance (2009), in which Kapoor plays the producer Rommy Rolly, and Sharmaji Namkeen (2022), the film Kapoor was shooting at his death, which the company completed by having Paresh Rawal play the remaining scenes as the same character.
biography: Ritesh Sidhwani produced Rishi Kapoor's final film and the role in which he most knowingly played a version of his own industry. With Farhan Akhtar he founded Excel Entertainment in 1999 and produced Dil Chahta Hai, which won National Awards and redirected mainstream Hindi cinema towards urban naturalism; the company later built one of India's first substantial streaming slates with Inside Edge, Mirzapur and Made in Heaven. Kapoor appears in Excel's Luck by Chance (2009) as Rommy Rolly, a producer who uses people and discards them, and in Sharmaji Namkeen, the gentle comedy about a retired man who takes up cooking that he was filming when he died in April 2020. Excel finished it with Paresh Rawal playing the remaining scenes as the same man, and released it in 2022.

name: Sajid–Farhad
career_background: A Hindi-film writing duo credited on comedies of the early 2010s, with no Wikipedia article under this name. They are credited on Housefull 2 as Sajid-Farhad, a spelling this workbook consolidates to the en-dash form used for composing and writing duos throughout.
major_works: With Kapoor: Housefull 2 (2012), Chashme Buddoor (2013).
recurring_themes: Large-ensemble farce built on mistaken identity and escalating confusion.
creative_style: Dialogue-led commercial comedy written for ensemble casts.
historical_importance: Not independently documented under the duo name.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both late comedies in which Kapoor is one element of a crowded cast: Housefull 2 (2012), where he and Randhir Kapoor play feuding brothers, and David Dhawan's remake Chashme Buddoor (2013). Both are scored by Sajid–Wajid, and both represent the kind of work available to a veteran star in a franchise comedy.
biography: Sajid–Farhad wrote two of Rishi Kapoor's late ensemble comedies, and the duo has no article under that name. Housefull 2 (2012) is the more interesting of the two for this filmography: in a cast of a dozen stars, Kapoor and his real-life elder brother Randhir Kapoor play feuding brothers, one of the few occasions the two appeared together on screen as adults. Chashme Buddoor (2013), David Dhawan's remake of the 1981 campus comedy, followed. Both films are scored by Sajid–Wajid, and both treat Kapoor as a recognisable veteran presence inside a franchise rather than as a performer with a part to play. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Sandeep Shirodkar
career_background: Sandeep Shirodkar is an Indian film score composer, music director and record producer who has also worked as an arranger of songs for other composers. He has composed background scores for Dabangg, Bodyguard, Once Upon A Time in Mumbaai and Prince, and more recently worked as an original song composer, including remakes for Judwaa 2 with Anu Malik.
debut: Working as an arranger before composing background scores in his own right.
major_works: With Kapoor: Housefull 2 (2012), Chashme Buddoor (2013). Elsewhere, the scores for Dabangg and Bodyguard.
recurring_themes: Background score for the mass-market action film and the ensemble comedy.
creative_style: An arranger-turned-score composer working in the loud, percussive register of the 2010s mass entertainer.
historical_importance: Representative of the specialised background-score profession that emerged in Hindi cinema in the 2000s.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both late ensemble comedies written by Sajid–Farhad and both with songs by Sajid–Wajid: Housefull 2 (2012) and Chashme Buddoor (2013). His contribution to each is the background score rather than the songs — the division of labour that characterises the films of Kapoor's final decade.
biography: Sandeep Shirodkar scored two of Rishi Kapoor's last comedies. An arranger who became one of Hindi cinema's specialist background-score composers, Shirodkar wrote the scores for Dabangg, Bodyguard and Once Upon A Time in Mumbaai — the loud, percussive idiom of the 2010s mass entertainer — and later moved into song composition, working with Anu Malik on remakes for Judwaa 2. His Kapoor films, Housefull 2 (2012) and Chashme Buddoor (2013), are both franchise comedies written by Sajid–Farhad with songs by Sajid–Wajid, in which his job was the underscore alone. The pattern is worth noting across this workbook: in Kapoor's youth one composer wrote everything a film needed, while by the end the songs, the score and the arrangement were three separate commissions.

name: Sanjeev Duggal
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active in the early 1990s, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bol Radha Bol (1992), Eena Meena Deeka (1994).
recurring_themes: Farce of mistaken identity and the double role.
creative_style: Not documented; on Bol Radha Bol he shares the writing credit with Anees Bazmee, who wrote the dialogue.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both David Dhawan comedies produced by Nitin Manmohan and scored by Anand–Milind: Bol Radha Bol (1992), the double-role farce that was among the last hits Kapoor carried, and Eena Meena Deeka (1994). The same unit made both.
biography: Sanjeev Duggal wrote two Rishi Kapoor comedies and has no documented biography. Bol Radha Bol (1992) is the better of the two by any measure: David Dhawan's farce in which Kapoor plays both a businessman and his criminal lookalike, with Juhi Chawla doubled as well, released the same year as Deewana and one of the last occasions he opened a hit alone. Eena Meena Deeka followed in 1994 with the same director, producer and composers. Duggal shares the Bol Radha Bol credit with Anees Bazmee, who went on to become one of Hindi cinema's most successful comedy directors while Duggal left no further trace. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: Shankar–Jaikishan
career_background: An Indian composing duo of Shankar Singh Ram Singh Raghuvanshi (15 October 1922 – 26 April 1987) and Jaikishan Dayabhai Panchal (4 November 1929 – 12 September 1971), known as S-J, who worked together from 1949 until Jaikishan's death in 1971 and composed for 136 films, introducing a new level of orchestral richness to Hindi film music. Their article describes them as widely considered the greatest composers of the Hindi film industry.
debut: Composing from 1949; they reached the front rank in 1955 with Shree 420 and Seema.
major_works: With Kapoor: Shree 420 (1955), Mera Naam Joker (1970). Elsewhere, Barsaat, Awaara, Chori Chori, Brahmachari and Pehchan.
recurring_themes: Large-orchestra romantic melody; the Raj Kapoor social melodrama; the songs of the 1950s and 1960s star vehicle.
creative_style: Orchestral richness unusual for its period, with a long association with Raj Kapoor and with the singers Mukesh, Lata Mangeshkar and Mohammed Rafi.
major_awards: Nine Filmfare Awards for Best Music Director, the first for Chori Chori, the sixth for Brahmachari — which also brought their first BFJA award — and the last for Be-Imaan; nominated for Mera Naam Joker.
historical_importance: The dominant composing team of 1950s and 1960s Hindi cinema and the musical voice of Raj Kapoor's studio.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and they are the first two in this filmography: Shree 420 (1955), in which a three-year-old Kapoor walks through 'Pyar Hua Iqrar Hua', and Mera Naam Joker (1970), his credited debut as the adolescent Raju, for which the duo received a Filmfare nomination. Both are Raj Kapoor films, and the second was among Jaikishan's last before his death in 1971. They scored the beginning of the career and nothing after it.
biography: Shankar–Jaikishan wrote the music Rishi Kapoor first appeared in front of, and the music of his credited debut. The duo of Shankar Raghuvanshi and Jaikishan Panchal worked from 1949 until Jaikishan's death in 1971, composing for 136 films, winning nine Filmfare Awards for Best Music Director and bringing an orchestral scale to Hindi film song that their own article calls unmatched. They were Raj Kapoor's composers, and so they scored Shree 420 in 1955 — the film in which his three-year-old son walks through 'Pyar Hua Iqrar Hua' — and Mera Naam Joker in 1970, in which the same boy, now seventeen, played his father's character as a schoolboy and won a National Film Award. Their association with the filmography ends there, a year before Jaikishan died and three before Bobby.

name: Sikandar Khanna
career_background: An Indian Hindi-film director whose Wikipedia article is a stub recording only that he worked in Bollywood and that he died during the making of Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zinda Dil (1975), Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan (1978).
recurring_themes: Romance and melodrama of the mid-1970s commercial mainstream.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not substantially documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films from Kapoor's first flush of stardom, and the second was unfinished at the director's death: his article records that he died during the making of Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan (1978). Zinda Dil (1975), with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score, came two years after Bobby, when Kapoor was being cast in as many romances as the market would take.
biography: Sikandar Khanna directed two Rishi Kapoor films and died during the second. His Wikipedia article is barely more than a line, recording his work as a Bollywood director and his death in the course of making Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan, released in 1978. The earlier film, Zinda Dil (1975), belongs to the rush of romances Kapoor made immediately after Bobby, when producers were casting him in anything that needed a young lover; it was scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, who wrote the music for thirty-two films in this filmography. Khanna is the only director here known to have died mid-production on a Kapoor film, and almost the only one about whom Wikipedia records a death but not a birth.

name: Sneha Khanwalkar
career_background: Sneha Khanwalkar (born 28 April 1983 in Indore) is an Indian music director working in Hindi films. She was nominated for Best Music Director at the 58th Filmfare Awards for Gangs of Wasseypur, becoming only the second woman nominated in that category, twenty-eight years after Usha Khanna. She also presented the television series Sound Trippin.
debut: Composing from 2004; her breakthrough was Anurag Kashyap's Gangs of Wasseypur duology.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018), Sharmaji Namkeen (2022). Elsewhere, Oye Lucky! Lucky Oye! and Gangs of Wasseypur.
recurring_themes: Field-recorded and regional musical idioms brought into film scoring; music assembled from found voices rather than studio singers.
creative_style: A collector's method: travelling to record local singers and sounds and building soundtracks from them, documented in her television series Sound Trippin.
major_awards: Filmfare nomination for Best Music Director for Gangs of Wasseypur at the 58th awards — only the second for a woman in that category.
historical_importance: The most prominent female composer in Hindi cinema of her generation, and one of only two ever nominated for the Filmfare Best Music Director award.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both at the very end of the career and both unlike anything in his lead years: Nandita Das's Manto (2018), in which Kapoor has a small part in a biographical film about the Urdu writer, and Sharmaji Namkeen (2022), his last film, released posthumously. She is one of a very small number of women among the 561 collaborators in this workbook, and the only female composer.
biography: Sneha Khanwalkar is the only female composer in this filmography, and she scored Rishi Kapoor's last film. Born in Indore in 1983, she built a reputation on a method unusual in Hindi cinema — travelling to record regional singers and incidental sound and assembling soundtracks from them, a practice she turned into the television series Sound Trippin — and became only the second woman nominated for the Filmfare Award for Best Music Director, for Gangs of Wasseypur, twenty-eight years after Usha Khanna. Her two Kapoor films are Nandita Das's Manto (2018), in which he appears briefly, and Sharmaji Namkeen, which he was shooting when he died and which was completed with Paresh Rawal in the remaining scenes. That his final soundtrack came from her is a sharp measure of the distance between the industry he entered and the one he left.

name: Soham Rockstar Entertainment
career_background: The production banner founded by the producer Deepak Mukut, under which he made mid-budget Hindi films in the late 2010s. The company has no Wikipedia article of its own; its founding by Mukut is recorded in his article, which is cited on his row in this sheet.
major_works: With Kapoor: Mulk (2018), Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019). Elsewhere, Sanam Teri Kasam and Dhaakad.
recurring_themes: Issue-driven drama alongside broad comedy, at mid-range budgets.
creative_style: Not documented beyond its founder's practice of backing modestly budgeted films across genres.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films from Kapoor's last two years, and they could hardly be more different: Anubhav Sinha's Mulk (2018), in which he plays Murad Ali Mohammed, the head of a Varanasi Muslim family defending itself against a terrorism accusation — one of the most substantial roles of his late career — and the farce Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
biography: Soham Rockstar Entertainment produced the last serious role of Rishi Kapoor's career. The banner belongs to Deepak Mukut, a distributor-turned-producer from Jaipur whose article records that he founded it, and under it he made Anubhav Sinha's Mulk in 2018: Kapoor plays the patriarch of a Muslim family in Varanasi whose nephew is accused of terrorism, a performance widely counted among his best. The company's second Kapoor film, Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), is a broad comedy with no such ambitions, and was one of his last releases. The pairing is a fair portrait of what an independent mid-budget banner could offer a veteran star at the end of the 2010s: one role worth having and one that paid.

name: Subhash Ghai
career_background: Subhash Ghai (born 24 January 1945 in Nagpur) is an Indian director, producer, actor, lyricist and screenwriter, and one of the most prominent Hindi filmmakers of the 1980s and 1990s. He founded Mukta Arts in 1982, which became a public company in 2000.
debut: Working from 1967; his breakthrough as a director was Kalicharan (1976).
major_works: With Kapoor: Karz (1980), Kaanchi: The Unbreakable (2014). Elsewhere, Kalicharan, Vidhaata, Hero, Karma, Ram Lakhan, Saudagar, Khalnayak, Pardes and Taal.
recurring_themes: The showman's melodrama: reincarnation and revenge, mothers and brothers, and the star entrance staged as spectacle.
creative_style: Large-scale commercial filmmaking with strong musical set pieces and an instinct for star image; a long collaboration with Dilip Kumar in Vidhaata, Karma and Saudagar.
major_awards: A Filmfare Award for Best Director for Saudagar among other honours, and the National Film Award for Best Film on Other Social Issues as the producer of Iqbal.
historical_importance: One of the defining commercial directors of 1980s and 1990s Hindi cinema, routinely called its showman after Raj Kapoor.
relationship_with_actor: Two films thirty-four years apart. Karz (1980) is the significant one: Ghai's reincarnation thriller gave Kapoor the most durable role of his early career as Monty, the singer who recovers the memory of his murder, with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score that outlived the film and has been remade and sampled repeatedly. Kaanchi: The Unbreakable (2014) came at the other end, a late Ghai film with Kapoor in support.
biography: Subhash Ghai directed the film that gave Rishi Kapoor his most imitated role. Born in Nagpur in 1945 and the dominant commercial showman of Hindi cinema in the 1980s and 1990s — Hero, Karma, Ram Lakhan, Saudagar, Khalnayak, Pardes, Taal — Ghai made Karz in 1980, a reincarnation thriller in which Kapoor's stage singer Monty is haunted by the murder of his previous self. The film was not an immediate triumph, but its Laxmikant–Pyarelal songs and its structure have been recycled ever since, including in an outright remake, and 'Om Shanti Om' became one of the defining numbers of Kapoor's career. Ghai also founded Mukta Arts in 1982 and later produced Iqbal, which won a National Film Award. He used Kapoor once more, in Kaanchi, thirty-four years after Karz.

name: Sukhwinder Singh
career_background: Sukhwinder Singh (born 18 July 1971 in Amritsar) is an Indian playback singer, composer, lyricist and music producer who has recorded in many Indian languages. He was noticed early by Laxmikant–Pyarelal and worked as a musical arranger on their projects in the late 1980s and early 1990s before his own career as a singer and composer.
debut: Recording from 1991, after arranging for Laxmikant–Pyarelal.
major_works: With Kapoor: Halla Bol (2008), Chintu Ji (2009). Elsewhere, as a singer, 'Chaiyya Chaiyya' and 'Jai Ho', and the award-winning 'Bismil' from Haider.
recurring_themes: Punjabi folk energy brought into the Hindi film song; the large anthemic number.
creative_style: A singer-composer whose own voice is the defining instrument of his work.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Male Playback Singer for 'Bismil' from Haider (2014), and two Filmfare Awards for Best Male Playback Singer, including for 'Chaiyya Chaiyya'.
historical_importance: One of the most recognisable playback voices of post-1998 Hindi cinema, best known for 'Chaiyya Chaiyya' and 'Jai Ho'.
relationship_with_actor: Two films as composer rather than singer, both from 2008–09 and both small: Rajkumar Santoshi's Halla Bol (2008) and Chintu Ji (2009), in which Kapoor plays a fictionalised version of himself. There is a neat line back through his biography: he began as an arranger for Laxmikant–Pyarelal, the duo who scored thirty-two Kapoor films, before composing two of his last.
biography: Sukhwinder Singh composed two late Rishi Kapoor films, having begun his career inside the orchestra of Kapoor's most frequent composers. Born in Amritsar in 1971, Singh was spotted by Laxmikant–Pyarelal and arranged for them before becoming one of the most recognisable playback voices in India, winning a National Film Award for 'Bismil' from Haider and two Filmfare Awards, with 'Chaiyya Chaiyya' and 'Jai Ho' among his recordings. As a composer he wrote for Rajkumar Santoshi's Halla Bol (2008) and for Chintu Ji (2009), the self-referential comedy in which Kapoor plays a star called Chintu Ji — his own childhood nickname — returning to his birthplace. The arc from arranging Laxmikant–Pyarelal's Kapoor scores to writing one himself spans almost exactly the length of the actor's career.

name: Suresh Nair
career_background: A Hindi-film writer active in the late 2000s and early 2010s, with no Wikipedia article of his own; the similarly named article that the bare credit resolves to belongs to an artist, not to this writer.
major_works: With Kapoor: Namastey London (2007), D-Day (2013).
recurring_themes: The diaspora family comedy and the espionage thriller — two registers with little in common beyond their scale.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: Two films from Kapoor's character-actor phase, both commercially substantial: Namastey London (2007), in which he plays the Punjabi father insisting on an Indian marriage for his British daughter, and Nikkhil Advani's D-Day (2013), in which he plays an underworld boss hiding in Karachi. The two parts are at opposite ends of his late range.
biography: Suresh Nair wrote two of Rishi Kapoor's better late films and has no documented biography. Namastey London (2007) gave him one of his most widely seen roles, the London Punjabi father who tricks his anglicised daughter into an Indian marriage — a part that traded on exactly the warmth audiences remembered from his romantic years. D-Day (2013) is the opposite: Kapoor as Iqbal Seth, a Dawood Ibrahim-like crime boss living under protection in Karachi, in a thriller that treats him as a figure of menace. That both scripts came from the same writer, in a career otherwise undocumented, is a reminder of how thinly Hindi cinema records its screenwriters even in the 2010s. This row is built from film credits alone.

name: T-Series Films
career_background: Super Cassettes Industries Private Limited, trading as T-Series, is an Indian record label and film studio founded by Gulshan Kumar on 11 July 1983 and now run by his son Bhushan Kumar with his brother Krishan Kumar. It is the largest music label in India with up to a 35 per cent share of the market, owns the most-viewed YouTube channel in the world, and has produced more than a hundred films.
debut: Founded in 1983 as a music label; film production followed.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patiala House (2011), Sanam Re (2016). Elsewhere, a large slate of 2010s Hindi films alongside its dominant music catalogue.
recurring_themes: Films commissioned partly to generate soundtrack catalogue; multi-composer albums.
creative_style: A music company producing films, with soundtracks typically divided among several composers and marketed independently of the film.
historical_importance: The dominant force in Indian recorded music and, since the 2000s, one of its most prolific film producers.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both late supporting roles: Patiala House (2011), in which Kapoor plays the London patriarch forbidding his son's cricket career, and Sanam Re (2016). Both were produced by Bhushan Kumar and Krishan Kumar, who have separate rows here, and both carry soundtracks split between several composers — the production model that characterises the last decade of the filmography.
biography: T-Series produced two of Rishi Kapoor's late films, and its presence in this workbook marks how much the industry's centre of gravity had shifted by the 2010s. Founded by Gulshan Kumar in 1983 and built into India's largest record label — with roughly a third of the market and, latterly, the most-viewed YouTube channel in the world — the company moved into film production under his son Bhushan Kumar and brother Krishan Kumar, commissioning films partly to feed its music catalogue. Kapoor appears in Patiala House (2011), as the embittered Southall father who forbids his son's cricket, and in Sanam Re (2016) as a grandfather. In his youth a film's songs belonged to its composer and its producer; in these, the film belongs to the music company.

name: T. Rama Rao
career_background: Tatineni Rama Rao (29 May 1938 – 20 April 2022), born in Kapileswarapuram in the Madras Presidency, was an Indian filmmaker who directed 75 Hindi and Telugu feature films between 1966 and 2000. He died in Chennai.
debut: Directing from 1966 in Telugu cinema, later moving into Hindi remakes.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naseeb Apna Apna (1986), Dosti Dushmani (1986). Elsewhere, a long run of Telugu films and their Hindi remakes.
recurring_themes: Family melodrama and revenge drama, frequently remade from Telugu originals for the Hindi market.
creative_style: A high-volume director working in two industries, specialising in transplanting southern commercial formulas into Hindi.
historical_importance: One of the most prolific directors of the southern-to-Hindi remake, a significant commercial current of 1980s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both released in 1986 and both multi-star melodramas: Naseeb Apna Apna, produced by K. C. Bokadia with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score, and Dosti Dushmani, written with Rahi Masoom Raza. They belong to the stretch in which a substantial share of Kapoor's films were made by South Indian directors reworking southern material, a pattern that shaped his mid-1980s output more than any single Hindi filmmaker did.
biography: T. Rama Rao directed two Rishi Kapoor films in a single year, and his presence identifies a distinct phase of the filmography. A Telugu director who made 75 features across two industries between 1966 and 2000, Rama Rao was among the most productive practitioners of the southern-to-Hindi remake, importing proven formulas into Bombay with large casts and strong melodrama. In 1986 he made both Naseeb Apna Apna, produced by K. C. Bokadia, and Dosti Dushmani with Kapoor, who was then taking whatever substantial lead work was available in a thin decade. Several other films of his middle period came from the same southern pipeline. Rama Rao died in Chennai in April 2022.

name: Tanishk Bagchi
career_background: Tanishk Bagchi (born 23 November 1980 in Kolkata) is an Indian music producer, composer, singer and lyricist working in Hindi films, also credited as half of Tanishk-Vayu and known for reworking older songs for new films.
debut: Working from 2007; prominent as a composer from the mid-2010s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kapoor & Sons (2016), The Body (2019). Elsewhere, Badrinath Ki Dulhania, Kesari and a long list of recreated songs.
recurring_themes: The recreated song — older melodies rebuilt for contemporary films — and the single-track commission.
creative_style: A producer-composer working one song at a time within multi-composer soundtracks, with a specialism in reworking existing material.
major_awards: Filmfare nomination for Best Lyricist for 'Ve Maahi' from Kesari at the 65th awards.
historical_importance: The composer most identified with the 2010s practice of rebuilding old Hindi songs for new films — a practice that has repeatedly reused the soundtracks of Kapoor's own era.
relationship_with_actor: Two films at the end of the career, both multi-composer soundtracks: Kapoor & Sons (2016) and The Body (2019), the last film released in Kapoor's lifetime. The connection carries an irony worth recording: Bagchi's stock in trade is the recreation of hits from the 1970s and 1980s, the decades in which Kapoor's own films supplied many of the originals.
biography: Tanishk Bagchi contributed songs to two of Rishi Kapoor's last films. A Kolkata-born producer and composer who became one of the most employed names in 2010s Hindi film music, Bagchi is best known for recreations — rebuilding older Hindi songs, many of them from the 1970s and 1980s, for contemporary films — and for working a single track at a time inside soundtracks shared among several composers. He wrote for Kapoor & Sons (2016), the Dharma family ensemble in which Kapoor played the ninety-year-old grandfather, and for The Body (2019), released five months before his death. The pattern is a closed loop: the composer whose trade is refurbishing the music of Kapoor's heyday was also, at the end, writing new songs for the films he appeared in.

name: Taz
industry: British Asian popular music; Indian cinema
career_background: Tarsame Singh Saini (23 May 1967 – 29 April 2022), known as Taz or Taz Stereo Nation and earlier as Johnny Zee, was a British singer, composer and actor of Indian descent, born in Coventry. He was the lead singer of the band Stereo Nation, formed in 1996, and is credited with pioneering cross-cultural Asian fusion music.
debut: Recording from 1989; his film debut was Don't Stop Dreaming (2007), for which he composed the soundtrack, sang the playback and acted.
major_works: With Kapoor: Don't Stop Dreaming (2007), Sambar Salsa (2007). Elsewhere, the Stereo Nation albums and singles.
recurring_themes: Bhangra and Western pop fusion for a British Asian audience.
creative_style: A performer-composer working outside the Hindi film industry, in the British Asian music scene he helped create.
historical_importance: A pioneer of British Asian fusion music, and one of the few musicians from that scene to compose for Indian films.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and they are the two English-language films in this filmography, both written and directed by Kapoor's cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor and both released in 2007. Taz's article names Kapoor directly: it records that he made his film debut with the British film Don't Stop Dreaming, composing the soundtrack and singing the playback, and that he co-starred with Rishi Kapoor, Sunil Shetty and Richard Blackwood.
biography: Taz composed and starred in the two English-language films in this filmography, and his article is one of the few that names Rishi Kapoor outright. Born Tarsame Singh Saini in Coventry in 1967 and performing first as Johnny Zee, he led Stereo Nation from 1996 and is credited with pioneering the British Asian fusion of bhangra and Western pop. In 2007 he made his film debut in Don't Stop Dreaming, written and directed by Kapoor's cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor, composing the score and singing the playback as well as acting alongside Kapoor, Sunil Shetty and Richard Blackwood; Sambar Salsa followed the same year. These two small films sit outside the Hindi industry altogether, and are the least documented entries in the filmography. Taz died in April 2022.

name: Tinnu Anand
career_background: Tinnu Anand, born Virender Raj Anand on 12 October 1945 in Peshawar, is an Indian actor, director, writer and producer in Hindi cinema with some Telugu and Tamil work. He is a son of the writer Inder Raj Anand and a brother of the producer Bittu Anand; the director Siddharth Anand is his nephew and Mukul Anand was his cousin. His notable films as director include Shahenshah, Kaalia and Kaalapani.
debut: Directing from the late 1970s; also a prolific character actor.
major_works: With Kapoor: Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan (1984). Elsewhere, Kaalia, Shahenshah and Kaalapani.
recurring_themes: The star vehicle built around a single performer, most often Amitabh Bachchan.
creative_style: A director of broad commercial entertainments with a strong sense of star entrance and confrontation, and a parallel career as a character actor.
historical_importance: The director of Shahenshah and Kaalia, two of Amitabh Bachchan's defining vehicles, and a member of the Anand filmmaking family.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both family productions in the sense that his brother Bittu Anand produced them and their father Inder Raj Anand wrote one: Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979) and Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan (1984), both with Kapoor as a romantic lead. The Anands account for six credits across this filmography in four functions.
biography: Tinnu Anand directed two Rishi Kapoor romances, both produced by his own brother. Born in Peshawar in 1945 as Virender Raj Anand and the son of the Raj Kapoor screenwriter Inder Raj Anand, he is better known for the Amitabh Bachchan vehicles Kaalia and Shahenshah and for a long career as a character actor. His Kapoor films — Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), on which his father has a writing credit, and Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan (1984) — were both produced by his brother Bittu Anand with Naresh Malhotra, making them family enterprises on two sides. The Anand family's six credits here, spanning writing, direction and production across three generations, illustrate how much of Hindi cinema's working structure in this period ran through households rather than studios.

name: Vanraj Bhatia
industry: Hindi cinema; Indian New Wave; Western classical music in India
career_background: Vanraj Bhatia (31 May 1927 – 7 May 2021) was an Indian composer best known for his work in Indian New Wave cinema and one of the leading composers of Western classical music in India. He received the National Film Award for Best Music Direction for the television film Tamas (1988), the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award for Creative and Experimental Music in 1989, and the Padma Shri in 2012.
debut: Composing for film from the 1970s, principally for Shyam Benegal and the parallel cinema.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ajooba (1991), Damini (1993). Elsewhere, Ankur, Bhumika, Mandi, Tamas and a body of concert and chamber music.
recurring_themes: Score as dramatic argument rather than decoration; Indian material treated with Western classical technique.
creative_style: A classically trained composer who wrote sparely for the parallel cinema and occasionally for commercial films, with an output including opera, chamber and solo piano music.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Tamas; Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1989); Padma Shri (2012).
historical_importance: The pre-eminent composer of the Indian New Wave and a serious concert composer, an unusual combination in Indian music.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both as background-score composer and both commercial pictures far from his usual territory: Shashi Kapoor's Indo-Soviet fantasy Ajooba (1991), in which Rishi Kapoor was third-billed behind Amitabh Bachchan and Dimple Kapadia, and Rajkumar Santoshi's Damini (1993). That the New Wave's leading composer scored both is one of the odder facts in this filmography.
biography: Vanraj Bhatia, the composer of the Indian New Wave, wrote the background score for two Rishi Kapoor films. Classically trained and equally at home in concert music — his catalogue includes opera, chamber and piano works — Bhatia was Shyam Benegal's composer and the musical voice of the parallel cinema, winning the National Film Award for Tamas, the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award and the Padma Shri. His commercial credits are sparse, which makes these two striking: Ajooba (1991), the Indo-Soviet fantasy Shashi Kapoor directed with Amitabh Bachchan and a third-billed Rishi Kapoor, and Damini (1993), Rajkumar Santoshi's courtroom melodrama, in which Kapoor plays the weak husband. In a filmography scored overwhelmingly by commercial song composers, Bhatia is the one figure whose reputation rests on score rather than songs.

name: Vishal–Shekhar
career_background: An Indian composing, production, singing and songwriting duo of Vishal Dadlani and Shekhar Ravjiani, from Mumbai. They have featured on more than 350 film soundtracks, had 72 number-one singles, and recorded with international artists including Akon, Imogen Heap and Diplo.
debut: Working from 1999; their breakthrough was Jhankaar Beats (2003), which brought them the Filmfare RD Burman Award for New Music Talent.
major_works: With Kapoor: Om Shanti Om (2007), Student of the Year (2012). Elsewhere, Jhankaar Beats, Dus, Om Shanti Om, Chennai Express and Pathaan.
recurring_themes: Dance-pop and rock-inflected romance for the post-2000 star vehicle; pastiche of earlier Hindi film styles.
creative_style: A rock and pop sensibility applied to mainstream film music, with Dadlani's vocals and a strong production hand.
major_awards: Filmfare RD Burman Award for Jhankaar Beats; Filmfare nominations for Best Music Director including for Om Shanti Om; Best Composer at the 2nd Asian Film Awards for Om Shanti Om.
historical_importance: Among the defining composers of post-2000 commercial Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both of which use Kapoor as an emblem of the industry's past: Om Shanti Om (2007), where he appears as himself in a film openly pastiching the 1970s cinema he came from — and whose songs, including 'Dard-e-Disco' and 'Main Agar Kahoon', won the duo an Asian Film Award — and Student of the Year (2012), where he plays the dean. Their RD Burman Award is a further link: Burman scored twenty of Kapoor's films.
biography: Vishal–Shekhar scored two films in which Rishi Kapoor appears as a figure from Hindi cinema's past. Vishal Dadlani and Shekhar Ravjiani have worked together since 1999, featuring on more than 350 soundtracks and winning the Filmfare RD Burman Award for Jhankaar Beats — an award named for the composer of twenty Kapoor films. Their Om Shanti Om (2007), for which they won Best Composer at the Asian Film Awards, is a pastiche of exactly the 1970s industry in which Kapoor had been a young star, and he appears in it as himself among a crowd of others. Student of the Year (2012) cast him as a college dean. In both, the soundtrack imitates or remembers the era he belonged to, while he plays the part of the remembered thing.

name: A. Krishnamoorthi
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He is very probably the same person as A. Krishnamurthy, credited as producer on Sindoor (1987): both films were directed by K. Ravi Shankar, both credits are for production, and the two names are transliteration variants. The identification is not certain, so this workbook keeps the two credits in separate rows rather than merging a collaboration count on circumstantial evidence.
major_works: With Kapoor: Gharana (1989).
recurring_themes: Family melodrama of sacrifice and respectability.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Gharana (1989), co-produced with its director K. Ravi Shankar, in which Kapoor's character renounces the woman he loves and marries another for dowry money — an inversion of the lover-boy pattern. The film's article spells his name Krishnamoorthi.
biography: A. Krishnamoorthi co-produced Gharana (1989) with its director K. Ravi Shankar and has no documented biography. The film is one of the more interesting of Kapoor's middle period: he plays a man who appears mercenary — abandoning one woman and marrying another for her dowry — precisely because he is sacrificing himself, which reads as a deliberate inversion of the persona Bobby had established. The same director's Sindoor (1987) credits a producer named A. Krishnamurthy, almost certainly the same man under a different transliteration; this workbook records both credits separately and notes the likely identity rather than merging them on inference.

name: A. Krishnamurthy
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He is very probably the same person as A. Krishnamoorthi, credited as producer on Gharana (1989): both films were directed by K. Ravi Shankar and the names are transliteration variants. The identification is not certain and the two credits are kept as separate rows.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sindoor (1987).
recurring_themes: Family melodrama of honour and remarriage.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sindoor (1987), directed by K. Ravi Shankar, with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score — one of the mid-budget melodramas that made up most of Kapoor's work in the late 1980s.
biography: A. Krishnamurthy produced Sindoor (1987) for the director K. Ravi Shankar and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the dense run of family melodramas Kapoor made in the second half of the 1980s, scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, in which he played husbands and sons rather than lovers. Shankar's other Kapoor film, Gharana (1989), credits a producer named A. Krishnamoorthi, and the two are almost certainly the same man; this workbook notes the probability in both rows rather than merging them, since merging would assert a two-film collaboration that no source confirms.

name: AA Films
career_background: An Indian motion-picture distribution company owned by Anil Thadani and the actress Raveena Tandon, which mainly distributes Hindi and Hindi-dubbed films. Its article gives the founding year as 1993 in Mumbai, which is three years after the Kapoor film it is credited on; the discrepancy is unresolved and may indicate a later distribution credit or a different company of the same name.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sheshnaag (1990).
recurring_themes: Distribution rather than production; a broad commercial slate.
creative_style: A distributor rather than a creative house.
historical_importance: One of the significant Hindi-film distributors of the 2000s and 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on the snake-deity fantasy Sheshnaag (1990), which Iqbal Durrani directed in the wake of Nagina's success. Note the chronology: the company's own article dates its founding to 1993, after this film's release, so the credit either reflects a later distribution arrangement or a different entity.
biography: AA Films appears once in this filmography, on Sheshnaag (1990), and the credit does not sit easily with the company's own history. The firm, owned by Anil Thadani and Raveena Tandon, became one of Hindi cinema's busiest distributors, but its article dates its founding to 1993 — three years after the film. Either the credit records a later distribution of the title, or the banner named on the film is a different company. Sheshnaag itself is one of the folk-fantasy pictures Kapoor made after Nagina proved the formula, with Laxmikant–Pyarelal's music and a plot of serpent deities rather than courtship. The row records the inconsistency rather than resolving it, and is graded accordingly.

name: Aadesh K. Arjun
career_background: A Hindi-film writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994).
recurring_themes: Household melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994), a Nadeem–Shravan-scored melodrama from the last stretch of Kapoor's lead career.
biography: Aadesh K. Arjun has one credit in this filmography, as a writer on Saajan Ka Ghar (1994), and no documented biography. The film is one of four Kapoor released that year, all of them modest, and belongs to the Nadeem–Shravan period in which the soundtrack was usually a film's only durable asset. This row exists because the workbook records every credited collaborator, and it is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Aasia Films Pvt. Ltd.
career_background: The production banner credited on Ajooba (1991), the Indo-Soviet fantasy Shashi Kapoor directed and produced. The company has no Wikipedia article of its own; the film's own credits name Shashi Kapoor as producer alongside this banner and the Gorky Film Studio.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ajooba (1991).
recurring_themes: Not documented; its one credit here is a large-scale international co-production.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ajooba (1991), in which Rishi Kapoor was third-billed behind Amitabh Bachchan and Dimple Kapadia in a fantasy adventure directed by his uncle Shashi Kapoor and co-produced with the Soviet Gorky Film Studio. It was an expensive failure and one of the odder entries in the filmography.
biography: Aasia Films is the banner behind Ajooba (1991), the Indo-Soviet fantasy that Shashi Kapoor directed and produced with the Gorky Film Studio, and it has no recorded history of its own. The film cast Amitabh Bachchan as a masked avenger with Dimple Kapadia and a third-billed Rishi Kapoor, was shot partly in the Soviet Union with Soviet crew, and failed badly. For this filmography it is notable as the only international co-production and as one of three films in which Rishi Kapoor worked for his uncle. The banner's row rests on the film's credits alone.

name: Abbas–Mustan
career_background: An Indian filmmaking duo of the brothers Abbas Alibhai Burmawalla and Mustan Alibhai Burmawalla, born in 1950 in Mumbai, who work as directors and producers and are known for stylish suspense, action and romantic thrillers with dark-lit visuals.
debut: Directing from 1985.
major_works: With Kapoor: Daraar (1996). Elsewhere, Baazigar, Soldier, Ajnabee and Race.
recurring_themes: The obsessive antagonist, the deceived spouse, and the thriller plotted as a series of reveals.
creative_style: Glossy, tightly plotted suspense with a strong visual signature and a preference for casting stars against type.
historical_importance: Among the most commercially successful thriller directors of 1990s and 2000s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Daraar (1996), in which Kapoor plays the obsessive, violent husband from whom Juhi Chawla's character flees — one of the few outright menacing roles of his leading career and a deliberate use of his accumulated romantic goodwill against the audience's expectations. It is also among his last films as a lead.
biography: Abbas–Mustan directed one Rishi Kapoor film, and it is among the sharpest uses anyone made of his image. The Burmawalla brothers, working together since 1985, built a career on glossy thrillers in which a familiar star turns out to be the threat — Baazigar being the best-known case. In Daraar (1996) they cast Kapoor as a husband whose jealousy becomes violent and from whom his wife escapes, inverting twenty years of accumulated romantic sympathy. The film came at the very end of his run as a lead, and the role anticipates the late character work — the villain of Agneepath, the crime boss of D-Day — that would eventually re-establish him. Their other films with him do not exist: one credit, one performance, and a durable one.

name: Abdol Samee Siddiqui
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Halla Bol (2008).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rajkumar Santoshi's Halla Bol (2008), a drama about a film star who becomes a witness to a murder, in which Kapoor appears in support during the early years of his character-actor phase.
biography: Abdol Samee Siddiqui is credited as a producer on Halla Bol (2008) and has no documented biography. The film, directed by Rajkumar Santoshi, who had made Damini with Kapoor fifteen years earlier, is a drama about celebrity and moral courage in which Kapoor took a supporting part. The credit falls in the period just after Hum Tum and Fanaa, when Kapoor was taking whatever supporting work was offered and before the Dharma and Yash Raj films consolidated his second career. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Abhay Kanwar
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The article on the film's director, Raj Kanwar, names Abhay Raj Kanwar as one of his two sons, which is almost certainly this writer — the credit is on his father's film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sadiyaan (2010).
recurring_themes: Partition romance and family separation.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sadiyaan (2010), directed by his father Raj Kanwar — the director of Deewana (1992), the film in which Kapoor's leading career effectively ended. Eighteen years later the same director, now with his son writing, cast Kapoor in a supporting role in a partition-era romance.
biography: Abhay Kanwar wrote Sadiyaan (2010) for its director, who was by all appearances his father: Raj Kanwar's own article names Abhay Raj Kanwar among his children, and the credit sits on Raj Kanwar's film. The connection matters only as a detail of how this filmography works — Raj Kanwar had directed Deewana in 1992, the film in which Kapoor handed the romantic lead to Shah Rukh Khan, and he returned to Kapoor eighteen years later for a partition romance in which the ageing actor plays a supporting part, now from his son's script. Nothing else about the writer is documented, and this row rests on the film's credits.

name: Abhinav Kashyap
career_background: Abhinav Singh Kashyap (born 6 September 1974 in Obra, Uttar Pradesh) is an Indian actor, director and screenwriter who directed and co-wrote Dabangg (2010). He is a brother of the director Anurag Kashyap.
debut: Working from 1995; directorial debut Dabangg (2010).
major_works: With Kapoor: Besharam (2013). Elsewhere, Dabangg.
recurring_themes: The irreverent action comedy built around a star's swagger.
creative_style: Broad commercial comedy with an ironic edge, pitched at a mass audience.
historical_importance: The director of Dabangg, one of the biggest commercial successes of 2010s Hindi cinema and the start of a franchise.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and an unusual one: Besharam (2013), his follow-up to Dabangg, is the only film in which Rishi Kapoor, his wife Neetu Singh and their son Ranbir Kapoor all appear — the parents as a pair of police officers, the son as the title character. The film failed commercially, which makes its family curiosity its main claim on this filmography.
biography: Abhinav Kashyap directed the only film in which three generations of this Kapoor household appear together. After Dabangg (2010), which he directed and co-wrote and which became one of the decade's biggest hits, Kashyap made Besharam in 2013 with Ranbir Kapoor as a cheerful car thief and both of Ranbir's parents — Rishi Kapoor and Neetu Singh — as police officers pursuing him. It was a critical and commercial disappointment, and Kashyap's career did not recover its earlier momentum. For this filmography the film matters less as work than as a family document: Kapoor had acted opposite Neetu Singh in a dozen films in the 1970s, and this is the one where they share the screen with their son.

name: Abhishek Chaubey
career_background: Abhishek Chaubey, from Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh and educated at Hindu College, Delhi, is an Indian director, screenwriter and film producer working in Hindi cinema. His own films have won awards including a Critics Award for Best Film at the 65th Filmfare Awards.
debut: Working from 2002, initially as an assistant to Vishal Bhardwaj.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sharmaji Namkeen (2022). Elsewhere, Ishqiya, Udta Punjab and Sonchiriya as director.
recurring_themes: Regional milieu rendered precisely; moral ambiguity; the small town and its codes.
creative_style: A director of texture and dialect who also produces work by others in a similar register.
major_awards: Critics Award for Best Film at the 65th Filmfare Awards.
historical_importance: One of the most critically regarded Hindi directors of his generation.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, as a producer of Sharmaji Namkeen (2022) — the film Kapoor was shooting when he died in April 2020, completed with Paresh Rawal playing the remaining scenes as the same character and released posthumously. It is the last entry in this filmography.
biography: Abhishek Chaubey is credited as a producer on Rishi Kapoor's last film. A director from Ayodhya who came up as Vishal Bhardwaj's assistant and made Ishqiya, Udta Punjab and Sonchiriya — work that earned him a Critics Award for Best Film at the 65th Filmfare Awards — Chaubey also produces, and Sharmaji Namkeen was among those projects. Kapoor plays a retired man who discovers a talent for cooking and joins a women's kitchen party circuit; he had shot roughly half the film when he died in April 2020. Excel Entertainment completed it by having Paresh Rawal perform the remaining scenes as the same character, an arrangement without real precedent in Hindi cinema, and released it in 2022.

name: Abhishek-Ishteyak
career_background: A composing pair credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article under this name.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chintu Ji (2009).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chintu Ji (2009), the comedy in which Kapoor plays a fictionalised version of himself — a star called Chintu Ji, his own lifelong nickname — returning to the village of his birth. They share the soundtrack with Sukhwinder Singh.
biography: Abhishek-Ishteyak composed songs for Chintu Ji (2009) alongside Sukhwinder Singh, and nothing about the pair is documented. The film is one of the most self-referential in the filmography: Kapoor plays a film star named Chintu Ji, which was his own nickname from childhood and the name the industry used for him, who returns to the village where he was born and is received as a celebrity. It belongs to the brief period after Hum Tum when Kapoor was experimenting with roles built directly on his own public persona. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ajay Devgn
career_background: Vishal Virender Devgan (born 2 April 1969), known as Ajay Devgn, is an Indian actor, director and producer who has appeared in over 100 Hindi films. He has won four National Film Awards and four Filmfare Awards and received the Padma Shri in 2016. He made his debut with Phool Aur Kaante (1991) and founded the production house Ajay Devgn FFilms.
debut: Acting debut Phool Aur Kaante (1991); his production company's first film was Raju Chacha (2000).
major_works: With Kapoor: Raju Chacha (2000). Elsewhere, Zakhm, The Legend of Bhagat Singh, Singham and Drishyam.
recurring_themes: As a producer, star-driven vehicles for himself; as an actor, intensity and understatement.
creative_style: A star-producer whose company exists primarily to make his own films.
major_awards: Four National Film Awards, including Best Actor for Zakhm and for The Legend of Bhagat Singh, four Filmfare Awards, and the Padma Shri in 2016.
historical_importance: One of the most durable leading men of post-1991 Hindi cinema and a significant star-producer.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Raju Chacha (2000), which Devgn produced as the first release of his own company and starred in, with Kapoor in support. The film was an expensive failure. It belongs to the thin stretch between Kapoor's last leads and his 2004 reinvention, when his work consisted largely of supporting roles in other stars' vehicles.
biography: Ajay Devgn produced one film in this filmography, and it marks the low point between Rishi Kapoor's two careers. Devgn, who debuted in 1991 and became one of the most durable leading men of his generation with four National Film Awards and a Padma Shri, launched his own production company with Raju Chacha in 2000, a lavish children's fantasy he also starred in; it failed expensively. Kapoor appears in support, at a point when he was no longer being cast as a lead and had not yet been rediscovered as a character actor — the four-year gap that Hum Tum would close in 2004. The credit is a reminder that his reinvention was not continuous with his stardom but followed a genuine interval of diminished work.

name: Ajay–Atul
career_background: An Indian composing duo of the brothers Ajay Ashok Gogavale and Atul Ashok Gogavale, from Pune, working predominantly in Marathi and Hindi films. They have won a National Film Award, four Filmfare Marathi Awards, three Maharashtra State Film Awards, twelve Mirchi Music Awards and two Zee Cine Awards, and appeared in the Forbes India Celebrity 100 list.
debut: Composing from 2000, first in Marathi cinema.
major_works: With Kapoor: Agneepath (2012). Elsewhere, Sairat, Dhadak, Natarang and Jodhaa Akbar's Marathi counterparts.
recurring_themes: Live orchestral recording, folk and devotional Marathi forms, and the large emotional set piece.
creative_style: Their article notes that almost all their songs and albums are recorded with live instruments — Agneepath among the most notable — which distinguishes them from the programmed production standard of the period.
major_awards: A National Film Award and four Filmfare Marathi Awards among many others.
historical_importance: The leading composers of modern Marathi cinema and among the few to bring full live orchestration back into mainstream Hindi film music.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a significant one: Agneepath (2012), in which Kapoor plays Rauf Lala, the flesh-trading antagonist, in a performance widely counted among the best of his career. Their article names Agneepath as one of the most notable examples of their live-instrument recording.
biography: Ajay–Atul scored Agneepath, the film that gave Rishi Kapoor his most admired villain. The Gogavale brothers, from Pune, became the defining composers of modern Marathi cinema — Natarang, Sairat — and brought an unusual commitment to live orchestral recording into Hindi film music; their own article cites Agneepath as a prime example. In Karan Johar's 2012 remake Kapoor plays Rauf Lala, a trafficker in women whose geniality makes him more frightening, physically transformed and speaking in a register he had never used in forty years of romantic leads. The score's weight and scale are part of what the performance works against. It is the single clearest piece of evidence that his late-career range was not limited to benign fathers.

name: Ajit Andhare
career_background: Ajit Andhare (born 11 July 1973) is an Indian businessman and the chief operating officer of Viacom18 Studios. He holds a Bachelor of Technology from NIT Rourkela and an MBA from the Indian School of Business.
debut: A studio executive rather than a creative producer; his credits come through Viacom18.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018). Elsewhere, the Viacom18 Studios slate.
recurring_themes: Content-driven films produced within a corporate studio structure.
creative_style: A studio executive's production practice: commissioning and backing directors rather than developing material himself.
historical_importance: A senior figure in one of the first corporate film studios in India.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Nandita Das's Manto (2018), in which Kapoor has a small role in a biographical film about the Urdu writer Saadat Hasan Manto — a festival-facing production quite unlike anything in his lead career, and evidence of the range of work open to him at the end.
biography: Ajit Andhare produced Manto (2018) in his capacity as chief operating officer of Viacom18 Studios. An engineer and business graduate rather than a filmmaker, Andhare belongs to the corporate studio layer that entered Indian cinema in the late 2000s, commissioning work rather than developing it. Manto, directed by Nandita Das, is a biographical film about the Urdu short-story writer Saadat Hasan Manto and his obscenity trials, and Kapoor appears in it briefly. For this filmography the credit is useful mainly as a marker: the actor who spent the 1970s singing in Nasir Hussain musicals ended up, forty years later, taking small parts in literary biopics financed by television conglomerates.

name: Ajit Singh
career_background: A composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own; the bare name resolves to a disambiguation page of politicians and sportsmen.
major_works: With Kapoor: Akarshan (1988).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Akarshan (1988), one of the least documented entries in the filmography, from the stretch in which Kapoor was appearing in three or four films a year with little critical notice.
biography: Ajit Singh composed the songs for Akarshan (1988) and has no documented biography; his name on Wikipedia leads only to a disambiguation page of politicians, rulers and athletes. The film is among the most obscure in this filmography, made in the year Kapoor released several pictures that left almost no critical trace. The row exists because the workbook records every credited collaborator, and it is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Akhtar Farooqui
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Karz (1980).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented, though his one credit is on a film of lasting influence.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a consequential one: he co-produced Subhash Ghai's Karz (1980) with Jagjit Khurana. Kapoor's performance as Monty, the singer recovering the memory of his murdered previous life, is among the most durable of his career, and the film's Laxmikant–Pyarelal soundtrack has been remade and sampled for four decades.
biography: Akhtar Farooqui co-produced Karz (1980), one of the two or three films on which Rishi Kapoor's reputation rests, and nothing about him is documented. Subhash Ghai's reincarnation thriller gave Kapoor the role of Monty, a stage singer haunted by the murder of his earlier self, and produced in 'Om Shanti Om' and 'Dard-e-Dil' songs that have outlived most of the decade's cinema; the film was remade outright in 2008 and its structure borrowed repeatedly. That the producer who financed it left no biographical record at all is among the sharper illustrations in this workbook of how unevenly the Hindi industry of the period is documented. This row rests on the film's credits.

name: Akhtar ul Iman
career_background: Akhtar ul Iman (12 November 1915 – 9 March 1996) was a noted Urdu poet and screenwriter who had a major influence on modern Urdu nazm. He studied at Zakir Husain Delhi College and Aligarh Muslim University, and worked as a freelance and B. R. Films cine writer between 1960 and 1980. He won the Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue twice, for Dharmputra (1963) and Waqt (1966), and the Sahitya Akademi Award in Urdu in 1962 for his poetry collection Yadein.
debut: Writing for films from the 1940s; his award-winning dialogue work came in the 1960s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Vijay (1988). Elsewhere, Dharmputra, Waqt, Gumrah and Daag.
recurring_themes: Partition, displacement and moral compromise; the family divided by history.
creative_style: A major poet writing film dialogue, bringing a compressed literary Urdu to commercial melodrama.
major_awards: Two Filmfare Awards for Best Dialogue (Dharmputra, Waqt) and the 1962 Sahitya Akademi Award in Urdu for Yadein.
historical_importance: One of the central figures of modern Urdu poetry and, simultaneously, one of Hindi cinema's most distinguished dialogue writers.
relationship_with_actor: One film, late in his own career: Yash Chopra's Vijay (1988), an ensemble in which Kapoor appeared alongside Anil Kapoor and Rishi's own generation of co-stars. It is a modest end to a distinguished writing life, and the only point of contact between a Sahitya Akademi laureate and this filmography.
biography: Akhtar ul Iman, one of the most important Urdu poets of the twentieth century, wrote one film in this filmography. A Sahitya Akademi laureate for his collection Yadein and a central figure in the modernisation of the Urdu nazm, he spent two decades as a cine writer, much of it attached to B. R. Films, and won the Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue twice, for Dharmputra and Waqt — films about partition and family division that are among Hindi cinema's most serious. His single Kapoor credit is Yash Chopra's Vijay (1988), a late, crowded family melodrama in which Kapoor was one of several leads. The juxtaposition is instructive: the literary prestige of Hindi cinema's 1960s reached this filmography only once, and at the end of the writer's life.

name: Aleem Masrur
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tawaif (1985).
recurring_themes: The courtesan film and the respectable household that takes her in.
creative_style: Not documented; he is credited alongside Rahi Masoom Raza, Satish Bhatnagar and C. J. Pavri.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: B. R. Chopra's Tawaif (1985), for which Rahi Masoom Raza won his second Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue, and in which Kapoor plays a man who gives shelter to a courtesan and comes to love her — one of the few roles of his middle period that treats love as moral complication rather than courtship.
biography: Aleem Masrur is one of four writers credited on Tawaif (1985) and has no documented biography. The film is among the most substantial of Kapoor's middle period: B. R. Chopra's story of a courtesan taken into a respectable home, written chiefly by Rahi Masoom Raza, who won his second Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue for it. Kapoor plays the man who shelters her and falls in love, a part that asks for restraint rather than ardour. Collective writing credits of this kind are normal in the period, and in most cases — this one included — only the best-known name on the list has left any record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Allchemy Productions
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: All Is Well (2015).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on All Is Well (2015), Umesh Shukla's family road comedy in which Kapoor plays the father opposite Supriya Pathak as his wife, with Abhishek Bachchan as their son. The film was a T-Series production and a commercial failure.
biography: Allchemy Productions appears once in this filmography, on All Is Well (2015), and has no recorded history. The film, directed by Umesh Shukla between Oh My God and 102 Not Out, put Kapoor and Supriya Pathak on a road trip with their estranged son, played by Abhishek Bachchan, and failed both critically and commercially. It belongs to the late run of ensemble comedies — Housefull 2, Chashme Buddoor, Besharam — in which Kapoor was one familiar face among several and the films themselves added little to his reputation. Shukla would use him far better three years later in 102 Not Out. This row is built from the film's credits.

name: Aly Morani
career_background: Aly Morani is an Indian film producer whose credits include Dum, Raja Hindustani, Damini, Arjun and Dushmani: A Violent Love Story. With his brother Karim Morani he owns Cineyug, a production and event company.
debut: Producing from the late 1980s; Damini (1993) is among his best-known films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Damini (1993). Elsewhere, Raja Hindustani and Arjun.
recurring_themes: Mainstream melodrama and the star vehicle, produced alongside a live-events business.
creative_style: A commercial producer working with established directors rather than developing material himself.
historical_importance: Co-owner of Cineyug, one of India's significant film and live-event companies.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rajkumar Santoshi's Damini (1993), a blockbuster in which Kapoor plays the husband of a woman who witnesses a rape in his family's house and is disbelieved.
