The film is among the most critically substantial of his later career precisely because he is not its moral centre — Meenakshi Seshadri and Sunny Deol carry it, and his character's weakness is the point.
biography: Aly Morani produced Damini (1993), the most critically substantial hit of Rishi Kapoor's later career. With his brother Karim Morani he owns Cineyug, a production and live-events company, and his credits include Raja Hindustani and Arjun. Damini, directed by Rajkumar Santoshi, is built around a young wife who sees a servant raped by her brother-in-law and is systematically disbelieved; Kapoor plays her husband, a man whose loyalty to his family makes him complicit, and the film gives its moral authority to Meenakshi Seshadri's character and Sunny Deol's alcoholic lawyer. It won Santoshi his second consecutive Filmfare Award for Best Director. For Kapoor it was an early demonstration that he could be used against his own likeability.

name: Aman Jeffery
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001).
recurring_themes: Family comedy.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rahul Rawail's Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), a comedy in which Kapoor plays the father of twins separated by their parents' divorce, from the quiet stretch before his 2004 reinvention.
biography: Aman Jeffery is credited as a writer on Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001) and has no documented biography. The film, directed by Rahul Rawail — whose own directorial debut twenty-one years earlier had also starred Kapoor — is a remake-style family comedy of separated twins, made in the four-year gap between Kapoor's last leading roles and the Yash Raj supporting parts that restarted his career. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Amar-Utpal
career_background: A composing pair credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article under this name.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Ki Izzat (1994).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ghar Ki Izzat (1994), the last of Kalpataru's five family melodramas with Kapoor, written with Kader Khan and Keshav Rathod.
biography: Amar-Utpal composed the songs for Ghar Ki Izzat (1994) and are otherwise undocumented. The film closes the run of five household melodramas Kalpataru directed with Kapoor between 1988 and 1994 — pictures named for the family rather than the romance, written largely by Kader Khan, and reviewed almost nowhere. The composers of the last of them left no record at all, which is characteristic of this tier of production. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Amarlal Chabria
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ginny Aur Johnny (1976).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ginny Aur Johnny (1976), a Rajesh Roshan-scored film from the three years immediately after Bobby, when Kapoor was cast in as many youth romances as producers could finance.
biography: Amarlal Chabria produced Ginny Aur Johnny (1976) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the rush of small romances that followed Bobby, when a twenty-three-year-old Kapoor was the most bankable young lover in Hindi cinema and the market absorbed whatever he appeared in; its score was by Rajesh Roshan, at the start of his own career. Nothing further about the producer survives, and this row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Amartya Rahut
career_background: A composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aurangzeb (2013).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Aurangzeb (2013), a Yash Raj Films crime drama in which Kapoor plays a police officer, one of several late supporting roles for the banner that had employed him since 1976.
biography: Amartya Rahut is credited among the composers of Aurangzeb (2013) and has no documented biography. The film, a Yash Raj crime drama about twins on opposite sides of the law, gave Kapoor a supporting role as a policeman; it is one of six YRF films from his character-actor phase and one of the least remembered. As with most of the 2010s entries in this filmography, the soundtrack was divided among several composers, and only some of them have left any record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Amin Surani
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chalk N Duster (2016).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chalk N Duster (2016), a drama about schoolteachers resisting a commercialising management, in which Kapoor appears in support — one of the small, issue-minded films he took in his last years alongside the studio comedies.
biography: Amin Surani produced Chalk N Duster (2016) and has no documented biography. The film is a modest drama about two schoolteachers and the commercial pressures on their school, with an ensemble of veteran performers including Shabana Azmi and Juhi Chawla, and Kapoor in a supporting part. It belongs to the late pattern in which his name helped finance small socially minded pictures rather than carrying them. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Amjad Nadeem–Aamir
career_background: A composing group credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article under this name. The credit appears as Amjad Nadeem-Aamir, which this workbook renders with an en dash in line with its treatment of composing duos and trios.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), one of six composers or groups credited on a single soundtrack, in a farce released months before Kapoor's death.
biography: Amjad Nadeem–Aamir are credited among the composers of Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019) and are otherwise undocumented. The film's soundtrack carries six separate composing credits — Yo Yo Honey Singh, this group, Sanjeev–Ajay, Rahul Jain and two others — which is an extreme case of the fragmentation that characterises Hindi film music in Kapoor's final decade, and the exact opposite of the single-composer scores of his youth, when Laxmikant–Pyarelal wrote every song in thirty-two of his films. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Anand Sharma
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own; the bare name resolves to an unrelated Indian politician.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011), which Hema Malini directed, produced and co-wrote, and in which Kapoor appears in support alongside a large cast of veterans.
biography: Anand Sharma is credited as a writer on Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011) and has no documented biography; an earlier pass of this research attached to his name the article of an unrelated politician. The film was Hema Malini's third as director, a search-for-identity drama starring her daughter Esha Deol, with Kapoor among a cast of established actors taking small parts. It failed commercially and is among the least discussed films of his late period. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Anil Devgan
career_background: Anil Devgan (25 May 1969 – 5 October 2020) was an Indian filmmaker and screenwriter, the son of Prem Prakash Devgan and a first cousin of the actor Ajay Devgn. He directed Raju Chacha and Blackmail, and died of cardiac arrest at the age of 51.
debut: Working from 1996; his directorial debut was Raju Chacha (2000).
major_works: With Kapoor: Raju Chacha (2000). Elsewhere, Blackmail.
recurring_themes: Family fantasy and the star-led action drama.
creative_style: Not extensively documented; both of his features were vehicles for his cousin Ajay Devgn.
historical_importance: Not substantially documented beyond his two features.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Raju Chacha (2000), his directorial debut, produced by and starring his cousin Ajay Devgn, with Kapoor in support. The film was an expensive failure, and it falls in the four-year gap between Kapoor's last leads and his reinvention in Hum Tum.
biography: Anil Devgan directed one film in this filmography, and it is a marker of Rishi Kapoor's lowest professional point. A cousin of Ajay Devgn and the son of Prem Prakash Devgan, he made his debut with Raju Chacha in 2000 — a lavish children's fantasy that his cousin produced and starred in and that lost a great deal of money. Kapoor appears in support, during the interval when he was no longer cast as a lead and had not yet been rediscovered as a character actor. Anil Devgan directed only one further feature, Blackmail, and died of cardiac arrest in October 2020, five months after Kapoor.

name: Anil Ganguly
career_background: Anil Ganguly (26 January 1933 – 15 January 2016) was an Indian film director and screenwriter who worked in Hindi cinema from the 1970s to 2001. He is best known for Kora Kagaz (1974), starring Jaya Bhaduri, and Tapasya (1975), starring Raakhee, both of which won the National Film Award for Best Popular Film Providing Wholesome Entertainment, and for a series of further films with Raakhee including Trishna, Aanchal and Saaheb. He also adapted Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay's Parineeta as Sankoch (1976). His daughter is the actress Rupali Ganguly.
debut: Working from 1962; his breakthrough was Kora Kagaz (1974).
major_works: With Kapoor: Pyar Ke Kabil (1987). Elsewhere, Kora Kagaz, Tapasya, Sankoch and Saaheb.
recurring_themes: The woman's film: sacrifice, estrangement and endurance, usually with the heroine at the centre.
creative_style: Restrained melodrama built around a female lead, with literary adaptation a recurring interest.
major_awards: Two of his films won the National Film Award for Best Popular Film; their leads Jaya Bhaduri and Raakhee won Filmfare Best Actress awards for them.
historical_importance: A significant director of the 1970s woman-centred melodrama, a strand that ran parallel to the masala cinema of the same years.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and late in both careers: Pyar Ke Kabil (1987), a Bappi Lahiri-scored romance from Kapoor's weakest commercial decade. Ganguly's reputation rests on films built around actresses — Kora Kagaz, Tapasya — which makes this single, modest collaboration with a male romantic star an outlier in his filmography rather than a natural fit.
biography: Anil Ganguly directed one Rishi Kapoor film, and the pairing is instructive mainly by contrast. Ganguly's standing came from the woman-centred melodrama: Kora Kagaz with Jaya Bhaduri and Tapasya with Raakhee both won the National Film Award for Best Popular Film and brought their leads Filmfare Best Actress awards, and he made several further films with Raakhee. His cinema was organised around a heroine's endurance rather than a hero's courtship. Pyar Ke Kabil (1987), his one film with Kapoor, is a modest romance with a Bappi Lahiri score from the middle of the actor's thinnest decade. Ganguly worked until 2001 and died in January 2016; his daughter is the actress Rupali Ganguly.

name: Anil Nagrath
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Anmol (1993).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; he is credited alongside Prayag Raj and Honey Irani.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Anmol (1993), produced by Manmohan Desai and directed by his son Ketan Desai under the MKD Films Combine banner — a late attempt at the family's masala formula, with Kapoor opposite Manisha Koirala.
biography: Anil Nagrath is one of four writers credited on Anmol (1993) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the Desai family's long afterlife in Hindi cinema: produced by Manmohan Desai, directed by his son Ketan Desai, written in part by Prayag Raj and Honey Irani, and assembled from the elements of Amar Akbar Anthony and Naseeb for a market that had moved on. Kapoor plays opposite Manisha Koirala in one of his last leads. As with most collective writing credits of the period, only the better-known names on the list have left a record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Anil V. Kumar
career_background: Anil V. Kumar (born 4 June 1975) is an Indian television and film director and producer. He directed the Star Plus serials Kahaani Ghar Ghar Kii and Kahin To Hoga, and in 2010 founded the production house Flying Turtle Films with Shabbir Ahluwalia and Sakett Saawhney, which co-produced Zanjeer in 2013.
debut: Directing for television before film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kucch To Hai (2003). Elsewhere, the Balaji television serials and Zanjeer as co-producer.
recurring_themes: Television serial drama and its transfer to film.
creative_style: A television director working in the Balaji Telefilms idiom, with occasional film work.
historical_importance: Representative of the traffic between Indian television and film in the 2000s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kucch To Hai (2003), a Balaji Motion Pictures horror-slasher in which Kapoor appears in support. The credit is shared — Anurag Basu's article names the same film as his own directorial debut, so this workbook records both men as directors, which the film's credits support.
biography: Anil V. Kumar is one of two directors credited on Kucch To Hai (2003). A television director who made Kahaani Ghar Ghar Kii and Kahin To Hoga for Star Plus and later founded Flying Turtle Films, he belongs to the Balaji Telefilms world that moved into cinema in the early 2000s under Ekta Kapoor. Kucch To Hai, a horror-slasher produced by Balaji Motion Pictures, carries his name alongside Anurag Basu's, whose own article calls the film his directorial debut; both credits stand in this workbook. For Rishi Kapoor the film is one of several supporting parts from the interval before Hum Tum restored him to mainstream work.

name: Anjana Rawail
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own. She shares a surname with the film's director H. S. Rawail and with his son Rahul Rawail, who is also credited on it; two other women named Rawail — Ruhi and Rita — hold credits on later films in this workbook, so the name recurs across the family's productions, though the exact relationships are not documented here.
major_works: With Kapoor: Laila Majnu (1976).
recurring_themes: The classical tragic romance.
creative_style: Not documented; she is credited with Abrar Alvi and H. S. Rawail.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a notable one: H. S. Rawail's Laila Majnu (1976), in which Kapoor played Qais opposite Ranjeeta Kaur in the classical Arabic love legend — the first film to ask him for tragic rather than teenage love. She shares the writing credit with Abrar Alvi, the writer of Pyaasa.
biography: Anjana Rawail is credited as a writer on Laila Majnu (1976) and has no documented biography. The film is one of the more significant of Kapoor's early career: H. S. Rawail's version of the Qais and Laila legend, in which love destroys rather than rewards, and the first serious departure from the Bobby persona. She shares the credit with Abrar Alvi and with the director himself, and her surname places her inside the Rawail family that accounts for several credits in this workbook — H. S. Rawail directing, Rahul Rawail directing and writing, and Ruhi and Rita Rawail credited on later films. The relationships are not documented in the sources consulted here.

name: Ankit Tiwari
career_background: Ankit Tiwari, from Kanpur, is an Indian playback singer, composer and music director. He began with jingles and television background music after meeting Pradeep Sarkar, and was then offered Do Dooni Chaar (2010) and Saheb, Biwi Aur Gangster (2011), the latter beginning his career as a singer.
debut: Composing for film with Do Dooni Chaar (2010).
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Dooni Chaar (2010). Elsewhere, 'Galliyan' from Ek Villain, for which he won the Filmfare Award for Best Male Playback Singer.
recurring_themes: The romantic ballad sung by its own composer.
creative_style: A singer-composer whose voice is the identifying feature of his work.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Male Playback Singer for 'Galliyan' from Ek Villain, with further Filmfare nominations as composer and singer.
historical_importance: One of the composer-singers who emerged in the 2010s when soundtracks were commissioned song by song.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is the one that mattered most to Kapoor's late career: Do Dooni Chaar (2010) was Tiwari's first film as composer, and the film in which Kapoor and Neetu Singh played a Delhi schoolteacher and his wife — the performance that won Kapoor the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor and established him as a character actor.
biography: Ankit Tiwari's first film as a composer was also the film that remade Rishi Kapoor's career. A singer and composer from Kanpur who came into films through jingles and television work, Tiwari was offered Do Dooni Chaar in 2010 — a small, closely observed comedy about a Delhi mathematics teacher, his wife and their ambition to own a car. Kapoor played the teacher opposite Neetu Singh, his wife and his co-star from a dozen 1970s films, and won the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor; the film is routinely treated as the start of his second career. Tiwari went on to win a Filmfare Award for singing 'Galliyan' from Ek Villain. Both men's reputations turn, in part, on the same small film.

name: Anubhav Sinha
career_background: Anubhav Sinha (born 22 June 1965 in Allahabad) is an Indian director, producer and writer in Hindi cinema. After commercial films including Tum Bin (2001), Dus (2005) and Ra.One (2011) he turned to a series of socio-political films — Mulk (2018), Article 15 (2019), Thappad (2020), Anek (2022) and Bheed (2023) — and made the Netflix series IC 814: The Kandahar Hijack (2024).
debut: Working from 1993; Tum Bin (2001) was his breakthrough.
major_works: With Kapoor: Mulk (2018). Elsewhere, Tum Bin, Ra.One, Article 15 and Thappad.
recurring_themes: Citizenship, prejudice and the law; the family forced to argue its own legitimacy in public.
creative_style: Argument-driven social cinema with courtroom and confrontation structures, made in a realist register after 2018.
historical_importance: One of the principal makers of politically engaged mainstream Hindi cinema in the late 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and one of the best things Kapoor did: Mulk (2018), in which he plays Murad Ali Mohammed, the head of a Muslim family in Varanasi whose nephew commits a terrorist act and whose household is then forced to prove its loyalty in court. The role gave him a weight nothing in his lead career had asked for, and it came two years before his death.
biography: Anubhav Sinha directed the film that gave Rishi Kapoor his most serious late role. Sinha spent the 2000s in commercial cinema — Tum Bin, Dus, Ra.One — before turning in 2018 to a run of socio-political films that made his reputation: Mulk, Article 15, Thappad, Anek, Bheed. In Mulk, Kapoor plays Murad Ali Mohammed, a Varanasi lawyer's elder brother whose family is publicly suspected after his nephew joins a terrorist attack, and who must watch his own belonging be litigated. It is a performance of restraint from an actor whose fame rested on charm, and it came in the last two years of his life. Sinha later made the Netflix series IC 814: The Kandahar Hijack.

name: Anuj Sharma
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), a farce co-produced with Deepak Mukut and released months before Kapoor's death — one of his last appearances and among the least regarded films in the filmography.
biography: Anuj Sharma co-produced Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019) and has no documented biography. The film is a broad comedy of deception in which the surviving account of Kapoor's character is internally inconsistent — the article describes him in consecutive sentences as a Punjabi farmer and as a retired police inspector — and it was one of his final releases. It came from the same producer group as Mulk the year before, which gives a fair picture of the range an independent banner offered him at the end: one film of substance, one that simply paid. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Anuraag Parparna
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kucch To Hai (2003).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kucch To Hai (2003), the Balaji Motion Pictures horror-slasher credited to two directors, Anurag Basu and Anil V. Kumar, with Kapoor in support.
biography: Anuraag Parparna is credited as a writer on Kucch To Hai (2003) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to Balaji Telefilms' early move into cinema and is the directorial debut Anurag Basu's own article claims, though Anil V. Kumar is credited alongside him; Kapoor appears in a supporting role during the quiet years before Hum Tum. Little about the production is documented beyond its credits, and this row rests on them alone.

name: Anurag Basu
career_background: Anurag Basu (born 8 May 1970 in Bhilai) is an Indian director, screenwriter, cinematographer, producer and actor. After initial setbacks his breakthrough was Murder (2004), followed by Gangster: A Love Story (2006) and the ensemble urban drama Life in a... Metro (2007), which won him the Filmfare Award for Best Screenplay and a nomination for Best Director. He received two further Best Director nominations, including for Barfi! (2012).
debut: His article names the Balaji Motion Pictures horror film Kucch To Hai (2003) as his directorial debut.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kucch To Hai (2003). Elsewhere, Murder, Gangster, Life in a... Metro, Barfi! and Jagga Jasoos.
recurring_themes: The city as a web of intersecting lives; romance complicated by class and circumstance; the outsider protagonist.
creative_style: An ensemble storyteller with a strong visual and musical sense, frequently writing his own screenplays.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Screenplay for Life in a... Metro, with three Filmfare nominations for Best Director.
historical_importance: One of the defining directors of 2000s urban Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kucch To Hai (2003), which his article calls his directorial debut and which this workbook credits to him alongside Anil V. Kumar. Kapoor appears in support. The connection has a coda outside this filmography — Basu later directed Barfi! and Jagga Jasoos with Ranbir Kapoor, the actor's son.
biography: Anurag Basu's directorial debut, by his own article's account, was a film in which Rishi Kapoor took a supporting part. Kucch To Hai (2003) was a Balaji Motion Pictures horror-slasher, credited to Basu and Anil V. Kumar, made before the run of films that established him — Murder, Gangster, and Life in a... Metro, which won him the Filmfare Award for Best Screenplay and the first of three Best Director nominations. Kapoor was then between careers, taking whatever supporting work was available. Basu went on to direct Kapoor's son Ranbir twice, in Barfi! and Jagga Jasoos, so the association continued into the next generation even though he never worked with the father again.

name: Anurag Saikia
career_background: Anurag Saikia (born December 1988) is an Indian film score composer, music director, producer and instrumentalist from Moran in Assam. He is one of the youngest recipients of the Rajat Kamal for Best Non-Feature Film Music Direction, for Yugadrashta. His mother Dipali Saikia is an All India Radio artist and teacher and his father Dr. Anil Saikia an academician.
debut: Composing for Assamese and Hindi films from the 2010s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Mulk (2018). Elsewhere, Yugadrashta and Assamese film and independent work.
recurring_themes: Regional and devotional material in a restrained score; music that supports argument rather than spectacle.
creative_style: A score-first composer working across Assamese and Hindi cinema, trained in classical and folk forms.
major_awards: Rajat Kamal (National Film Award) for Best Non-Feature Film Music Direction for Yugadrashta.
historical_importance: One of the few composers from the Assamese industry to work regularly in mainstream Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Anubhav Sinha's Mulk (2018), in which Kapoor plays the head of a Muslim family in Varanasi defending its loyalty in court. The film's music is deliberately sparse, which suits a picture built on argument — a register that appears almost nowhere else in a filmography otherwise dominated by song.
biography: Anurag Saikia scored Mulk (2018), the film that gave Rishi Kapoor his most substantial late role. Born in Moran in Assam in 1988 to an All India Radio artist and an academician, Saikia is among the youngest winners of the Rajat Kamal for non-feature music direction and works across Assamese and Hindi cinema. Mulk, Anubhav Sinha's drama about a Varanasi Muslim family forced to prove its loyalty after a nephew's terrorist act, asks for restraint rather than melody, and Kapoor's performance as Murad Ali Mohammed depends on that quiet. In a filmography where thirty-two films were scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal and the songs usually carried the picture, a film in which the music stays out of the way is itself notable.

name: Anvita Dutt Guptan
career_background: Anvita Dutt (born 20 February 1972 in New Delhi), credited on this film as Anvita Dutt Guptan, is an Indian dialogue, screenplay and story writer, lyricist and director of Hindi films.
debut: Writing for films from 2005, initially as a lyricist and dialogue writer.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patiala House (2011), on which she is credited as both writer and lyricist. Elsewhere, her lyrics for a long run of 2000s Hindi films and her later work as a director.
recurring_themes: The woman's interior life; family authority questioned from within.
creative_style: A lyricist-writer with an ear for colloquial dialogue, later a director in her own right.
historical_importance: One of the few women writing dialogue and lyrics across mainstream 2000s Hindi cinema, and later a notable director.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Nikkhil Advani's Patiala House (2011), for which she wrote and also supplied the lyrics. Kapoor plays the Southall patriarch whose bitterness after a racist attack leads him to forbid his son's cricket career — a role built on paternal authority, which is exactly the structure her writing tends to question.
biography: Anvita Dutt wrote and supplied the lyrics for Patiala House (2011), one of the stronger films of Rishi Kapoor's late career. Born in New Delhi in 1972, she worked through the 2000s as a lyricist and dialogue writer on a long list of mainstream Hindi films before becoming a director herself. In Patiala House she wrote the role of Gurtej Singh Kahlon, the London Punjabi father whose experience of racist violence hardens into control over his son's life — the part gave Kapoor something colder than the benign patriarchs he was usually offered, and reunited him on screen with Dimple Kapadia for the fourth time since Bobby. She is one of very few women credited as writers anywhere in this workbook.

name: Anwar Khan
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography. He has no Wikipedia article of his own: the bare name leads to a disambiguation page listing cricketers, politicians and others, none of them this writer.
major_works: With Kapoor: Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal-scored film from the densest and least documented stretch of the filmography, when Kapoor was releasing three or four pictures a year to almost no critical attention.
biography: Anwar Khan is credited as a writer on Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990) and has no documented biography; his name on Wikipedia resolves only to a disambiguation page of cricketers and politicians. The film comes from the period between 1989 and 1991 in which Kapoor appeared in nine releases, most of them melodramas scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal and reviewed by nobody, and it is among the least documented entries in this workbook. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Apoorva Mehta
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own; the bare name resolves to an unrelated Canadian-American businessman. His credits here come through Dharma Productions, alongside Hiroo Yash Johar and Karan Johar.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kapoor & Sons (2016).
recurring_themes: The Dharma Productions slate of family and youth films.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kapoor & Sons (2016), in which Kapoor plays the ninety-year-old grandfather under heavy prosthetics — the performance that drew the warmest notices of his late career and won him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor. He is credited as producer with Hiroo Yash Johar and Karan Johar.
biography: Apoorva Mehta is credited as a producer on Kapoor & Sons (2016), and no biography of him can be sourced here — the name on Wikipedia belongs to an unrelated businessman, which is how an earlier pass of this research briefly attached the wrong article to him. The film itself is among the most important of Rishi Kapoor's second career: a Dharma Productions family drama in which he plays a mischievous ninety-year-old patriarch, buried in prosthetics, whose wish for a single photograph of the whole family frames the story. It won him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Arindam Chaudhuri
career_background: Arindam Chaudhuri is an Indian businessman best known for his involvement with the now-defunct Indian Institute of Planning and Management, an unaccredited institute widely criticised for false advertisement and fraudulent practices; he was arrested in August 2020 for tax evasion. Through Planman Motion Pictures he produced Bengali films including Sanjhbatir Rupkathara (2002) and Dosar (2006), the National Film Award-winning Faltu (2006), and The Last Lear, which won the National Film Award for Best Film in English.
debut: Film production through Planman Motion Pictures from the early 2000s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Dooni Chaar (2010). Elsewhere, Faltu, Dosar and The Last Lear.
recurring_themes: Small, award-minded films produced alongside an education business.
creative_style: A businessman-producer backing art-house and festival films rather than commercial vehicles.
major_awards: His productions won National Film Awards, including for Faltu and The Last Lear.
historical_importance: Documented mainly for the collapse of his education business; in film, for a short run of award-winning small productions.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is the hinge of Kapoor's late career: Planman Motion Pictures produced Do Dooni Chaar (2010), the modest comedy in which he and Neetu Singh played a Delhi schoolteacher and his wife, and for which he won the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor. That the film which restored his critical standing came from a producer now better known for an education scandal is among the odder facts in this filmography.
biography: Arindam Chaudhuri produced the film that re-established Rishi Kapoor as a serious actor. Chaudhuri's public reputation rests elsewhere — on the Indian Institute of Planning and Management, an unaccredited business school criticised for false advertising and later wound up, and on his 2020 arrest for tax evasion — but through Planman Motion Pictures he financed a short run of small, well-regarded films, among them the National Film Award winners Faltu and The Last Lear. Do Dooni Chaar (2010) belongs to that run: an unassuming comedy about a Delhi mathematics teacher saving for a car, with Kapoor opposite Neetu Singh, which won him the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor and is routinely cited as the start of his character-actor phase.

name: Arjun Dev Rashk
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naya Daur (1978).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Naya Daur (1978), an R. D. Burman-scored picture from Kapoor's early run as a young lead — not to be confused with the 1957 Dilip Kumar film of the same title.
biography: Arjun Dev Rashk is credited as a writer on Naya Daur (1978) and has no documented biography. The film shares its title with the far better-known 1957 Dilip Kumar film and has left correspondingly little trace; it belongs to the stretch five years after Bobby when Kapoor was releasing several romances a year with an R. D. Burman score attached to most of them. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Arjun Hingorani
career_background: Arjun Hingorani (15 November 1926 – 5 May 2018) was an Indian director, producer and actor. He launched Dharmendra and Sadhana Shivdasani in Indian cinema, and made Abana (1958), the first Sindhi film. His films include Kab? Kyoon? Aur Kahan?, Kahani Kismat Ki, Khel Khilari Ka and Katilon Ke Kaatil.
debut: Directing from the 1950s; Abana (1958) was the first Sindhi film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Katilon Ke Kaatil (1981). Elsewhere, Kahani Kismat Ki and Khel Khilari Ka, both with Dharmendra.
recurring_themes: Action melodrama with alliterative titles, built around Dharmendra.
creative_style: A commercial director with a long single-star association and a habit of titling films in matched sets.
historical_importance: The maker of the first Sindhi film and the filmmaker who gave Dharmendra his debut.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Katilon Ke Kaatil (1981), an action picture with a Kalyanji–Anandji score in which Kapoor shared the screen with Dharmendra — Hingorani's own discovery and the star of most of his films. It is one of the few outright action vehicles in Kapoor's filmography.
biography: Arjun Hingorani directed one Rishi Kapoor film, and it is an outlier in the filmography. Hingorani's place in Indian cinema rests on two things: he made Abana in 1958, the first film in Sindhi, and he gave Dharmendra his debut, then built most of his subsequent career around him. Katilon Ke Kaatil (1981) is an action picture in that mould, with Dharmendra alongside Kapoor and a Kalyanji–Anandji score, from a period when Kapoor was being paired with established action stars rather than carrying romances alone. He also launched Sadhana Shivdasani. Hingorani worked into the 1990s and died in May 2018.

name: Armaan Shahabi
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sahibaan (1993).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ramesh Talwar's Sahibaan (1993), a Shiv–Hari-scored romance and the last of Talwar's four films with Kapoor, made as his leading career closed.
biography: Armaan Shahabi is credited as a writer on Sahibaan (1993) and has no documented biography. The film was Ramesh Talwar's fourth and last with Kapoor — sixteen years after Doosra Aadmi, the debut in which Talwar had used the actor's youth against him — and it carries a Shiv–Hari score, the same classical duo who had written Chandni four years earlier. By 1993 Kapoor's romantic vehicles were being made by the same people in diminished circumstances, which is the pattern this row sits inside. It is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Arun Kaul
career_background: Arun Kaul (12 August 1933 – 21 July 2007) was a noted Kashmiri filmmaker and screenwriter. His own film Diksha (1991) won the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Movie and the Golden Lotus for Best Hindi Film at the National Film Awards. He worked as screenplay assistant to Gulzar on Ijaazat (1987) and Lekin (1990), and his article records that he wrote the screenplay for Yash Chopra's Chandni (1989).
debut: Working in film from the 1960s; his directorial work culminated in Diksha (1991).
major_works: With Kapoor: Chandni (1989). Elsewhere, Diksha as director, and screenplay work with Gulzar.
recurring_themes: Caste and social injustice in his own films; romance and longing in his commercial screenwriting.
creative_style: A parallel-cinema filmmaker who also wrote for the mainstream, bringing a literary sense of structure to commercial romance.
major_awards: Filmfare Critics Award for Best Movie and the Golden Lotus for Best Hindi Film at the National Film Awards, both for Diksha.
historical_importance: A figure of the Indian parallel cinema — he was among those who called for a new Indian cinema in the 1960s — who also wrote one of Hindi cinema's best-known romances.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a crucial one: his article credits him with the screenplay of Yash Chopra's Chandni (1989), the film that restored Kapoor to romantic leading man opposite Sridevi after a decade of melodrama. That a National Award-winning parallel filmmaker wrote it is not what the film's reputation would suggest.
biography: Arun Kaul wrote the screenplay of Chandni, the film that gave Rishi Kapoor his second life as a romantic lead. A Kashmiri filmmaker associated with the Indian parallel cinema, Kaul directed Diksha (1991), which won both the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Movie and the Golden Lotus for Best Hindi Film, and worked as screenplay assistant to Gulzar on Ijaazat and Lekin. His article also records the Chandni credit — a Yash Chopra romance built on music, chiffon and longing, in which Kapoor's Rohit is paralysed in an accident and pushes Sridevi's Chandni away. The combination is worth noting: the most commercially glossy film of Kapoor's middle years was written by a man whose own cinema was about caste and rural injustice.

name: Arun Rangachari
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He is named among the key people of DAR Motion Pictures in that company's article, which is cited on its own row in this sheet.
major_works: With Kapoor: D-Day (2013).
recurring_themes: Content-driven cinema produced through DAR Motion Pictures.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Nikkhil Advani's D-Day (2013), in which Kapoor plays Iqbal Seth, a Dawood Ibrahim-like crime boss living under protection in Karachi — one of the most unsympathetic roles of his career and part of the late widening of his range.
biography: Arun Rangachari produced D-Day (2013) through DAR Motion Pictures, whose article names him among its key people but who has no article of his own. The film is one of the strongest of Rishi Kapoor's late character roles: he plays Iqbal Seth, a fictionalised version of Dawood Ibrahim, hiding in Karachi under state protection while Indian agents plan his extraction. Cast against forty years of romantic goodwill, the performance is genial and chilling at once, and it belongs with Agneepath's Rauf Lala among the villains that redefined what he could be given. DAR Motion Pictures was founded in 2009 with a stated focus on content-driven cinema.

name: Aseem Bajaj
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rajma Chawal (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Leena Yadav's Rajma Chawal (2018), in which Kapoor plays a widowed father who creates a fake social-media profile to reach his estranged son — a small, late role built on loneliness rather than authority.
biography: Aseem Bajaj is credited as a producer on Rajma Chawal (2018) and has no documented biography. The film, directed by Leena Yadav and released on Netflix, gave Kapoor one of the gentler parts of his last years: a widower in old Delhi who, unable to talk to his son, poses online as a young woman to reach him. It belongs with Do Dooni Chaar and Sharmaji Namkeen among the late films that cast him as an ordinary, slightly ridiculous older man rather than a patriarch, and it was one of his final completed performances. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ashish Redij
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sambar Salsa (2007).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sambar Salsa (2007), one of the two English-language films in this filmography, both written and directed by Kapoor's cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor and both released that year. They are the least documented entries in the workbook.
biography: Ashish Redij produced Sambar Salsa (2007) and has no documented biography. The film is one of two English-language pictures Kapoor made that year, both written and directed by his cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor and both so slightly distributed that almost nothing about them is recorded — no reviews of substance, no commercial figures, and in this case no documented producer. They fall in the gap between his Yash Raj supporting roles and the Dharma films that followed, when family connections were supplying work. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Atul Sabharwal
career_background: An Indian director and writer credited on one film in this filmography. No Wikipedia article was located for him under this name during this research.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aurangzeb (2013).
recurring_themes: Crime drama built on doubling and family loyalty.
creative_style: Not documented here.
historical_importance: Not documented here.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Aurangzeb (2013), a Yash Raj Films crime drama about twin brothers on opposite sides of the law, in which Kapoor plays a police officer. It is one of six Yash Raj films from his character-actor phase, the banner that had also employed him as a young lead in the 1970s and restored him in Chandni.
biography: Atul Sabharwal wrote and directed Aurangzeb (2013), and no Wikipedia article for him was located in this research. The film is a Yash Raj crime drama set in Gurgaon's land mafia, built on a pair of separated twins — a device as old as the Manmohan Desai films Kapoor had made in the 1970s, here played straight as noir. Kapoor appears as a policeman, one of the supporting roles the banner gave him across six films after 2004. The absence of a locatable article for a working Yash Raj director is a reminder that the documentation gaps in this workbook are not confined to the 1980s.

name: Aydin Vance
career_background: A composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sanam Re (2016).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sanam Re (2016), a T-Series production directed by Divya Khosla Kumar in which Kapoor plays the hero's grandfather. The soundtrack is divided among several composers, of whom Mithoon — who wrote the title song — is the best known.
biography: Aydin Vance is credited among the composers of Sanam Re (2016) and has no documented biography. The film is a T-Series romance in which Kapoor plays the grandfather whose own remembered love frames the younger couple's story, and its soundtrack was assembled from several composers in the manner standard by then — Mithoon's title song became one of the most streamed Hindi recordings of its year, while the other contributors left no trace. The contrast with the single-composer soundtracks of Kapoor's youth is the point worth recording. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ayesha Devitre Dhillon
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kapoor & Sons (2016).
recurring_themes: The contemporary family and its unspoken resentments.
creative_style: Not documented; she shares the writing credit on a film built on overlapping family dialogue.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a significant one: Kapoor & Sons (2016), the Dharma family drama in which Kapoor plays the ninety-year-old grandfather and which won him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor. She is one of the small number of women credited as writers anywhere in this workbook.
biography: Ayesha Devitre Dhillon is credited as a writer on Kapoor & Sons (2016) and has no documented biography. The film is one of the two or three best of Rishi Kapoor's late career: a family drama in which three generations circle their own grievances, and in which Kapoor, under extensive prosthetics, plays a ninety-year-old who wants one photograph of the family together. It won him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor. Her presence is also worth recording in the aggregate: of 561 credited collaborators in this filmography, very few are women, and most of those appear in the last fifteen years. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Azure Entertainment
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: The Body (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on The Body (2019) with Viacom18 Motion Pictures — the last film released in Kapoor's lifetime, a thriller remade from a Spanish original in which he plays the investigating officer. He died five months after its release.
biography: Azure Entertainment co-produced The Body (2019), the last film released while Rishi Kapoor was alive, and has no recorded history of its own. Directed by the Malayalam filmmaker Jeethu Joseph and remade from a Spanish thriller, the film cast Kapoor as the police officer investigating a corpse's disappearance — a procedural role, far from the romantic parts that made him, and the final completed performance released in his lifetime. He died in April 2020, with Sharmaji Namkeen unfinished. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: B. H. Tharun Kumar
career_background: A director credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006), a variation on Indecent Proposal in which Kapoor is top-billed but functionally the antagonist, coercing a younger couple — one of the few outright unsympathetic parts of his career and, notably, one he took six years after Karobaar had used the same premise with him on the other side of it.
biography: B. H. Tharun Kumar directed Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006) and has no documented biography. The film is a reworking of the Indecent Proposal situation, with Kapoor as the wealthy older man who buys his way into a young couple's marriage — top-billed but effectively the villain, and playing the position he had been on the receiving end of in Karobaar six years earlier. Films like this one, in the interval before Dharma and Yash Raj reframed him, show him experimenting with unsympathetic roles well before Agneepath made that turn respectable. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: B. K. Parivar
career_background: The producer credit recorded on Ghar Parivar (1991). The name has no Wikipedia article, and its resemblance to the film's own title invites suspicion of a transcription error; the film's Wikipedia article, however, gives the producer as B. K. Parivar exactly, so the credit is reproduced here as the source states it.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Parivar (1991).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ghar Parivar (1991), directed by Mohanji Prasad with a Kalyanji–Anandji score, in which Kapoor appeared with Rajesh Khanna, Moushumi Chatterjee and Meenakshi Seshadri — a multi-star family melodrama from the end of his lead career.
biography: B. K. Parivar is the producer credit on Ghar Parivar (1991), and the name is as opaque as it looks. Because it echoes the film's title, this research checked the film's own Wikipedia article rather than trusting the extraction, and the article gives the producer as B. K. Parivar in exactly that form; the credit is therefore reproduced as the source has it, with the caveat recorded here. The film itself is a crowded family melodrama directed by Mohanji Prasad, with Rajesh Khanna, Moushumi Chatterjee and Meenakshi Seshadri alongside Kapoor, from the stretch at the turn of the 1990s when his vehicles had become ensembles of declining stars.

name: B.K. Jaiswal
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989).
recurring_themes: The household melodrama of class and marriage.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989), directed by Kalpataru and written with Kader Khan — one of the five domestic melodramas that made up the densest and least documented stretch of Kapoor's lead career.
biography: B.K. Jaiswal produced Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989) and has no documented biography. The film is one of five that Kalpataru directed with Kapoor between 1988 and 1994, all of them titled for the household rather than the romance and most written with Kader Khan: domestic melodramas of dowry, duty and in-law cruelty in which Kapoor plays sons and husbands. Nine of his films were released between 1989 and 1991, and this tier of production — small producers, prolific directors, no critical record — accounts for most of them. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

relationship_with_actor: One film: Rahul Rawail's Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), co-produced with Rita Rawail and the Nandys, in which Kapoor plays the father of twins separated by their parents' divorce — one of the few roles he had in the quiet years before Hum Tum.
biography: B.L. Saboo co-produced Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001) and has no documented biography. The film reunited Kapoor with Rahul Rawail, who had given him his lead in Gunahgaar twenty-one years earlier, and cast him as the father of twin daughters raised apart after a divorce. It belongs to the four-year interval between the end of his leading career and Hum Tum, when his work consisted of a handful of supporting and paternal roles in films that made little impression. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: BMB Combines
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naseeb Apna Apna (1986).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Naseeb Apna Apna (1986), which T. Rama Rao directed and K. C. Bokadia produced, with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score and Kapoor opposite Farha — one of the southern-formula remakes that made up much of his mid-1980s work.
biography: BMB Combines is the banner on Naseeb Apna Apna (1986) and has no recorded history. The film is characteristic of Kapoor's middle period in several ways at once: directed by T. Rama Rao, one of the most prolific importers of Telugu formulas into Hindi; produced by K. C. Bokadia, whose own article is the only reason another film in this workbook has a director credit; scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, who wrote for thirty-two of these films; and written in part by Mushtaq Jalili, an Urdu screenwriter whose father was a poet. The banner that financed it left nothing behind. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Badshah
career_background: Aditya Prateek Singh, known professionally as Badshah, is an Indian rapper, singer-songwriter, composer, reality-television judge and businessman from Delhi, influential in both Indian hip-hop and Hindi film music and widely credited with helping Indian hip-hop reach mainstream global audiences. His article notes that he is known for high-energy commercial songs and for a series of controversies.
debut: Recording from 2006; wide recognition followed his 2012 single 'Saturday Saturday', used in the soundtrack of Humpty Sharma Ki Dulhania (2014).
major_works: With Kapoor: Kapoor & Sons (2016). Elsewhere, 'Abhi Toh Party Shuru Hui Hai' from Khoobsurat and a long run of film and non-film singles.
recurring_themes: Party and club records written as standalone singles and then placed in films.
creative_style: Hip-hop and dance-pop built for streaming and radio, usually rapped by himself, commissioned a song at a time.
historical_importance: One of the central figures in Indian hip-hop's move into the commercial mainstream.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kapoor & Sons (2016), where he is one of six credited song composers — the infobox lists Amaal Mallik, Badshah, Arko, Tanishk Bagchi, Benny Dayal and Nucleya under 'Songs' and Sameer Uddin under 'Score'. Kapoor plays the ninety-year-old grandfather in it, under prosthetics, and won the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor.
biography: Badshah contributed a song to Kapoor & Sons (2016), and the credit is a small marker of how far Hindi film music had travelled during Rishi Kapoor's career. A Delhi rapper who came up outside the film industry and reached a mass audience with 'Saturday Saturday' before Bollywood absorbed him, Badshah is one of six composers on a single soundtrack — an arrangement unimaginable in 1973, when Laxmikant–Pyarelal wrote every song in Bobby. The film itself is among the best of Kapoor's late work: a family drama in which he plays a mischievous nonagenarian who wants one photograph of everyone together, a performance that won him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor.

name: Balaji Films Ltd.
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article under this name. The credit belongs to the Balaji group founded by Ekta Kapoor, whose own article is cited on her row in this sheet.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kucch To Hai (2003).
recurring_themes: The transfer of television serial production into film.
creative_style: Not documented under this name.
historical_importance: Not independently documented under this name; the wider Balaji group is a dominant force in Indian television.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Kucch To Hai (2003), the horror-slasher credited to two directors — Anurag Basu, whose article calls it his debut, and Anil V. Kumar — with Kapoor in support. It falls in the interval between his last leads and Hum Tum.
biography: Balaji Films is the banner on Kucch To Hai (2003), and has no article under that name. The credit places the film inside Ekta Kapoor's Balaji group, which dominated Indian television in the early 2000s and was then moving into cinema; Kucch To Hai was one of its early features, a horror-slasher aimed at a young audience, credited to Anurag Basu and Anil V. Kumar and featuring Rishi Kapoor in a supporting part. For Kapoor it belongs to the quietest stretch of his working life, the four years between the end of his leading roles and the Yash Raj films that restarted him. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Benaras Media Works
career_background: The production banner of the director Anubhav Sinha, credited on Mulk (2018). It has no Wikipedia article of its own — the name redirects to Sinha himself, whose article is cited on his row in this sheet.
major_works: With Kapoor: Mulk (2018).
recurring_themes: Socially engaged drama; the citizen before the law.
creative_style: A director's own banner, used for the run of political films Sinha began in 2018.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Mulk (2018), in which Kapoor plays Murad Ali Mohammed, the head of a Varanasi Muslim family whose loyalty is put on trial after his nephew joins a terrorist attack. It is the most substantial role of his last years.
biography: Benaras Media Works is Anubhav Sinha's own banner, and it produced the film that gave Rishi Kapoor his best late dramatic role. The company has no separate article — its name redirects to Sinha — and it exists to make the socially engaged films he turned to from 2018: Mulk, Article 15, Thappad. In Mulk, Kapoor plays a Varanasi patriarch forced to defend his family's belonging in open court, a performance of stillness from an actor whose fame had rested on charm. The banner's name, invoking Benaras, points at the film's setting. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Benchmark Pictures
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: 102 Not Out (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on 102 Not Out (2018), Umesh Shukla's two-hander in which the 65-year-old Kapoor plays the 75-year-old son of Amitabh Bachchan's 102-year-old father — his last leading role and the ninth film the two men made together.
biography: Benchmark Pictures co-produced 102 Not Out (2018) and has no recorded history of its own. The film is the last lead role of Rishi Kapoor's career: adapted by Umesh Shukla from his own Gujarati play, it puts Kapoor as a morose seventy-five-year-old against Amitabh Bachchan's irrepressible centenarian father, the two of them alone in a house for most of its length. They had first appeared together in Amar Akbar Anthony forty-one years earlier, and this is the only one of their nine films in which Kapoor plays the younger generation. He died two years after its release. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Benny Dayal
industry: Hindi cinema; Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and other Indian cinema
career_background: Benny Dayal (born 13 May 1979 in Abu Dhabi) is an Indian playback singer based in the United Arab Emirates who records in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada, Bengali, Gujarati and Marathi. He is a member of the band S5, launched by the SS Music channel, through which A. R. Rahman noticed him, and he made an acting debut in the Malayalam film By the People.
debut: Recording from 2002; brought into film music by A. R. Rahman.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kapoor & Sons (2016). Elsewhere, a large catalogue of playback work across Indian languages.
recurring_themes: High-energy playback singing across languages; the single-song film commission.
creative_style: Primarily a playback singer, credited here among a film's composers in the multi-contributor manner of 2010s soundtracks.
historical_importance: One of the most widely recorded multilingual playback singers of his generation.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kapoor & Sons (2016), where the infobox lists him among six names under 'Songs'. Kapoor plays the ninety-year-old grandfather in it, the performance that won him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor.
biography: Benny Dayal is credited among the song composers of Kapoor & Sons (2016), a film whose soundtrack was divided between six contributors. Born in Abu Dhabi in 1979 and based in the UAE, Dayal is better known as a playback singer — one of the most prolific multilingual voices of his generation, brought into film music by A. R. Rahman after being noticed with the band S5 — and his presence in a composer credit is characteristic of how loosely those credits are assigned in the streaming era. The film itself gave Kapoor his Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor, as a nonagenarian patriarch played under heavy prosthetics.

name: Bhagwan Chitra Mandir
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Deewana (1992).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented, though its one credit here is on a film of real consequence.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and on the pivotal film of the later career: Deewana (1992), Raj Kanwar's directorial debut, in which Kapoor plays the singer presumed dead whose widow marries the younger man played by a debuting Shah Rukh Khan. The film was a hit and is read as the handover of the romantic lead between generations.
biography: Bhagwan Chitra Mandir is the banner on Deewana (1992) and has no recorded history. The film matters more than almost any other in the second half of this filmography: Kapoor plays Ravi, a wealthy singer who marries Divya Bharti's character and is believed killed, and Shah Rukh Khan, in his film debut, plays the man she later marries. It was Raj Kanwar's first film as director, a commercial success, and the moment at which Hindi cinema's romantic lead visibly passed from Kapoor's generation to the next — with Kapoor performing the transfer himself. The company that financed it left nothing else behind. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Bhappi Sonie
career_background: Bhappi Sonie (31 July 1928 – 5 September 2001) was an Indian director and producer in Hindi cinema. He assisted Raj Khosla on Milap (1955), C.I.D. (1956) and Solva Saal (1958) before making his directorial debut with Ek Phool Char Kaante, starring Sunil Dutt and Waheeda Rehman. He is best known for the Shammi Kapoor and Dharmendra hits Janwar (1965) and Brahmachari (1968), and won the Filmfare Award for Best Film.
debut: Assistant to Raj Khosla from 1955; directorial debut Ek Phool Char Kaante.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bade Dilwala (1983). Elsewhere, Janwar and Brahmachari.
recurring_themes: Light romantic comedy built around a charismatic male star.
creative_style: Breezy star vehicles with strong song placement, in the 1960s Shammi Kapoor idiom.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Film, for Brahmachari.
historical_importance: A significant director of the 1960s star comedy, and the maker of two of Shammi Kapoor's defining films.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Bade Dilwala (1983), an R. D. Burman-scored melodrama written in part by Rahi Masoom Raza and Gulshan Nanda. The interest lies in the lineage — Sonie had directed Janwar and Brahmachari with Shammi Kapoor, Rishi's uncle, and came to the nephew two decades later for a film neither is remembered for.
biography: Bhappi Sonie directed one Rishi Kapoor film, late in a career built on another Kapoor. Sonie learned the trade assisting Raj Khosla on Milap, C.I.D. and Solva Saal, then made his name with Janwar (1965) and Brahmachari (1968), both starring Shammi Kapoor — Rishi's uncle — and the second winning him the Filmfare Award for Best Film. His one film with the nephew, Bade Dilwala (1983), is a melodrama with an R. D. Burman score and a script shared between Rahi Masoom Raza, Gulshan Nanda and C. J. Pavri, and it made no impression. The pairing is one of several in this workbook where a director associated with the previous generation of Kapoors reached Rishi only after his own best work was behind him.

name: Bharat B. Bhalla
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ajooba (1991).
recurring_themes: Fantasy adventure.
creative_style: Not documented; he is credited with Prayag Raj and Brij Katyal, and with two Soviet writers.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ajooba (1991), the Indo-Soviet fantasy Shashi Kapoor directed with Gennady Vasilyev, in which Rishi Kapoor was third-billed behind Amitabh Bachchan and Dimple Kapadia. The writing credit is shared with Prayag Raj, Brij Katyal and the Soviet writers Yu Avetikov and Valentin Ezhov.
biography: Bharat B. Bhalla is one of five writers credited on Ajooba (1991) and has no documented biography. The film is the strangest production in this filmography: an Indo-Soviet co-production shot partly at the Gorky Film Studio with Soviet crew and a Soviet co-director, directed and produced by Shashi Kapoor, with Amitabh Bachchan as a masked avenger and his nephew Rishi third-billed. It cost a great deal and failed. Five writers from two countries are credited, of whom only Prayag Raj and the Soviet screenwriter Valentin Ezhov have any wider record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

biography: Bharat Film Works is a banner on Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001) and has no recorded history. The film reunited Kapoor with Rahul Rawail, who had given him a lead in his own directorial debut Gunahgaar twenty-one years earlier; here Kapoor plays a father and the picture is pitched at family audiences. It belongs to the quiet interval around 2000 when his work was sporadic and largely paternal, before Hum Tum established the character-actor phase. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Bharat Patel
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own; the bare name resolves to an unrelated Zimbabwean judge.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017), a comedy of a Gujarati-Punjabi marriage in which Kapoor plays the Gujarati father opposite Paresh Rawal — three years before Rawal would complete Kapoor's unfinished last film.
biography: Bharat Patel produced Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017) and has no documented biography; an earlier pass of this research attached to the name the article of a Zimbabwean judge. The film is a culture-clash comedy about a Gujarati family and a Punjabi one, with Kapoor as the Gujarati patriarch and Paresh Rawal opposite him — a pairing that acquired an unexpected significance three years later, when Rawal stepped in to complete Sharmaji Namkeen after Kapoor's death, playing the same character in the unshot scenes. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Bholenath Movies
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017), the Gujarati-Punjabi marriage comedy in which Kapoor plays the father of the bride opposite Paresh Rawal, with Lalit Pandit's songs.
biography: Bholenath Movies is a banner on Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017) and has no recorded history. The film belongs to the late run of small comedies in which Kapoor played fathers for producers with no public profile, three years before his death; its music came from Lalit Pandit, working solo after the end of Jatin–Lalit. Several of the companies behind these final films — this one, Bholenath Movies, Allchemy Productions, Azure Entertainment — exist in this workbook only as names on a credit list. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Bholu Khan
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), Rahul Rawail's family comedy of separated twins, with Kapoor as their father.
biography: Bholu Khan is credited as a writer on Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001) and has no documented biography. The film is one of four collaborators' worth of writing credits on a modest family comedy, directed by Rahul Rawail twenty-one years after his own debut with Kapoor, and released in the quiet patch before Hum Tum reopened the actor's career. As with most single-credit writers in this workbook, the film's cast list is the only evidence of his working life. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Binod Pradhan
career_background: Binod Pradhan, from Kalimpong, is an Indian cinematographer, director and actor. His award-winning work as a cinematographer includes 1942: A Love Story, Devdas, Rang De Basanti, Mission Kashmir and Munna Bhai M.B.B.S.
debut: A cinematographer first; he has directed occasionally.
major_works: With Kapoor: Wedding Pullav (2015). Elsewhere, as cinematographer, Devdas and Rang De Basanti.
recurring_themes: Visual scale and colour; the romantic melodrama photographed as spectacle.
creative_style: One of Hindi cinema's foremost cinematographers, whose direction is a sideline to that career.
major_awards: Multiple awards and nominations for cinematography, including Filmfare and IIFA recognition.
historical_importance: A leading Indian cinematographer of the 1990s and 2000s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Wedding Pullav (2015), which Pradhan directed and in which Kapoor appears in support — a slight picture by any measure, and an odd item in the filmography of a cinematographer of his standing. Salim–Sulaiman wrote the songs.
biography: Binod Pradhan, one of Hindi cinema's most distinguished cinematographers, directed one film in this filmography. His reputation rests on his camerawork — 1942: A Love Story, Mission Kashmir, Devdas, Munna Bhai M.B.B.S., Rang De Basanti — a body of work that defined the look of mainstream Hindi cinema across two decades. Wedding Pullav (2015), which he directed, is a small romantic comedy with Kapoor in a supporting role and songs by Salim–Sulaiman, and it made no impression. It sits among the late ensemble films in which Kapoor's presence was a reassurance to financiers rather than a part worth writing. Pradhan returned to cinematography afterwards.

name: Bobby Bedi
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He is named as managing director of Kaleidoscope Entertainment in that company's article, which is cited on its own row in this sheet; Kaleidoscope's productions include Bandit Queen, Fire, Maqbool and Mangal Pandey: The Rising.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chintu Ji (2009). Elsewhere, through Kaleidoscope, Bandit Queen and Maqbool.
recurring_themes: Independent and art-house Indian cinema produced for an international as well as a domestic audience.
creative_style: A producer associated with directors outside the commercial mainstream.
historical_importance: Not documented in his own right, though the company he runs is among India's significant independent production houses.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chintu Ji (2009), in which Kapoor plays a fictionalised version of himself — a star named Chintu Ji, his own childhood nickname — who returns to the village of his birth. That a producer identified with Bandit Queen and Maqbool made it suggests the film was conceived as something more than a vehicle.
biography: Bobby Bedi produced Chintu Ji (2009), the most self-referential film in this filmography, and has no Wikipedia article of his own. He is named as managing director of Kaleidoscope Entertainment, the company behind Bandit Queen, Fire, Maqbool and Mangal Pandey: The Rising — a body of work squarely outside the commercial mainstream. Chintu Ji casts Kapoor as a film star called Chintu Ji, which was his own nickname from childhood and the name the industry used for him, returning to the village where he was born to be received as a celebrity and a disappointment. It is an unusual piece of work for a 1970s romantic lead to take, and the producer's background helps explain why it exists.

name: Brar Productions
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pehla Pehla Pyar (1994).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Pehla Pehla Pyar (1994), a romance written by Rumi Jaffery and Honey Irani with music by Anand–Milind — one of four films Kapoor released that year, all of them pitched at a romantic persona that had stopped selling.
biography: Brar Productions is a banner on Pehla Pehla Pyar (1994) and has no recorded history. The film is one of the clearest examples of the problem Kapoor faced in the mid-1990s: a romance written to his established image by Rumi Jaffery and Honey Irani, scored by Anand–Milind, released at a point when audiences had transferred their affections to Shah Rukh Khan, Aamir Khan and Salman Khan. Four of his films came out that year and none registered. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Brij Katyal
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ajooba (1991).
recurring_themes: Fantasy adventure.
creative_style: Not documented; credited with Prayag Raj, Bharat B. Bhalla and two Soviet writers.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ajooba (1991), the Indo-Soviet fantasy co-directed by Shashi Kapoor and Gennady Vasilyev and shot partly at the Gorky Film Studio, in which Rishi Kapoor was third-billed behind Amitabh Bachchan and Dimple Kapadia.
biography: Brij Katyal is one of five writers credited on Ajooba (1991) and has no documented biography. The film was an Indo-Soviet co-production — Shashi Kapoor directing with the Russian Gennady Vasilyev, Soviet cinematographers, the Gorky Film Studio as co-producer — built as a swashbuckling fantasy around Amitabh Bachchan, with Rishi Kapoor third-billed. It is the only international co-production in this filmography and one of its most expensive failures. The writing was divided between three Indian and two Soviet credits, of which this is the least documented. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Bunty Soorma
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Damini (1993).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rajkumar Santoshi's Damini (1993), the blockbuster in which Kapoor plays the husband of a woman who witnesses a rape in his family's house and is disbelieved — one of the few films of his later career in which he is deliberately not the moral centre.
biography: Bunty Soorma is credited as a producer on Damini (1993) and has no documented biography. The film is among the most substantial of Rishi Kapoor's later career and among the least flattering to him: Meenakshi Seshadri's Damini sees a servant raped by her brother-in-law and is systematically disbelieved, Sunny Deol's alcoholic lawyer takes her case, and Kapoor plays the husband whose loyalty to his family makes him complicit. It won Rajkumar Santoshi his second consecutive Filmfare Award for Best Director. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Cineyug
career_background: A production and event company owned by the brothers Aly Morani and Karim Morani, as recorded in Aly Morani's Wikipedia article, which is cited on his row in this sheet. The company has no article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Damini (1993). Elsewhere, Raja Hindustani and Arjun.
recurring_themes: Mainstream star vehicles produced alongside a live-events business.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: One of India's significant film and live-event companies, though not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Damini (1993), in which Kapoor plays the weak husband in a film whose moral weight belongs to Meenakshi Seshadri and Sunny Deol. It is among the strongest films of his later career and among the least concerned with his charm.
biography: Cineyug produced Damini (1993) and has no article of its own; what is documented appears in the article on Aly Morani, who owns the company with his brother Karim Morani and whose own row in this sheet carries that source. The company's slate ran from Damini to Raja Hindustani while also building a live-events business. Damini is the significant credit here: a courtroom melodrama about a woman disbelieved after witnessing a rape, in which Kapoor's husband is complicit through family loyalty — a part that uses his accumulated likeability as a liability rather than an asset, and one of the clearest signs before 2010 that he could be cast against type.

name: Clinton Cerejo
career_background: Clinton Cerejo is an Indian singer and composer from Mumbai, active since 1999, who has worked extensively as a music producer for other composers as well as composing and singing in his own right. He is married to the singer Dominique Cerejo.
debut: Working in film music from 1999, initially as a producer and arranger.
major_works: With Kapoor: The Body (2019). Elsewhere, his production work for other composers and his non-film recordings.
recurring_themes: Background score and arrangement rather than songs; fusion of Indian and Western idioms.
