creative_style: A producer-composer best known for arranging and realising other composers' work, with a parallel career as a singer.
historical_importance: One of the most employed music producers in Hindi cinema of his period.
relationship_with_actor: One film: The Body (2019), the last film released in Kapoor's lifetime — a thriller remade from a Spanish original, directed by the Malayalam filmmaker Jeethu Joseph, in which Kapoor plays the investigating police officer. Cerejo wrote the score; the songs were by Shamir Tandon, Arko and Tanishk Bagchi.
biography: Clinton Cerejo wrote the background score for the last Rishi Kapoor film released while he was alive. A Mumbai singer and composer working since 1999, Cerejo built his career largely as a music producer realising other composers' soundtracks, with his own composing and singing alongside it. The Body (2019) is a remake of a Spanish thriller about a corpse that vanishes from a morgue, directed by Jeethu Joseph, with Kapoor as the police officer running the investigation — a procedural part, a long way from the romances that made him. Its songs came from three other composers while Cerejo supplied the score, the standard division of labour in the period. Kapoor died five months after its release.

name: Crystal Films
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal-scored film from the stretch between 1989 and 1991 in which Kapoor released nine pictures, most of them unreviewed.
biography: Crystal Films is the banner on Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990) and has no recorded history. The film belongs to the densest and least documented period of the filmography: between 1989 and 1991 Kapoor appeared in nine releases, most of them melodramas scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, produced by companies with no public profile and reviewed by nobody. This row exists because the workbook records every credited collaborator, and it is built from the film's credits alone.

name: D.K. Chawla
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sahibaan (1993).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ramesh Talwar's Sahibaan (1993), a Shiv–Hari-scored romance and the last of Talwar's four films with Kapoor, made as his leading career closed.
biography: D.K. Chawla produced Sahibaan (1993) and has no documented biography. The film was Ramesh Talwar's fourth and final collaboration with Kapoor, sixteen years after Doosra Aadmi had cast the young star as the object of an older woman's grief, and it carries a score by Shiv–Hari, the classical duo who had written Chandni four years earlier. By 1993 the same directors and composers were making Kapoor's romances in markedly reduced circumstances. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: D.R. Kaushal
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Honeymoon (1992).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Honeymoon (1992), directed and produced by Surendra Mohan with songs by Anand–Milind, from the year of Deewana and Bol Radha Bol — the point at which Kapoor's lead career was ending.
biography: D.R. Kaushal is credited as a writer on Honeymoon (1992) and has no documented biography. The film came out in the same year as Deewana and Bol Radha Bol, the two pictures that between them closed Kapoor's run as a romantic lead — one by handing the part to Shah Rukh Khan on screen, the other by giving him a last solo hit. Honeymoon, by contrast, left no trace; it was the third and last of Surendra Mohan's films with the actor. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: DAR Motion Pictures
career_background: DAR Motion Pictures, founded in 2009, is an Indian film production and distribution company based in Mumbai and wholly owned by the DAR Capital Group. Its article describes a focus on content-driven cinema and names Arun Rangachari, Vivek Rangachari and Sethumadhavan Napan among its key people; it has worked with directors including Ritesh Batra, Nikhil Advani and Anurag Kashyap, and its films include City of Gold, D-Day and The Lunchbox.
debut: Opened with Lalbaug Parel (Marathi) and City of Gold (2010).
major_works: With Kapoor: D-Day (2013). Elsewhere, The Lunchbox and City of Gold.
recurring_themes: Content-driven cinema: urban realism, the thriller with a political edge, and festival-facing drama.
creative_style: A corporate production and distribution house that backs directors rather than imposing a house style.
historical_importance: One of the production companies behind the critically successful independent Hindi cinema of the 2010s, including The Lunchbox.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Nikkhil Advani's D-Day (2013), in which Kapoor plays Iqbal Seth, a Dawood Ibrahim-like crime boss hiding in Karachi — among the most unsympathetic parts of his career, and part of the late widening of his range that began with Agneepath the year before.
biography: DAR Motion Pictures produced D-Day (2013), one of the films that redefined what Rishi Kapoor could be cast as. Founded in 2009 as part of the DAR Capital Group and run by Arun and Vivek Rangachari, the company made its name on content-driven cinema — City of Gold, and then The Lunchbox, one of the most internationally successful Indian films of the decade. In D-Day, Nikkhil Advani's thriller about an operation to extract a fugitive gangster from Karachi, Kapoor plays the gangster: genial, paternal and entirely without conscience. Coming a year after Agneepath's Rauf Lala, it confirmed that the actor's late career would not be confined to indulgent fathers.

name: Daboo Malik
career_background: Israr Sardar Malik, known as Daboo Malik, is an Indian music director, composer, singer, actor and scriptwriter, born in Mumbai to the composer Sardar Malik. He is known for Tumko Na Bhool Paayenge and I Proud to Be an Indian. His brothers are the composers Anu Malik and Abu Malik, his sons are Amaal Mallik and Armaan Malik, and the lyricist Hasrat Jaipuri was his maternal uncle.
debut: Acting in the 1980s and 1990s before composing from the 2000s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006). Elsewhere, Tumko Na Bhool Paayenge and I Proud to Be an Indian.
recurring_themes: Mainstream commercial songs for action and romance.
creative_style: A family composer working in the Malik idiom, with a parallel career as an actor and writer.
historical_importance: Not independently prominent, but a member of one of Hindi film music's most persistent dynasties — four Maliks and two Mallik sons hold credits across this workbook's period.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006), in which Kapoor is top-billed but functionally the antagonist, coercing a younger couple. The family pattern is notable: his brother Anu Malik scored seven Kapoor films and his son Amaal Mallik three, so the Maliks appear across eleven films in this filmography.
biography: Daboo Malik scored one Rishi Kapoor film, and his row is most useful as a record of a musical dynasty. The son of the composer Sardar Malik and nephew of the lyricist Hasrat Jaipuri, he acted before composing and is remembered chiefly for Tumko Na Bhool Paayenge; his brothers Anu and Abu Malik are composers, and his sons Amaal Mallik and Armaan Malik became a composer and a singer in the next generation. Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006) gave Kapoor one of his very few unsympathetic leads, a wealthy man buying his way into a young marriage. Between Daboo, Anu and Amaal, the Malik family accounts for eleven credits in this filmography across four decades.

name: Deepak Adhiya
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sheshnaag (1990).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sheshnaag (1990), Iqbal Durrani's snake-deity fantasy made in the wake of Nagina's success, with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score — one of the genre pictures that filled the end of Kapoor's lead career.
biography: Deepak Adhiya is one of three producers credited on Sheshnaag (1990) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the folk-fantasy cycle that followed Nagina's success in 1986, in which Kapoor's romantic function was subordinated to curses, serpent deities and transformation plots. Nine of his films were released between 1989 and 1991, most of them in this register, scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal and financed by producers who left no record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Deepak Anand
career_background: A director credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own; the bare name resolves to an unrelated Canadian politician.
major_works: With Kapoor: Shreemaan Aashique (1993).
recurring_themes: Romantic comedy.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Shreemaan Aashique (1993), a romantic comedy written by Rumi Jaffery and Kamlesh Pandey with Nadeem–Shravan's songs, and one of the last films written squarely to Kapoor's lover-boy persona before it stopped selling.
biography: Deepak Anand directed Shreemaan Aashique (1993) and has no documented biography; an earlier pass of this research briefly attached to the name the article of a Canadian politician. The film is a late example of the formula Kapoor had carried since the 1970s — a romantic comedy built on his charm, written by Rumi Jaffery and Kamlesh Pandey with a Nadeem–Shravan soundtrack — released a year after Deewana had publicly handed the romantic lead to Shah Rukh Khan. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Deepak Sareen
career_background: An Indian film director and assistant director whose Wikipedia article is a stub recording only that his first film as director was Ranbhoomi and his last was Albela.
debut: Ranbhoomi (1991), his first film as director.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ranbhoomi (1991). Elsewhere, Albela.
recurring_themes: Multi-star action melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not substantially documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it was this director's debut: Ranbhoomi (1991), a multi-star melodrama with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score, written in part by K. K. Singh, who had begun his own career as an assistant director on Raj Kapoor's Prem Rog. It belongs to the crowded stretch at the turn of the 1990s when Kapoor appeared in nine films in three years.
biography: Deepak Sareen made his directorial debut with a Rishi Kapoor film, and his Wikipedia article records almost nothing else: that Ranbhoomi was his first film as director and Albela his last. Ranbhoomi (1991) is a multi-star melodrama with Laxmikant–Pyarelal's music, written in part by K. K. Singh, who had entered films as an assistant director on Raj Kapoor's Prem Rog and would win Filmfare awards for Krantiveer four years later. The film sits in the densest and least documented patch of this filmography, and its director is among several who left only a one-line record.

name: Dev Anand
career_background: Dev Anand, born Dharamdev Pishorimal Anand (26 September 1923 – 3 December 2011), was an Indian actor, writer, director and producer, considered one of the greatest and most successful actors in Indian cinema. Across more than six decades he worked in over 100 films. He received four Filmfare Awards, including two for Best Actor, the Padma Bhushan in 2001 and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 2002, and died in London.
debut: On screen from 1946; directing from the 1970s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love at Times Square (2003), which he wrote, produced and directed. Elsewhere, as actor, Kala Pani, Guide, Jewel Thief and Hare Rama Hare Krishna.
recurring_themes: The restless modern hero; the romance staged against travel, youth culture and the city.
creative_style: A star-director whose later films were written, produced and directed by himself, often to launch new performers, and marked by an insistence on contemporaneity.
major_awards: Four Filmfare Awards including two for Best Actor; Padma Bhushan (2001); Dadasaheb Phalke Award (2002).
historical_importance: One of the three defining male stars of post-independence Hindi cinema, alongside Raj Kapoor and Dilip Kumar, and later a prolific independent filmmaker.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Love at Times Square (2003), which Dev Anand wrote, produced and directed at the age of seventy-nine, with Kapoor in support. The pairing is of some historical interest — Dev Anand was the contemporary and rival of Raj Kapoor, Rishi's father, and he directed the son in a film made four decades after that rivalry defined Hindi stardom.
biography: Dev Anand directed one Rishi Kapoor film, and the fact of it closes a long circle in Hindi cinema. One of the three great male stars of the post-independence era — with Raj Kapoor and Dilip Kumar — Anand appeared in more than a hundred films, won four Filmfare Awards and received the Padma Bhushan and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, and spent his later decades writing, producing and directing his own pictures, usually to launch unknown performers. Love at Times Square (2003) is one of those late films, made when he was seventy-nine, with Kapoor in a supporting role and songs by Bappi Lahiri, Rajesh Roshan and Lucky Ali. That Raj Kapoor's great rival should direct Raj Kapoor's son is the kind of detail this filmography turns up repeatedly.

name: Dev Goradia
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006), in which Kapoor is top-billed but effectively the antagonist, coercing a younger couple in a variation on Indecent Proposal — one of the few outright unsympathetic leads of his career.
biography: Dev Goradia produced Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006) and has no documented biography. The film is one of the odder entries in this filmography: Kapoor takes top billing as a rich man who buys his way into a young couple's marriage, playing the coercer rather than the lover, six years after Karobaar had used the same premise with him on the other side of it. Films like this one, made in the thin years before Dharma and Yash Raj reframed him, show him testing unsympathetic roles well before Agneepath made that turn visible. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Devgans Films
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own. The name indicates the Devgan family company behind Raju Chacha.
major_works: With Kapoor: Raju Chacha (2000).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Raju Chacha (2000), produced by and starring Ajay Devgn and directed by his cousin Anil Devgan, with Kapoor in support. The film was an expensive failure, and it falls in the four-year gap between Kapoor's last leads and Hum Tum.
biography: Devgans Films is the banner on Raju Chacha (2000) and has no recorded history. The film was a Devgan family enterprise — produced by and starring Ajay Devgn, directed by his cousin Anil Devgan — and a costly children's fantasy that failed badly. Kapoor appears in support. Its place in this filmography is as a marker of the interval around 2000, when his leading career had ended, the character-actor phase had not begun, and his work consisted of supporting parts in other stars' vehicles. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Devika Bhagat
career_background: Devika Bhagat (born 25 October 1979) is an Indian screenwriter working in Hindi films. She has written Manorama Six Feet Under (2007), Bachna Ae Haseeno (2008) and Ladies vs Ricky Bahl (2011) among others.
debut: Writing from the 2000s; Manorama Six Feet Under (2007) brought her notice.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jab Tak Hai Jaan (2012). Elsewhere, Manorama Six Feet Under, Bachna Ae Haseeno and Ladies vs Ricky Bahl.
recurring_themes: Contemporary urban relationships; the noir reworked for small-town India.
creative_style: A screenwriter of modern romance and genre material, mostly for Yash Raj Films.
historical_importance: One of the small number of women writing mainstream Hindi screenplays in the 2000s and 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Yash Chopra's Jab Tak Hai Jaan (2012), the director's last film, released after his death during its production, with Kapoor in a supporting role. It is the final entry in the long Kapoor–Yash Raj association that began with Kabhie Kabhie in 1976.
biography: Devika Bhagat wrote Jab Tak Hai Jaan (2012), the last film Yash Chopra directed and the end of a thirty-six-year association between that filmmaker and Rishi Kapoor. Born in 1979, Bhagat came to notice with Manorama Six Feet Under and then wrote for Yash Raj — Bachna Ae Haseeno, Ladies vs Ricky Bahl — becoming one of the few women writing mainstream Hindi screenplays in the period. Chopra died of dengue fever during the production of Jab Tak Hai Jaan; Kapoor, whom he had first cast in Kabhie Kabhie in 1976 and restored to romantic leading man in Chandni in 1989, appears in support. Both careers end in the same film.

name: Dhirendra Bohra
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He shares a surname with Surendra Bohra, the director and co-producer of the same film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994).
recurring_themes: Household melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994), directed by Surendra Bohra with a Nadeem–Shravan score and Nutan among its producers, from the last year in which Kapoor was routinely cast as a lead.
biography: Dhirendra Bohra is credited as a writer on Saajan Ka Ghar (1994) and has no documented biography; he shares a surname with the film's director and co-producer Surendra Bohra, which suggests a family production. The film is one of four Kapoor released in 1994, all modest, all pitched at a romantic persona that the market had stopped buying, and all remembered — where they are remembered at all — for their Nadeem–Shravan soundtracks. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Dinesh B. Patel
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. He may be the same person as Dinesh Patel, credited as producer on Dhartiputra (1993), two years earlier; the names differ only by an initial and no source distinguishes them, so this workbook keeps the two credits in separate rows rather than merging a collaboration count on inference.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saajan Ki Baahon Mein (1995).
recurring_themes: Romantic melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Saajan Ki Baahon Mein (1995), written by Sachin Bhowmick and Rumi Jaffery with a Nadeem–Shravan score, from the final stretch of Kapoor's lead career.
biography: Dinesh B. Patel produced Saajan Ki Baahon Mein (1995) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the last cluster of Kapoor's romantic vehicles — written by Sachin Bhowmick, who had supplied the plots of his 1970s successes, with songs by Nadeem–Shravan, the composers of Deewana — made at a point when the formula no longer worked commercially. A producer named Dinesh Patel is credited on Dhartiputra two years earlier, and the two may well be the same man; this workbook records the possibility in both rows without merging them.

name: Dinesh Patel
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own; the bare name resolves to an unrelated baseball player. He may be the same person as Dinesh B. Patel, credited on Saajan Ki Baahon Mein (1995), but no source distinguishes or connects them, and the two credits are kept as separate rows.
major_works: With Kapoor: Dhartiputra (1993).
recurring_themes: Melodrama and folk-mythological material.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Dhartiputra (1993), written and directed by Iqbal Durrani with a Nadeem–Shravan score — one of the genre pictures that filled the close of Kapoor's leading career.
biography: Dinesh Patel produced Dhartiputra (1993) and has no documented biography; an earlier pass of this research attached to the name the article of an Indian-born baseball pitcher. The film, written and directed by Iqbal Durrani, belongs to the folk and mythological strand of Kapoor's late lead work, scored by Nadeem–Shravan at the height of their dominance. A producer credited as Dinesh B. Patel appears on another Kapoor film two years later and may be the same man; this workbook notes the possibility in both rows rather than asserting it.

name: Dinesh Vijan
career_background: Dinesh Vijan is an Indian film producer and director from Mumbai, the founder of Maddock Films, under which he has produced more than 35 films including Love Aaj Kal (2009), Cocktail (2012), Badlapur (2015), Hindi Medium (2017), Stree (2018), Luka Chuppi (2019), Bala (2019), Angrezi Medium (2020) and Mimi (2021).
debut: Producing from 2005; Love Aaj Kal (2009) was among his early successes.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Aaj Kal (2009). Elsewhere, Cocktail, Hindi Medium, Stree and the horror-comedy universe built from it.
recurring_themes: Contemporary urban romance; the small-town comedy; and from 2018 a connected horror-comedy franchise.
creative_style: A producer with a strong instinct for commercial trends, backing writer-directors and building franchises.
historical_importance: One of the most commercially successful independent producers in contemporary Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Imtiaz Ali's Love Aaj Kal (2009), in which Kapoor plays the elderly Veer Singh, whose remembered courtship in 1960s Delhi forms the film's period strand against the contemporary one. The role uses his own screen past as the content of the film's nostalgia, which is unusual even among his late parts.
biography: Dinesh Vijan produced Love Aaj Kal (2009), the film that put Rishi Kapoor's own romantic history on screen as history. The founder of Maddock Films and one of the most commercially astute producers of his generation — Cocktail, Badlapur, Hindi Medium, Stree — Vijan backed Imtiaz Ali's double narrative, in which a modern couple's casual romance is set against the patient, decades-long courtship of an older man, Veer Singh, played by Kapoor in the present and by a younger actor in flashback. Casting the 1970s' definitive lover-boy as the embodiment of a slower, more devoted idea of love is the film's most pointed decision, and it belongs to the period when Kapoor's past had become usable material.

name: Divya Khosla Kumar
career_background: Divya Khosla Kumar, née Khosla, is an Indian model, actress, producer and director working mainly in Hindi cinema. She began as a model and appeared in music videos, studied cinematography and editing, and directed music videos before making her directorial debut with Yaariyan (2014), followed by Sanam Re (2016). She is married to the T-Series head Bhushan Kumar.
debut: Directorial debut Yaariyan (2014).
major_works: With Kapoor: Sanam Re (2016). Elsewhere, Yaariyan as director and a number of T-Series productions.
recurring_themes: Youth romance built around music, in the T-Series house style.
creative_style: A director from a music-video background, with songs placed at the centre of the storytelling.
historical_importance: One of the few women directing mainstream commercial Hindi romances in the 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sanam Re (2016), her second feature, a T-Series romance in which Kapoor plays the hero's grandfather and whose title song, by Mithoon, became one of the most streamed Hindi recordings of its year. Kapoor's late work for T-Series — this film, All Is Well, Patiala House — came through the company her husband runs.
biography: Divya Khosla Kumar directed Sanam Re (2016), one of Rishi Kapoor's last supporting roles. A model and music-video director who studied cinematography and editing before making Yaariyan in 2014, she is among the very few women to have directed mainstream commercial Hindi romances in the period, and her films are built around their soundtracks in the T-Series manner — the company her husband Bhushan Kumar runs and which produced three of Kapoor's late films. In Sanam Re he plays the grandfather whose own remembered love frames the younger couple's story, a role that, like several of his last parts, trades on the audience's memory of him as a lover rather than asking him to be one.

name: Ekta Kapoor
career_background: Ekta R. Kapoor (born 7 June 1975) is an Indian television and film producer, the founder of Balaji Telefilms, where she is joint managing director and creative head. She began at seventeen and became known for producing a large number of Hindi soap operas. She received the Padma Shri in 2020 and the International Emmy Directorate Award in 2023.
debut: Producing television from 1995; her company moved into film production in the early 2000s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kucch To Hai (2003). Elsewhere, the Balaji television output and films including The Dirty Picture and Udta Punjab.
recurring_themes: Family melodrama for television; genre cinema aimed at young audiences.
creative_style: A high-volume producer who industrialised Hindi serial drama and carried its methods into film.
major_awards: Padma Shri (2020); International Emmy Directorate Award (2023); Best Entrepreneur of the Year (2001).
historical_importance: The dominant figure in Indian television drama from the late 1990s, and a significant film producer thereafter.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kucch To Hai (2003), an early Balaji Motion Pictures feature credited to two directors — Anurag Basu, whose article calls it his debut, and Anil V. Kumar — with Kapoor in support during the quietest years of his career.
biography: Ekta Kapoor produced one film in this filmography, early in her company's move from television into cinema. The founder of Balaji Telefilms, she reshaped Indian television from the late 1990s with a vast output of family serials, and was later honoured with the Padma Shri and an International Emmy Directorate Award. Kucch To Hai (2003) was among Balaji Motion Pictures' first features — a horror-slasher aimed at a young audience, credited to Anurag Basu and Anil V. Kumar — and gave Rishi Kapoor a supporting part at a point when little else was on offer. The credit is a useful reminder that his lean years coincided exactly with the arrival of television money in Hindi film production.

name: Emmay Entertainment
career_background: Emmay Entertainment and Motion Pictures LLP is an Indian content production company based in Mumbai, founded in 2011 by Nikkhil Advani, Monisha Advani and Madhu Bhojwani. It began with feature films and expanded into television, short films, telefilms and digital content. Its first feature production was D-Day.
debut: D-Day (2013), the company's first feature.
major_works: With Kapoor: D-Day (2013). Elsewhere, Airlift, Katti Batti and Hero.
recurring_themes: The ensemble thriller and the issue-driven commercial film.
creative_style: A director-founded company producing Advani's own films alongside others' work.
historical_importance: Not independently prominent, but a notable example of the director-owned production companies that proliferated in 2010s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and it is the company's own first film: D-Day (2013), in which Kapoor plays Iqbal Seth, a Dawood Ibrahim-like crime boss living under protection in Karachi. The role is among the most unsympathetic of his career and part of the late widening of his range.
biography: Emmay Entertainment's first film gave Rishi Kapoor one of his best late roles. Founded in 2011 by Nikkhil Advani with his sister Monisha Advani and Madhu Bhojwani, the company opened with D-Day in 2013 — Advani's thriller about an Indian intelligence operation to extract a fugitive gangster from Karachi — and cast Kapoor as the gangster. Coming a year after Agneepath's Rauf Lala, the performance confirmed that his second career would include genuine menace as well as benign fathers. The company went on to produce Airlift, Katti Batti and Hero, and to expand into television and digital work.

name: Epic Bhangra
career_background: A music act credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article under this name.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sanam Re (2016).
recurring_themes: Bhangra-inflected dance music.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sanam Re (2016), a T-Series romance directed by Divya Khosla Kumar in which Kapoor plays the hero's grandfather. The soundtrack is divided among several composers, of whom Mithoon is the best known.
biography: Epic Bhangra is credited among the composers of Sanam Re (2016) and has no documented history. The film is a T-Series production whose soundtrack was assembled from several contributors in the manner standard by the mid-2010s, with Mithoon's title song becoming one of the most streamed Hindi recordings of its year while the remaining credits left no trace. Kapoor appears as the grandfather whose remembered love frames the story. The contrast with the single-composer soundtracks of his youth is the point worth recording. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Eros International
career_background: Eros International is an Indian motion-picture production and distribution company founded in Mumbai by Arjan Lulla in 1977 and managed by his sons Kishore and Sunil Lulla. It is a subsidiary of Eros Media World, formed in 2020 and formerly known as Eros International Plc.
debut: Operating as a distributor from 1977 and later as a producer.
major_works: With Kapoor: Wedding Pullav (2015). Elsewhere, a very large distribution catalogue of Hindi films.
recurring_themes: Distribution and co-production across the commercial Hindi slate.
creative_style: A distributor-producer rather than a house with a creative signature.
historical_importance: One of the longest-established and most internationally active Indian film distributors.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Wedding Pullav (2015), the small romantic comedy the cinematographer Binod Pradhan directed, with Kapoor in support and songs by Salim–Sulaiman. It is among the slightest films of his last decade.
biography: Eros International appears once in this filmography, on Wedding Pullav (2015). Founded by Arjan Lulla in 1977 and run by his sons, the company became one of India's largest film distributors and a significant international presence, later reorganised as Eros Media World. Its one Kapoor credit is a minor romantic comedy directed by the cinematographer Binod Pradhan, with Salim–Sulaiman's songs and Kapoor in a supporting role — one of the several late films in which his participation was a mark of respectability rather than a part worth writing. The company's distribution catalogue, by contrast, includes a substantial share of the Hindi cinema of his lifetime.

name: F. A. Nadiadwala
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The Nadiadwala name recurs in this workbook — I. A. Nadiadwala and Sajid Nadiadwala also hold credits — indicating the long-running Bombay production family of that name.
major_works: With Kapoor: Hathyar (1989).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Hathyar (1989), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal-scored film from the crowded stretch at the turn of the 1990s when Kapoor released nine pictures in three years, most of them unreviewed.
biography: F. A. Nadiadwala produced Hathyar (1989) and has no documented biography. The name belongs to one of Bombay cinema's production families — I. A. Nadiadwala is credited elsewhere in this filmography, and Sajid Nadiadwala produced Housefull 2 two decades later — but the individual leaves no record. The film itself comes from the densest and least documented period of Kapoor's lead career, between 1989 and 1991, when his vehicles were mid-budget melodramas financed by small producers and scored, almost invariably, by Laxmikant–Pyarelal. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Farah Khan
career_background: Farah Khan Kunder (born 9 January 1965) is an Indian film director, choreographer, dancer, writer, producer and actress. She has choreographed more than a hundred songs in over eighty films, winning the National Film Award for Best Choreography and seven Filmfare Awards for Best Choreography. Her directorial debut Main Hoon Na (2004) and Om Shanti Om (2007) both earned her Filmfare nominations for Best Director, making her the second woman nominated in that category.
debut: Choreographing from 1987; directorial debut Main Hoon Na (2004).
major_works: With Kapoor: Om Shanti Om (2007). Elsewhere, Main Hoon Na, Tees Maar Khan and Happy New Year.
recurring_themes: Hindi cinema's own history as subject and joke; the reincarnation plot; the song as spectacle.
creative_style: A choreographer's cinema — set pieces first, built on affectionate pastiche of earlier Hindi film styles.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Choreography and seven Filmfare Awards for Best Choreography; two Filmfare nominations for Best Director.
historical_importance: The most prominent choreographer-turned-director in Hindi cinema, and only the second woman nominated for the Filmfare Best Director award.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Om Shanti Om (2007), in which Kapoor appears as himself. The film is a pastiche of the 1970s industry in which he had been a young star, and its reincarnation plot borrows directly from Karz (1980), one of his own defining films — so he appears in a film that is partly a tribute to his own period and partly a remake of its structure.
biography: Farah Khan directed the film that turned the cinema of Rishi Kapoor's youth into a subject. A choreographer of more than a hundred songs who won the National Film Award and seven Filmfare Awards in that craft before directing, Khan made Om Shanti Om in 2007: a reincarnation story set half in the 1970s Hindi film industry and half in the present, whose plot openly echoes Karz, the Subhash Ghai film that had given Kapoor his most durable role in 1980. Kapoor appears as himself, one of dozens of stars in a sequence of industry self-reference. It was his first film with Shah Rukh Khan's company, fifteen years after Deewana, and it marks the point at which his own past had become material for other people's films.

name: Farooq
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography under a single name, with no Wikipedia article identifiable to him; the bare name resolves to a disambiguation of unrelated figures.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994), co-produced with the actress Nutan and Surendra Bohra, who also directed — one of four Kapoor films released that year, all of them modest.
biography: Farooq is credited as one of three producers on Saajan Ka Ghar (1994) and cannot be identified further; the single-name credit resolves to nothing. The film is notable for a different name on the same list: the actress Nutan, one of the great leading ladies of the 1950s and 1960s, is credited as a co-producer. It was directed by Surendra Bohra with a Nadeem–Shravan score and belongs to the last year in which Kapoor was routinely cast as a lead. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: FilmStoc
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Nandita Das's Manto (2018), a biographical film about the Urdu writer Saadat Hasan Manto in which Kapoor has a small role — a festival-facing production quite unlike anything in his lead career.
biography: FilmStoc is one of four banners credited on Manto (2018) and has no recorded history. The film, directed by Nandita Das, follows the Urdu short-story writer Saadat Hasan Manto through his obscenity trials and his migration to Pakistan, and Kapoor appears briefly in it. Its music credits were mislabelled in the source data this workbook drew on — the infobox groups composers under 'Songs' and 'Background Score', which an earlier pass read as names — and its producer list runs to six people across four companies, of which this is the least documented. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: G. P. Sippy
career_background: Gopaldas Parmanand Sipahimalani (14 September 1914 – 25 December 2007), known as G. P. Sippy, was an Indian film producer and director. He produced Seeta Aur Geeta (1972), Shaan (1980), Saagar (1985) and Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (1992), and his magnum opus Sholay. He chaired the Film and Television Producers Guild of India for several years and won Filmfare Awards in 1968 and 1982. His son is the director Ramesh Sippy and his grandson the director Rohan Sippy.
debut: Producing from the 1950s; Sholay (1975) was his greatest success.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saagar (1985). Elsewhere, Sholay, Seeta Aur Geeta and Shaan.
recurring_themes: The large-scale commercial entertainment, made with the biggest stars available.
creative_style: A producer of scale who worked almost exclusively with his son Ramesh Sippy as director in his most successful years.
major_awards: Filmfare Awards in 1968 and 1982; long-serving chairman of the Film and Television Producers Guild of India.
historical_importance: The producer of Sholay, the most commercially and culturally significant Hindi film of its era.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Saagar (1985), directed by his son Ramesh Sippy, in which Kapoor plays Raja, the fisherman who loves Dimple Kapadia's Mona and loses her to Kamal Haasan's character. It is among the finest performances of his career and earned R. D. Burman a Filmfare nomination for one of the decade's best-selling soundtracks — a rare high point in an otherwise weak decade for him.
biography: G. P. Sippy produced Saagar, the best film Rishi Kapoor appeared in during his thinnest decade. The producer of Sholay and of Seeta Aur Geeta, Shaan and Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman, Sippy worked at the largest scale Hindi cinema offered and for years chaired its producers' guild. Saagar (1985), directed by his son Ramesh Sippy, reunited Kapoor with Dimple Kapadia twelve years after Bobby — her return to films after marriage — and cast him as the fisherman who loves her and loses. The performance is among his most admired, the R. D. Burman soundtrack among the decade's best-selling, and the film a reminder that when a major producer and director were behind him, his range was never the limitation.

name: G.M. Singh Nindrajog
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a serious one: Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986), adapted from Rajinder Singh Bedi's Urdu novel, in which Kapoor plays a man made to marry his dead brother's widow. It is among the few genuinely literary projects of his middle period, with Phani Majumdar and Madan Joshi credited as writers.
biography: G.M. Singh Nindrajog produced Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986) and has no documented biography. The film is one of the most substantial Rishi Kapoor made in his weakest decade: an adaptation of Rajinder Singh Bedi's Sahitya Akademi-winning Urdu novel about a widow compelled by custom to marry her late husband's younger brother, with Kapoor as the brother and Hema Malini as the widow. Phani Majumdar, a director working since 1938, was among its writers. That the producer of such a film left no record is characteristic of this workbook's lower tiers. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: GR8 Entertainment
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Wedding Pullav (2015).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Wedding Pullav (2015), the romantic comedy directed by the cinematographer Binod Pradhan with songs by Salim–Sulaiman and Kapoor in support — among the slightest films of his last decade.
biography: GR8 Entertainment is one of the banners on Wedding Pullav (2015) and has no recorded history. The film is a minor romantic comedy, notable only for having been directed by Binod Pradhan, one of Hindi cinema's most distinguished cinematographers, and for Kapoor's supporting presence. It belongs to the group of late films — Chalk N Duster, Wedding Pullav, All Is Well — in which his name lent respectability to productions that asked little of him. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Gautam Talwar
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chintu Ji (2009).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chintu Ji (2009), co-produced with Bobby Bedi of Kaleidoscope Entertainment, in which Kapoor plays a film star called Chintu Ji — his own childhood nickname — who returns to the village of his birth. It is the most directly self-referential film in the filmography.
biography: Gautam Talwar co-produced Chintu Ji (2009) and has no documented biography. The film is an oddity worth its place in this workbook: Kapoor plays a fictionalised version of himself, a star named Chintu Ji — the nickname he had carried since childhood and by which the industry knew him — who returns to his birthplace and is received as both celebrity and disappointment. His co-producer was Bobby Bedi, whose Kaleidoscope Entertainment had made Bandit Queen and Maqbool, which suggests the film was conceived as something more ambitious than a vehicle. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Gava
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography under a single name, with no Wikipedia article identifiable to him; the bare name resolves to a list of unrelated places.
major_works: With Kapoor: Karobaar (2000).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Karobaar: The Business of Love (2000), directed and produced by Rakesh Roshan with a Rajesh Roshan score, in which Kapoor's character is on the receiving end of a bargain over his wife — a premise he would play from the other side six years later in Love Ke Chakkar Mein.
biography: Gava is credited as a producer on Karobaar (2000) and cannot be identified further. The film is one of the last of Kapoor's leading roles, a Rakesh Roshan production scored by his brother Rajesh Roshan — the two-family combination behind four films in this workbook — built on a variation of the Indecent Proposal situation. Kapoor plays the husband whose marriage is bought; six years later, in Love Ke Chakkar Mein, he would play the buyer. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Gennady Vasilyev
career_background: Gennadi Leonidovich Vasilyev (31 August 1940 – 21 October 1999) was a Russian film director, best known for his fairy-tale film Finist, the Brave Falcon (1975).
debut: Directing in Soviet cinema from the early 1970s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ajooba (1991). Elsewhere, Finist, the Brave Falcon.
recurring_themes: The folk tale and the fantasy adventure.
creative_style: A Soviet director of fairy-tale spectacle, which is precisely what Ajooba required.
historical_importance: Not a major figure in Soviet cinema, but the co-director of one of the very few Indo-Soviet feature co-productions.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ajooba (1991), which he co-directed with Shashi Kapoor — an Indo-Soviet fantasy adventure shot partly at the Gorky Film Studio with Soviet crew, in which Rishi Kapoor was third-billed behind Amitabh Bachchan and Dimple Kapadia. It is the only international co-production in this filmography and one of its most expensive failures.
biography: Gennady Vasilyev is the only non-Indian director in this filmography. A Russian filmmaker known at home for the fairy-tale film Finist, the Brave Falcon, he co-directed Ajooba (1991) with Shashi Kapoor — an Indo-Soviet co-production with the Gorky Film Studio, Soviet cinematographers and the Soviet actress Ariadna Shengelaya in the cast, built as a swashbuckling fantasy around Amitabh Bachchan's masked avenger. Rishi Kapoor was third-billed. The film cost a great deal, failed in both countries, and remains a curiosity: a Hindi fantasy made under a bilateral cultural arrangement that was about to disappear with the Soviet Union itself. Vasilyev died in 1999.

name: George Joseph
career_background: A background-score composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article identifiable to him; the bare name resolves to a disambiguation page of unrelated figures.
major_works: With Kapoor: 102 Not Out (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: 102 Not Out (2018), Umesh Shukla's two-hander in which the 65-year-old Kapoor plays the 75-year-old son of Amitabh Bachchan's 102-year-old father — his last leading role. He wrote the score; the songs were by Salim–Sulaiman and others.
biography: George Joseph wrote the background score for 102 Not Out (2018) and cannot be identified further from the sources consulted here. The film is Rishi Kapoor's last leading role: adapted by Umesh Shukla from his own Gujarati play, it confines Kapoor and Amitabh Bachchan to a Mumbai house as a sulking seventy-five-year-old son and his relentlessly cheerful centenarian father. The two had first appeared together in Amar Akbar Anthony forty-one years earlier, and this was the ninth and last of their films — the only one in which Kapoor played the younger man. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Gorky Film Studio
career_background: Gorky Film Studio is a municipally owned film studio in Moscow, one of the oldest active studios in Russia. By the end of the Soviet Union it had produced more than a thousand films, many of them classics, some of which won international festival awards.
debut: Operating since the early Soviet period.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ajooba (1991). Elsewhere, more than a thousand Soviet films.
recurring_themes: The full range of Soviet production, including children's films and fairy tales.
creative_style: A state studio rather than a house with an authorial signature.
historical_importance: One of the principal studios of Soviet cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Ajooba (1991), the Indo-Soviet fantasy Shashi Kapoor co-directed with Gennady Vasilyev. Parts of the film were shot at the studio with Soviet crew, and Rishi Kapoor was third-billed behind Amitabh Bachchan and Dimple Kapadia. It is the only foreign studio credited anywhere in this filmography.
biography: Gorky Film Studio is the only foreign production house in this filmography. A municipal Moscow studio and one of the oldest in Russia, it produced more than a thousand films before the Soviet Union ended, and in 1991 it co-produced Ajooba with Shashi Kapoor — an Indo-Soviet fantasy adventure, partly shot at the studio, with Soviet cinematographers, a Soviet co-director in Gennady Vasilyev and the actress Ariadna Shengelaya in the cast. Rishi Kapoor was third-billed behind Amitabh Bachchan and Dimple Kapadia. The film failed, and the bilateral arrangements that made such co-productions possible dissolved with the state that had funded them.

name: Grand Master Movies
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Izzat Ki Roti (1993).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Izzat Ki Roti (1993), directed by K. Pappu with a Bappi Lahiri score and written in part by Ranbir Pushp — one of the modest melodramas of Kapoor's final years as a lead.
biography: Grand Master Movies is the banner on Izzat Ki Roti (1993) and has no recorded history. The film was directed by K. Pappu — a brother of Raj Kanwar, who had directed Deewana the previous year — with Bappi Lahiri's music and a script shared with Ranbir Pushp, and it belongs to the long tail of Kapoor's lead career, when his films were financed by companies that made one picture and vanished. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Guddu Dhanoa
career_background: Guddu Dhanoa is an Indian writer, producer and director of Hindi films, known for the action pictures Ziddi with Sunny Deol and Bichhoo with Bobby Deol. He is a cousin of Dharmendra and so related to the Deol family. His article records that he began as a producer for Shah Rukh Khan, who starred in Dhanoa's 1992 film Deewana.
debut: Producing from 1992 with Deewana; later directed action films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Deewana (1992). Elsewhere, Ziddi, Bichhoo and Jaani Dushman.
recurring_themes: The action melodrama built around a Deol.
creative_style: A commercial producer-director working largely within his extended family's star network.
historical_importance: The producer of Deewana, the film that introduced Shah Rukh Khan.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and the pivotal one of the later career: he produced Deewana (1992), in which Kapoor plays the singer presumed dead and the debuting Shah Rukh Khan the younger man his widow marries. His own article frames the film as the start of Khan's career — 'he started as a producer for Shahrukh Khan who starred in Dhanoa's 1992 film Deewana' — which is precisely how the film is remembered, and precisely why it marks the end of Kapoor's run as a romantic lead.
biography: Guddu Dhanoa produced the single most consequential film of Rishi Kapoor's later career, and his own article describes it from the other side. A cousin of Dharmendra who worked largely within the Deol family's orbit and later directed the action pictures Ziddi and Bichhoo, Dhanoa produced Deewana in 1992: Kapoor plays Ravi, a wealthy singer believed killed, and Shah Rukh Khan, in his film debut, the man his widow marries. Dhanoa's article records the film as the start of Khan's career. For Kapoor it was the end of something — the moment, performed on screen, at which the Hindi romantic lead passed to the next generation. The film was a hit, and he never carried another romance of that scale.

name: Gulab Singh Tanwar
career_background: Gulab Singh Tanwar, also known as Captain Gulab Singh (born 1964), is an Indian film producer and business figure who was formerly a pilot with Indian Airlines. His productions include Parched, Te3n and Rajma Chawal, and his article names 72 Hoorain among the films he is known for.
debut: Producing from 1999.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rajma Chawal (2018). Elsewhere, Parched and Te3n.
recurring_themes: Small and mid-budget films, including festival-facing work such as Parched.
creative_style: A producer from outside the industry backing directors with independent sensibilities.
historical_importance: Not substantially documented, though his slate includes internationally screened independent films.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Leena Yadav's Rajma Chawal (2018), in which Kapoor plays a widowed father in old Delhi who creates a fake online profile to reach his estranged son. Tanwar had earlier produced Yadav's Parched, which premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival, so the pairing brought Kapoor into a genuinely independent production.
biography: Gulab Singh Tanwar produced one of Rishi Kapoor's last and quietest performances. A former Indian Airlines pilot turned producer, Tanwar backed Leena Yadav's Parched, which premiered at Toronto, and then her Rajma Chawal in 2018 — a Netflix release in which Kapoor plays a widower in the old city of Delhi who, unable to speak to his son, poses online as a young woman to reach him. It is a small, melancholy part, of a kind unavailable to him in his leading years, and it belongs with Do Dooni Chaar and Sharmaji Namkeen among the late films that found something ordinary in him. He died two years later.

name: H. S. Bhattacharya
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Barood (1976).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Barood (1976), one of the run of films Kapoor made in the three years after Bobby, with a story by Sachin Bhowmick and lyrics by Anand Bakshi.
biography: H. S. Bhattacharya is credited as a producer on Barood (1976) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the rush of work that followed Bobby, when Kapoor at twenty-three was the most saleable young lover in Hindi cinema and producers financed almost anything he would appear in; Sachin Bhowmick supplied the story, as he did for several of the early successes, and Anand Bakshi the lyrics. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: HP Studios
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Nandita Das's Manto (2018), the biographical film about the Urdu writer Saadat Hasan Manto in which Kapoor has a small role. Four banners and six producers are credited on it, of which this is among the least documented.
biography: HP Studios is one of four banners credited on Manto (2018) and has no recorded history. The film follows the Urdu short-story writer Saadat Hasan Manto through obscenity trials in Bombay and his migration to Pakistan, and Kapoor appears briefly in it — one of the small parts he took in his last years in productions with no commercial expectations of him. Its financing was spread across six producers and four companies, a structure characteristic of festival-facing Indian cinema of the period. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Hari Om Entertainment
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own; the name redirects to a differently named company, so no history can be attributed to it with confidence here.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patiala House (2011).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Nikkhil Advani's Patiala House (2011), in which Kapoor plays the Southall patriarch whose bitterness after a racist attack leads him to forbid his son's cricket career — one of the stronger roles of his late period, and his fourth film opposite Dimple Kapadia.
biography: Hari Om Entertainment is one of three banners on Patiala House (2011) and has no verifiable history — its name redirects on Wikipedia to a company of another name, which this workbook declines to treat as the same entity. The film itself is among the better of Kapoor's late roles: Gurtej Singh Kahlon, a London Punjabi whose experience of racist violence has hardened into control over his son's life, played opposite Dimple Kapadia as his wife, the fourth of their four films together after Bobby, Saagar and Pyaar Mein Twist. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Hasina Moin
industry: Pakistani television and theatre; Hindi cinema
career_background: Haseena Moin (20 November 1941 – 26 March 2021) was a Pakistani dramatist, playwright and scriptwriter who wrote for stage, radio and television, including Pakistan Television's first original script, Kiran Kahani, in the early 1970s. She received the Pride of Performance award from the President of Pakistan in 1987 and worked as a school principal and educationist. Her article records that Raj Kapoor asked her to write the dialogue for his project Henna.
debut: Writing for Pakistani radio and television from 1970; Kiran Kahani was PTV's first original script.
major_works: With Kapoor: Henna (1991). Elsewhere, a large body of Pakistani television drama.
recurring_themes: Women's lives in middle-class Pakistani settings, written with unusual wit and independence.
creative_style: A television dramatist whose dialogue was prized for its naturalism and humour, and whose heroines were notably self-possessed.
major_awards: Pride of Performance, awarded by the President of Pakistan in 1987.
historical_importance: One of the most important Pakistani television writers of her generation, and the author of PTV's first original script.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a notable piece of film history: Henna (1991), the cross-border romance in which Kapoor's Indian engineer loses his memory and is sheltered by a Pakistani village girl. Her article records that Raj Kapoor wanted her to write the dialogue for the project, and the choice of a Pakistani dramatist for a film about the border is the clearest statement of what he intended by it. Raj Kapoor died before completing the film; his son Randhir finished it.
biography: Haseena Moin wrote dialogue for Henna, the last project Raj Kapoor conceived and the most politically pointed film in this filmography. A Pakistani dramatist who wrote PTV's first original script and became the most admired television writer of her generation there, honoured with the Pride of Performance in 1987, she was approached by Raj Kapoor — her article records that he wanted her for the dialogue of his dream project. Henna casts Rishi Kapoor as an Indian who loses his memory across the border and is cared for by a Pakistani woman, and hiring a Pakistani writer to voice that half of the film was a deliberate act. Raj Kapoor died in 1988 before shooting was complete; Randhir Kapoor finished it and released it in 1991. Moin died in Karachi in 2021.

name: Hema Malini
career_background: Hema Malini (born 16 October 1948) is an Indian actress, director, producer and politician. One of the most successful leading actresses of Hindi cinema in the 1970s, she won the Filmfare Award for Best Actress and later the Filmfare Lifetime Achievement Award in 2000 and a Filmfare Special Award in 2019 for fifty years in cinema. She received the Padma Shri in 2000, served in the Rajya Sabha from 2003 to 2009 and from 2011 to 2012, and has been the Bharatiya Janata Party member of the Lok Sabha for Mathura since 2014.
debut: Acting from 1963; directing from the 1990s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011), which she directed, produced and co-wrote. Elsewhere, as an actress, Sholay, Seeta Aur Geeta and Dream Girl.
recurring_themes: As a director, family melodrama and the search for identity; as an actress, the self-possessed heroine of the 1970s.
creative_style: A star-director whose films are built around family relationships and, latterly, her own daughter's casting.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Actress; Filmfare Lifetime Achievement Award (2000); Filmfare Special Award (2019); Padma Shri (2000).
historical_importance: One of the defining female stars of 1970s Hindi cinema and, since 2014, a sitting member of parliament.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011), which she wrote, produced and directed, starring her daughter Esha Deol, with Kapoor among a cast of veteran actors in supporting parts. Their careers had run in parallel for forty years without intersecting — she was the leading female star of the decade in which he became a leading man — and this late, little-seen film is their only joint credit in this filmography.
biography: Hema Malini directed the only film she and Rishi Kapoor made together, four decades after they became stars in the same industry. The dominant female lead of 1970s Hindi cinema — Sholay, Seeta Aur Geeta, Dream Girl — and later a Padma Shri recipient, Rajya Sabha member and, since 2014, the BJP's member of parliament for Mathura, she turned to directing in her later career. Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011) was her third film as director: a search-for-identity drama she also wrote and produced, built around her daughter Esha Deol, with Kapoor and several contemporaries in support. It failed commercially and is among the least discussed entries in this filmography, which makes the absence of any earlier collaboration between two of the decade's biggest stars the more striking fact.

name: Hema Malini Creations
career_background: The production banner of the actress and filmmaker Hema Malini, credited on Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011). The company has no Wikipedia article of its own; her article is cited on her own row in this sheet.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011).
recurring_themes: Family drama and the search for identity.
creative_style: A star's own banner, used for the films she directed.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011), which Hema Malini wrote, produced and directed and in which her daughter Esha Deol starred, with Kapoor among a cast of veterans in support. It is the only joint credit in this filmography between Kapoor and the leading female star of the decade in which he became a lead.
biography: Hema Malini Creations is the banner behind Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011) and has no history of its own beyond its proprietor's. The film was Hema Malini's third as director — she also wrote and produced it — and was built around her daughter Esha Deol, with Rishi Kapoor and several of his contemporaries in supporting parts. Its chief interest for this filmography is the absence it exposes: Hema Malini was the dominant female star of the 1970s, exactly the decade in which Kapoor became a leading man, and this late, little-seen film is the only credit they share. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Himanshu Mehra
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Besharam (2013).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Besharam (2013), Abhinav Kashyap's comedy and the only film in which Rishi Kapoor, his wife Neetu Singh and their son Ranbir Kapoor all appear — the parents as police officers, the son as the title character. It failed commercially.
biography: Himanshu Mehra produced Besharam (2013) and has no documented biography. The film is a family document more than a work: Abhinav Kashyap's follow-up to Dabangg cast Ranbir Kapoor as a cheerful car thief and both his parents — Rishi Kapoor and Neetu Singh, who had been paired as romantic leads in a dozen films of the 1970s — as the police officers pursuing him. It is the only film in which all three appear, and it was a critical and commercial failure. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Hitesh Bhatia
career_background: An Indian director and writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sharmaji Namkeen (2022).
recurring_themes: The retired man's second life; gentle domestic comedy.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is the last in this filmography: Sharmaji Namkeen (2022), which Bhatia wrote and directed. Kapoor plays a newly retired man who discovers a talent for cooking and joins a women's kitchen-party circuit; he had shot roughly half of it when he died in April 2020, and Excel Entertainment completed the film by having Paresh Rawal perform the remaining scenes as the same character — an arrangement without real precedent in Hindi cinema.
biography: Hitesh Bhatia wrote and directed Rishi Kapoor's last film, and almost nothing about him is documented. Sharmaji Namkeen (2022) is a small, warm comedy about a man forced into retirement who finds purpose cooking for other people's parties — the kind of ordinary, unglamorous part that only became available to Kapoor after Do Dooni Chaar. He died in April 2020 with the film half shot, and rather than recast or abandon it, the producers had Paresh Rawal play the remaining scenes as the same man, so that two actors alternate in the role. The film was released posthumously in 2022 and closes this filmography. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Honey Trehan
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sharmaji Namkeen (2022).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sharmaji Namkeen (2022), Kapoor's last, which he was shooting when he died in April 2020 and which was completed with Paresh Rawal playing the remaining scenes as the same character.
biography: Honey Trehan is credited as a producer on Sharmaji Namkeen (2022) and has no documented biography. The film is the last entry in this filmography and the only one in which Kapoor's performance is incomplete: he had shot about half of Hitesh Bhatia's comedy about a retired man who takes up cooking when he died in April 2020, and the producers chose to finish it with Paresh Rawal in the remaining scenes rather than abandon it. Kapoor had acted opposite Rawal five years earlier in Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Hriday Shetty
career_background: Hriday Shetty is an Indian film director, the son of the stuntman and actor M. B. Shetty and the half-brother of the director and producer Rohit Shetty. His films include Chaalis Chauraasi, Godfather: The Legend Continues, Pyaar Mein Twist, Daag – Shades of Love and Plan.
debut: Directing from the 1990s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pyaar Mein Twist (2005). Elsewhere, Plan and Chaalis Chauraasi.
recurring_themes: Crime comedy and the ensemble caper; occasionally the late-life romance.
creative_style: A commercial director working in modest budgets across genres.
historical_importance: Not substantially documented, though his family is central to contemporary Hindi action cinema through his half-brother Rohit Shetty.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is one of the most interesting in the whole filmography: Pyaar Mein Twist (2005), which Kapoor himself produced, casts him and Dimple Kapadia — his co-star from Bobby thirty-two years earlier — as a widower and widow whose late romance is opposed by their adult children. It is Bobby's structure with the generations reversed: the lovers are old, and the obstacle is filial rather than parental.
biography: Hriday Shetty directed the single most revealing film of Rishi Kapoor's late career. The son of the stuntman M. B. Shetty and half-brother of Rohit Shetty, he has worked as a commercial director since the 1990s on films including Plan and Chaalis Chauraasi. Pyaar Mein Twist (2005) is a small picture that Kapoor produced himself: he and Dimple Kapadia, the girl of Bobby, play a widower and a widow in their fifties whose courtship their grown children try to stop. Thirty-two years after the film that made them, the same pair are performing the same situation with the opposition inverted — a deliberate echo, and the clearest evidence in this workbook that Kapoor understood his own romantic persona as material.

name: Hussain Dalal
career_background: Hussain Dalal (born 27 March 1989 in Mumbai) is an Indian actor and screenwriter known for dialogue writing in Hindi films, including Yeh Jawaani Hai Deewani (2013), Margarita with a Straw (2014), 2 States (2014) and Brahmāstra: Part One – Shiva (2022). In 2017 he appeared as one of three mentors on a television show.
debut: Writing from 2012.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sanam Re (2016). Elsewhere, Yeh Jawaani Hai Deewani, 2 States and Brahmāstra.
recurring_themes: Contemporary youth dialogue; the urban romance of the 2010s.
creative_style: A dialogue specialist with an ear for how young urban Indians actually speak.
historical_importance: One of the most employed dialogue writers of 2010s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sanam Re (2016), the T-Series romance in which Kapoor plays the hero's grandfather. The generational link is the more interesting fact — two of Dalal's best-known films, Yeh Jawaani Hai Deewani and Brahmāstra, were vehicles for Ranbir Kapoor, so the writer worked for the son far more often than for the father.
biography: Hussain Dalal wrote dialogue for one Rishi Kapoor film and for several of his son's. Born in Mumbai in 1989 and writing from 2012, Dalal became one of the busiest dialogue writers of the 2010s, with Yeh Jawaani Hai Deewani, 2 States, Margarita with a Straw and Brahmāstra to his name — the first and last of those built around Ranbir Kapoor. His single credit with Rishi Kapoor is Sanam Re (2016), a T-Series romance in which the older actor plays the grandfather whose remembered love frames the younger couple's story. The pattern recurs across this workbook's final stretch: the writers and directors of the 2010s mostly encountered the father as a supporting presence while working for the son.

name: I. A. Nadiadwala
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The Nadiadwala name recurs here — F. A. Nadiadwala and Sajid Nadiadwala also hold credits — indicating the long-running Bombay production family.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rafoo Chakkar (1975).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rafoo Chakkar (1975), the cross-dressing comedy — a Hindi reworking of Some Like It Hot — in which Kapoor and Paintal disguise themselves as women to escape gangsters. It is among the few outright farces of his early career and came two years after Bobby.
biography: I. A. Nadiadwala produced Rafoo Chakkar (1975) and has no documented biography. The film is Hindi cinema's best-known reworking of Some Like It Hot, with Kapoor spending much of it in women's clothing to hide from gangsters, written by Kader Khan and K. K. Shukla and scored by Kalyanji–Anandji. It demonstrates something the romantic record obscures: within two years of Bobby he was already being cast in broad comedy, and the farcical register would return repeatedly, through Bol Radha Bol and the Housefull films. The Nadiadwala name recurs across this workbook without any individual leaving a record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ila Bedi Dutta
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Agneepath (2012).
recurring_themes: The revenge epic and the criminal family.
creative_style: Not documented; she is credited alongside Karan Malhotra on the remake's screenplay.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a significant one: Karan Malhotra's Agneepath (2012), the Dharma Productions remake in which Kapoor plays Rauf Lala, a trafficker in women whose geniality makes him frightening. The performance is widely counted among the best of his career and the clearest proof that his late range extended well beyond benign fathers. She is one of the few women credited as writers in this workbook.
biography: Ila Bedi Dutta co-wrote Agneepath (2012) and has no documented biography. The film is Karan Malhotra's remake of the 1990 Amitabh Bachchan picture, produced by Dharma, and it gave Rishi Kapoor the role of Rauf Lala — a Mumbai trader in women and drugs, played with a warmth that makes him worse rather than better, under prosthetic teeth and a skullcap. For an actor who had spent forty years being likeable, it was a genuine transformation, and it reset expectations of what he could be cast as in the eight years he had left. She is among the very small number of women credited as writers anywhere in this filmography.

name: Illuminati Films
career_background: The production banner credited on Love Aaj Kal (2009). It has no Wikipedia article of its own — the name redirects to the actor Saif Ali Khan, who founded the company — so no independent history can be attributed to it here.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Aaj Kal (2009).
recurring_themes: Contemporary urban romance.
creative_style: A star-owned banner producing vehicles for its proprietor.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Imtiaz Ali's Love Aaj Kal (2009), in which Kapoor plays the elderly Veer Singh whose decades-long courtship in 1960s Delhi forms the film's period strand against a modern couple's casual romance. The role uses his own screen history as the content of the film's nostalgia.
biography: Illuminati Films produced Love Aaj Kal (2009), and the company exists in this workbook only as a name: its Wikipedia entry redirects to Saif Ali Khan, who founded it and starred in the film. The film itself is among the most pointed uses of Rishi Kapoor's past. Imtiaz Ali sets a contemporary couple's casual, self-interested romance against the patient courtship of an older man, Veer Singh, played by Kapoor in the present day and by a younger actor in the 1960s flashbacks. Casting the definitive lover-boy of the 1970s as the embodiment of a slower and more devoted idea of love is the film's argument in miniature. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Imtiaz Ali
career_background: Imtiaz Ali (born 16 June 1971 in Jamshedpur) is an Indian filmmaker best known for writing and directing the romantic comedies Socha Na Tha (2005), Jab We Met (2007) and Love Aaj Kal (2009), and the dramas Rockstar (2011), Highway (2014), Tamasha (2015) and Jab Harry Met Sejal (2017). His uncle is the theatre figure Khalid Ahmed.
debut: Working from 1994 in television; directorial debut Socha Na Tha (2005).
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Aaj Kal (2009). Elsewhere, Jab We Met, Rockstar, Highway and Tamasha.
recurring_themes: Love across time and distance; the journey as self-discovery; the romantic who cannot recognise his own feeling until too late.
creative_style: A writer-director of romance whose films are structured on travel and on deferred recognition, with music used as narration.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue and three Filmfare nominations for Best Director.
historical_importance: The most distinctive director of romance in Hindi cinema after Yash Chopra, and the filmmaker most responsible for its contemporary idiom.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and an unusually pointed one: Love Aaj Kal (2009), in which Kapoor plays the elderly Veer Singh, whose patient decades-long courtship in 1960s Delhi is set against a modern couple's casual, self-protective romance. Casting the defining lover-boy of 1970s cinema as the embodiment of an older, more devoted idea of love makes his own screen past the film's argument. Ali later directed Ranbir Kapoor in Rockstar and Tamasha, so his association with the family continued through the son.
biography: Imtiaz Ali gave Rishi Kapoor the role that most explicitly used his own history as a romantic lead. Born in Jamshedpur in 1971, Ali became the most distinctive director of Hindi romance of his generation — Jab We Met, Rockstar, Highway, Tamasha — building films on travel, deferred recognition and music, and winning a Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue with three Best Director nominations. In Love Aaj Kal (2009) he set a contemporary couple's wary romance against the story of Veer Singh, an older man whose courtship took decades; Kapoor plays Veer in the present, narrating his own past. The casting is the point: the actor who had embodied uncomplicated devotion in the 1970s appears as its last witness. Ali went on to direct Kapoor's son Ranbir twice.

name: Inderjit Films Combine
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sadiyaan (2010).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Sadiyaan (2010), Raj Kanwar's partition-era romance written in part by his son Abhay Kanwar, with Kapoor in a supporting role — eighteen years after Kanwar had directed him in Deewana.
biography: Inderjit Films Combine is the banner on Sadiyaan (2010) and has no recorded history. The film reunited Kapoor with Raj Kanwar, the director whose debut Deewana had, in 1992, staged the handover of the Hindi romantic lead from Kapoor to Shah Rukh Khan. Eighteen years later Kanwar cast him in support in a partition romance, from a script his own son Abhay Kanwar worked on, and the film passed unnoticed. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ismail Darbar
career_background: Ismail Darbar, from Surat in Gujarat, is an Indian film score composer, music director, instrumentalist, singer and violinist. He won the National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam (1999).
debut: Composing from the late 1990s; Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam (1999) was his breakthrough.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kaanchi: The Unbreakable (2014). Elsewhere, Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam and Devdas.
