recurring_themes: Grand, classically inflected romantic scores for large-scale melodrama.
creative_style: A violinist's orchestration, built on classical Indian forms and used at operatic scale, closely associated with Sanjay Leela Bhansali's early films.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam (1999).
historical_importance: The composer of two of the most musically ambitious Hindi films of the turn of the century, Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam and Devdas.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and late in both careers: Subhash Ghai's Kaanchi: The Unbreakable (2014), with Kapoor in support. Darbar shares the soundtrack credit with Salim–Sulaiman. The film failed, and neither man's reputation rests on it.
biography: Ismail Darbar scored one film in this filmography, long after the work that made him. A violinist from Surat, Darbar won the National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam in 1999 and then wrote Devdas, two soundtracks of unusual classical ambition that defined Sanjay Leela Bhansali's early cinema. By 2014 he was sharing the credit on Subhash Ghai's Kaanchi: The Unbreakable with Salim–Sulaiman, a film that failed and in which Kapoor appeared in support — thirty-four years after Ghai had directed him in Karz. Both the composer and the actor were working well below their best in it.

name: J. C. Bhagat
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Barood (1976).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Barood (1976), from the run of films Kapoor made in the three years after Bobby, with a Sachin Bhowmick story and Anand Bakshi's lyrics.
biography: J. C. Bhagat is one of the producers credited on Barood (1976) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the glut of work that followed Bobby, when a twenty-three-year-old Kapoor was the most saleable young lover in Hindi cinema and producers financed almost anything he would appear in — Sachin Bhowmick supplying the story, Anand Bakshi the lyrics, and the picture itself leaving little trace. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: J. P. Dutta
career_background: Jyoti Prakash Dutta, known as J. P. Dutta, is an Indian director, writer and producer in Hindi cinema, born in Bombay and best known for Ghulami (1985), Yateem (1988), Batwara (1989), Kshatriya (1993) and Border (1997). He is married to the actress Bindiya Goswami.
debut: Directing from 1985 with Ghulami.
major_works: With Kapoor: Hathyar (1989). Elsewhere, Ghulami, Batwara, Kshatriya, Border and LOC Kargil.
recurring_themes: Feud, honour and vengeance in rural Rajasthan; later the war film as national epic.
creative_style: Large-canvas melodrama with ensemble casts, long running times and a taste for the ballad of masculine honour.
historical_importance: The director of Border, one of the most commercially successful war films in Indian cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Hathyar (1989), a crime drama from the period when Kapoor was releasing three or four films a year. It belongs to Dutta's early run of honour-and-vengeance pictures rather than to Kapoor's romantic line, and gave the actor one of the harder registers he occasionally tried in that decade.
biography: J. P. Dutta directed one Rishi Kapoor film, and it sits oddly in both filmographies. Dutta made his name on rural feud dramas — Ghulami, Batwara, Kshatriya — before Border in 1997 made him the most commercially successful war-film director in India. Hathyar (1989), his film with Kapoor, is a Bombay crime drama from the densest stretch of the actor's career, when nine of his films appeared in three years and most were melodramas. Dutta's cinema is organised around masculine honour and violence rather than courtship, which makes the pairing an experiment on Kapoor's part — one of several in that decade, when the romantic formula was no longer reliably selling.

name: Jagdish C. Sharma
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zamana (1985).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Zamana (1985), directed by Ramesh Talwar from a Salim–Javed script written before the duo's split — one of the few Salim–Javed properties Kapoor appeared in, and by his article's account one of only two Talwar films that succeeded.
biography: Jagdish C. Sharma produced Zamana (1985) and has no documented biography. The film is of modest interest for a structural reason: it was made from material written by Salim–Javed, the duo whose angry-young-man scripts had defined 1970s Hindi cinema around Amitabh Bachchan rather than around romantic leads like Kapoor, and it reached the screen only after the pair had separated. Ramesh Talwar directed; his own article records that Zamana was one of just two of his seven films to succeed commercially. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Jagdish Sidana
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sher Dil (1990).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sher Dil (1990), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal-scored picture from the stretch between 1989 and 1991 in which Kapoor released nine films, nearly all of them unreviewed.
biography: Jagdish Sidana produced Sher Dil (1990) and has no documented biography. The film comes from the least documented period of this filmography: between 1989 and 1991 Kapoor appeared in nine releases, financed by small producers, directed by men with one-line records, and scored almost without exception by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, whose thirty-two credits here are concentrated in exactly these years. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Jagjit Khurana
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Karz (1980).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented, though his one credit is on a film of lasting influence.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a consequential one: he co-produced Subhash Ghai's Karz (1980) with Akhtar Farooqui. Kapoor's Monty — the stage singer who recovers the memory of his own murder — is among the most durable roles of his career, and the film's Laxmikant–Pyarelal songs have been remade and sampled for four decades.
biography: Jagjit Khurana co-produced Karz (1980) and has no documented biography. Subhash Ghai's reincarnation thriller is one of the two or three films on which Rishi Kapoor's reputation rests: he plays Monty, a stage performer haunted by the murder of his previous self, and the film's songs — 'Om Shanti Om', 'Dard-e-Dil' — outlived almost everything else released that year. It was remade outright in 2008 and its structure borrowed repeatedly, including by Farah Khan's Om Shanti Om, in which Kapoor himself appears. Neither of its two producers left any biographical record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Jaideep Sahni
career_background: Jaideep Sahni, from New Delhi, is an Indian screenwriter and lyricist known for Bunty Aur Babli (2005), Chak De! India (2007), Rocket Singh: Salesman of the Year (2009) and Shuddh Desi Romance (2013). He won the Filmfare Awards for Best Dialogue and Best Story for Company (2002) and the Filmfare Award for Best Screenplay for Khosla Ka Ghosla (2006), as well as the IIFA Award for Best Story for Chak De! India.
debut: Writing from 2000; his breakthrough was Company (2002).
major_works: With Kapoor: Shuddh Desi Romance (2013). Elsewhere, Company, Khosla Ka Ghosla, Bunty Aur Babli, Chak De! India and Rocket Singh.
recurring_themes: Small-town and lower-middle-class India rendered precisely; work, aspiration and institutional frustration; the unheroic protagonist.
creative_style: One of the most admired screenwriters of his generation, writing in close observational detail and in the actual idiom of the places he sets his films.
major_awards: Filmfare Awards for Best Dialogue and Best Story (Company) and Best Screenplay (Khosla Ka Ghosla); IIFA Award for Best Story (Chak De! India).
historical_importance: Among the writers who reoriented mainstream Hindi cinema towards ordinary Indian lives in the 2000s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Shuddh Desi Romance (2013), a Yash Raj romance about commitment-shy young people in Jaipur, in which Kapoor plays a wedding contractor. It is a small part, but the pairing is notable — the writer most identified with unglamorous realism working with the actor who had embodied Hindi cinema's most idealised romance.
biography: Jaideep Sahni wrote one film in which Rishi Kapoor appears, and the contrast between their sensibilities is instructive. Sahni is among the most respected screenwriters in Hindi cinema — Company, Khosla Ka Ghosla, Bunty Aur Babli, Chak De! India, Rocket Singh — a writer of work, class and small-town specificity who has won Filmfare Awards for dialogue, story and screenplay. Shuddh Desi Romance (2013) applies that method to romance itself: young people in Jaipur who keep abandoning weddings because they cannot commit. Kapoor plays the wedding contractor who keeps having to arrange them. The actor whose career was built on love as destiny appears, at the end of it, in a film about love as hesitation.

name: Jaidev
career_background: Jaidev Verma (3 August 1918 – 6 January 1987), known as Jaidev, was a music composer in Hindi films, born in Nairobi and resident in Bombay. He is best known for Hum Dono (1961), Reshma Aur Shera (1971), Prem Parbat, Gharaonda (1977) and Gaman (1978), and won the National Film Award for Best Music Direction three times — for Reshma Aur Shera, Gaman and Ankahee.
debut: Working in film from the 1930s as a performer, later composing.
major_works: With Kapoor: Laila Majnu (1976). Elsewhere, Hum Dono, Reshma Aur Shera, Gharaonda and Gaman.
recurring_themes: The ghazal and the restrained, classically grounded film song; parallel-cinema scores.
creative_style: A composer of austere, melodically exact songs, valued more by critics and musicians than by the commercial market.
major_awards: Three National Film Awards for Best Music Direction — Reshma Aur Shera (1972), Gaman (1979) and Ankahee (1985).
historical_importance: One of the most critically admired Hindi film composers, and among the few to win the National Film Award for music three times.
relationship_with_actor: One film: H. S. Rawail's Laila Majnu (1976), in which Kapoor played Qais in the classical Arabic love tragedy. The film carries two composer credits, Jaidev and Madan Mohan, and this workbook records both as credited rather than assigning the score to either; Madan Mohan had died in July 1975, the year before the film's release.
biography: Jaidev is among the most critically admired composers in this filmography, and he worked on one of its most ambitious films. A three-time National Film Award winner for Reshma Aur Shera, Gaman and Ankahee, he wrote in a spare, classically grounded idiom — Hum Dono, Gharaonda — that earned more respect than money. His Kapoor credit is Laila Majnu (1976), H. S. Rawail's version of the Qais and Laila legend, which asked the twenty-four-year-old star for tragic rather than teenage love and succeeded commercially. The film carries two composer credits, Jaidev and Madan Mohan, the latter having died in July 1975; this workbook records both as credited without deciding how the work was divided. Jaidev died in January 1987.

name: Jatish Varma
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Nandita Das's Manto (2018), the biographical film about the Urdu writer Saadat Hasan Manto, screened at Cannes in the Un Certain Regard section, in which Kapoor has a small role.
biography: Jatish Varma is one of six producers credited on Manto (2018) and has no documented biography. The film, which Nandita Das wrote and directed, follows the Urdu short-story writer Saadat Hasan Manto through obscenity trials in Bombay and his migration to Pakistan, and was screened at Cannes in Un Certain Regard; Kapoor appears briefly. Its financing was spread across six producers and four companies, a structure typical of festival-facing Indian cinema, and most of those names leave no trace. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Jawaharlal Bafna
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani (1988).
recurring_themes: The joint-family melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani (1988), the first of Kalpataru's five household melodramas with Kapoor, a remake of a Telugu film whose real subject is a mother-in-law's cruelty to her daughters-in-law, with Kader Khan among its writers.
biography: Jawaharlal Bafna produced Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani (1988) and has no documented biography. The film opens the run of five family melodramas Kalpataru directed with Kapoor between 1988 and 1994 — the densest and least documented cluster in this filmography — and is a remake of a Telugu original in which the drama belongs to the household's women rather than to any romance. Kapoor plays a son whose marriage is destroyed by his own suspicion, with a second relationship scored separately in this workbook. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Jay Prakash
career_background: A director and writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saajan Ki Baahon Mein (1995).
recurring_themes: Romantic melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Saajan Ki Baahon Mein (1995), written by Sachin Bhowmick and Rumi Jaffery with a Nadeem–Shravan score — one of the last romances built on Kapoor's leading persona before it was retired.
biography: Jay Prakash directed Saajan Ki Baahon Mein (1995) and has no documented biography. The film is among the last romances written to Rishi Kapoor's established image: Sachin Bhowmick, who had supplied the plots of Khel Khel Mein and Karz two decades earlier, wrote the story; Rumi Jaffery, the David Dhawan comedy specialist, shared the script; Nadeem–Shravan, the dominant composers of the decade, wrote the songs. The formula was intact and the audience had gone. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Jayant Dharmadhikari
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rafoo Chakkar (1975).
recurring_themes: Farce and disguise.
creative_style: Not documented; he is credited alongside Kader Khan and K. K. Shukla.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rafoo Chakkar (1975), the Hindi reworking of Some Like It Hot in which Kapoor spends much of the picture disguised as a woman — one of the earliest demonstrations that his range included broad comedy as well as romance.
biography: Jayant Dharmadhikari is credited as a writer on Rafoo Chakkar (1975) and has no documented biography. The film, written with Kader Khan and K. K. Shukla and scored by Kalyanji–Anandji, transplants Some Like It Hot to Bombay, with Kapoor and Paintal hiding from gangsters in women's clothes. It came two years after Bobby and is evidence against reading his early career as uninterrupted romance: the farce was there from the start, and it returned in Bol Radha Bol and the late Housefull films. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Jayant Gilatar
career_background: A director credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chalk N Duster (2016).
recurring_themes: The institutional drama; teachers and schools.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chalk N Duster (2016), a drama about schoolteachers resisting a commercialising management, with an ensemble including Shabana Azmi and Juhi Chawla and Kapoor in support — one of the small, socially minded pictures of his last years.
biography: Jayant Gilatar directed Chalk N Duster (2016) and has no documented biography. The film is a modest drama about two teachers and the pressures of commercialised schooling, cast with veterans — Shabana Azmi, Juhi Chawla, Divya Dutta — and Kapoor in a supporting role. It belongs with Chalk N Duster's near-contemporaries Wedding Pullav and All Is Well among the late films in which his participation lent credibility to small productions rather than carrying them. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Jeet Gannguli
career_background: Jeet Gannguli, born Chandrajeet Ganguly on 24 May 1971, is an Indian playback singer and composer working in Hindi and Bengali cinema. He is from Baranagar in Kolkata and has recorded for Sony Music, T-Series, Saregama, Zee Music and SVF.
debut: Composing from 2001, initially as co-composer with Pritam on Tere Liye.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sanam Re (2016). Elsewhere, a large body of Bengali film music and Hindi romantic ballads.
recurring_themes: The romantic ballad; melody-led songwriting for both Bengali and Hindi audiences.
creative_style: A melodist working in the tradition of Bengali film song, with a parallel career as a singer.
historical_importance: One of the most prolific composers in modern Bengali cinema and a regular contributor to Hindi romantic soundtracks.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sanam Re (2016), a T-Series romance directed by Divya Khosla Kumar in which Kapoor plays the hero's grandfather. He is one of several composers on the soundtrack, of whom Mithoon — who wrote the title song — is the best known.
biography: Jeet Gannguli contributed to the soundtrack of Sanam Re (2016), one of Rishi Kapoor's last supporting roles. Born Chandrajeet Ganguly in Kolkata in 1971, Gannguli began in Hindi cinema as Pritam's co-composer on Tere Liye in 2001 and went on to become one of the most prolific composers in Bengali film music while supplying romantic ballads to Hindi productions. Sanam Re is a T-Series film whose soundtrack was split among several composers — the norm by then — with Mithoon's title song carrying the picture commercially. Kapoor plays the grandfather whose remembered love frames the younger couple's story, one of several late parts that traded on the audience's memory of him.

name: Jeetendra
career_background: Ravi Kapoor, known professionally as Jeetendra, is an Indian actor, producer and businessman regarded as one of the most successful stars of Hindi cinema, with more than 200 films and, by his article's account, over 120 hits across six decades. He received the Filmfare Lifetime Achievement Award at the 48th ceremony. His home banner is Tirupati Films, and the director Abhishek Kapoor is his nephew.
debut: On screen from 1959; a leading star from the mid-1960s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Deedar-E-Yaar (1982), which he presented through Tirupati Films. Elsewhere, Farz, Caravan, Himmatwala and a long run of 1980s hits.
recurring_themes: The dancing hero of the 1970s and the southern-remake action melodrama of the 1980s.
creative_style: A star whose production involvement served his own vehicles and those of filmmakers in his orbit.
major_awards: Filmfare Lifetime Achievement Award at the 48th Filmfare Awards.
historical_importance: One of the most commercially successful Hindi stars of the 1970s and 1980s, and a contemporary of Kapoor's in exactly those years.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, as the presenter of H. S. Rawail's Deedar-E-Yaar (1982) under his own Tirupati Films banner. His article describes the outcome plainly: the film, which also starred Rekha, Rishi Kapoor and Tina Munim, 'failed to live up to the expectations and proved to be a major box office flop with minimal recovery of the investment'. One further note for this workbook: Jeetendra's real name is Ravi Kapoor, which is also the name of an unrelated screenwriter with five credits in this filmography.
biography: Jeetendra presented Deedar-E-Yaar (1982), one of the most expensive failures in this filmography, under his own Tirupati Films banner. Born Ravi Kapoor and one of the biggest stars of the 1970s and 1980s — more than 200 films, over 120 of them hits by his article's reckoning, and a Filmfare Lifetime Achievement Award — he was Rishi Kapoor's direct contemporary and competitor for much of that period. Deedar-E-Yaar, H. S. Rawail's lavish Muslim social with Rekha, Tina Munim and Kapoor, lost most of its investment, as Jeetendra's own article records. The coincidence of his birth name with that of an unrelated writer credited on five Kapoor films is noted here to prevent the two being conflated.

name: Jeethu Joseph
career_background: Jeethu Joseph, from Muvattupuzha in Kerala, is an Indian director and screenwriter working principally in Malayalam cinema since 2007.
debut: Directing from 2007 in Malayalam.
major_works: With Kapoor: The Body (2019). Elsewhere, his Malayalam thrillers.
recurring_themes: The procedural thriller built on concealment and reversal.
creative_style: A thriller specialist whose films turn on a withheld piece of information.
historical_importance: One of the most commercially successful directors of Malayalam thrillers of his period.
relationship_with_actor: One film: The Body (2019), a Hindi remake of the Spanish thriller of the same name, in which Kapoor plays the police officer investigating a corpse's disappearance from a morgue. It was the last film released in his lifetime — he died five months later — and a procedural part of a kind entirely absent from his leading years.
biography: Jeethu Joseph directed the last film released in Rishi Kapoor's lifetime. A Malayalam filmmaker from Muvattupuzha working since 2007 and known for tightly plotted thrillers, Joseph was brought in to remake the Spanish film The Body, whose original writer-director Oriol Paulo also appears in this workbook's credits. Kapoor plays the police officer running the investigation after a body vanishes from a morgue — a cold, procedural role of a kind he was never offered as a leading man, and the last of the late parts that widened his range. The film opened in December 2019; he died in April 2020, leaving Sharmaji Namkeen unfinished.

name: Jitu Thakar
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Barood (1976).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Barood (1976), from the glut of work that followed Bobby, with a Sachin Bhowmick story and Anand Bakshi's lyrics.
biography: Jitu Thakar is among the producers credited on Barood (1976) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the three years after Bobby, when Kapoor at twenty-three was the most saleable young lover in Hindi cinema and producers financed almost anything he appeared in. Three separate producers are credited on it, none of them documented — a pattern repeated across the lower tiers of this workbook, where the financing of a 1970s mid-budget film has left no record beyond the names on its titles. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: K. Bapaiah
career_background: Kovelamudi Bapayya, known as K. Bapaiah, is an Indian film director who has directed about eighty films in Telugu and Hindi. He is a cousin of the director K. Raghavendra Rao and a nephew of the director and producer K. S. Prakash Rao.
debut: Directing in Telugu cinema before moving into Hindi remakes.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kasak (1992). Elsewhere, a long run of Telugu films and their Hindi versions.
recurring_themes: Family melodrama and revenge drama transplanted from Telugu originals.
creative_style: A high-volume director working in two industries, specialising in the southern formula remade for Hindi audiences.
historical_importance: One of the most prolific directors of the Telugu-to-Hindi remake, a significant commercial current of 1980s and early 1990s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kasak (1992), a Rajesh Roshan-scored melodrama from the year in which Kapoor's leading career effectively ended. It belongs to the southern pipeline — T. Rama Rao, K. Bapaiah, K. Ravi Shankar — that supplied a substantial share of his work from the mid-1980s on.
biography: K. Bapaiah directed one Rishi Kapoor film, and his presence identifies a current that runs through the actor's middle period. Born Kovelamudi Bapayya into a filmmaking family — cousin of K. Raghavendra Rao, nephew of K. S. Prakash Rao — he directed some eighty films across Telugu and Hindi cinema, most of them transplanting proven southern melodrama into Hindi. Kasak (1992), with a Rajesh Roshan score, came in the year of Deewana and Bol Radha Bol, as Kapoor's run as a lead was closing. Several directors from the same pipeline, T. Rama Rao and K. Ravi Shankar among them, account for a notable share of his films after 1985, when the Bombay mainstream had begun to look elsewhere.

name: K. L. Bhatia
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zinda Dil (1975).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Zinda Dil (1975), directed by Sikandar Khanna with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score, from the rush of romances Kapoor made in the two years after Bobby.
biography: K. L. Bhatia is among the producers credited on Zinda Dil (1975) and has no documented biography. The film came two years after Bobby, directed by Sikandar Khanna — who would die during the making of his next Kapoor film — and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, whose thirty-two credits make them the most frequent collaborators in this filmography. It belongs to the period when the market would absorb any romance with Kapoor in it, and when the people financing those films left almost no record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: K. Pappu
career_background: K. Pappu (died 11 July 2005) was an Indian film director, producer and screenwriter who directed Ucha Dar Babe Nanak Da (1982), Jigri Yaar (1984), Mohabbat Ki Kasam (1986), Vishnu-Devaa (1991), Ayee Milan Ki Raat (1991), Izzat Ki Roti (1993), Maha Shaktishaali (1994) and Raghuveer (1995). He was a brother of the director Raj Kanwar.
debut: Directing from the early 1980s, including in Punjabi cinema.
major_works: With Kapoor: Izzat Ki Roti (1993). Elsewhere, Ayee Milan Ki Raat and Vishnu-Devaa.
recurring_themes: Action melodrama and the family honour plot, in Hindi and Punjabi.
creative_style: A commercial director of mid-budget melodrama across two languages.
historical_importance: Not substantially documented beyond his filmography.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Izzat Ki Roti (1993), with a Bappi Lahiri score and Ranbir Pushp among its writers. The family connection is worth noting — his brother Raj Kanwar had directed Deewana the previous year, the film in which Kapoor's romantic lead passed to Shah Rukh Khan, so both brothers worked with him in consecutive years at the close of that career.
biography: K. Pappu directed Izzat Ki Roti (1993), and his row records a family coincidence of some interest. He was a brother of Raj Kanwar, whose directorial debut Deewana had, the year before, staged the handover of the Hindi romantic lead from Rishi Kapoor to Shah Rukh Khan. Pappu's own career ran through Hindi and Punjabi melodrama — Ucha Dar Babe Nanak Da, Ayee Milan Ki Raat, Vishnu-Devaa — and Izzat Ki Roti, with a Bappi Lahiri score and Ranbir Pushp among its writers, is a modest entry from the end of Kapoor's lead years. He died in July 2005.

name: K. Rangaraj
career_background: K. Rangaraj is an Indian film director, screenwriter and producer who was active mainly in Tamil cinema in the 1980s.
debut: Working from 1983.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sindoor (1987).
recurring_themes: Family melodrama of honour and remarriage, in the southern commercial tradition.
creative_style: Not extensively documented; a Tamil filmmaker whose material reached Hindi through remakes.
historical_importance: Not substantially documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sindoor (1987), directed by K. Ravi Shankar with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score — one of several Kapoor films of the period that drew on southern source material and southern filmmakers.
biography: K. Rangaraj is credited as a writer on Sindoor (1987), and his article records only that he was a Tamil filmmaker active mainly in the 1980s. The film, directed by K. Ravi Shankar with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score, belongs to the pipeline that supplied much of Kapoor's work in that decade: southern writers, directors and formulas remade for the Hindi market. Of the five or six people associated with this film, three — its producer, its co-writer and its director — are documented only in fragments, and the credit for its direction had to be recovered for this workbook from the director's own article.

name: K. Shankar
industry: Tamil cinema; Hindi cinema; other Indian languages
career_background: Kannan Shankar (17 March 1926 – 5 March 2006) was an Indian film editor, screenwriter and director who directed more than eighty films in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada and Hindi, as well as one in Sinhala. He gave Sivaji Ganesan the hit Aalayamani (1962) and went on to direct Andavan Kattalai, Anbu Karangal and many others.
debut: Working as an editor before directing; Aalayamani (1962) was an early success.
major_works: With Kapoor: Raaja (1975). Elsewhere, Aalayamani and a long list of southern films.
recurring_themes: Family melodrama and the star vehicle, across five languages.
creative_style: An editor-turned-director of great volume, moving between industries.
historical_importance: One of the most prolific directors in Indian cinema, with more than eighty films across five languages.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Raaja (1975), an R. D. Burman-scored picture written in part by Inder Raj Anand, from the two years after Bobby. It is the earliest instance in this filmography of a southern director being brought in for a Kapoor film — a pattern that would become common a decade later.
biography: K. Shankar directed Raaja (1975), and he is among the most prolific filmmakers in this workbook. Born Kannan Shankar in 1926, he began as an editor and directed more than eighty films in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada and Hindi — plus one in Sinhala — including Aalayamani, a hit for Sivaji Ganesan. Raaja came two years after Bobby, with an R. D. Burman score and a script in part by Inder Raj Anand, Raj Kapoor's long-serving writer. It is the first sign in this filmography of a pattern that would dominate Kapoor's mid-1980s: southern directors working in Hindi, on material and formulas proven elsewhere. Shankar died in 2006.

name: K. Shorey
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zinda Dil (1975).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Zinda Dil (1975), directed by Sikandar Khanna with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score, from the rush of romances that followed Bobby.
biography: K. Shorey is among the producers credited on Zinda Dil (1975) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the two years after Bobby, when Kapoor's name alone could finance a romance; it was directed by Sikandar Khanna, who died during production of his next film with the actor, and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal. Like most of the producers in this tier of the workbook, Shorey is attested only by the credits of the film he financed. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: K. Viswanath
career_background: Kasinadhuni Viswanath (19 February 1930 – 2 February 2023) was an Indian director, screenwriter, lyricist and actor who worked predominantly in Telugu cinema and was known for blending parallel cinema with the mainstream. He received the Prize of the Public at the Besançon Film Festival in 1981, the Padma Shri in 1992, the Raghupathi Venkaiah Award, and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 2016. He won five National Film Awards, seven Nandi Awards, ten Filmfare Awards South and one Filmfare Award in Hindi.
debut: Working from 1951; his Hindi films include Sargam (1979), Kaamchor (1982), Sur Sangam (1985) and Sanjog (1985).
major_works: With Kapoor: Sargam (1979). Elsewhere, Sankarabharanam, Sagara Sangamam, Swathi Muthyam and Sur Sangam.
recurring_themes: Classical Indian art — music, dance, sculpture — as the subject and moral centre of popular melodrama; disability and social exclusion.
creative_style: A director who made art and performance the engine of mass entertainment, bringing classical forms into commercial cinema without condescension.
major_awards: Five National Film Awards, the Padma Shri (1992) and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award (2016), among many others.
historical_importance: One of the most honoured Indian filmmakers of his generation and the figure most associated with the classical-arts melodrama.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a defining one: Sargam (1979), Viswanath's Hindi remake of his own Telugu film, in which Kapoor plays opposite Jaya Prada as a man who loves a mute woman and courts her through the dholak. The soundtrack by Laxmikant–Pyarelal was a phenomenon, and the film is one of the three or four on which Kapoor's image as a singing romantic hero rests.
biography: K. Viswanath directed Sargam, one of the films that fixed Rishi Kapoor's identity as a musical romantic hero. The most honoured Telugu filmmaker of his generation — five National Film Awards, the Padma Shri, the Dadasaheb Phalke Award — Viswanath built his cinema on classical Indian art forms, making dance, music and sculpture the moral centre of popular melodrama. Sargam (1979), a Hindi remake of his own Telugu film, cast Kapoor opposite Jaya Prada as a man in love with a woman who cannot speak, courting her with a dholak; the Laxmikant–Pyarelal songs were among the biggest of the decade. It is the clearest case in this filmography of a director from outside the Bombay mainstream giving Kapoor his most characteristic role.

name: K.R. Reddy
career_background: A director credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sheshnaag (1990).
recurring_themes: The folk-mythological fantasy.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sheshnaag (1990), the snake-deity fantasy made in the wake of Nagina's success. The film carries two director credits in this workbook's sources, his and Iqbal Durrani's, and no source consulted here resolves how the work was divided; both are recorded.
biography: K.R. Reddy is credited as a director of Sheshnaag (1990) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the folk-fantasy cycle that followed Nagina in 1986, with Laxmikant–Pyarelal's music and a plot of serpent deities rather than courtship, and it carries two director credits — Reddy's and Iqbal Durrani's — which the sources consulted here do not reconcile. This workbook records both rather than choosing between them. The pattern of shared or contested credits recurs through Kapoor's late-1980s films, which were made quickly and documented barely at all. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Kalapi Nagada
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017), a culture-clash comedy in which Kapoor plays the Gujarati father of the bride opposite Paresh Rawal — three years before Rawal would complete Kapoor's unfinished final film.
biography: Kalapi Nagada is among the producers of Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017) and has no documented biography. The film is a broad comedy about a Gujarati family marrying into a Punjabi one, with Kapoor and Paresh Rawal as the opposing patriarchs and songs by Lalit Pandit. Its pairing of the two actors acquired a retrospective significance: when Kapoor died in April 2020 with Sharmaji Namkeen half shot, it was Rawal who played the remaining scenes as the same character. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Kaleidoscope Entertainment
career_background: Kaleidoscope Entertainment Pvt. Ltd., founded in 1989 and managed by Bobby Bedi, is an Indian film and television production company. Its films include Bandit Queen, Fire, Electric Moon, Saathiya, Maqbool, American Daylight and Mangal Pandey: The Rising, and it is described in its article as one of the leading production houses in the Indian film and television industry.
debut: Producing from 1989; Bandit Queen (1994) brought it international attention.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chintu Ji (2009). Elsewhere, Bandit Queen, Fire, Maqbool and Mangal Pandey: The Rising.
recurring_themes: Independent Indian cinema for domestic and international audiences; adaptations and politically charged subjects.
creative_style: A producer's house identified with directors outside the commercial mainstream — Shekhar Kapur, Deepa Mehta, Vishal Bhardwaj.
historical_importance: One of the most significant independent production companies in Indian cinema of the 1990s and 2000s.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Chintu Ji (2009), in which Kapoor plays a fictionalised version of himself — a star named Chintu Ji, his own lifelong nickname — returning to the village of his birth. That the company behind Bandit Queen and Maqbool made it indicates the film was conceived as more than a vehicle, and it is the most directly self-referential entry in this filmography.
biography: Kaleidoscope Entertainment produced the strangest and most self-aware film in this filmography. Founded in 1989 and run by Bobby Bedi, the company made Bandit Queen, Fire, Maqbool and Mangal Pandey: The Rising — a body of work associated with Shekhar Kapur, Deepa Mehta and Vishal Bhardwaj rather than with commercial Hindi cinema. Chintu Ji (2009) casts Rishi Kapoor as a film star called Chintu Ji, the nickname he had carried since childhood and by which the whole industry knew him, who returns to the village of his birth and is received as both celebrity and disappointment. Coming a year before Do Dooni Chaar, it belongs to the period when Kapoor was beginning to treat his own persona as material.

name: Kamlesh Doshi
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kaun Sachcha Kaun Jhootha (1997).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kaun Sachcha Kaun Jhootha (1997), a Rakesh Roshan production scored by his brother Rajesh Roshan and written in part by Ranbir Pushp — one of the last films in which Kapoor took a leading role.
biography: Kamlesh Doshi is credited as a producer on Kaun Sachcha Kaun Jhootha (1997) and has no documented biography. The film is one of the last of Rishi Kapoor's leading roles, made by the Roshan family unit — Rakesh Roshan producing and directing, his brother Rajesh Roshan scoring — that accounts for four films in this filmography. Within three years Rakesh Roshan would launch his son Hrithik in Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai and Kapoor would be taking supporting parts. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Kamleshwar
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography. No Wikipedia article could be resolved for him in this research: the bare name returns a page too short to use, and no disambiguated title was identified, so nothing beyond the credit is recorded here.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pati Patni Aur Woh (1978).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not documented here.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and an interesting one: B. R. Chopra's Pati Patni Aur Woh (1978), a comedy of adultery in which Kapoor plays the husband who deceives both his wife and his mistress — one of the few films of his young-star period that treats marriage rather than courtship, and one of only two Chopra films in the filmography.
biography: Kamleshwar is credited as a writer on Pati Patni Aur Woh (1978), and this research could not resolve an article for him — the bare name returns a page too brief to use, so the row records the credit and nothing more. The film is among the more unusual of Kapoor's early career: B. R. Chopra, Hindi cinema's foremost maker of social problem films, directing a comedy about a husband conducting an affair and lying to both women, with Ravindra Jain's music and Anand Bakshi's lyrics. In a filmography dominated by courtship, it is one of the few entries that takes marriage and its failures as the subject.

name: Kanchan Ketan Desai
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own. The article on her husband, the director Ketan Desai, records that he is married to Kanchan Kapoor, a daughter of the actor Shammi Kapoor — which makes her Rishi Kapoor's first cousin and the credit a family one.
major_works: With Kapoor: Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002).
recurring_themes: The late Desai-family masala comedy.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002), directed by her husband Ketan Desai under the MKD Films Combine banner, with Kapoor in a supporting role as the older generation to Salman Khan's lead. She is his first cousin — the daughter of Shammi Kapoor — so this is one of several credits in this filmography that run through the family rather than the industry.
biography: Kanchan Ketan Desai produced Yeh Hai Jalwa (2002), and the credit is a family one twice over. Her husband Ketan Desai, who directed it, was the son of Manmohan Desai, the maker of Amar Akbar Anthony, Naseeb and Coolie; she is, according to his article, Kanchan Kapoor, a daughter of Shammi Kapoor, and therefore Rishi Kapoor's first cousin. The film was the last attempt to revive the Desai masala formula, with Kapoor now playing the older generation to Salman Khan's lead. Between the Desais and the Kapoors, the production was almost entirely a matter of two intermarried film families. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Kanu Chauhan
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Ki Izzat (1994).
recurring_themes: The household melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ghar Ki Izzat (1994), the last of Kalpataru's five family melodramas with Kapoor, written with Kader Khan and Keshav Rathod.
biography: Kanu Chauhan produced Ghar Ki Izzat (1994) and has no documented biography. The film closes the run of five household melodramas Kalpataru directed with Kapoor between 1988 and 1994 — pictures named for the family rather than the romance, written largely by Kader Khan, financed by producers with no public profile and reviewed almost nowhere. Taken together they are the clearest evidence of what Kapoor's lead career had become by the early 1990s. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Kapil Kapoor
career_background: A director credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The bare name resolves to an unrelated professor of linguistics at Jawaharlal Nehru University, which is how an earlier pass of this research briefly attached the wrong article to him.
major_works: With Kapoor: Yeh Vaada Raha (1982).
recurring_themes: Romantic melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Yeh Vaada Raha (1982), an R. D. Burman-scored romance from the early 1980s, when Kapoor's vehicles were still being built around his singing-hero persona.
biography: Kapil Kapoor directed Yeh Vaada Raha (1982) and has no documented biography; the name on Wikipedia belongs to a Sanskrit and linguistics scholar at JNU, no relation. The film is a romance with an R. D. Burman score from the stretch when Burman was still writing Kapoor's soundtracks — twenty films between 1974 and 1985 — and when the actor's vehicles were constructed around songs. The coincidence of surname is worth noting only because this filmography already contains several unrelated Kapoors, including a screenwriter and the actor Jeetendra, whose birth name was Ravi Kapoor. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Karan Malhotra
career_background: Karan Ravi Malhotra is an Indian film director and screenwriter working in Hindi cinema, best known for directing Agneepath (2012), his directorial debut and a remake of the 1990 film of the same name. He worked as an assistant director before that, and is married to Ekta Pathak.
debut: Directorial debut Agneepath (2012).
major_works: With Kapoor: Agneepath (2012). Elsewhere, Brothers and Shamshera.
recurring_themes: The revenge epic; the criminal patriarch; violence staged as spectacle.
creative_style: Large-scale, operatic melodrama with heavy production design and extended set pieces.
historical_importance: The director of one of Dharma Productions' biggest commercial successes and of a remake that reframed a canonical 1990 film.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and one of the two or three best things Kapoor ever did: Agneepath (2012), in which he plays Rauf Lala, a Mumbai trafficker in women and drugs whose geniality is what makes him frightening. Transformed by prosthetic teeth, a skullcap and an unfamiliar register, he was widely held to have stolen the film from Hrithik Roshan and Sanjay Dutt, and the performance reset what directors would offer him in his last eight years.
biography: Karan Malhotra gave Rishi Kapoor the role that proved his late career could include genuine menace. Malhotra's directorial debut was Agneepath (2012), Dharma Productions' remake of the 1990 Amitabh Bachchan film, an operatic revenge epic with Hrithik Roshan in the lead. Kapoor plays Rauf Lala, a Mumbai dealer in women and narcotics — avuncular, chuckling, entirely pitiless — in prosthetics and a vocal register he had never used in forty years of leading roles. Most notices singled him out. Coming eight years after Hum Tum had restarted his career as a benign father, it was the performance that broke that typecasting, and D-Day's gangster followed the next year.

name: Karim Morani
career_background: Karim Morani is an Indian film producer who produced Arjun (1985) and Damini (1993), and later co-produced Chennai Express and Ra.One with Shah Rukh Khan. With his brother Aly Morani he co-owns Cineyug, a film production and event-management company. His article also records his involvement in the 2G spectrum case and other controversies.
debut: Producing from the mid-1980s with Arjun.
major_works: With Kapoor: Damini (1993). Elsewhere, Arjun, Chennai Express and Ra.One.
recurring_themes: Mainstream star vehicles produced alongside a live-events business.
creative_style: A commercial producer working with established directors and, latterly, with Shah Rukh Khan's company.
historical_importance: Co-owner of Cineyug, one of India's significant film and live-event companies.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rajkumar Santoshi's Damini (1993), which his article names directly — 'the universally acclaimed 1993 film Damini which starred Sunny Deol, Meenakshi Seshadri and Rishi Kapoor'. Kapoor plays the husband of a woman who witnesses a rape in his family's house and is disbelieved; the film's moral authority belongs to others, and his character's weakness is the point.
biography: Karim Morani produced Damini, the most critically substantial hit of Rishi Kapoor's later career, and his article names Kapoor among its stars. With his brother Aly Morani he owns Cineyug, a production and live-events company, and his credits run from Arjun in 1985 to Chennai Express and Ra.One with Shah Rukh Khan's banner. Damini (1993) is built around Meenakshi Seshadri's character, who sees a servant raped by her brother-in-law and is systematically disbelieved, and Sunny Deol's alcoholic lawyer; Kapoor plays the husband whose family loyalty makes him complicit. It won Rajkumar Santoshi his second consecutive Filmfare Award for Best Director. Morani's article also records his involvement in the 2G spectrum case.

name: Kashi Richard
career_background: A composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), on which six composers or groups are credited — Yo Yo Honey Singh, Amjad Nadeem–Aamir, Sanjeev–Ajay, Rahul Jain, this composer and one other. It was among Kapoor's last releases.
biography: Kashi Richard is one of six composing credits on Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019) and has no documented biography. The film, a farce released months before Kapoor's death, is the extreme case of a pattern this workbook traces across fifty years: in 1973 Laxmikant–Pyarelal wrote every song in Bobby, and they went on to score thirty-two of his films; by 2019 a single soundtrack was divided among six separate parties, most of whom left no record. The row exists because the workbook records every credited collaborator, and it is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Kaushal Bharti
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan (1978).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan (1978), the second of Sikandar Khanna's two films with Kapoor and the one during whose making the director died. The script is shared with Rajendra Krishan, the lyricist and screenwriter.
biography: Kaushal Bharti is credited as a writer on Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan (1978) and has no documented biography. The film is remembered, to the extent it is remembered at all, for its director's death: Sikandar Khanna's article records that he died during its making. It was his second film with Kapoor after Zinda Dil, scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, and written with Rajendra Krishan, the veteran lyricist and screenwriter. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Kaybe Pictures
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sambar Salsa (2007).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Sambar Salsa (2007), one of the two English-language films in this filmography, both written and directed by Kapoor's cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor and both released that year. They are the least documented entries in the workbook.
biography: Kaybe Pictures is the banner on Sambar Salsa (2007) and has no recorded history. The film is one of two English-language pictures Rishi Kapoor made that year, both written and directed by his first cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor — the son of Shammi Kapoor — and both so slightly distributed that this workbook can record almost nothing about them: no reviews of substance, no commercial figures, and producers and banners with no documentation at all. They fall in the gap between his Yash Raj supporting roles and the Dharma films that followed. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Keshu Ramsay
career_background: Keshu Ramsay (1955–2010) was an Indian producer and film director, one of the Ramsay Brothers — the sibling group of directors, producers and editors that included Shyam, Kumar, Tulsi and Kiran Ramsay and that defined Hindi horror cinema. He is noted particularly for producing the Khiladi series.
debut: Working within the Ramsay family's production unit from the 1970s and 1980s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Khoj (1989). Elsewhere, the Khiladi films.
recurring_themes: Genre filmmaking: horror in the family tradition, and later the action thriller.
creative_style: A commercial producer-director who moved the family business from low-budget horror into mainstream action.
historical_importance: A member of the family that created the Hindi horror film as a commercial genre, and the producer of the Khiladi series.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Khoj (1989), a thriller with a Bappi Lahiri score, co-produced by his brother Kiran Ramsay — one of the nine films Kapoor released between 1989 and 1991 and among the least documented. The Ramsay connection is the point of interest: a family synonymous with horror making a mainstream picture with a romantic star at the end of his lead career.
biography: Keshu Ramsay directed Khoj (1989), and his row records an unexpected intersection. The Ramsay Brothers — Shyam, Kumar, Tulsi, Kiran, Keshu and others — were the family that invented the Hindi horror film as a commercial genre, working at the bottom of the market with their own crews. Keshu moved the family business towards mainstream action and produced the Khiladi series. Khoj, a thriller with a Bappi Lahiri score co-produced by his brother Kiran, belongs to the crowded 1989–91 stretch when Kapoor was making three or four films a year for whoever offered work. He died in 2010 at fifty-five.

name: Khalid Mohammed
career_background: Khalid Mohamed is an Indian journalist, editor, film critic, screenwriter and director. He worked for The Times of India for twenty-seven years and later for DNA and the Hindustan Times, and was the lead editor of Filmfare magazine. He is the son of the singer Zubeida Begum, on whose life he based the screenplay of Shyam Benegal's Zubeidaa (2001), and is known as a filmmaker for Fiza and Silsiilay.
debut: Screenwriting from the 1990s; directing from the 2000s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tehzeeb (2003), which he wrote and directed. Elsewhere, Fiza, Mammo and Zubeidaa as screenwriter.
recurring_themes: The Muslim family and its women; performance, memory and the mother who cannot be forgiven.
creative_style: A critic's cinema: literate, dialogue-led and concerned with the inner lives of its female characters.
historical_importance: One of India's most prominent film critics and editors, and the writer of a notable trilogy of Muslim-social films directed by Shyam Benegal.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Tehzeeb (2003), which he wrote and directed, with Kapoor as the dying husband of Shabana Azmi's celebrated singer in a story of mother and daughter. For the actor it is an unusual credit — a literate family drama in the Muslim-social tradition, made in the middle of the quiet years before Hum Tum, with music by A. R. Rahman and dialogue by Javed Siddiqui.
biography: Khalid Mohamed wrote and directed Tehzeeb, one of the more serious films Rishi Kapoor made between his leading career and his reinvention. A film critic and editor for nearly three decades — The Times of India, DNA, the Hindustan Times, and the editorship of Filmfare — Mohamed also wrote Shyam Benegal's Mammo, Zubeidaa and Sardari Begum, the last two drawing on his own family: his mother was the singer Zubeida Begum. Tehzeeb (2003) is his second film as director, a drama of a famous singer and her estranged daughter, with Shabana Azmi, Urmila Matondkar and Kapoor as the dying husband, A. R. Rahman's music and Javed Siddiqui's dialogue. It is one of the few genuinely literary projects in the whole filmography.

name: Khayyam
career_background: Mohammed Zahur Khayyam Hashmi (18 February 1927 – 19 August 2019), known as Khayyam, was an Indian music director and background-score composer whose career spanned four decades. He won three Filmfare Awards — Best Music in 1977 for Kabhie Kabhie and in 1982 for Umrao Jaan, and a lifetime achievement award in 2010 — the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award for Creative Music in 2007, and the Padma Bhushan in 2011. He is known for Umrao Jaan, Kabhi Kabhie, Noorie, Thodisi Bewafaii, Dil-e-Nadaan and Razia Sultan.
debut: Composing from the late 1940s; his critical and commercial peak came with Kabhie Kabhie (1976) and Umrao Jaan (1981).
major_works: With Kapoor: Kabhie Kabhie (1976). Elsewhere, Umrao Jaan, Noorie and Razia Sultan.
recurring_themes: The ghazal and the Urdu lyric set with unusual restraint; music conceived for the poem rather than the star.
creative_style: A composer of deliberate sparseness and classical discipline, celebrated for giving the lyric primacy over the arrangement.
major_awards: Three Filmfare Awards, including Best Music for Kabhie Kabhie (1977) and Umrao Jaan (1982); Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (2007); Padma Bhushan (2011).
historical_importance: One of the most critically revered composers in Hindi film history, and the composer of Umrao Jaan.
relationship_with_actor: One film — and Khayyam won the Filmfare Award for Best Music for it. Yash Chopra's Kabhie Kabhie (1976) is the ensemble in which Kapoor and Neetu Singh's young romance plays against an older marriage haunted by a first love, written by Sagar Sarhadi, and its title song is among the most admired in Hindi cinema. It is the only Kapoor film in this workbook whose score won its composer that award.
biography: Khayyam wrote the music for Kabhie Kabhie, and won the Filmfare Award for Best Music for it — the only score in this filmography to take that prize. One of the most revered composers in Hindi cinema, honoured with the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award and the Padma Bhushan and remembered above all for Umrao Jaan, Khayyam worked in a deliberately spare idiom that gave the Urdu lyric primacy over arrangement. Yash Chopra's Kabhie Kabhie (1976) was his breakthrough in the mainstream: Kapoor and Neetu Singh as the young couple, Amitabh Bachchan and Raakhee as the older marriage shadowed by a first love, and a title song that has outlasted nearly everything else either man made that decade. Khayyam died in 2019, eight months before Kapoor.

name: Kiran Ramsay
career_background: Karan Ramsay, also known as Kiran Ramsay, is a producer, sound designer and director of Hindi films and one of the Ramsay Brothers, the sibling group — Shyam, Kumar, Keshu, Tulsi, Gangu and Arjun Ramsay — that made Hindi horror cinema a commercial genre.
debut: Working within the family's production unit.
major_works: With Kapoor: Khoj (1989).
recurring_themes: Genre filmmaking within a family production unit; sound as much as production.
creative_style: A producer and sound designer rather than a director of record.
historical_importance: A member of the Ramsay family, whose low-budget horror films of the 1970s and 1980s created a durable Indian genre.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Khoj (1989), which his brother Keshu Ramsay directed, with a Bappi Lahiri score — one of the nine films Kapoor released between 1989 and 1991 and among the least documented in the workbook.
biography: Kiran Ramsay co-produced Khoj (1989) with his brother Keshu, who directed it. The Ramsays were a production family in the fullest sense: seven brothers working as directors, producers, cinematographers, editors and sound men, who built Hindi horror into a commercial genre from the 1970s on with their own crews and almost no outside money. Khoj is not a horror film but a thriller, scored by Bappi Lahiri, and it belongs to the crowded 1989–91 stretch when Kapoor took whatever lead work was available. The family's presence in this filmography is a reminder of how much of the Hindi industry was organised around households rather than studios.

name: Kunal Kohli Productions
career_background: The production company founded by the director Kunal Kohli. According to his article, its first production was his own fantasy comedy-drama Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic (2008), co-produced by Yash Raj Films, and it went on to make Break Ke Baad (2010), Teri Meri Kahaani (2012) and Phir Se... (2018). The company has no article of its own; Kohli's is cited on his row in this sheet.
major_works: With Kapoor: Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic (2008). Elsewhere, Break Ke Baad and Teri Meri Kahaani.
recurring_themes: Light romance and fantasy in the Yash Raj register.
creative_style: A director's own banner, producing his films and those of others in a similar mode.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and it was the company's first film: Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic (2008), the third of Kohli's three consecutive films with Kapoor after Hum Tum and Fanaa. Those three, made between 2004 and 2008, are what re-established Kapoor as a bankable supporting presence in mainstream Hindi cinema.
biography: Kunal Kohli Productions made its first film with Rishi Kapoor in it. Kohli had directed him in Hum Tum (2004) — the film that reopened his career — and Fanaa (2006) before founding the company, whose debut production, co-financed by Yash Raj Films, was his own fantasy comedy Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic in 2008. It completed a run of three films in five years with the same director, the sequence that turned Kapoor from a star without work into a reliable character actor. The banner has no separate documentation; what is known of it comes from Kohli's own article, which this row cites rather than duplicating.

name: Kundan A. Thadani
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Premee (1980).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Do Premee (1980), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal-scored romance written by the novelist Gulshan Nanda, from the period when Kapoor's romantic vehicles were still being made at scale.
biography: Kundan A. Thadani produced Do Premee (1980) and has no documented biography. The film is a romance from the start of the 1980s with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score and a story by Gulshan Nanda, the most widely read Hindi popular novelist of his generation, whose plots of concealment and thwarted love had supplied a dozen hits in the preceding decades. It was among Nanda's last credits — he died in 1985 — and among the last of Kapoor's romances to be built on that older melodramatic model. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Lalit Kapoor
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. There is no evidence in the credits of any relation to the Kapoor family of this filmography.
major_works: With Kapoor: Deewana (1992).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and the pivotal one: Deewana (1992), Raj Kanwar's directorial debut, in which Kapoor plays the singer presumed dead whose widow marries the younger man played by a debuting Shah Rukh Khan. The film was a hit and marks the handover of the Hindi romantic lead between generations.
biography: Lalit Kapoor is one of several producers credited on Deewana (1992) and has no documented biography; the surname appears to be coincidental, as nothing in the credits connects him to the Kapoor family. The film is the single most consequential entry in the second half of this filmography: Rishi Kapoor as Ravi, the wealthy singer believed killed, and Shah Rukh Khan in his film debut as the man his widow marries. It succeeded commercially, won Khan a Filmfare award for best debut, and is read — then and since — as the moment the romantic lead passed from one generation to the next. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Leena Yadav
career_background: Leena Yadav (born 6 January 1971) is an Indian film director, producer, screenwriter and editor who began in television before moving to features. Her first international feature, Parched, premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2015. She is married to the cinematographer and producer Aseem Bajaj, who is also credited on this film, and her father-in-law is the theatre figure Ram Gopal Bajaj.
debut: Television before features; Parched (2015) brought her international notice.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rajma Chawal (2018). Elsewhere, Parched and Teen Patti.
recurring_themes: Women's lives outside the mainstream frame; isolation and the possibility of connection.
creative_style: A director from an editing and television background whose features are character-led and shot with an independent sensibility.
historical_importance: One of the few Indian women directing internationally distributed features in the 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rajma Chawal (2018), which she wrote, produced and directed — a Netflix release in which Kapoor plays a widowed father in old Delhi who, unable to speak to his estranged son, poses online as a young woman to reach him. It is among the quietest and most sympathetic of his last parts, and her husband Aseem Bajaj is credited as a producer on the same film.
biography: Leena Yadav directed one of Rishi Kapoor's last and most affecting performances. A television professional turned filmmaker whose Parched premiered at Toronto in 2015, Yadav works at an independent scale and writes about people the mainstream frame excludes. Rajma Chawal (2018), made for Netflix, casts Kapoor as a widower in the old city of Delhi who cannot talk to his son and so invents a young woman's social-media profile to reach him — a role built on loneliness and foolishness rather than authority, and unavailable to him in the years when he was a star. Her husband, Aseem Bajaj, produced it. The film came two years before his death.

name: Lucky Ali
career_background: Maqsood Mahmood Ali, known as Lucky Ali (born 19 September 1958 in Bangalore), is an Indian singer, songwriter and actor who emerged as a significant figure of Indipop in the 1990s with a series of popular singles and albums. He won the Filmfare Award for Best Male Playback Singer in 2001 for 'Ek Pal Ka Jeena' and was nominated again for 'Aa Bhi Jaa' from Sur at the 48th Filmfare Awards. He is a son of the actor and director Mehmood.
debut: Recording from 1978; his breakthrough as a non-film artist came in the mid-1990s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love at Times Square (2003). Elsewhere, his albums Sunoh, Sifar and Aks, and 'Ek Pal Ka Jeena' from Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai.
recurring_themes: Melancholy, guitar-led non-film pop brought occasionally into cinema.
creative_style: A singer-songwriter working largely outside the film industry, with a distinctive unforced vocal style.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Male Playback Singer (2001) for 'Ek Pal Ka Jeena', with a further nomination for Sur.
historical_importance: One of the defining voices of 1990s Indipop, the non-film movement that briefly rivalled film music in India.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Love at Times Square (2003), which Dev Anand wrote, produced and directed. The family pattern is the striking part — Lucky Ali's father, the comedian and filmmaker Mehmood, directed Ginny Aur Johnny (1976), so father and son each hold a single credit in this filmography, twenty-seven years apart.
biography: Lucky Ali composed for one Rishi Kapoor film, and his row records a generational coincidence. The son of Mehmood — the great comic actor who also directed Ginny Aur Johnny, in which Kapoor starred in 1976 — Lucky Ali became one of the defining voices of 1990s Indipop with Sunoh and Sifar, working largely outside the film industry, and won the Filmfare Award for Best Male Playback Singer in 2001 for 'Ek Pal Ka Jeena'. His single film credit here is Love at Times Square (2003), the late picture Dev Anand wrote, produced and directed at seventy-nine, with Kapoor in support. Father and son thus appear in this workbook twenty-seven years apart, in two of its most obscure entries.

name: M. D. Sunder
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Dosti Dushmani (1986).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside Rahi Masoom Raza and M. Balamurugan.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: T. Rama Rao's Dosti Dushmani (1986), a multi-star melodrama from the southern-remake pipeline that supplied much of Kapoor's mid-1980s work, with a script shared with Rahi Masoom Raza.
biography: M. D. Sunder is one of three writers credited on Dosti Dushmani (1986) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the current of southern filmmaking that dominated Kapoor's middle period: T. Rama Rao directing, a Telugu formula transplanted into Hindi, Laxmikant–Pyarelal scoring, and a cast assembled for breadth rather than coherence. His co-writers were Rahi Masoom Raza, a Sahitya Akademi-level Urdu novelist, and M. Balamurugan, who is equally undocumented — a juxtaposition typical of the period's collective credits. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: M. Parvez
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Izzat Ki Roti (1993).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Izzat Ki Roti (1993), directed by K. Pappu — a brother of Raj Kanwar, who had directed Deewana the previous year — with a Bappi Lahiri score and Ranbir Pushp among its writers.
biography: M. Parvez is credited as a writer on Izzat Ki Roti (1993) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the final stretch of Kapoor's lead career, directed by K. Pappu whose brother Raj Kanwar had, a year earlier, made Deewana — the film in which Kapoor handed the romantic lead to Shah Rukh Khan. Two brothers, two consecutive years, two very different outcomes: one of the most consequential films of the decade and one that left no trace. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: M.M.C. Cooper
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rishta To Ho Aisa (1992).
recurring_themes: The household melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rishta To Ho Aisa (1992), the fourth of Kalpataru's five family melodramas with Kapoor, written with Kader Khan and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal.
biography: M.M.C. Cooper produced Rishta To Ho Aisa (1992) and has no documented biography. The film is one of five household melodramas Kalpataru directed with Kapoor between 1988 and 1994 — titled for the family rather than any romance, written largely by Kader Khan, scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, and reviewed essentially nowhere. Released in the same year as Deewana and Bol Radha Bol, it shows what the bulk of his output looked like even as those two films were deciding the shape of his later career. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: MacGuffin Pictures
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sharmaji Namkeen (2022).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Sharmaji Namkeen (2022) — the last film in this filmography, which Kapoor was shooting when he died in April 2020 and which was completed with Paresh Rawal performing the remaining scenes as the same character.
biography: MacGuffin Pictures is one of the banners on Sharmaji Namkeen (2022) and has no recorded history. The film closes this filmography: Hitesh Bhatia's gentle comedy about a man forced into retirement who finds purpose cooking for other people's parties, with Kapoor in the title role. He had shot about half of it when he died in April 2020, and rather than abandon or recast the film, the producers had Paresh Rawal play the remaining scenes as the same man — so that two actors alternate in one part. It was released posthumously in 2022. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Madan Mohan
career_background: Madan Mohan Kohli (25 June 1924 – 14 July 1975), known as Madan Mohan, was an Indian music director of the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, considered one of the most melodious composers in Hindi cinema and particularly remembered for his ghazals and for his work with Lata Mangeshkar. He won the National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Dastak (1971) and was nominated for the Filmfare Award for Woh Kaun Thi in 1964; he was posthumously awarded the IIFA Award for Best Music Director in 2005 for Veer-Zaara, which used tunes he had left unrecorded.
debut: Composing from 1950.
major_works: With Kapoor: Laila Majnu (1976). Elsewhere, Woh Kaun Thi, Anpadh, Dastak and the posthumous Veer-Zaara.
recurring_themes: The ghazal in film; melody of unusual refinement, written for the voice rather than the arrangement.
creative_style: A composer of exceptional melodic precision, celebrated by musicians more than by the box office, who worked largely with Lata Mangeshkar and Mohammed Rafi.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Dastak (1971); posthumous IIFA Award for Veer-Zaara (2005).
historical_importance: Widely regarded as the finest composer of ghazals in Hindi cinema, and the only one whose unused tunes became a hit soundtrack thirty years after his death.
relationship_with_actor: One film: H. S. Rawail's Laila Majnu (1976). His article names three of its songs — 'Hoke Mayus Tere Dar Se', 'Tere Dar Pe Aaya Hu' and 'Barbad-e-Mohabbat', all recorded with Mohammed Rafi — among the hits of his last years. He died in July 1975, before the film's release, and Jaidev is also credited on it; this workbook records both composers as credited.
biography: Madan Mohan wrote the songs of Laila Majnu and did not live to see the film open. One of the most admired composers in Hindi cinema — a National Film Award winner for Dastak and the acknowledged master of the film ghazal, whose unrecorded tunes were used thirty years after his death for Veer-Zaara — he was at the end of his career when H. S. Rawail cast the twenty-four-year-old Rishi Kapoor as Qais in the classical Arabic love tragedy. His article names 'Hoke Mayus Tere Dar Se', 'Tere Dar Pe Aaya Hu' and 'Barbad-e-Mohabbat', all sung by Mohammed Rafi, among the hits of his final years. Madan Mohan died in July 1975; the film was released in 1976 with Jaidev also credited.

name: Maddock Films
career_background: Maddock Films is an Indian film production company founded by the producer and director Dinesh Vijan in 2005 and based in Mumbai. Its productions include Love Aaj Kal (2009), Cocktail (2012), Badlapur (2015), Hindi Medium (2017) and its sequel Angrezi Medium, Luka Chuppi (2019), Bala (2019), Mimi (2021) and Chhaava (2025).
debut: Founded in 2005; Love Aaj Kal (2009) was among its early productions.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Aaj Kal (2009). Elsewhere, Cocktail, Hindi Medium, Stree and the horror-comedy films built from it.
recurring_themes: Contemporary urban romance; the small-town comedy; and latterly a connected horror-comedy universe.
creative_style: A producer-led house with a strong instinct for commercial trends, backing writer-directors and building franchises.
historical_importance: One of the most commercially successful independent production companies in contemporary Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Imtiaz Ali's Love Aaj Kal (2009), in which Kapoor plays the elderly Veer Singh whose decades-long courtship in 1960s Delhi is set against a modern couple's casual romance. The casting makes his own screen past the film's subject — the lover-boy of the 1970s appearing as the witness to an older idea of love.
biography: Maddock Films produced Love Aaj Kal, the film that turned Rishi Kapoor's romantic history into narrative material. Founded by Dinesh Vijan in 2005, the company became one of the most commercially astute independents in Hindi cinema, with Cocktail, Badlapur, Hindi Medium and the Stree horror-comedies to its name. Love Aaj Kal (2009) runs two romances in parallel: a contemporary couple who protect themselves from commitment, and the patient decades-long courtship of Veer Singh, played in the present by Kapoor. Casting the actor who had embodied uncomplicated devotion in the 1970s as the last witness to it is the film's argument, and one of the clearest instances in this workbook of his past being used deliberately.

name: Madhu Bhojwani
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own. The article on Emmay Entertainment, cited on that company's row in this sheet, names her as a co-founder alongside Nikkhil Advani and Monisha Advani.
major_works: With Kapoor: D-Day (2013).
recurring_themes: The ensemble thriller and the issue-driven commercial film, through Emmay Entertainment.
creative_style: Not documented individually.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Nikkhil Advani's D-Day (2013), the first feature her company produced, in which Kapoor plays Iqbal Seth, a Dawood Ibrahim-like crime boss hiding in Karachi — one of the most unsympathetic roles of his career and part of the late widening of his range.
biography: Madhu Bhojwani co-produced D-Day (2013), the first film made by Emmay Entertainment, the company she founded in 2011 with Nikkhil Advani and Monisha Advani. She has no Wikipedia article of her own; what is recorded of her appears in the company's. D-Day is among the strongest of Rishi Kapoor's late character roles: an Indian intelligence operation to extract a fugitive gangster from Karachi, with Kapoor as the gangster — genial, paternal and pitiless.
