Coming a year after Agneepath's Rauf Lala, it confirmed that his second career would not be confined to indulgent fathers. She is also one of the few women among this workbook's 561 credited collaborators.

name: Mahendra Saral
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Badaltey Rishtey (1978).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside Madan Joshi and Phani Majumdar.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Badaltey Rishtey (1978), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal-scored triangle from the end of Kapoor's first flush of stardom, with Phani Majumdar — a director working since 1938 — among its writers.
biography: Mahendra Saral is one of several writers credited on Badaltey Rishtey (1978) and has no documented biography. The film is a triangle from the late 1970s, scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal and written with Madan Joshi and Phani Majumdar, the last a pioneering director whose own career had begun in 1938. Collective writing credits of this kind are the norm across Kapoor's filmography, and in most cases — this one included — only one or two names on the list have left any record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Mahesh Bhatt
career_background: Mahesh Bhatt (born 20 September 1948) is a retired Indian film director, producer and screenwriter, known for unconventional narratives and bold themes and counted among the most prominent filmmakers of 1980s and 1990s Hindi cinema. He has received five National Film Awards and four Filmfare Awards, including the National Film Award – Special Jury Award for Hum Hain Rahi Pyar Ke (1993), and his Tamanna won the National Film Award for Best Film on Other Social Issues.
debut: Directing from the mid-1970s; his breakthrough was Arth (1982).
major_works: With Kapoor: Naya Daur (1978). Elsewhere, Arth, Saaransh, Naam, Sadak, Hum Hain Rahi Pyar Ke and Zakhm.
recurring_themes: Autobiographical material reworked as melodrama; adultery, addiction and illegitimacy; the woman left to manage the consequences.
creative_style: A director of intense, dialogue-driven chamber melodrama, drawing openly on his own life.
major_awards: Five National Film Awards and four Filmfare Awards.
historical_importance: One of the defining Hindi filmmakers of the 1980s and 1990s, and the founder of a family production dynasty.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it came before either man was established: Naya Daur (1978), an early Bhatt film with an R. D. Burman score, made four years before Arth made his reputation. The two never worked together again — Bhatt's cinema of adultery, addiction and self-laceration had little use for the lover-boy persona, and by the time he was dominant in the 1990s Kapoor's lead career was ending.
biography: Mahesh Bhatt directed one Rishi Kapoor film, early and inconsequentially, and the absence of any later collaboration is the more interesting fact. Naya Daur (1978) came four years before Arth, the film that made Bhatt's name, and shares its title with the far better-known 1957 Dilip Kumar picture. Bhatt went on to five National Film Awards and four Filmfare Awards and to dominate a strand of 1980s and 1990s Hindi cinema built on adultery, addiction and autobiography — Arth, Saaransh, Naam, Zakhm — material for which Kapoor's screen persona was almost comically unsuited. Their paths crossed once, before either had found his register.

name: Makhan Singh
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article identifiable to him; the bare name resolves to a disambiguation page of trade unionists and sportsmen.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a substantial one: Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986), adapted from Rajinder Singh Bedi's Sahitya Akademi-winning Urdu novel, in which Kapoor plays a man compelled by custom to marry his dead brother's widow, opposite Hema Malini. It is among the few genuinely literary films of his middle period.
biography: Makhan Singh is credited as a writer on Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986) and cannot be identified further; the name on Wikipedia leads only to a disambiguation page. The film is one of the most serious in this filmography: Rajinder Singh Bedi's novel about a widow forced by custom into marriage with her husband's younger brother, which had won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1965 and had already been filmed in Pakistan, with Kapoor as the brother and Hema Malini as the widow. Several writers are credited, among them the veteran director Phani Majumdar. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Manash Productions
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006), in which Kapoor is top-billed but functionally the antagonist, coercing a younger couple in a variation on Indecent Proposal — one of very few unsympathetic leads in his career, and one he took six years after Karobaar had used the same premise with him on the other side of it.
biography: Manash Productions is the banner on Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006) and has no recorded history. The film is among the odder entries in the filmography: Kapoor takes top billing as a wealthy man who buys his way into a young couple's marriage, playing the coercer rather than the lover. It belongs to the thin period before Dharma and Yash Raj reframed him, and shows him testing unsympathetic roles well before Agneepath made that turn respectable. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Maneesh Sharma
career_background: Maneesh Sharma (born 6 January 1978 in Delhi) is an Indian filmmaker educated at Hansraj College and the California Institute of the Arts. He has directed Band Baaja Baaraat (2010), Ladies vs Ricky Bahl (2011), Shuddh Desi Romance (2013), Fan (2016) and Tiger 3 (2023), and won the Filmfare Award for Best Debut Director for his first film.
debut: Band Baaja Baaraat (2010), which won him the Filmfare Award for Best Debut Director.
major_works: With Kapoor: Shuddh Desi Romance (2013). Elsewhere, Band Baaja Baaraat, Fan and Tiger 3.
recurring_themes: Young people negotiating marriage and work in north Indian cities; the romance treated as a practical problem.
creative_style: A Yash Raj-trained director working in a naturalistic contemporary register, with location-specific detail and non-star casting.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Debut Director for Band Baaja Baaraat.
historical_importance: One of the directors Yash Raj Films developed in-house during its studio phase, and a maker of its modern small-town romances.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Shuddh Desi Romance (2013), written by Jaideep Sahni and set among commitment-shy young people in Jaipur, with Kapoor as a wedding contractor. His article names the film's leads — Sushant Singh Rajput, Parineeti Chopra and the debuting Vaani Kapoor — without mentioning him, which fairly reflects the size of the part.
biography: Maneesh Sharma directed one of Rishi Kapoor's late supporting roles, in a film whose subject is the opposite of everything Kapoor's own romances asserted. A Yash Raj-trained filmmaker who won the Filmfare Award for Best Debut Director for Band Baaja Baaraat and went on to make Fan and Tiger 3, Sharma specialises in young north Indians treating love as a practical difficulty. Shuddh Desi Romance (2013), written by Jaideep Sahni, follows people who keep abandoning their own weddings; Kapoor plays the contractor who keeps having to arrange them. In 1973 he had played a boy willing to lose everything for love; forty years later he was the man hired to put up the tent.

name: Mangesh Dhakde
career_background: A background-score composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Mulk (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Anubhav Sinha's Mulk (2018), in which Kapoor plays Murad Ali Mohammed, the head of a Varanasi Muslim family forced to defend its loyalty in court after a nephew's terrorist act — the most substantial role of his last years, in a film whose music is deliberately restrained.
biography: Mangesh Dhakde wrote the background score for Mulk (2018) and has no documented biography. The film gave Rishi Kapoor his best late dramatic part: a Varanasi patriarch whose family's belonging is litigated in open court, played with a stillness his romantic career had never required. Mulk belongs to a register almost absent from the rest of this workbook — a film carried by argument rather than song, where the score stays out of the way. In a filmography of which thirty-two films were scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, that restraint is itself notable. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Mani Ratnam
career_background: Gopalaratnam Subramaniam (born 2 June 1956 in Madurai), known as Mani Ratnam, is an Indian director, producer and screenwriter working predominantly in Tamil cinema and occasionally in Hindi, Malayalam, Telugu and Kannada. He is widely regarded as one of the most prominent and successful directors in Indian cinema, with seven National Film Awards, four Filmfare Awards, seven Filmfare Awards South and numerous international festival awards. He received the Padma Shri in 2002.
debut: Directing from 1983; Mouna Ragam (1986) and Nayakan (1987) established him.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kasak (1992), on which he holds a writing credit. Elsewhere, Nayakan, Roja, Bombay, Dil Se and Guru as director.
recurring_themes: Love set against political violence; the city; marriages made and unmade under pressure.
creative_style: A director of visual and musical sophistication who brought art-cinema technique into mass Indian filmmaking.
major_awards: Seven National Film Awards, four Filmfare Awards, seven Filmfare Awards South and the Padma Shri (2002).
historical_importance: One of the most influential Indian filmmakers of the past four decades.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and an indirect one: he is credited as a writer on Kasak (1992), the Hindi film K. Bapaiah directed with Kapoor. Bapaiah's career was built on transplanting southern material into Hindi, so the credit most likely reflects a Tamil original of Ratnam's rather than any work on the Hindi film itself; the sources consulted here do not name that original, and the connection is recorded as a credit without further inference.
biography: Mani Ratnam appears once in this filmography, and almost certainly at second hand. One of the most important Indian filmmakers of the past forty years — Nayakan, Roja, Bombay, Guru, seven National Film Awards and the Padma Shri — he is credited as a writer on Kasak (1992), a Hindi melodrama directed by K. Bapaiah with Rishi Kapoor and a Rajesh Roshan score. Bapaiah made some eighty films largely by remaking southern successes in Hindi, so the credit most plausibly records a Tamil original rather than any direct involvement; this workbook's sources do not identify it. The row is worth keeping for the fact itself: the filmography of Hindi cinema's great romantic lead touches Ratnam's only through a remake nobody remembers.

name: Manivannan
career_background: Manivannan (31 July 1954 – 15 June 2013) was an Indian actor, film director, screenwriter, voice artist, playback singer and social activist who worked in Tamil cinema. He began as a story and dialogue writer for the director Bharathiraja between 1980 and 1982, became a successful director who experimented across genres, and later worked prolifically as a character actor.
debut: Writing for Bharathiraja from 1980; directing thereafter.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naseeb Apna Apna (1986). Elsewhere, a large body of Tamil films as director and actor.
recurring_themes: Rural Tamil melodrama and political satire; the common man against institutions.
creative_style: A writer-director from the Bharathiraja school, later one of Tamil cinema's most recognisable supporting actors.
historical_importance: A significant figure in 1980s Tamil cinema as both director and writer, and later a ubiquitous character actor.
relationship_with_actor: One credit: he is credited as a writer on Naseeb Apna Apna (1986), the T. Rama Rao film produced by K. C. Bokadia with Kapoor opposite Farha. Like Mani Ratnam's credit on Kasak, it almost certainly reflects a Tamil original remade for the Hindi market rather than work on the Hindi film, and it marks the same southern pipeline that supplied much of Kapoor's mid-1980s output.
biography: Manivannan's single credit in this filmography belongs to the southern remake trade. A writer for Bharathiraja who became a prolific Tamil director and then one of that industry's most familiar character actors, he is credited as a writer on Naseeb Apna Apna (1986) — a Hindi film directed by T. Rama Rao, who made a career of transplanting Telugu and Tamil successes into Hindi, produced by K. C. Bokadia and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal. The credit most likely records a Tamil original. Its interest for this workbook is structural: between 1985 and 1992 a substantial share of Kapoor's films came through this pipeline, with southern writers and directors supplying material the Bombay mainstream had stopped offering him.

name: Manmohan Singh
career_background: Manmohan Singh is an Indian cinematographer and film director. As a cinematographer he worked repeatedly for Yash Chopra and Aditya Chopra, shooting Chandni (1989), Lamhe (1991), Darr (1993), Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995), Dil To Pagal Hai (1997) and Mohabbatein (2000), and won two Filmfare Awards, for Chandni and Darr. He directed his first Hindi film, Pehla Pehla Pyar, in 1994 and his first Punjabi film, Jee Aayan Nu, in 2003, becoming a leading figure in Punjabi cinema.
debut: Cinematography from the 1970s; directing from Pehla Pehla Pyar (1994).
major_works: With Kapoor: Pehla Pehla Pyar (1994) as director — and, earlier, Chandni (1989) as cinematographer. Elsewhere, Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge and the Punjabi films from Jee Aayan Nu onwards.
recurring_themes: The Yash Raj romance photographed as landscape and chiffon; later, Punjabi family drama.
creative_style: A cinematographer whose images defined the look of 1990s Hindi romance, and a director of warm, music-led Punjabi cinema.
major_awards: Two Filmfare Awards for cinematography, for Chandni and Darr.
historical_importance: The cinematographer most responsible for the visual style of Yash Raj Films' romances, and a founding figure of the modern Punjabi film industry.
relationship_with_actor: Two points of contact, of which the workbook records one as a credit. He directed Kapoor in Pehla Pehla Pyar (1994), his own first Hindi film; five years earlier he had photographed Chandni, the Yash Chopra romance that restored Kapoor to leading-man status opposite Sridevi, and won the Filmfare Award for Best Cinematography for it. The look of Kapoor's most important late-career romance is therefore his.
biography: Manmohan Singh photographed the film that revived Rishi Kapoor's romantic career and then directed him in one that did not. As Yash Chopra's cinematographer he shot Chandni (1989) — the film that returned Kapoor to leading man opposite Sridevi — and won the Filmfare Award for it, before going on to Lamhe, Darr, Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge and Mohabbatein, the run of films that fixed the visual language of 1990s Hindi romance. His first film as director was Pehla Pehla Pyar (1994), a modest romance with Kapoor, written by Rumi Jaffery and Honey Irani; it made no impression. He later became one of the central figures of modern Punjabi cinema, beginning with Jee Aayan Nu in 2003.

name: Manu Rishi Chadha
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article resolved for him in this research.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rajma Chawal (2018).
recurring_themes: Contemporary Delhi dialogue and the generational gap.
creative_style: Not documented here.
historical_importance: Not documented here.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Leena Yadav's Rajma Chawal (2018), in which Kapoor plays a widowed father in old Delhi who creates a fake social-media profile to reach his estranged son — among the gentlest and most sympathetic parts of his final years.
biography: Manu Rishi Chadha is credited as a writer on Rajma Chawal (2018), and no article for him was resolved in this research. The film, directed by Leena Yadav for Netflix, casts Kapoor as a widower in the old city of Delhi who, unable to talk to his son, invents a young woman's online profile in order to reach him. It is a role built on loneliness and self-deception rather than authority, of a kind unavailable to him during his years as a star, and it belongs with Do Dooni Chaar and Sharmaji Namkeen among the late films that found something ordinary in him. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Marco Enterprises
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rishta To Ho Aisa (1992).
recurring_themes: The household melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Rishta To Ho Aisa (1992), the fourth of Kalpataru's five family melodramas with Kapoor, written with Kader Khan and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal.
biography: Marco Enterprises is a banner on Rishta To Ho Aisa (1992) and has no recorded history. The film is one of five household melodramas Kalpataru made with Kapoor between 1988 and 1994 — pictures named for the family rather than for any romance, written largely by Kader Khan, scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, financed by companies with no public profile and reviewed almost nowhere. It was released in the same year as Deewana and Bol Radha Bol, which shows what the bulk of his output looked like even as those two films decided the shape of his later career. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Mayank Arts
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Deewana (1992).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented, though its one credit is on a film of real consequence.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and on the pivotal film of the later career: Deewana (1992), Raj Kanwar's directorial debut, in which Kapoor plays the singer presumed dead whose widow marries the younger man played by a debuting Shah Rukh Khan.
biography: Mayank Arts is one of the banners on Deewana (1992) and has no recorded history. The film is the single most consequential entry in the second half of this filmography: Kapoor as Ravi, the wealthy singer believed killed, and Shah Rukh Khan in his film debut as the man his widow marries. It was a commercial success, won Khan a Filmfare award for best debut, and is read as the moment Hindi cinema's romantic lead passed between generations — with Kapoor performing the handover on screen. Several producers and two banners are credited on it, none of them documented. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Mayur Puri
career_background: Mayur Puri, from Ajmer in Rajasthan, is an Indian screenwriter, lyricist, actor and filmmaker based in Mumbai. His song and dialogue work includes Farah Khan's Om Shanti Om (2007) and Happy New Year (2014) and the ABCD: Any Body Can Dance films, and he directed his first short film, Firdaws, in 2017.
debut: Writing songs and dialogue from the mid-2000s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011). Elsewhere, Om Shanti Om, Happy New Year and the ABCD films.
recurring_themes: Spectacle, dance and self-aware Hindi film pastiche.
creative_style: A lyricist-screenwriter attached to large commercial entertainments, especially Farah Khan's.
historical_importance: Not independently prominent, but a regular contributor to some of the biggest Hindi films of the 2000s and 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011), which Hema Malini wrote, produced and directed, with Kapoor among a cast of veterans in support. Puri also wrote for Om Shanti Om (2007), in which Kapoor appears as himself, though this workbook's credits for that film do not list him.
biography: Mayur Puri wrote for Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011), one of the least seen films in this filmography. A screenwriter and lyricist from Ajmer whose work runs through Farah Khan's biggest pictures — Om Shanti Om, Happy New Year — and the ABCD dance films, Puri belongs to the machinery of large commercial Hindi cinema. Tell Me O Kkhuda was Hema Malini's third film as director, built around her daughter Esha Deol, with Kapoor and several of his contemporaries taking small parts; it failed commercially. It is the only credit shared by Kapoor and Hema Malini, the leading female star of the decade in which he became a lead.

name: Mehboob Studios
career_background: Mehboob Studio is an Indian film and recording studio in Bandra, Mumbai, founded in 1954 by the director and producer Mehboob Khan, who had earlier owned Mehboob Productions, founded in 1942. It is most associated with Mother India (1957), which won the Filmfare Awards for Best Film and Best Director and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.
debut: Operating as a studio from 1954.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chala Murari Hero Banne (1977). Elsewhere, it is the facility at which a large part of Hindi cinema was shot and recorded.
recurring_themes: A facility rather than a production house with a slate.
creative_style: Not applicable; it is a studio and recording stage.
historical_importance: One of the most historically significant film facilities in India, founded by the maker of Mother India.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Asrani's Chala Murari Hero Banne (1977) — a satire about a man trying to become a film star, in which the real stars, Kapoor among them, appear within the joke. That the credit is a studio rather than a producer is fitting for a film about the industry's own machinery.
biography: Mehboob Studio appears once in this filmography, on a film about the film industry. Founded in Bandra in 1954 by Mehboob Khan — the maker of Mother India, which won Filmfare's Best Film and Best Director and an Academy Award nomination — the studio became one of the most used facilities in Indian cinema, a place rather than a production house. Its credit here is on Chala Murari Hero Banne (1977), the satire Asrani wrote, directed and starred in about a hopeful trying to become a hero, with the real stars appearing as themselves. Kapoor was four years past Bobby and already famous enough to be part of the joke.

name: Mehmood
career_background: Mehmood Ali (29 September 1932 – 23 July 2004), known as Mehmood, was an Indian actor, singer, director and producer who appeared in over 300 Hindi films across more than four decades, playing comic, serious and emotional roles, and was known as Bollywood's original Bhaijaan. He received twenty-five award nominations. Meena Kumari was his sister-in-law, and his children include the singer Lucky Ali and the actress Ginny.
debut: Acting from the 1940s; directing and producing from the 1960s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ginny Aur Johnny (1976), which he directed. Elsewhere, Padosan, Pyar Kiye Jaa and Bombay to Goa.
recurring_themes: Comedy built on mimicry and regional caricature; family productions starring his own children.
creative_style: A comedian-director whose own films were vehicles for family members and for his particular brand of performance.
historical_importance: The most popular comic actor in Hindi cinema for two decades and one of the few to become a director and producer in his own right.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ginny Aur Johnny (1976), which he directed. His article records that it starred his daughter Ginny and was based on the 1973 American film Paper Moon — so Kapoor, three years after Bobby, was cast as the adult foil to a child star in a Hindi version of a Hollywood picture. His son Lucky Ali also holds a credit in this filmography, as a composer on Love at Times Square (2003), twenty-seven years later.
biography: Mehmood directed Rishi Kapoor in a Hindi version of Paper Moon. The most popular comic actor in Hindi cinema for two decades, with more than 300 films behind him, Mehmood also produced and directed, usually building films around his own family. Ginny Aur Johnny (1976), his article records, starred his daughter Ginny and was based on Peter Bogdanovich's 1973 film about a conman and a child; Kapoor, twenty-three and three years past Bobby, played opposite the child. The family connection extends further: Mehmood's son Lucky Ali composed for Love at Times Square in 2003, so father and son each hold one credit in this workbook, twenty-seven years apart and both in obscure films.

name: Mirza Brothers
career_background: A writing credit on one film in this filmography, given as a pair under a collective name, with no Wikipedia article identifiable to it.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aap Ke Deewane (1980).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside Madan Joshi.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Aap Ke Deewane (1980), the first production of Rakesh Roshan's Filmkraft, directed by Surendra Mohan with a Rajesh Roshan score. The film failed, and the surviving account of its plot does not record how its triangle resolves.
biography: The Mirza Brothers are credited as writers on Aap Ke Deewane (1980) and cannot be identified further. The film has a small place in industrial history as the first production of Filmkraft, the company Rakesh Roshan founded that year and which went on to make Khudgarz, Karan Arjun and the Krrish films; it was a box-office failure, and the plot summary this workbook could recover breaks off without resolving its triangle. Collective credits under a family name — Mirza Brothers, Ramsay Brothers, Sippy — recur through the Hindi industry of the period. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Mohan Sehgal
career_background: A director credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article resolved for him in this research.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sher Dil (1990).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not documented here.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sher Dil (1990), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal-scored picture from the stretch between 1989 and 1991 in which Kapoor released nine films, nearly all of them unreviewed and several directed by men with no surviving record.
biography: Mohan Sehgal directed Sher Dil (1990), and no article for him was resolved in this research. The film belongs to the least documented period in this filmography: nine releases between 1989 and 1991, financed by small producers, scored almost without exception by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, and directed by figures — Kalpataru, Surendra Mohan, Deepak Sareen, this one — whose records range from a single sentence to nothing at all. The aggregate is more informative than any individual row: at the point where Kapoor was working hardest, the industry was documenting him least. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Monisha Advani
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own. The article on Emmay Entertainment names her as a co-founder of that company in 2011, with her brother Nikkhil Advani and Madhu Bhojwani.
major_works: With Kapoor: D-Day (2013). Elsewhere, Emmay's slate including Airlift and Batla House.
recurring_themes: The ensemble thriller and the issue-driven commercial film.
creative_style: Not documented individually.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Nikkhil Advani's D-Day (2013), the first feature her company produced, in which Kapoor plays Iqbal Seth, a Dawood Ibrahim-like crime boss living under protection in Karachi — among the most unsympathetic roles of his career.
biography: Monisha Advani co-produced D-Day (2013), the first film from Emmay Entertainment, the company she founded in 2011 with her brother Nikkhil Advani and Madhu Bhojwani. She has no article of her own; what is recorded of her appears in the company's. D-Day gave Rishi Kapoor one of his strongest late roles: the fugitive gangster in Karachi, played with a geniality that makes the character worse rather than better. Coming a year after Agneepath's Rauf Lala, it confirmed that the second half of his career would include real menace alongside the indulgent fathers. She is one of relatively few women among this workbook's 561 credited collaborators.

name: Movie Temple Productions
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Besharam (2013).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Besharam (2013), Abhinav Kashyap's comedy and the only film in which Rishi Kapoor, his wife Neetu Singh and their son Ranbir Kapoor all appear — the parents as police officers, the son as the title character.
biography: Movie Temple Productions is a banner on Besharam (2013) and has no recorded history. The film matters to this filmography as a family document rather than as work: Abhinav Kashyap's follow-up to Dabangg cast Ranbir Kapoor as a cheerful car thief with both his parents as the police officers pursuing him — Rishi Kapoor and Neetu Singh, who had been paired as romantic leads in a dozen films of the 1970s. It is the only film in which all three appear, and it failed both critically and commercially. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Mukesh Talreja
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patiala House (2011).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Nikkhil Advani's Patiala House (2011), in which Kapoor plays the Southall patriarch whose bitterness after a racist attack leads him to forbid his son's cricket career — one of the stronger roles of his late period, and his fourth film opposite Dimple Kapadia after Bobby, Saagar and Pyaar Mein Twist.
biography: Mukesh Talreja is one of five producers credited on Patiala House (2011) and has no documented biography. The film gave Kapoor a genuinely cold part: Gurtej Singh Kahlon, a London Punjabi whose experience of racist violence has hardened into control over his son's life, forbidding him the cricket career he wants. It also reunited him with Dimple Kapadia for the fourth time since Bobby, now as a long-married couple. Five producers across three banners are credited, which is characteristic of T-Series-era financing. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Mukta Arts
career_background: Mukta Arts is the production company founded by the director Subhash Ghai in 1982, which became a public company in 2000. Its article names Ghai and Rahul Puri among its key people.
debut: Founded in 1982; it produced Ghai's films from Vidhaata onwards.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kaanchi: The Unbreakable (2014). Elsewhere, Ram Lakhan, Saudagar, Khalnayak, Pardes, Taal and Iqbal.
recurring_themes: The showman's melodrama; from the 2000s, a broader slate including small award-winning films.
creative_style: A director's own company, built to produce his films and later to train filmmakers through an associated institute.
historical_importance: One of the most prominent director-owned production houses in Hindi cinema, and among the first to list publicly.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Kaanchi: The Unbreakable (2014), a late Subhash Ghai film with Kapoor in support. The more consequential connection is outside this credit: Ghai had directed Kapoor in Karz (1980), two years before founding the company, and that film remains one of the two or three on which the actor's reputation rests.
biography: Mukta Arts, Subhash Ghai's company, appears once in this filmography — and late. Founded in 1982, two years after Ghai directed Rishi Kapoor in Karz, the company produced the run of films that made him Hindi cinema's showman of the 1980s and 1990s: Ram Lakhan, Saudagar, Khalnayak, Pardes, Taal. It listed publicly in 2000 and later produced the National Award-winning Iqbal. Its one Kapoor credit is Kaanchi: The Unbreakable (2014), a failure in which the actor took a supporting part thirty-four years after Karz had given him Monty, the reincarnated singer. The gap between the two credits is the whole arc of both careers.

name: Munir Ahmad
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article identifiable to him; the bare name resolves to an unrelated Afghan cricketer.
major_works: With Kapoor: Don't Stop Dreaming (2007).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Don't Stop Dreaming (2007), one of the two English-language films in this filmography, both written and directed by Kapoor's cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor. Taz of Stereo Nation composed its soundtrack and co-starred; his article names Kapoor, Sunil Shetty and Richard Blackwood among the cast.
biography: Munir Ahmad is credited as a producer on Don't Stop Dreaming (2007) and cannot be identified further. The film is one of two English-language pictures Kapoor made that year, both written and directed by his first cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor and both so slightly released that almost nothing about them is documented. What is known comes from an unexpected direction: the British Asian singer Taz, who composed the soundtrack and acted in it, has an article that names Kapoor among his co-stars — one of the few places either film is recorded at all. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Mushtaq Jalili
career_background: Mushtaq Jalili (27 October 1927 – 14 October 2004) was an Indian screenwriter born in Hyderabad, the son of the Urdu poet Fasahat Jung Jaleel, known as Jaleel Manikpuri. He began as an assistant story writer with A. R. Kardar, worked from 1955 in the story department under P. N. Arora, then as an assistant writer with Pandit Mukhram Sharma, and was writing films in his own right from 1963.
debut: Writing independently from 1963, after apprenticeships with A. R. Kardar, P. N. Arora and Pandit Mukhram Sharma.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naseeb Apna Apna (1986).
recurring_themes: Melodrama in the Urdu-inflected tradition he was trained in.
creative_style: A writer formed by three successive apprenticeships in the old Bombay story departments.
historical_importance: Not substantially documented, though his training places him in a direct line from the 1940s studio system.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Naseeb Apna Apna (1986), the T. Rama Rao film produced by K. C. Bokadia with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score, in which Kapoor starred opposite Farha. He shares the writing credit with Manivannan, whose own credit almost certainly reflects the Tamil original the film was remade from.
biography: Mushtaq Jalili's single credit in this filmography carries an unusual amount of history. The son of the Urdu poet Jaleel Manikpuri, he learned screenwriting through three apprenticeships in the Bombay story departments — with A. R. Kardar, then under P. N. Arora from 1955, then with Pandit Mukhram Sharma — before writing on his own account from 1963. By the time he worked on Naseeb Apna Apna (1986), a southern remake directed by T. Rama Rao with Kapoor opposite Farha, that whole apprenticeship system had gone. His co-writer on the film, Manivannan, was a Tamil director whose credit reflects the original rather than the Hindi version.

name: Mushtaq Shiekh
career_background: Mushtaq Shiekh, from Mumbai, is an Indian screenwriter, author, producer and actor, known mainly for writing the screenplays of Ra.One, Om Shanti Om and Billu.
debut: Writing for Hindi films in the 2000s, in close association with Farah Khan and Shah Rukh Khan's productions.
major_works: With Kapoor: Om Shanti Om (2007). Elsewhere, Ra.One and Billu.
recurring_themes: Hindi cinema's own history and machinery as subject matter.
creative_style: A screenwriter and author working within the Red Chillies and Farah Khan orbit, with books on the industry alongside his scripts.
historical_importance: Not independently prominent, though his credits include two of the largest Hindi productions of their period.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Om Shanti Om (2007), in which Kapoor appears as himself among dozens of stars. The film is a pastiche of the 1970s industry in which he had been a young lead, and its reincarnation plot echoes Karz (1980), one of his own defining films — so the screenplay places him inside a knowing reconstruction of his own era.
biography: Mushtaq Shiekh co-wrote Om Shanti Om, the film that turned the cinema of Rishi Kapoor's youth into material. A Mumbai screenwriter and author best known for Om Shanti Om, Ra.One and Billu, Shiekh worked within the Farah Khan and Red Chillies orbit, and also published books about the industry. Om Shanti Om (2007) sets half its action in the 1970s Hindi film world and borrows its reincarnation structure from Karz, the Subhash Ghai film that had given Kapoor his most durable role in 1980. Kapoor appears as himself. It is the clearest instance in this workbook of his past being recycled as content by the generation that followed him.

name: N. N. Sippy
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The Sippy name recurs in Hindi cinema — G. P. Sippy and Ramesh Sippy also hold credits here — but no source consulted connects them to him.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sargam (1979).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a major one: Sargam (1979), K. Viswanath's Hindi remake of his own Telugu film, in which Kapoor courts Jaya Prada's mute heroine through the dholak. Its Laxmikant–Pyarelal soundtrack was among the biggest of the decade, and the film is one of the three or four on which Kapoor's image as a singing romantic hero rests.
biography: N. N. Sippy produced Sargam (1979) and has no documented biography. The film is one of the most important in this filmography: directed by K. Viswanath, the most honoured Telugu filmmaker of his generation, as a Hindi version of his own earlier film, it cast Kapoor as a man in love with a woman who cannot speak and gave him a soundtrack — Laxmikant–Pyarelal's — that defined his singing-hero persona as firmly as Bobby had defined his romantic one. That its producer left no record is one more instance of the pattern this workbook keeps encountering: consequential films financed by people history did not keep.

name: Nadiadwala Grandson Entertainment
career_background: Nadiadwala Grandson Entertainment Pvt Ltd is an Indian film production company based in Mumbai, established by Sajid Nadiadwala in 1992 and involved in motion pictures, radio, television and other entertainment activities.
debut: Established in 1992.
major_works: With Kapoor: Housefull 2 (2012). Elsewhere, the Housefull series, Kick and Baaghi.
recurring_themes: Large-ensemble comedy and mass-market action franchises.
creative_style: A producer-led house specialising in franchise entertainment with very large casts.
historical_importance: One of the most commercially successful production companies in contemporary Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Housefull 2 (2012), in which Kapoor and his elder brother Randhir Kapoor play feuding brothers in a cast of a dozen stars — one of the very few occasions the two appeared together on screen as adults. The Nadiadwala name recurs in this filmography through F. A. and I. A. Nadiadwala, producers on films from 1975 and 1989.
biography: Nadiadwala Grandson Entertainment produced Housefull 2, and the credit records a small family curiosity. Established by Sajid Nadiadwala in 1992, the company became one of the most commercially successful in Hindi cinema on the strength of franchise comedies and action films. Housefull 2 (2012) is a farce with a dozen stars, in which Rishi Kapoor and Randhir Kapoor play feuding brothers — a rare on-screen pairing of the two Kapoor brothers as adults, forty years after they had appeared together as children in Shree 420. The Nadiadwala name appears twice more in this workbook, on films from 1975 and 1989, through producers about whom nothing is recorded.

name: Nalini Shankar
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sheshnaag (1990).
recurring_themes: The folk-mythological fantasy.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sheshnaag (1990), the snake-deity fantasy made in the wake of Nagina's success, with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score and two director credits. She is one of three producers on it and one of the few women credited as a producer anywhere in this filmography.
biography: Nalini Shankar is one of three producers credited on Sheshnaag (1990) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the folk-fantasy cycle that followed Nagina in 1986, in which Kapoor's romantic function was subordinated to curses and serpent deities; it carries two director credits that no source consulted here reconciles. Her row is worth noting in the aggregate: women are scarce among the 561 collaborators in this workbook, and those who appear are concentrated either in the late films or, as here, in single producer credits on pictures nobody wrote about. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Namrata Goyal
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own; the bare name resolves to an unrelated businessman, which is how an earlier pass of this research briefly attached the wrong article.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Nandita Das's Manto (2018), the biographical film about the Urdu writer Saadat Hasan Manto, screened at Cannes in Un Certain Regard, in which Kapoor has a small role.
biography: Namrata Goyal is one of six producers credited on Manto (2018) and has no documented biography. The film follows the Urdu short-story writer Saadat Hasan Manto through obscenity trials in Bombay and his migration to Pakistan; Kapoor appears briefly. Its financing was spread across six producers and four companies, which is typical of festival-facing Indian cinema, and most of those names leave no trace — in this case the trace that does exist belongs to someone else entirely. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Nandita Das
career_background: Nandita Das (born 7 November 1969) is an Indian actress and director who has acted in more than forty feature films in ten languages, including Fire (1996), Earth (1998), Bawandar (2000), Kannathil Muthamittal (2002) and Before the Rains (2007). Her directorial debut Firaaq (2008) premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival, and her second film as director, Manto (2018), was screened at the Cannes Film Festival in the Un Certain Regard section.
debut: Acting from 1987; directorial debut Firaaq (2008).
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018), which she wrote, produced and directed. Elsewhere, Fire and Earth as an actress and Firaaq as a director.
recurring_themes: Communal violence and its aftermath; the writer or artist under state and social pressure; women's autonomy.
creative_style: A director from the parallel-cinema tradition working in a restrained, research-driven register, often on politically difficult subjects.
historical_importance: One of the most internationally visible Indian actor-directors, associated with Deepa Mehta's elements trilogy and with her own films on communalism and censorship.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Manto (2018), in which Kapoor takes a small role in a biographical film about the Urdu writer Saadat Hasan Manto and his obscenity trials. For an actor whose career was built on commercial romance, a Cannes-screened literary biopic is as far from Bobby as this filmography reaches, and it came two years before his death.
biography: Nandita Das directed the most unlikely film in this filmography. An actress of more than forty features in ten languages — Fire, Earth, Bawandar — she turned director with Firaaq, about the aftermath of the 2002 Gujarat violence, and then made Manto (2018), a biographical film about the Urdu short-story writer who was tried for obscenity in both India and Pakistan. It screened at Cannes in Un Certain Regard. Rishi Kapoor appears briefly in it. Nothing in his fifty years of commercial cinema prepares for the credit, and that is its interest: in his last years his name could be attached to a festival film about literary censorship, and he took the part.

name: Nandita Das Initiatives LLP
career_background: The production vehicle of the director Nandita Das, credited on Manto (2018). It has no Wikipedia article of its own; her article is cited on her row in this sheet.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018).
recurring_themes: Politically engaged independent cinema.
creative_style: A director's own company, used to make her films.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Manto (2018), the Cannes-screened biographical film about the Urdu writer Saadat Hasan Manto in which Kapoor has a small role — the furthest this filmography reaches from the commercial romance that made him.
biography: Nandita Das Initiatives is the company through which Nandita Das made Manto (2018), and it has no separate documentation. The film, which she wrote, produced and directed, follows Saadat Hasan Manto through the obscenity trials that pursued him in Bombay and Lahore, and was screened at Cannes in Un Certain Regard; Kapoor appears briefly. Four companies and six producers share the credits, an arrangement typical of Indian films made for festivals rather than for the domestic box office. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Narender Bedi
career_background: Narendra Bedi (1 January 1937 – 21 October 1982) was a Hindi film director and the son of the Urdu writer Rajinder Singh Bedi. He is best known for Jawani Diwani (1972), starring Randhir Kapoor and Jaya Bhaduri, for several Rajesh Khanna films, and for the Amitabh Bachchan pictures Benaam (1974) and Adalat (1977).
debut: Directing from 1965; his breakthrough was Jawani Diwani (1972).
major_works: With Kapoor: Rafoo Chakkar (1975). Elsewhere, Jawani Diwani, Benaam and Adalat.
recurring_themes: Youth comedy and the urban thriller; the star vehicle built on energy rather than melodrama.
creative_style: A brisk commercial director with a feel for young audiences, working across comedy and crime.
historical_importance: A significant director of 1970s Hindi cinema, cut short by his death at forty-five.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rafoo Chakkar (1975), the Hindi reworking of Some Like It Hot in which Kapoor and Paintal hide from gangsters in women's clothes — one of the earliest demonstrations that his range included broad farce. The family connection runs further: Bedi's father, Rajinder Singh Bedi, wrote the novel adapted as Ek Chadar Maili Si, in which Kapoor starred in 1986, and he had earlier directed Kapoor's brother Randhir in Jawani Diwani.
biography: Narender Bedi directed the film that showed Rishi Kapoor could play farce, and his family appears twice more in this workbook. The son of Rajinder Singh Bedi — the Urdu novelist whose Ek Chadar Maili Si would be filmed with Kapoor in 1986 — Bedi made his name with Jawani Diwani in 1972, which starred Kapoor's elder brother Randhir, and went on to direct Rajesh Khanna and Amitabh Bachchan. Rafoo Chakkar (1975), his film with Rishi Kapoor, transplants Some Like It Hot to Bombay, with the star spending much of it in women's clothing two years after Bobby. Bedi died in 1982 at forty-five.

name: Nasir Hussain Films
career_background: The production banner of the writer-director-producer Nasir Hussain, credited on Hum Kisise Kum Naheen. It has no Wikipedia article of its own; Hussain's article is cited on his row in this sheet, where his career and influence are set out.
major_works: With Kapoor: Hum Kisise Kum Naheen (1977).
recurring_themes: The musical of disguise and rivalry; youth, performance and courtship through song.
creative_style: A family banner built to make Hussain's own musicals, with R. D. Burman scoring and new performers introduced by the films themselves.
historical_importance: The company behind several of the films credited with establishing both the 1970s masala musical and, later, the 1990s romance template.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Hum Kisise Kum Naheen (1977), the purest expression of Kapoor's youth persona: a musical of masquerade and competition with an R. D. Burman soundtrack in which the hero sings his way through the plot. It is among the three or four films that fixed his image as the singing romantic lead.
biography: Nasir Hussain Films produced Hum Kisise Kum Naheen, one of the defining films of Rishi Kapoor's youth. The banner belonged to Nasir Hussain, the filmmaker credited with creating the masala form with Yaadon Ki Baraat and, a decade later, the 1990s romance template with Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak. The 1977 film is a musical of disguise and rivalry carried by an R. D. Burman score, in which Kapoor sings, flirts and competes rather than suffers — the register his early stardom rests on. The company has no documentation of its own; what is known comes through Hussain's article, cited on his row rather than duplicated here.

name: Neetu Verma
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chalk N Duster (2016).
recurring_themes: The institutional drama; teachers and schools.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chalk N Duster (2016), a drama about schoolteachers resisting a commercialising management, with an ensemble including Shabana Azmi and Juhi Chawla and Kapoor in support — one of the small, socially minded films of his last years.
biography: Neetu Verma is credited as a writer on Chalk N Duster (2016) and has no documented biography. The film is a modest drama about two teachers and the pressures of commercialised schooling, cast with veterans and with Kapoor in a supporting part. She is one of the women credited as writers in this workbook — a small group, concentrated almost entirely in the final fifteen years of the filmography, which is itself a finding worth recording about the industry Kapoor worked in. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Neha Arts
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own. It is the banner associated with the producer Nitin Manmohan, who has a separate row in this sheet.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bol Radha Bol (1992).
recurring_themes: The David Dhawan comedy vehicle.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Bol Radha Bol (1992), David Dhawan's double-role farce in which Kapoor plays both a businessman and his criminal lookalike opposite a doubled Juhi Chawla. Released months after Deewana, it was among the last hits he carried alone.
biography: Neha Arts is the banner on Bol Radha Bol (1992), the last outright hit Rishi Kapoor carried by himself. The company has no recorded history; it belongs to the producer Nitin Manmohan, who made two Dhawan comedies with Kapoor. The film is a double-role farce — Kapoor as a businessman and as the lookalike criminal who takes his place, Juhi Chawla doubled as well — and it came out in the same year as Deewana, where the romantic lead passed to Shah Rukh Khan. The two films together make 1992 the decisive year in this filmography. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Nikhil–Vinay
career_background: Nikhil–Vinay were an Indian composing duo consisting of Nikhil Kamath and Vinay Tiwari, both trained in classical music, active in Hindi cinema from 1991 until their split in 2006. According to their article, the singer Anuradha Paudwal discovered them and recommended them to Gulshan Kumar of T-Series.
debut: Composing from 1991, under the patronage of T-Series.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006). Elsewhere, a long run of 1990s T-Series soundtracks.
recurring_themes: Melodic romance in the T-Series idiom of the 1990s.
creative_style: Classically trained melodists working for the music-company production model that dominated 1990s Hindi film song.
historical_importance: Representative of the composers T-Series built its catalogue on in the 1990s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006), the last year of the duo's partnership, in which Kapoor is top-billed but effectively the antagonist. The credit on that film also appeared in a mangled form as a stray 'Nikhil' alongside the duo's name, which this workbook has consolidated.
biography: Nikhil–Vinay scored one Rishi Kapoor film, in the final year of their partnership. Nikhil Kamath and Vinay Tiwari were classically trained musicians brought into films by Anuradha Paudwal's recommendation to Gulshan Kumar of T-Series, and they spent the 1990s supplying melodic romance to that company's catalogue — the music-industry production model that dominated the decade. Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006) is a late and unflattering credit for both parties: Kapoor top-billed as a man who buys his way into a young couple's marriage, the duo splitting up the same year. The film's composer credits reached this workbook partly garbled and had to be reconciled.

name: Niranjan Iyengar
career_background: Niranjan Iyengar, born in Dombivali, Maharashtra, is an Indian screenwriter and lyricist particularly known for his work with the director Karan Johar. He wrote the book The Making of Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham and has hosted the talk show Look Who's Talking with Niranjan on Zee Café. He was nominated for the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist for 'Sajda'.
debut: Writing for Hindi films from the early 2000s, within Dharma Productions.
major_works: With Kapoor: Student of the Year (2012). Elsewhere, Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna, My Name Is Khan and Agneepath as writer or dialogue writer.
recurring_themes: Family, friendship and desire inside the Dharma house style; dialogue as emotional set piece.
creative_style: A dialogue specialist formed in Karan Johar's filmmaking, with a parallel career in television presenting.
major_awards: Filmfare nomination for Best Lyricist for 'Sajda'.
historical_importance: One of the principal writers of Dharma Productions' output in the 2000s and 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Student of the Year (2012), Karan Johar's youth ensemble in which Kapoor plays the dean of a fantasy college and which launched three debutant actors. The casting of a veteran beside newcomers is the structural point: his presence supplied the credibility the cast lacked.
biography: Niranjan Iyengar wrote Student of the Year, one of three Dharma Productions films that remade Rishi Kapoor's late career. A screenwriter and lyricist formed inside Karan Johar's filmmaking — Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna, My Name Is Khan — and the author of a book about the making of Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham, Iyengar also presents television. Student of the Year (2012) cast three debutants, Sidharth Malhotra, Alia Bhatt and Varun Dhawan, and needed a familiar older presence to anchor them; Kapoor played the dean. In the same year the same company's Agneepath gave him Rauf Lala. Between them, those two films established the two registers — comic elder and genuine villain — that his last decade would alternate.

name: Niren Bhatt
career_background: Niren Bhatt is an Indian screenwriter and lyricist working predominantly in Hindi films. He has written the films of the Maddock horror-comedy universe, most notably Stree 2 (2024), which became one of the highest-grossing Hindi films of all time.
debut: Writing from 2008, initially in television and Gujarati cinema.
major_works: With Kapoor: All Is Well (2015). Elsewhere, Bala, Stree 2 and the Maddock horror-comedy films.
recurring_themes: Comedy built on small-town social anxiety; genre reworked for a mass audience.
creative_style: A comedy writer with a strong ear for regional idiom, working across Gujarati and Hindi.
historical_importance: One of the most commercially successful screenwriters of 2020s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Umesh Shukla's All Is Well (2015), a family road comedy in which Kapoor plays the father opposite Supriya Pathak, with Abhishek Bachchan as their estranged son. The film failed; Shukla would use Kapoor far better three years later in 102 Not Out.
biography: Niren Bhatt wrote All Is Well (2015), one of the weaker late Rishi Kapoor films, before becoming one of the most commercially successful screenwriters in Hindi cinema. His later work — Bala, and the Maddock horror-comedies culminating in Stree 2, among the highest-grossing Hindi films ever made — came after this credit. All Is Well is a road comedy about an estranged family, directed by Umesh Shukla between Oh My God and 102 Not Out, with Kapoor as the father and Abhishek Bachchan as the son; it was a critical and commercial failure. Shukla's next use of Kapoor, in 102 Not Out, gave him his last leading role.

name: Nishi Kohli
career_background: Nishi Kohli, born Krishna Kumari Sharma on 1 January 1935 in Sialkot and known professionally as Nishi, is an Indian former actress who worked in Punjabi and Hindi films between 1955 and 1970, frequently opposite Dara Singh. She is known for Railway Platform, Pind di Kudi and Bhangra (1959). She is married to the director Rajkumar Kohli; their sons are Armaan Kohli and Gogi Kohli.
debut: Acting from 1955; later a producer on her husband's films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naukar Biwi Ka (1983). Elsewhere, her own acting career in Punjabi and Hindi cinema.
recurring_themes: Family production within a director's household.
creative_style: An actress of the 1950s and 1960s who moved into production alongside her husband.
historical_importance: A leading actress of Punjabi cinema in her era, and part of the Kohli filmmaking family.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Naukar Biwi Ka (1983), which her husband Rajkumar Kohli directed and she produced — a household enterprise in the pattern that recurs through this filmography. Kapoor leads a comedy about a husband reduced to his wife's servant, with a Bappi Lahiri score.
biography: Nishi Kohli produced Naukar Biwi Ka (1983) for her husband to direct, and her own career came earlier. Born Krishna Kumari Sharma in Sialkot in 1935, she acted in Punjabi and Hindi films from 1955 to 1970, often opposite Dara Singh, and was known in Punjabi cinema for Bhangra and Pind di Kudi before marrying the director Rajkumar Kohli. Their film with Kapoor is a comedy in which a husband is reduced to serving his own wife, scored by Bappi Lahiri. Husband-and-wife credits on the same picture recur across this workbook — the Desais, the Bohras, the Advanis, the Yadavs — and are one of its clearest findings about how the industry was organised.

name: Nucleya
career_background: Udyan Sagar, known by the stage name Nucleya, is an Indian electronic music producer and DJ, born in Agra and based in Ahmedabad, working since 1998.
debut: Producing electronic music from 1998; prominent as a solo artist from the 2010s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kapoor & Sons (2016). Elsewhere, his bass-music albums and festival work.
recurring_themes: Indian bass music — electronic production built on regional samples and folk vocals.
creative_style: A producer and DJ from outside the film industry whose work reaches cinema through single-song commissions.
historical_importance: One of the most prominent figures in Indian electronic dance music.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kapoor & Sons (2016), where he is one of six credited song composers alongside Amaal Mallik, Badshah, Arko, Tanishk Bagchi and Benny Dayal. Kapoor plays the ninety-year-old grandfather in it, under prosthetics, and won the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor.
biography: Nucleya contributed to the soundtrack of Kapoor & Sons (2016), and the credit measures the distance this filmography covers. An electronic producer and DJ working since 1998, Udyan Sagar built a following in Indian bass music entirely outside cinema before films began commissioning individual tracks from him; on Kapoor & Sons he is one of six composers credited under 'Songs'. The film gave Rishi Kapoor his Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor as a mischievous nonagenarian. Forty-three years earlier, Bobby's entire soundtrack had come from one composing duo. The same actor's last significant hit was scored by a committee that included a DJ.

name: Nupur Asthana
career_background: Nupur Asthana, from Uttar Pradesh, is an Indian film and television director and writer. She made her television debut with the series Hip Hip Hurray in 1998 and her film debut with the youth film Mujhse Fraaandship Karoge (2011), produced by Y-Films, the youth arm of Yash Raj Films.
debut: Television from 1998; film debut Mujhse Fraaandship Karoge (2011).
major_works: With Kapoor: Bewakoofiyaan (2014). Elsewhere, Mujhse Fraaandship Karoge and the television series Hip Hip Hurray.
recurring_themes: Young people negotiating work, money and family expectation.
creative_style: A director from television working in a light contemporary register for the Yash Raj studio.
historical_importance: One of the small number of women directing mainstream Hindi features in the 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Bewakoofiyaan (2014), a Yash Raj romance about a couple strained by unemployment, in which Kapoor plays the heroine's father — a bureaucrat whose objection to her boyfriend is frankly economic. It is one of six Yash Raj films from his character-actor phase, and he is the senior presence against two young leads.
biography: Nupur Asthana directed Rishi Kapoor in Bewakoofiyaan (2014), one of his late Yash Raj supporting roles. She came up through television — Hip Hip Hurray, in 1998, was among the first Indian series aimed at teenagers — and made her first feature for Y-Films, the studio's youth label, before this one. Bewakoofiyaan, written by Habib Faisal, is about a young couple whose relationship frays when he loses his job; Kapoor plays her father, a government officer who disapproves on precisely financial grounds. It is a small part, and she is one of very few women to have directed him in a career of 160 films.

name: Nutan
career_background: Nutan Samarth-Bahl (4 June 1936 – 21 February 1991) was an Indian actress regarded as one of the finest in the history of Indian cinema, noted for naturalistic performances in parts of conflicted and often unconventional women. In a career spanning four decades she received seven Filmfare Awards, including a then-record five for Best Actress — the first for Seema (1955) and the last, in the Best Supporting Actress category, for Meri Jung — and the Padma Shri in 1974. Her son is the actor Mohnish Bahl, and she belonged to the Mukherjee-Samarth family.
debut: On screen from 1950; Seema (1955) brought her the first of five Best Actress awards.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994), as producer. Elsewhere, as an actress, Seema, Sujata, Bandini and Milan.
recurring_themes: As an actress, women refusing the roles their families assign them; as a producer, a single late family film.
creative_style: An actress of extraordinary restraint in an era of declamation; her production credit is an isolated late venture.
major_awards: Seven Filmfare Awards, including a then-record five for Best Actress; the Padma Shri in 1974.
historical_importance: One of the greatest actresses in Indian cinema, and the holder of the record for Filmfare Best Actress awards in her lifetime.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and a surprising one: she is named as a producer of Saajan Ka Ghar (1994), directed by Surendra Bohra with a Nadeem–Shravan score — a modest melodrama released three years after her death, in a function entirely unlike the work that made her. She and Kapoor never appeared together as actors.
biography: Nutan appears in this filmography once, and not as an actress. One of the greatest performers in Indian cinema — five Filmfare Best Actress awards, a then-record, for Seema, Sujata, Bandini and others, a Padma Shri in 1974, and a style of unadorned realism decades ahead of the industry around her — she is credited here as a producer of Saajan Ka Ghar (1994), a Nadeem–Shravan-scored melodrama directed by Surendra Bohra. Nutan died in February 1991, three years before its release, so the credit records involvement in a project she did not live to see out. That she and Rishi Kapoor never shared a scene in fifty years of overlapping careers is the more striking fact.

name: Om Prakash Mittal
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Banjaran (1991).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Banjaran (1991), directed by Harmesh Malhotra with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score — the fifth and last of Malhotra's films with Kapoor, and one of nine the actor released between 1989 and 1991.
biography: Om Prakash Mittal produced Banjaran (1991) and has no documented biography. The film closes Harmesh Malhotra's run of five pictures with Kapoor — a sequence that had begun with the hit Nagina in 1986 and ran through its sequel Nigahen to this and Amiri Garibi — all of them scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal and all aimed at the single-screen market. It belongs to the densest stretch of the filmography, nine releases in three years, and to its least documented tier. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Oriol Paulo
career_background: Oriol Paulo (born 30 July 1975 in Barcelona) is a Spanish screenwriter and director known for the crime thrillers The Body (2012) and The Invisible Guest (2016), both of which were internationally acclaimed and remade in several languages. He was nominated for Best New Director at the Goya Awards and won the Best Film award at the Fantastic Film Festival in Paris for The Body.
debut: Writing from 2004; his feature directing debut was The Body (2012), which he also wrote.
major_works: With Kapoor: The Body (2019), the Hindi remake of his own film. Elsewhere, The Invisible Guest and Mirage.
recurring_themes: The withheld fact; thrillers built on a single reversal and on characters lying to each other.
creative_style: A writer-director of tightly engineered puzzle thrillers whose scripts have proved unusually portable across languages.
major_awards: Goya nomination for Best New Director; Best Film at the Fantastic Film Festival, Paris, for The Body.
historical_importance: One of the most widely remade European thriller writers of his generation.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and the only foreign writing credit in this filmography: the Hindi The Body (2019), directed by Jeethu Joseph from Paulo's Spanish original, in which Kapoor plays the police officer investigating a corpse's disappearance from a morgue. It was the last film released in his lifetime.
biography: Oriol Paulo wrote the original of the last film released in Rishi Kapoor's lifetime. A Barcelona screenwriter and director, Paulo made The Body in 2012 — a thriller about a body vanishing from a morgue and the detective who will not let it go — and followed it with The Invisible Guest; both were remade repeatedly across Asia. The Hindi version, directed by the Malayalam filmmaker Jeethu Joseph in 2019, cast Kapoor as the investigating officer, a cold procedural role unlike anything his leading career offered. He died five months after its release. Paulo's is the only non-Indian writing credit in this workbook's 561 collaborators.

name: P. Madhavan
career_background: Palakrishnan Madhavan (1 January 1928 – 16 December 2003) was an Indian film director and producer who worked in Tamil cinema in the 1960s and 1970s. He directed forty-nine films and produced thirty-nine under the banner Arun Prasad Movies, and died in Chennai.
debut: Directing from 1963.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985). Elsewhere, a long run of Tamil films as director and producer.
recurring_themes: Family melodrama in the southern commercial tradition.
creative_style: A prolific director-producer of the Tamil industry who occasionally worked in Hindi.
historical_importance: A significant figure in 1960s and 1970s Tamil commercial cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985), an R. D. Burman-scored melodrama produced by Harish Shah, from the weakest commercial stretch of Kapoor's lead career. It is one of several of his mid-1980s films made by southern directors working in Hindi — the pipeline that supplied much of his work in that decade.
biography: P. Madhavan directed one Rishi Kapoor film, and it belongs to a pattern rather than to either man's best work. A Tamil director-producer with forty-nine films directed and thirty-nine produced under his own Arun Prasad Movies banner, Madhavan worked mainly in the 1960s and 1970s in Madras. Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985) is a late Hindi credit, scored by R. D. Burman and produced by Harish Shah, from the year in which Kapoor released five forgotten films. Between 1985 and 1992 a substantial share of his work came from southern directors — T. Rama Rao, K. Bapaiah, K. Ravi Shankar, K. Shankar, this one — reworking proven material for the Hindi market.

name: Palagummi Padmaraju
industry: Telugu literature; Telugu and Hindi cinema
career_background: Palagummi Padmaraju (24 June 1915 – 17 February 1983), known as P. Padmaraju, was a Telugu writer, poet, lyricist, screenwriter and lecturer, and a winner of the Sahitya Akademi Award. He is known for his work in Telugu literature and Telugu cinema, with Galivana among his notable works.
debut: A literary career from the 1930s and 1940s, with film writing alongside it.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani (1988). Elsewhere, his Telugu short stories and novels, including the Sahitya Akademi-honoured work.
recurring_themes: The moral life of ordinary families; Telugu social realism carried into popular cinema.
creative_style: A literary writer of standing whose film credits arise mainly from adaptations of his own or others' Telugu material.
major_awards: Sahitya Akademi Award.
historical_importance: A significant figure in twentieth-century Telugu literature, remembered particularly for his short stories.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and at second hand: Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani (1988), the first of Kalpataru's five household melodramas with Kapoor, is a remake of a Telugu film, and Padmaraju's credit almost certainly belongs to that original rather than to the Hindi version. The film's real subject is a mother-in-law's cruelty to her daughters-in-law.
biography: Palagummi Padmaraju, a Sahitya Akademi laureate in Telugu, holds one credit in this filmography — and almost certainly for work he did not do on the Hindi film. One of the notable Telugu writers of the twentieth century, remembered for his short stories and for Galivana, Padmaraju also wrote for Telugu cinema. Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani (1988), the first of Kalpataru's five family melodramas with Kapoor, is a remake of a Telugu original, and his credit belongs there. The pattern recurs in this workbook with Mani Ratnam, Manivannan and K. Rangaraj: distinguished southern names appear on Kapoor's Hindi films because the material was imported, not because they worked with him.

name: Pamela Chopra
career_background: Pamela Chopra, née Singh (29 July 1948 – 20 April 2023), was an Indian playback singer who was also a film writer and producer. She was the wife of the director Yash Chopra; their sons are the producer-director Aditya Chopra and the actor Uday Chopra, and the actress Simi Garewal was her first cousin.
debut: Singing and writing for her husband's films from the 1970s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kabhie Kabhie (1976). Elsewhere, her playback singing and story work across the Yash Raj Films catalogue.
recurring_themes: The Yash Raj romance — longing, music and the marriage shadowed by an earlier love.
creative_style: A writer, singer and informal creative partner within her husband's studio rather than an independent author.
historical_importance: A central figure in the Yash Raj Films household, which accounts for eleven films in this filmography.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Yash Chopra's Kabhie Kabhie (1976) — the ensemble in which Kapoor and Neetu Singh's young romance plays against an older marriage haunted by a first love, with Khayyam's Filmfare-winning score. Her family connection reaches much further into this workbook: her husband directed or produced five Kapoor films and her son Aditya Chopra produced seven.
biography: Pamela Chopra is credited on Kabhie Kabhie, the first Yash Raj film in this filmography, and her family accounts for more of it than any other outside Kapoor's own. A playback singer who also wrote and produced, she was married to Yash Chopra, who directed or produced five of Kapoor's films and in Chandni restored him to romantic leading man; their son Aditya Chopra produced seven more, and the Yash Raj banner accounts for eleven in total. Kabhie Kabhie (1976) is where that long association begins: Kapoor and Neetu Singh as the young couple, Amitabh Bachchan and Raakhee as the older marriage, and a Khayyam score that won the Filmfare Award for Best Music. She died in April 2023.

name: Paresh Talpade
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tehzeeb (2003).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Tehzeeb (2003), written and directed by the film critic Khalid Mohamed, with A. R. Rahman's music and Javed Siddiqui's dialogue, in which Kapoor plays the dying husband of Shabana Azmi's celebrated singer. It is among the few genuinely literary projects in the filmography.
biography: Paresh Talpade produced Tehzeeb (2003) and has no documented biography. The film is one of the more serious things Rishi Kapoor did between the end of his leading career and his reinvention in Hum Tum: a drama of a famous singer and her estranged daughter, written and directed by Khalid Mohamed — for twenty-seven years a critic at The Times of India and a former editor of Filmfare — with music by A. R. Rahman and dialogue by Javed Siddiqui. Kapoor plays the dying husband. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Partho Ghosh
career_background: Partho Ghosh (8 June 1949 – 9 June 2025) was an Indian film director and producer who worked in Hindi and Bengali cinema. His successful films include 100 Days with Jackie Shroff and Madhuri Dixit, Teesra Kaun, Dalaal with Mithun Chakraborty and Agni Sakshi with Jackie Shroff and Nana Patekar.
debut: Directing from 1980; 100 Days (1991) was among his successes.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kaun Sachcha Kaun Jhootha (1997). Elsewhere, 100 Days, Teesra Kaun and Agni Sakshi.
recurring_themes: The thriller of obsession and mistaken identity; the woman in danger.
creative_style: A commercial director of suspense melodrama with a strong taste for the reveal.
historical_importance: A dependable thriller director of 1990s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kaun Sachcha Kaun Jhootha (1997), a Rakesh Roshan production scored by his brother Rajesh Roshan and written in part by Ranbir Pushp — one of the last films in which Kapoor took a leading role before the four-year gap that preceded Hum Tum.
biography: Partho Ghosh directed one of Rishi Kapoor's last leading roles. A Bengali filmmaker working in both industries from 1980, Ghosh had commercial success with 100 Days, Dalaal and Agni Sakshi — thrillers built on obsession and concealment, usually with a woman in danger at the centre. Kaun Sachcha Kaun Jhootha (1997) was made for the Roshan family unit that accounts for four films in this filmography, with Rajesh Roshan's music and Ranbir Pushp among its writers. Within three years Rakesh Roshan would launch his son Hrithik and Kapoor would be taking supporting parts. Ghosh died in June 2025, a day after his seventy-sixth birthday.

name: People Tree Films
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patiala House (2011).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Nikkhil Advani's Patiala House (2011), in which Kapoor plays the Southall patriarch whose bitterness after a racist attack leads him to forbid his son's cricket career — one of the stronger roles of his late period, opposite Dimple Kapadia for the fourth time since Bobby.
biography: People Tree Films is one of three banners on Patiala House (2011) and has no recorded history. The film itself matters: Kapoor plays Gurtej Singh Kahlon, a London Punjabi whose experience of racist violence has calcified into control over his son's life, in a part that allowed him to be genuinely unpleasant rather than merely stern. It was also his fourth film with Dimple Kapadia, after Bobby, Saagar and Pyaar Mein Twist, this time as a long-married couple. Three banners and five producers are credited, the standard structure for a T-Series-financed film of the period. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Percept Picture Company
career_background: The Percept Picture Company is an Indian film production company established in 2002 as a division of Percept Limited, an entertainment, media and communications company based in Mumbai.
