Its films include Dhol, MP3: Mera Pehla Pehla Pyaar, Malamaal Weekly, Hanuman, Yahaan and Pyaar Mein Twist.
debut: Established in 2002.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pyaar Mein Twist (2005). Elsewhere, Hanuman, Yahaan and Malamaal Weekly.
recurring_themes: A mixed slate from animation to small comedies and dramas.
creative_style: A corporate media company's film division rather than a house with an authorial signature.
historical_importance: An early example of the corporate entertainment company moving into Hindi film production.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and on one of the most revealing films of the late career: Pyaar Mein Twist (2005), which Kapoor co-produced himself, casting him and Dimple Kapadia — the girl of Bobby — as a widower and widow whose romance is opposed by their adult children. It is Bobby's structure with the generations reversed.
biography: Percept Picture Company produced the film in which Rishi Kapoor deliberately restaged his own most famous situation. Established in 2002 as the film arm of the Mumbai media group Percept Limited, the company made a varied slate — the animated Hanuman, the Kashmir drama Yahaan, the comedy Malamaal Weekly — and in 2005 Pyaar Mein Twist, which Kapoor co-produced. He and Dimple Kapadia, thirty-two years after Bobby, play a widower and a widow in their fifties whose late courtship their grown children try to prevent: the same prohibition, with the opposition moved one generation down. It is the clearest evidence in this workbook that he understood his own persona as material.

name: Planman Motion Pictures
career_background: The film production arm of Arindam Chaudhuri's Planman group, credited on Do Dooni Chaar. It has no Wikipedia article of its own; Chaudhuri's article, cited on his row in this sheet, records that the company produced the Bengali films Sanjhbatir Rupkathara and Dosar, the National Film Award-winning Faltu, and The Last Lear, which won the National Film Award for Best Film in English.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Dooni Chaar (2010). Elsewhere, Faltu, Dosar and The Last Lear.
recurring_themes: Small, award-minded films made outside the commercial mainstream.
creative_style: A businessman's production arm backing art-house and festival work rather than star vehicles.
historical_importance: Not independently documented, though its slate includes two National Film Award winners.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and it is the hinge of the late career: Do Dooni Chaar (2010), the modest comedy in which Kapoor and Neetu Singh play a Delhi schoolteacher and his wife saving for a car. It won him the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor and is routinely cited as the start of his character-actor phase.
biography: Planman Motion Pictures produced the film that re-established Rishi Kapoor as a serious actor, and it belongs to an improbable backer. The company was the film arm of Arindam Chaudhuri's Planman group — Chaudhuri being far better known for the Indian Institute of Planning and Management, an unaccredited business school later wound up amid criticism, and for his 2020 arrest for tax evasion — yet it financed a run of small, well-regarded films including the National Award winners Faltu and The Last Lear. Do Dooni Chaar (2010) is one of them: a Delhi mathematics teacher, his wife, and a scooter they want to replace with a car. It won Kapoor the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor.

name: Pooja Entertainment
career_background: Pooja Entertainment is an Indian production and distribution company established by Vashu Bhagnani in 1986 and based in Mumbai. It is known for the comedies Coolie No. 1 (1995), Hero No. 1 (1997) and Biwi No.1 (1999), and had produced over forty films as of 2024. Its key people include Vashu Bhagnani, Jackky Bhagnani and Deepshikha Deshmukh.
debut: Established in 1986; its David Dhawan comedies of the 1990s made its name.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009). Elsewhere, the Coolie No. 1, Hero No. 1 and Biwi No.1 comedies.
recurring_themes: The star comedy, usually with David Dhawan directing and Govinda or Salman Khan leading.
creative_style: A producer-led house specialising in broad comedy and, latterly, launching its proprietor's son.
historical_importance: One of the production companies behind the 1990s Hindi comedy cycle.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Kal Kissne Dekha (2009), a youth film launching the producer's son Jackky Bhagnani, with a Sajid–Wajid score and Kapoor in support. The company's connection to his work is otherwise indirect but substantial: its 1990s comedies were made with David Dhawan, who directed Kapoor five times, more than any other director in this filmography.
biography: Pooja Entertainment produced Kal Kissne Dekha (2009), one of the slighter films of Rishi Kapoor's late period. Established by Vashu Bhagnani in 1986 and responsible for the Coolie No. 1, Hero No. 1 and Biwi No.1 comedies that made David Dhawan and Govinda the dominant comic pairing of the 1990s, the company had made more than forty films by 2024. Kal Kissne Dekha was a vehicle for Bhagnani's son Jackky, with Kapoor in a supporting role. The indirect connection matters more than the credit: Dhawan, the company's house director, directed Kapoor five times — more than anyone else in this workbook.

name: Prabhakar Tamhane
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Biwi-O-Biwi (1981).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Biwi-O-Biwi (1981), an R. K. Films production directed by Rahul Rawail with an R. D. Burman score — one of the six R. K. films in this filmography and one of the few comedies among them.
biography: Prabhakar Tamhane is credited as a writer on Biwi-O-Biwi (1981) and has no documented biography. The film is one of six R. K. Films productions in this filmography — the family studio that gave Kapoor his debut in Mera Naam Joker and his stardom in Bobby — and one of the lightest: a comedy directed by Rahul Rawail, scored by R. D. Burman, made while Raj Kapoor was preparing Prem Rog. It sits between the two Raj Kapoor melodramas that frame Kapoor's work for the studio. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Pradeep Sharma
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Amiri Garibi (1990).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Amiri Garibi (1990), directed by Harmesh Malhotra with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score and Achala Nagar among its writers — one of nine films Kapoor released between 1989 and 1991.
biography: Pradeep Sharma produced Amiri Garibi (1990) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to Harmesh Malhotra's run of five pictures with Kapoor, which had begun with the hit Nagina in 1986 and by 1990 had declined into mid-budget melodrama scored, as almost all of them were, by Laxmikant–Pyarelal. It is one of nine releases in three years, the densest and least documented stretch of the filmography. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Praful Parekh
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside Rajeev Kaul and Raghuvir Shekhawat.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006), in which Kapoor is top-billed but functionally the antagonist, coercing a younger couple — one of very few unsympathetic leads in his career.
biography: Praful Parekh is one of three writers credited on Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006) and has no documented biography. The film reworks the Indecent Proposal situation with Kapoor as the wealthy man who buys his way into a young marriage — the position he had played from the other side in Karobaar six years earlier. Films like this one, made before Dharma and Yash Raj reframed him, show him experimenting with unpleasant roles well before Agneepath made that turn visible. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Pragati Chitra International
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zehreela Insaan (1974).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Zehreela Insaan (1974) — Kapoor's first film after Bobby, directed by the Kannada filmmaker Puttanna Kanagal with an R. D. Burman score. It was the beginning of both his R. D. Burman association, which ran to twenty films, and of the southern-director pattern that would recur through his career.
biography: Pragati Chitra International is the banner on Zehreela Insaan (1974) and has no recorded history. The film matters for its position: it was the first Rishi Kapoor released after Bobby had made him a star, and it was directed not by a Bombay filmmaker but by Puttanna Kanagal, one of the most influential figures in Kannada cinema, with an R. D. Burman score. Burman would go on to write twenty of Kapoor's films, the second-largest composing association in this workbook, and southern directors would supply a substantial share of his work from the mid-1980s on. Both patterns start here.

name: Pramod Chakravorty
career_background: Pramod Chakravorty (15 August 1929 – 12 December 2004) was an Indian Hindi-film producer and director, born in Calcutta and working from 1955 to 1998.
debut: Directing and producing from the mid-1950s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Barood (1976). Elsewhere, a long run of commercial Hindi films across four decades.
recurring_themes: Mainstream action and romance built for a mass audience.
creative_style: A commercial producer-director of the old Bombay school, working steadily across four decades.
historical_importance: A dependable commercial filmmaker of the 1960s and 1970s, though not substantially documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Barood (1976), from the rush of films that followed Bobby, with a story by Sachin Bhowmick and lyrics by Anand Bakshi. Three producers are credited on it, none of them documented.
biography: Pramod Chakravorty directed Barood (1976), one of the films that filled Rishi Kapoor's diary in the three years after Bobby. A Calcutta-born producer-director who worked from 1955 to 1998, Chakravorty belonged to the generation of commercial filmmakers who kept the Bombay industry running without ever acquiring an authorial reputation; his article records the span of his career and little else. Barood was written from a Sachin Bhowmick story — Bhowmick supplied the plots of several of Kapoor's early successes — with Anand Bakshi's lyrics, and it left no particular trace.

name: Pramod Kumar Saraswat
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Akarshan (1988).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Akarshan (1988), among the most obscure entries in this filmography — a year in which Kapoor had several releases that left almost no critical or commercial record.
biography: Pramod Kumar Saraswat produced Akarshan (1988) and has no documented biography. The film is among the least traceable in this workbook: its composer, Ajit Singh, is equally undocumented, and the picture itself appears in Kapoor's filmography largely as a title and a year. It belongs to the period when he was appearing in three or four films annually, financed by producers who made one picture and disappeared. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Prasad Sashte
career_background: A composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Mulk (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Anubhav Sinha's Mulk (2018), in which Kapoor plays Murad Ali Mohammed, the head of a Varanasi Muslim family forced to defend its loyalty in court — the most substantial dramatic role of his last years, in a film whose music is deliberately restrained.
biography: Prasad Sashte is credited among the composers of Mulk (2018) and has no documented biography. The film gave Rishi Kapoor the best dramatic part of his late career, and it is one of the few in this workbook where the music is asked to stay out of the way: a courtroom drama about a family's citizenship, scored sparely by Anurag Saikia with additional credits including this one. In a filmography of which thirty-two films were scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal and where songs usually carried the picture, that restraint is itself notable. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Prasan Kapoor
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. Nothing in the credits connects him to the Kapoor family of this filmography.
major_works: With Kapoor: Deedar-E-Yaar (1982).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: H. S. Rawail's Deedar-E-Yaar (1982), the lavish Muslim social presented by Jeetendra under his Tirupati Films banner, with Rekha, Tina Munim and Kapoor. Jeetendra's own article records that it 'failed to live up to the expectations and proved to be a major box office flop with minimal recovery of the investment'.
biography: Prasan Kapoor produced Deedar-E-Yaar (1982), one of the most expensive failures in this filmography, and has no documented biography. The film was H. S. Rawail's attempt at a grand Muslim social in the manner of his own Mere Mehboob, written by Rahi Masoom Raza with Rahul Rawail among the co-writers and presented by the star Jeetendra through his Tirupati Films banner; Jeetendra's article is unusually blunt about the result. The surname is coincidental: nothing in the credits links this producer to the Kapoor family. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Prasoon Joshi
career_background: Prasoon Joshi (born 16 September 1971 in Almora) is an Indian poet, writer, lyricist, screenwriter and advertising executive. He was CEO of McCann Worldgroup India and chairman for the Asia-Pacific region, and served as chairperson of the Central Board of Film Certification. He has won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist three times — in 2007, 2008 and again in 2014 for Bhaag Milkha Bhaag — and the National Film Award for Best Lyrics twice, for Taare Zameen Par (2007) and Chittagong (2013). He received a Cannes Lions Gold in 2003 and the Padma Shri in 2015.
debut: Writing from 1992, in advertising and then film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Delhi-6 (2009) as writer, and the lyrics of 'Chand Sifarish' from Fanaa (2006), for which he won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist. Elsewhere, Rang De Basanti, Taare Zameen Par and Bhaag Milkha Bhaag.
recurring_themes: The nation examined through its young people; childhood; language of great economy.
creative_style: A poet and advertising man whose film lyrics are unusually plain-spoken, and whose screenwriting shares that directness.
major_awards: Three Filmfare Awards for Best Lyricist, two National Film Awards for Best Lyrics, a Cannes Lions Gold and the Padma Shri (2015).
historical_importance: One of the most honoured lyricists of post-2000 Hindi cinema and, as CBFC chairperson, a figure in India's film-certification debates.
relationship_with_actor: Two points of contact. He is credited as a writer on Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra's Delhi-6 (2009), in which Kapoor plays a Chandni Chowk elder; and his Filmfare-winning lyric 'Chand Sifarish' comes from Fanaa (2006), in which Kapoor plays the Kashmiri father of Kajol's blind heroine. Both belong to his character-actor phase, and both to films whose authorship lay elsewhere.
biography: Prasoon Joshi's work touches this filmography twice, in both cases late. An Almora-born poet who became CEO of McCann India and later chairperson of the Central Board of Film Certification, Joshi is among the most honoured lyricists of his era — three Filmfare Awards, two National Film Awards for Taare Zameen Par and Chittagong, and the Padma Shri. His lyric 'Chand Sifarish', from Fanaa (2006), won the first of those Filmfare awards, and Kapoor appears in that film as the heroine's father; three years later Joshi co-wrote Delhi-6, in which Kapoor is one voice in a Chandni Chowk ensemble pulled apart by religious tension. Neither film is his, and that is the point: by then his presence was a texture in other people's work.

name: Pritish Nandy
industry: Hindi cinema; Indian journalism and literature
career_background: Pritish Nandy (15 January 1951 – 8 January 2025) was an Indian poet, painter, journalist, politician and maker of film and television content. He was publishing director of The Times of India Group between 1982 and 1991 and edited The Illustrated Weekly of India, The Independent and Filmfare. He was nominated a Poet Laureate by the World Academy of Arts and Culture in 1981, received the Padma Shri in 1977 for his contribution to Indian literature, and served in the Rajya Sabha. His brothers are the scholars Ashis Nandy and Manish Nandy.
debut: A poet and editor before moving into film and television production.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001). Elsewhere, the television and film output of Pritish Nandy Communications.
recurring_themes: Urban, English-speaking India; animal welfare and other causes, pursued in parallel with his media work.
creative_style: A writer and editor who built a content company rather than a studio, producing for television and streaming as much as for cinema.
major_awards: Padma Shri (1977); named Poet Laureate by the World Academy of Arts and Culture (1981).
historical_importance: A significant figure in Indian English-language publishing and journalism, and the editor of Filmfare, before becoming a producer.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rahul Rawail's Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), produced with his daughter Rangita Pritish Nandy, in which Kapoor plays the father of twin daughters raised apart after a divorce. It belongs to the thin years before Hum Tum reopened his career. The connection has an additional irony: Nandy had edited Filmfare, the magazine whose awards punctuate this entire workbook.
biography: Pritish Nandy produced one Rishi Kapoor film, and his own life sits oddly beside it. A poet honoured with the Padma Shri at twenty-six and named a Poet Laureate by the World Academy of Arts and Culture, Nandy was publishing director of The Times of India Group for a decade and edited The Illustrated Weekly of India, The Independent and — relevantly for this workbook — Filmfare, whose awards recur on almost every page of it. He later served in the Rajya Sabha and built a content company. Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), produced with his daughter Rangita, cast Kapoor as the father of separated twins in a film nobody remembers. He died in January 2025.

name: Pushpa Sharma
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Amar Akbar Anthony (1977).
recurring_themes: The masala construction of separated families and coincidence.
creative_style: Not documented; she is credited alongside Kader Khan, K. K. Shukla, Jeevanprabha M. Desai and Prayag Raj.
historical_importance: Not independently documented, though her one credit is on the biggest commercial success in this filmography.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is the largest hit of Kapoor's career: Manmohan Desai's Amar Akbar Anthony (1977), in which he plays Akbar, the qawwali-singing Muslim brother, alongside Amitabh Bachchan and Vinod Khanna. She is one of two women among its five credited writers, the other being the director's wife Jeevanprabha M. Desai.
biography: Pushpa Sharma is one of five writers credited on Amar Akbar Anthony (1977), the biggest commercial success in this filmography, and has no documented biography. The film — three brothers separated in childhood and raised Hindu, Muslim and Christian, reunited through coincidence — was the definitive masala picture, and Kapoor's Akbar gave him the music and the courtship while Amitabh Bachchan took the comedy. Two of its five writers were women, she and the director's wife Jeevanprabha M. Desai, which is itself unusual for the period; neither has left a record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Puttanna Kanagal
career_background: Shubraveshti Ramaswamiah Seetharama Sharma (1 December 1933 – 5 June 1985), known as S. R. Puttanna Kanagal, was an Indian filmmaker known for his work in Kannada cinema and often counted among Indian cinema's most influential directors. He gave early platforms to a long list of actors including Kalpana, Aarathi, Jayanthi, Srinath, Rajinikanth, Vishnuvardhan and Ambareesh.
debut: Directing from 1957 in Kannada cinema.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zehreela Insaan (1974). Elsewhere, Bellimoda, Gejje Pooje, Sharapanjara and Nagarahaavu.
recurring_themes: Psychological interiority and social transgression — adultery, prostitution, mental illness — treated seriously within popular cinema.
creative_style: Known as 'the visualiser', a director of unusual psychological ambition who worked with novels and with new performers.
historical_importance: One of the most influential directors in Kannada cinema and a significant figure in Indian cinema generally.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it came at a critical moment: Zehreela Insaan (1974) was the first Rishi Kapoor release after Bobby, with an R. D. Burman score. That the follow-up to the biggest teen romance of the decade was handed to a Kannada director known for psychological seriousness rather than to a Bombay romance specialist is among the more interesting decisions in the early career.
biography: Puttanna Kanagal directed the film Rishi Kapoor made immediately after Bobby. One of the most influential filmmakers in Kannada cinema — Bellimoda, Gejje Pooje, Sharapanjara, Nagarahaavu — Kanagal was known for taking novels and psychological subjects seriously inside popular cinema, and for launching performers who would dominate the following decades, Rajinikanth and Vishnuvardhan among them. Zehreela Insaan (1974), his Hindi film with Kapoor, carries an R. D. Burman score and began the actor's twenty-film association with that composer. It is the earliest instance in this workbook of a southern director being brought to a Kapoor film, a pattern that would recur for the next twenty years.

name: Pyramid Saimira
career_background: Pyramid Saimira was an Indian multinational entertainment company operating in six countries, with businesses spanning theatre exhibition, film and television production, distribution, soundtrack distribution, hospitality, animation and advertising. Its article describes it as one of the world's fastest-growing entertainment groups before a collapse into debt and closure.
debut: Expanding rapidly in the mid-2000s before its collapse.
major_works: With Kapoor: Halla Bol (2008). Elsewhere, Tamil film production and a large exhibition chain.
recurring_themes: Vertical integration across exhibition, production and distribution.
creative_style: A corporate group rather than a creative house.
historical_importance: A cautionary case in Indian film business history: rapid expansion across six countries followed by debt and closure.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Rajkumar Santoshi's Halla Bol (2008), a drama about a film star who witnesses a murder, with Kapoor in support. The company's own failure came soon after, which makes the credit a small record of a business model that did not survive.
biography: Pyramid Saimira produced Halla Bol (2008), and its own story is the more dramatic one. An Indian entertainment group that expanded across six countries — cinemas, production, distribution, animation, hospitality — it was described as one of the fastest-growing companies in the sector before debt brought it down and it closed. Halla Bol, directed by Rajkumar Santoshi fifteen years after Damini, is about a successful film star who sees a murder and must decide whether to testify; Kapoor appears in support. It is one of the small, issue-minded films he took in the years when the Dharma and Yash Raj work was establishing his second career.

name: R. C. Kumar
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tawaif (1985).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a substantial one: B. R. Chopra's Tawaif (1985), written chiefly by Rahi Masoom Raza, who won his second Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue for it, in which Kapoor plays a man who shelters a courtesan and comes to love her. It is one of the few films of his middle period that treats love as moral complication.
biography: R. C. Kumar produced Tawaif (1985) and has no documented biography. The film is among the more serious of Rishi Kapoor's middle period: B. R. Chopra, Hindi cinema's foremost maker of social problem films, directing Rahi Masoom Raza's script about a courtesan given shelter in a respectable home and the man who falls in love with her. Raza won his second Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue for it. Four writers are credited, two of them undocumented, and so is the producer — the usual proportion in this workbook. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: R. Jhalani
career_background: A director credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article resolved for him in this research.
major_works: With Kapoor: Badaltey Rishtey (1978).
recurring_themes: The romantic triangle.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not documented here.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Badaltey Rishtey (1978), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal-scored triangle from the end of Kapoor's first flush of stardom, with the veteran director Phani Majumdar among its writers.
biography: R. Jhalani directed Badaltey Rishtey (1978) and no article for him was resolved in this research. The film is a triangle from the period when Kapoor was five years past Bobby and still being cast almost exclusively as a lover; it was scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal and written by a group that included Phani Majumdar, whose own directing career had begun in 1938. The disparity recurs across this workbook: films in which one credited name belongs to Indian cinema's history and the rest have vanished. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Raamlaxman
career_background: Raamlaxman was an Indian composing duo consisting of Vijay Patil (16 September 1942 – 22 May 2021), who worked under the name Laxman, and Surendra, who died in 1976; Patil continued to compose under the duo's original name. He was a composer, pianist and accordionist, and is best known for his long association with Rajshri Productions.
debut: Composing from the mid-1970s; the association with Rajshri Productions made the name.
major_works: With Kapoor: Anmol (1993). Elsewhere, Maine Pyar Kiya, Hum Aapke Hain Koun..! and Nadiya Ke Paar.
recurring_themes: Melodic, devotional and wedding-centred songs for the family film.
creative_style: Sweet-toned melody written for the conservative family audience, with heavy use of the accordion and piano.
historical_importance: The composer of Maine Pyar Kiya and Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!, two of the biggest-selling Hindi soundtracks of their era.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Anmol (1993), the late Desai-family masala film directed by Ketan Desai with Kapoor opposite Manisha Koirala. The timing is pointed — Raamlaxman had just scored the two largest family-film soundtracks of the era for Rajshri, while this picture, made on the old multi-star formula, failed.
biography: Raamlaxman scored one Rishi Kapoor film, at the height of the duo's own commercial power and the end of Kapoor's. The name belonged first to two men — Vijay Patil, working as Laxman, and Surendra, who died in 1976 — after which Patil continued alone under it. His association with Rajshri Productions produced Maine Pyar Kiya and Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!, soundtracks that defined the family film of the late 1980s and 1990s. Anmol (1993) is a different proposition: Ketan Desai attempting the old Desai masala formula with Kapoor and Manisha Koirala, for an audience that had moved on. Patil died in May 2021.

name: Raftaar
career_background: Dilin Nair (born 16 November 1988 in Trivandrum), known as Raftaar, is an Indian rapper, lyricist, music producer, composer, dancer and television personality associated with Hindi, Punjabi and Haryanvi music.
debut: Recording from 2008; prominent in Indian hip-hop through the 2010s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018), for which he wrote and performed 'Mantoiyat'. Elsewhere, a large catalogue of Hindi and Punjabi hip-hop.
recurring_themes: Hip-hop as argument; verse built on wordplay and social comment.
creative_style: A rapper-producer who writes his own verses, working between the independent scene and film commissions.
historical_importance: One of the central figures in the rise of Indian hip-hop as a mainstream form.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Nandita Das's Manto (2018), in which Kapoor has a small role. Raftaar's track 'Mantoiyat' was praised, his article records, for its lyrical content and for bringing conscious hip-hop into Hindi film music — an unusually apt commission for a film about a writer prosecuted for obscenity.
biography: Raftaar wrote 'Mantoiyat' for Manto (2018), the film in which Rishi Kapoor takes a small part. A Trivandrum-born rapper and producer who became one of the central figures of Indian hip-hop, Raftaar was commissioned for Nandita Das's biographical film about Saadat Hasan Manto — the Urdu short-story writer tried for obscenity in both India and Pakistan — and his article records that the track was praised for its lyrical content and for bringing conscious hip-hop into Hindi film music. The pairing of a rapper's polemic with a film about literary censorship is among the more thoughtful commissions in this workbook, and it sits two years before Kapoor's death.

name: Raghu Dixit
industry: Kannada cinema; Hindi cinema; Indian independent music
career_background: Raghupati Dwarakanath Dixit (born 11 November 1974 in Nasik) is an Indian singer, composer, producer and film score composer, and the frontman of the multilingual folk band The Raghu Dixit Project. He works prominently in Kannada cinema as a soundtrack composer, and his music combines Indian folk forms with other styles. The Raghu Dixit Project won Best Newcomer at the Songlines Music Awards in 2011.
debut: Recording and composing from 2005.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bewakoofiyaan (2014). Elsewhere, his band's albums and his Kannada film scores.
recurring_themes: Indian folk idioms arranged for a contemporary audience.
creative_style: A performer-composer working from the independent music scene into film, with folk instrumentation at the centre.
major_awards: Best Newcomer at the Songlines Music Awards (2011) with The Raghu Dixit Project.
historical_importance: One of the most internationally visible figures in Indian independent music.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Bewakoofiyaan (2014), the Yash Raj romance about a couple strained by unemployment, directed by Nupur Asthana and written by Habib Faisal, in which Kapoor plays the heroine's father — a bureaucrat whose objection to her boyfriend is frankly economic.
biography: Raghu Dixit scored Bewakoofiyaan (2014), one of Rishi Kapoor's late Yash Raj supporting roles. A folk musician from the independent scene — frontman of The Raghu Dixit Project, which won Best Newcomer at the Songlines Awards, and a busy composer in Kannada cinema — Dixit belongs to the generation of musicians who reached Hindi film music from outside it, in the period when soundtracks were being assembled from such commissions. The film, written by Habib Faisal and directed by Nupur Asthana, has Kapoor as a government officer who opposes his daughter's unemployed boyfriend on strictly financial grounds. It is a small, well-observed part of the kind his last decade specialised in.

name: Raghuvir Shekhawat
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside Rajeev Kaul and Praful Parekh.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006), in which Kapoor is top-billed but functionally the antagonist, coercing a younger couple — one of very few unsympathetic leads of his career, and one he took six years after Karobaar had used the same premise with him on the other side of it.
biography: Raghuvir Shekhawat is one of three writers credited on Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006) and has no documented biography. The film is a reworking of the Indecent Proposal situation, with Kapoor as the rich man who buys his way into a young marriage. Its interest for this workbook lies in the role rather than the film: in the years before Dharma and Yash Raj reframed him as a benign elder, he was already taking parts that traded on his accumulated goodwill in order to unsettle it — a line that runs to Agneepath and D-Day. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rahil Qazi
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Dooni Chaar (2010).
recurring_themes: The lower-middle-class household and its economics.
creative_style: Not documented; he is credited alongside the film's director Habib Faisal.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is the hinge of the late career: Do Dooni Chaar (2010), in which Kapoor and Neetu Singh play a Delhi schoolteacher and his wife saving for a car. It won Kapoor the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor and is routinely treated as the start of his character-actor phase.
biography: Rahil Qazi is credited as a writer on Do Dooni Chaar (2010) and has no documented biography — which is worth recording, because the film reset Rishi Kapoor's career. Habib Faisal's directorial debut is a small, closely observed comedy about a Delhi mathematics teacher, his wife and their ambition to replace a scooter with a car; casting Kapoor opposite Neetu Singh, his wife and his co-star from a dozen 1970s films, gave it its warmth and him the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor. After thirty years of diminishing melodrama, an unglamorous part in a modest film is what restored him. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rahul Jain
career_background: Rahul Jain is an Indian singer, music composer and lyricist. He made his Hindi-film debut with the song 'Teri Yaad' in Fever (2016) and has composed more than 250 tracks. He was nominated for the Mirchi Music Award for Upcoming Male Vocalist of the Year at the 11th Mirchi Music Awards for 'Aanewale Kal' from 1921 (2018).
debut: Hindi-film debut with 'Teri Yaad' in Fever (2016).
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019). Elsewhere, 'Teri Yaad' and 'Aanewale Kal'.
recurring_themes: The romantic single commissioned for a film rather than written as part of a score.
creative_style: A singer-composer working one song at a time in the fragmented soundtrack economy of the late 2010s.
major_awards: Mirchi Music Award nomination for Upcoming Male Vocalist of the Year.
historical_importance: Representative of the song-by-song commissioning model that replaced the single-composer soundtrack.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), on which six composers or groups are credited — the extreme case of soundtrack fragmentation in this workbook, and the opposite of the arrangement under which Laxmikant–Pyarelal wrote every song in thirty-two Kapoor films. It was among his last releases.
biography: Rahul Jain is one of six composing credits on Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), among Rishi Kapoor's last releases. A singer-composer who debuted with 'Teri Yaad' in Fever (2016) and claims more than 250 tracks, Jain belongs entirely to the commissioning model that replaced the film soundtrack: a producer buys one song from one artist, and the album is assembled from six such transactions. The contrast with the start of this filmography is the clearest single measure of how the industry changed around Kapoor — Bobby's songs came from one duo who went on to score thirty-two of his films; his penultimate release divided its music among six parties, most of them undocumented.

name: Raj Bharti
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Premee (1980).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside the novelist Gulshan Nanda.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Do Premee (1980), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal-scored romance written with Gulshan Nanda, the most widely read Hindi popular novelist of his generation, and among the last of Kapoor's romances built on that older melodramatic model.
biography: Raj Bharti is credited as a writer on Do Premee (1980) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to the turn of the 1980s, with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score and a story shared with Gulshan Nanda, whose novels had supplied a dozen hits in the preceding decades and who died in 1985. It is one of the last Kapoor romances constructed on the pre-1980s melodramatic template of concealment and thwarted love, before the market moved to action and, later, to a younger generation of romantic leads. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Raj Khosla
career_background: Raj Khosla, born Desraj Khosla (31 May 1925 – 9 June 1991), was among the leading directors, producers and screenwriters of Hindi cinema from the 1950s to the 1980s. His article credits him with bringing neo-noir style into Indian cinema and calls him a women's director for the way he showcased actresses: Woh Kaun Thi (1964) gave Sadhana her signature role as the mystery girl and Do Badan (1966) made Asha Parekh a serious actress and won Simi Garewal a Filmfare Award. Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki (1978) won the Filmfare Award for Best Film.
debut: Working from 1949; his breakthrough came with the thrillers of the early 1960s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Premee (1980). Elsewhere, Woh Kaun Thi, Mera Saaya, Do Badan, Mera Gaon Mera Desh, Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki and Dostana.
recurring_themes: The mystery woman and the noir-inflected thriller; the actress as the film's centre; the village revenge drama.
creative_style: Style-conscious direction with a strong visual signature and an unusual attentiveness to his leading women.
major_awards: Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki won the Filmfare Award for Best Film; several of his films brought awards to their actresses.
historical_importance: One of the most stylish commercial directors of Hindi cinema and the filmmaker most responsible for its neo-noir strain.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and late in Khosla's career: Do Premee (1980), a Laxmikant–Pyarelal-scored romance written with the novelist Gulshan Nanda. The indirect link is sharper — Khosla's Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki (1978) won Rahi Masoom Raza the first of his three Filmfare dialogue awards, and Raza went on to write six Kapoor films in the 1980s.
biography: Raj Khosla directed one Rishi Kapoor film, in the last decade of a career that had shaped Hindi cinema's visual style. A director from 1949 whose thrillers — Woh Kaun Thi, Mera Saaya, Do Badan — brought a neo-noir manner into Indian film and who was known for building films around his actresses, Khosla also made Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki, a Filmfare Best Film winner. Do Premee (1980), his film with Kapoor, is a romance from a Gulshan Nanda story with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score, and it is a minor entry for both men. The more consequential connection runs through Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki, which won Rahi Masoom Raza the dialogue award that preceded his six films with Kapoor.

name: Raj N. Sippy
career_background: Raj N. Sippy (born 6 March 1948 in Bombay), also known as Raj Sippy, is an Indian film director and producer who was prominent in the 1980s with Inkaar, Satyamev Jayate and Mahaadev with Vinod Khanna, Satte Pe Satta with Amitabh Bachchan, and Boxer and Baazi with Mithun Chakraborty.
debut: Directing from 1978.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sitamgar (1985). Elsewhere, Satte Pe Satta, Inkaar and Satyamev Jayate.
recurring_themes: The action thriller and the vigilante drama of the 1980s.
creative_style: A commercial director of star-led action, working mainly with Vinod Khanna, Amitabh Bachchan and Mithun Chakraborty.
historical_importance: A dependable director of 1980s Hindi action cinema, remembered particularly for Satte Pe Satta.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sitamgar (1985), an R. D. Burman-scored picture written in part by Humayun Mirza, from the year in which Kapoor released five films that left little trace. Sippy's reputation rests on action vehicles for other stars, which makes this a marginal credit in both careers.
biography: Raj N. Sippy directed one Rishi Kapoor film, and it sits at the edge of both filmographies. Sippy's 1980s were built on action and vigilante pictures for Vinod Khanna, Amitabh Bachchan and Mithun Chakraborty — Satte Pe Satta, Inkaar, Satyamev Jayate, Boxer — a register in which Kapoor's romantic persona had no obvious place. Sitamgar (1985), with an R. D. Burman score, came in the weakest year of Kapoor's lead career, when five of his films were released and none registered. The Sippy name recurs in this workbook through G. P. Sippy and Ramesh Sippy, the producer and director of Saagar, though no source consulted here connects them to him.

name: Raj Sun Films
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Ki Izzat (1994).
recurring_themes: The household melodrama.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Ghar Ki Izzat (1994), the last of Kalpataru's five family melodramas with Kapoor, written with Kader Khan and Keshav Rathod.
biography: Raj Sun Films is the banner on Ghar Ki Izzat (1994) and has no recorded history. The film closes the run of five household melodramas Kalpataru directed with Kapoor between 1988 and 1994, all named for the family rather than any romance, most written with Kader Khan, and reviewed essentially nowhere. Taken together they are the clearest evidence of what his lead career had become by the early 1990s, and almost none of the companies that financed them left a trace. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rajeev Barnwal
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Besharam (2013).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Besharam (2013), Abhinav Kashyap's comedy and the only film in which Rishi Kapoor, his wife Neetu Singh and their son Ranbir Kapoor all appear — the parents as police officers, the son as the title character.
biography: Rajeev Barnwal is credited as a writer on Besharam (2013) and has no documented biography. The film matters as a family record rather than as work: Abhinav Kashyap's follow-up to Dabangg cast Ranbir Kapoor as a cheerful car thief with both his parents as the police officers pursuing him — Rishi Kapoor and Neetu Singh, who had been paired as romantic leads a dozen times in the 1970s. It is the only film in which all three appear, and it failed on both counts. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rajeev Jhaveri
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kucch To Hai (2003).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kucch To Hai (2003), the Balaji Motion Pictures horror-slasher credited to two directors — Anurag Basu, whose article calls it his debut, and Anil V. Kumar — with Kapoor in support during the quietest stretch of his career.
biography: Rajeev Jhaveri is credited as a writer on Kucch To Hai (2003) and has no documented biography. The film belongs to Balaji Telefilms' early move from television into cinema under Ekta Kapoor, and is the directorial debut Anurag Basu's own article claims, though Anil V. Kumar shares the credit. Rishi Kapoor appears in a supporting role, in the four-year interval between the end of his leading career and Hum Tum. Four writers are credited on the film, none of them documented. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rajeev Kaul
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside Praful Parekh and Raghuvir Shekhawat.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006), in which Kapoor is top-billed but functionally the antagonist, coercing a younger couple in a variation on Indecent Proposal — one of very few unsympathetic leads in his career.
biography: Rajeev Kaul is one of three writers credited on Love Ke Chakkar Mein (2006) and has no documented biography. The film gives Kapoor top billing in a part that works against him: the wealthy older man who buys his way into a young couple's marriage, the position he had played from the other side in Karobaar six years earlier. It belongs to the interval before Dharma and Yash Raj recast him as a benign elder, and shows that the late appetite for unsympathetic roles — Rauf Lala, Iqbal Seth — had earlier precedents. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rajeev Kumar
career_background: A director credited on one film in this filmography. No Wikipedia article could be resolved for him: the bare name leads to a disambiguation page of police officers, politicians and a reality-show singer, none of them this filmmaker.
major_works: With Kapoor: Prem Yog (1994).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not documented here.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Prem Yog (1994), produced by B. S. Shaad with a Bappi Lahiri score and Rumi Jaffery and Honey Irani among its writers — one of four Kapoor films released that year, all of them romances pitched at a persona that had stopped selling.
biography: Rajeev Kumar directed Prem Yog (1994), and no article for him could be resolved in this research — the name on Wikipedia leads to police officers and politicians. The film is one of four Kapoor released in 1994, written by Rumi Jaffery and Honey Irani and scored by Bappi Lahiri, and it is characteristic of that year: romances built on an image audiences had transferred to Shah Rukh Khan, Aamir Khan and Salman Khan two years earlier. None of the four registered. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rajendra Krishan
career_background: Rajinder Krishan Duggal (6 June 1919 – 23 September 1987), also credited as Rajendra Krishan, was an Indian poet, lyricist, dialogue and screenplay writer, born in Jalalpur Jattan in Punjab — now in Pakistan — and resident in Bombay. He won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist in 1966.
debut: Writing for films from 1948.
major_works: With Kapoor: Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan (1978). Elsewhere, four decades of Hindi film lyrics and screenplays.
recurring_themes: Urdu-inflected lyric writing of great fluency, and the comedy screenplay.
creative_style: A lyricist first, with a parallel career in dialogue and screenplay, working at high volume from 1948 until his death.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist (1966).
historical_importance: One of the most prolific and successful lyricists of the 1950s and 1960s Hindi film song.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan (1978) — the second of Sikandar Khanna's two films with Kapoor and the one during whose making the director died. Krishan wrote it with Kaushal Bharti; it was scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal.
biography: Rajendra Krishan wrote one Rishi Kapoor film, late in a long and distinguished career. A poet and lyricist from Jalalpur Jattan who worked in Hindi cinema from 1948 until his death in 1987, Krishan was among the most prolific songwriters of the 1950s and 1960s and won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist in 1966; he also wrote dialogue and screenplays, including for comedies. Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan (1978) is a minor entry for him and an unlucky one for its director, Sikandar Khanna, who died during its making. The film was scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, by then well into the thirty-two-film association that dominates this workbook.

name: Rajendra Singh
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article identifiable to him; the bare name resolves to an unrelated environmentalist, which is how an earlier pass of this research briefly attached the wrong article.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sheshnaag (1990).
recurring_themes: The folk-mythological fantasy.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sheshnaag (1990), the snake-deity fantasy made in the wake of Nagina's success, with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score and two director credits that no source consulted here reconciles.
biography: Rajendra Singh is credited as a writer on Sheshnaag (1990) and cannot be identified further. The film belongs to the folk-fantasy cycle that followed Nagina in 1986, in which Kapoor's romantic function was subordinated to curses and serpent deities, and which accounts for a surprising share of his work between 1986 and 1993. Three producers, two directors and several writers are credited on it, almost none of them documented. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rajinder Singh Bedi
career_background: Rajinder Singh Bedi (1 September 1915 – 11 November 1984) was an Indian Urdu writer of the progressive writers' movement and a playwright who later worked in Hindi cinema as a director, screenwriter and dialogue writer. He won the Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue for Madhumati (1958) and Satyakam (1969), and the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1965 for his novel Ek Chadar Maili Si, which Khushwant Singh translated into English as I Take This Woman. His son was the director Narendra Bedi; the actors Rajat and Manek Bedi are his grandsons.
debut: Writing from 1933; in films from the 1950s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986), from his own novel. Elsewhere, Madhumati, Satyakam, Garm Hava and Abhimaan.
recurring_themes: Women bound by custom; the Punjabi village and the compromises of poverty; Partition.
creative_style: One of the major Urdu prose writers of the century, who brought the same unsentimental attention to film dialogue.
major_awards: Two Filmfare Awards for Best Dialogue (Madhumati, Satyakam) and the 1965 Sahitya Akademi Award for Ek Chadar Maili Si.
historical_importance: A central figure of twentieth-century Urdu fiction and one of Hindi cinema's most distinguished dialogue writers.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, and it is the source of one of the most serious films in this filmography: Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986) is adapted from his Sahitya Akademi-winning novel about a widow compelled by custom to marry her dead husband's younger brother, with Kapoor as the brother and Hema Malini as the widow. His article records that the novella had already been filmed in Pakistan as Mutthi Bhar Chawal (1978). His son Narendra Bedi directed Kapoor in Rafoo Chakkar (1975), so father and son both appear in this workbook.
biography: Rajinder Singh Bedi wrote the novel behind the most literary film in this filmography. One of the major Urdu prose writers of the twentieth century and a figure of the progressive writers' movement, Bedi also worked in Hindi cinema, winning Filmfare Awards for the dialogue of Madhumati and Satyakam. His novel Ek Chadar Maili Si — the story of a widow forced by custom to marry her husband's younger brother — won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1965, was translated by Khushwant Singh as I Take This Woman, and was filmed in Pakistan before the 1986 Hindi version in which Rishi Kapoor played the brother opposite Hema Malini. Bedi died in 1984, two years before it reached the screen. His son Narendra Bedi had directed Kapoor in Rafoo Chakkar.

name: Rajkumar Kohli
career_background: Rajkumar Kohli (14 September 1930 – 24 November 2023) was an Indian film director, born in Lahore, known for Lootera (1965) with Dara Singh and the actress Nishi, whom he later married, and for Punjabi films including Dulla Bhatti (1966). His best-known Hindi films are large ensemble pictures: Nagin (1976), Jaani Dushman (1979), Badle Ki Aag (1982), Naukar Biwi Ka (1983) and Raaj Tilak (1984). His sons are Armaan Kohli and Rajnish Kohli.
debut: Directing from 1963, initially in Punjabi cinema.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naukar Biwi Ka (1983). Elsewhere, Nagin, Jaani Dushman and Raaj Tilak.
recurring_themes: The multi-star ensemble; the snake-woman and revenge fantasy; the comedy of domestic reversal.
creative_style: A director of crowded, high-concept entertainments assembled from as many stars as a budget allowed.
historical_importance: The maker of Nagin and Jaani Dushman, two of the biggest multi-star genre hits of the 1970s, and of the fantasy formula that Nagina later revived.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Naukar Biwi Ka (1983), a comedy in which Kapoor's husband is reduced to serving his own wife, with a Bappi Lahiri score, produced by Kohli's wife Nishi Kohli. The indirect connection is larger: Kohli's Nagin (1976) established the snake-woman formula that Harmesh Malhotra's Nagina would use in 1986 to give Kapoor the biggest hit of his middle period.
biography: Rajkumar Kohli directed one Rishi Kapoor film, and invented the genre that would later rescue him. Born in Lahore in 1930, Kohli made his name with Lootera and Punjabi films before building a career on crowded multi-star entertainments — Nagin (1976), Jaani Dushman (1979), Raaj Tilak — of which Nagin, a snake-woman revenge fantasy, was the template that Nagina revived a decade later to give Kapoor his biggest hit since Amar Akbar Anthony. Their own film together, Naukar Biwi Ka (1983), is a domestic comedy produced by Kohli's wife, the former actress Nishi, in which Kapoor's husband is reduced to his wife's servant. Kohli died in November 2023.

name: Raju Kothari
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Deewana (1992).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented, though his one credit is on the pivotal film of the later career.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Deewana (1992), Raj Kanwar's directorial debut, in which Kapoor plays the singer presumed dead whose widow marries the younger man played by a debuting Shah Rukh Khan. The film was a hit and is read as the handover of the Hindi romantic lead between generations.
biography: Raju Kothari is among the producers credited on Deewana (1992) and has no documented biography. The film is the single most consequential entry in the second half of this filmography: Kapoor as Ravi, the wealthy singer believed killed, and Shah Rukh Khan in his film debut as the man his widow marries. It succeeded commercially, won Khan a Filmfare award for best debut, and is remembered as the moment Hindi cinema's romantic lead changed hands — with Kapoor performing the transfer himself. Four producers and two banners are credited on it, and not one of them is documented. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Raju Rao
career_background: A background-score composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sadiyaan (2010).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sadiyaan (2010), Raj Kanwar's partition-era romance written in part by his son Abhay Kanwar, with Kapoor in a supporting role — eighteen years after Kanwar had directed him in Deewana.
biography: Raju Rao wrote the background score for Sadiyaan (2010) and has no documented biography. The film reunited Kapoor with Raj Kanwar, whose directorial debut Deewana had, in 1992, staged the handover of the Hindi romantic lead to Shah Rukh Khan; eighteen years later Kanwar cast him in support in a partition romance written partly by his own son, and the film passed unnoticed. Its songs were by Adnan Sami, its score by this composer, and almost nobody involved left a record. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rakesh Kumar
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography. No Wikipedia article could be resolved for him: the bare name leads to a disambiguation page of cricketers, a kabaddi player, a lyricist and a politician, none of them this writer.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naya Daur (1978).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not documented here.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Naya Daur (1978), an early Mahesh Bhatt film with an R. D. Burman score — made four years before Arth established Bhatt's reputation, and sharing its title with the far better-known 1957 Dilip Kumar picture.
biography: Rakesh Kumar is credited as a writer on Naya Daur (1978) and cannot be identified further. The film's interest lies elsewhere: it was directed by Mahesh Bhatt four years before Arth made him one of the defining filmmakers of the 1980s, and it is the only film Bhatt and Kapoor made together — their sensibilities diverged sharply afterwards, Bhatt towards autobiography, adultery and addiction, Kapoor towards romance and family melodrama. The film also shares a title with the 1957 Dilip Kumar classic, which has not helped its visibility. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra
career_background: Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra (born 7 July 1963 in Delhi) is an Indian film director, screenwriter and occasional actor. He is best known for writing and directing Rang De Basanti (2006) and the biographical sports film Bhaag Milkha Bhaag (2013), winning two Filmfare Awards for Best Director; both films also won the National Film Award for Best Popular Film Providing Wholesome Entertainment. He also wrote and directed the supernatural thriller Aks (2001) and the drama Delhi-6 (2009).
debut: Advertising films from 1986; feature debut Aks (2001).
major_works: With Kapoor: Delhi-6 (2009). Elsewhere, Rang De Basanti and Bhaag Milkha Bhaag.
recurring_themes: The nation examined through its young; the neighbourhood as a body politic; history reopened in the present.
creative_style: An advertising-trained director with a strong visual signature who works on large ensembles and uses music as narration.
major_awards: Two Filmfare Awards for Best Film and Best Director (Rang De Basanti, Bhaag Milkha Bhaag) and two National Film Awards for Best Popular Film.
historical_importance: One of the most significant Hindi directors of the 2000s, and the maker of Rang De Basanti, a film with a measurable effect on Indian public protest.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Delhi-6 (2009), in which Kapoor plays a Chandni Chowk elder in an ensemble pulled apart by religious tension. Mehra's article names the cast directly — 'Abhishek Bachchan, Sonam Kapoor, Aditi Rao Hydari, Rishi Kapoor, Supriya Pathak' — and the film, with its A. R. Rahman score and Prasoon Joshi lyrics, is among the most ambitious in which Kapoor took a supporting part.
biography: Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra directed Rishi Kapoor in Delhi-6, one of the most ambitious films of his late career. Mehra came from advertising to features with Aks in 2001, then made Rang De Basanti (2006), a film about young Indians and political violence that won him Filmfare Awards for Best Film and Best Director and had a measurable effect on how protest was staged in India, and Bhaag Milkha Bhaag (2013), which repeated the double. Between them came Delhi-6 (2009), set in the lanes of Chandni Chowk, with an A. R. Rahman score, Prasoon Joshi's lyrics and an ensemble in which Mehra's own article lists Kapoor. It failed commercially and remains among the more interesting films of his second career.

name: Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra Pictures
career_background: The production banner of the director Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra, credited on Delhi-6. It has no Wikipedia article of its own — the name redirects to Mehra himself, whose article is cited on his row in this sheet and records the films he wrote, directed and produced.
major_works: With Kapoor: Delhi-6 (2009).
recurring_themes: The ensemble film about contemporary India, made within the director's own company.
creative_style: A director's own banner, used for his films.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One credit, on Delhi-6 (2009), in which Kapoor plays a Chandni Chowk elder in an ensemble that Mehra's own article lists as including him alongside Abhishek Bachchan, Sonam Kapoor, Aditi Rao Hydari and Supriya Pathak. The film has an A. R. Rahman score and lyrics by Prasoon Joshi.
biography: Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra Pictures is the director's own banner and has no separate documentation; its name redirects to him. Under it he made Delhi-6 (2009), a film set in the lanes of Chandni Chowk in which a neighbourhood tears itself apart over religion, with an A. R. Rahman score, Prasoon Joshi's lyrics and an ensemble cast that includes Rishi Kapoor as a local elder. It came between Rang De Basanti and Bhaag Milkha Bhaag, the two films that made Mehra's reputation, and failed commercially where they had succeeded. For Kapoor it is among the most serious films of his character-actor phase.

name: Ram B.C.
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Laila Majnu (1976).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a significant one: H. S. Rawail's Laila Majnu (1976), in which Kapoor played Qais opposite Ranjeeta Kaur in the classical Arabic love tragedy — the first film to ask him for love as destruction rather than courtship. Its songs were by Madan Mohan, who died before release, and Jaidev.
biography: Ram B.C. is credited as a producer on Laila Majnu (1976) and has no documented biography. The film is among the most ambitious of Kapoor's early career: H. S. Rawail's version of the Qais and Laila legend, with Abrar Alvi — the writer of Pyaasa — among its writers, songs by Madan Mohan, who died in July 1975 before it was finished, and Jaidev, a three-time National Award winner, completing the credit. Rawail's own article records that the film was a success. That its producer left no record is characteristic of this workbook's lower tiers. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ram Kelkar
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Hawalaat (1987).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside Ranbir Pushp.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Hawalaat (1987), directed and produced by Surendra Mohan with an Anu Malik score, a multi-starrer in which Kapoor appeared with Mithun Chakraborty — one of the ensemble pictures that filled his middle period.
biography: Ram Kelkar is credited as a writer on Hawalaat (1987) and has no documented biography. The film is a multi-star melodrama directed and produced by Surendra Bohra's contemporary Surendra Mohan, scored by Anu Malik early in his career and co-written with Ranbir Pushp, who would later write Deewana. Ranbir Pushp's own article names Hawalaat and Kapoor among his credits, which is the only reason the film appears in any biography at all. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ram Singh
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article identifiable to him; the bare name resolves to a disambiguation page of Indian rulers and others.
major_works: With Kapoor: Banjaran (1991).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Banjaran (1991), directed by Harmesh Malhotra with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score — the fifth and last of Malhotra's films with Kapoor, and one of nine the actor released between 1989 and 1991.
biography: Ram Singh is credited as a producer on Banjaran (1991) and cannot be identified further. The film closes Harmesh Malhotra's five-film run with Kapoor, which had begun with the hit Nagina in 1986 and declined through its sequel Nigahen into mid-budget melodrama. It belongs to the densest and least documented stretch of the filmography — nine releases in three years — in which the producers are almost uniformly untraceable and the composers almost uniformly Laxmikant–Pyarelal. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ramesh Behl
career_background: Ramesh Behl was an Indian film director and producer of the Behl film family. He produced The Train and Kasme Vaade (1978) and directed Pukar (1983), Jawaani (1984) and Apne Apne (1987). His article records that he is the only filmmaker to have had R. D. Burman as the composer for all his films. The actor Kamal Kapoor was his father-in-law and Rajendra Kumar his brother-in-law; his son is the filmmaker Goldie Behl and the actor Ravi Behl is his nephew.
debut: Producing from the late 1960s; directing from 1983.
major_works: With Kapoor: Yeh Vaada Raha (1982). Elsewhere, The Train, Kasme Vaade and Jawaani.
recurring_themes: Youth romance and thriller, all of it scored by R. D. Burman.
creative_style: A producer whose defining decision was a single lifelong musical partnership.
historical_importance: Notable for an unusual record: every film he made was scored by R. D. Burman.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Yeh Vaada Raha (1982), directed by Kapil Kapoor with — inevitably — an R. D. Burman score. Burman wrote twenty of Kapoor's films, the second-largest composing association in this workbook, and Behl's own article notes that he worked with no other composer at all.
biography: Ramesh Behl produced Yeh Vaada Raha (1982), and his place in this workbook is secured by a single fact: his article records him as the only filmmaker to have had R. D. Burman score every one of his films. Behl produced The Train and Kasme Vaade and directed Pukar, Jawaani and Apne Apne, all with Burman; he was also well connected by marriage, with Kamal Kapoor as a father-in-law and Rajendra Kumar as a brother-in-law. His one Kapoor film is a romance directed by Kapil Kapoor, and its Burman songs belong to the twenty-film association that defined the actor's youth. Behl's son Goldie Behl later became a filmmaker himself.

name: Ramesh Sippy
career_background: Ramesh Sippy is an Indian director, producer and actor in Hindi cinema, best known as the director of Sholay (1975), often regarded as one of the most influential Indian films ever made. He is the son of the producer G. P. Sippy, received the Padma Shri in 2013, and founded the Ramesh Sippy Academy of Cinema in 2017. His children include the director Rohan Sippy.
debut: Directing from 1971; Sholay (1975) made his reputation.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saagar (1985). Elsewhere, Sholay, Seeta Aur Geeta, Shaan and Shakti.
recurring_themes: The large-canvas ensemble; friendship and vengeance; romance staged against landscape.
creative_style: A director of scale and precision, with an unusual command of ensemble staging and of the widescreen image.
major_awards: Padma Shri (2013); his Sholay received the Filmfare Best Film of 50 Years award in 2005.
historical_importance: The director of Sholay, the most culturally pervasive Hindi film ever made.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and it is among Kapoor's finest: Saagar (1985), which Sippy directed for his father G. P. Sippy's production. His article records that it starred Rishi Kapoor and Kamal Haasan and marked Dimple Kapadia's return to films twelve years after her debut in Bobby — so the film reunited Kapoor with his first leading lady, and cast him as the fisherman who loves her and loses. R. D. Burman's score was among the decade's best-selling.
biography: Ramesh Sippy directed the best film Rishi Kapoor appeared in during his worst decade. The director of Sholay, a Padma Shri recipient and the son of the producer G. P. Sippy, Sippy made Saagar in 1985: his own article records that it starred Kapoor and Kamal Haasan and marked Dimple Kapadia's comeback twelve years after Bobby, the film in which she and Kapoor had become stars together. He plays Raja, the fisherman who loves her and is not chosen; the performance is among his most admired and R. D. Burman's score among the best-selling Hindi albums of the 1980s. In a decade of forgotten melodramas, Saagar is the exception that shows what he could still do.

name: Rangita Pritish Nandy
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own; the name resolves to her father, the poet, editor and parliamentarian Pritish Nandy, whose article is cited on his own row in this sheet.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001).
recurring_themes: Urban English-speaking India, through her father's content company.
creative_style: Not documented individually.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rahul Rawail's Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), produced with her father Pritish Nandy, in which Kapoor plays the father of twin daughters raised apart after a divorce. It belongs to the quiet years before Hum Tum reopened his career.
biography: Rangita Pritish Nandy co-produced Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001) with her father, and has no article of her own — the name leads to his. Pritish Nandy was a Padma Shri-winning poet, publishing director of The Times of India Group and a former editor of Filmfare, whose awards recur throughout this workbook; the family's content company made television and film. Their one Kapoor film is a family comedy of separated twins directed by Rahul Rawail, who had given Kapoor a lead in his own debut twenty-one years earlier. It made no impression. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ranjeev Verma
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chalk N Duster (2016).
recurring_themes: The institutional drama; teachers and schools.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chalk N Duster (2016), a drama about schoolteachers resisting a commercialising management, with an ensemble including Shabana Azmi and Juhi Chawla and Kapoor in support — one of the small, socially minded films of his last years.
biography: Ranjeev Verma is credited as a writer on Chalk N Duster (2016) and has no documented biography. The film is a modest drama about two teachers and the commercial pressures on their school, cast with veterans and with Kapoor in a supporting part. It belongs with Wedding Pullav and All Is Well among the late films in which his name lent respectability to productions that asked little of him, and it came four years before his death. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ranjit Kapoor
career_background: A director and writer credited on one film in this filmography. No Wikipedia article could be resolved for him: the bare name redirects to the 2021 film Chehre, and no disambiguated title was found. There is no evidence in the credits of any relation to the Kapoor family of this filmography.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chintu Ji (2009).
recurring_themes: Satire of celebrity and of the village's relation to it.
creative_style: Not documented here.
historical_importance: Not documented here.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and the most self-referential in the filmography: Chintu Ji (2009), which he wrote and directed, casts Kapoor as a film star named Chintu Ji — the nickname he had carried since childhood and by which the industry knew him — who returns to the village of his birth and is received as both celebrity and disappointment. Bobby Bedi of Kaleidoscope Entertainment produced it.
biography: Ranjit Kapoor wrote and directed Chintu Ji (2009), the film in which Rishi Kapoor plays a version of himself, and no article for him could be resolved in this research. The premise is unusually bold: a star called Chintu Ji — Kapoor's own lifelong nickname — goes back to the village where he was born, where the inhabitants have their own ideas about what he owes them. That it was produced by Bobby Bedi, whose Kaleidoscope Entertainment made Bandit Queen and Maqbool, suggests the film was conceived as satire rather than vanity. It came a year before Do Dooni Chaar, in the period when Kapoor had begun treating his own persona as material.

name: Ratan Khatri
career_background: Ratan Khatri (c. 1932 – 9 May 2020) was an Indian gambling figure and film producer, widely known as the Matka King for his central role in turning matka — a form of betting — into one of Bombay's most lucrative underground industries.
debut: A bookmaker before his film production; his article treats the gambling career as the principal subject.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rangila Ratan (1976).
recurring_themes: Not documented as a producer; his article concerns the matka business, its rise and its decline.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: A major figure in the history of illegal gambling in Bombay, and a reminder of how that money reached the film industry.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rangila Ratan (1976), a Kalyanji–Anandji-scored comedy from the rush of work that followed Bobby. The title's second word is his own name, which may or may not be coincidence; the film is otherwise undocumented. The credit is the clearest instance in this workbook of the industry's well-known dependence on money from outside it.
biography: Ratan Khatri, the Matka King of Bombay, produced a Rishi Kapoor film. Khatri's article is about gambling rather than cinema: he was the central figure in transforming matka betting into one of the city's largest underground industries, and he died in May 2020, three weeks after Kapoor. His one credit here is Rangila Ratan (1976) — a comedy from the glut of films that followed Bobby, scored by Kalyanji–Anandji, whose title carries his own name. The relationship between the Hindi film industry's financing and Bombay's unofficial economies is widely discussed and rarely documented; this is one of the few places in this workbook where it appears on a credit list.

name: Ravi
career_background: A composer credited on one film in this filmography under a single name. No Wikipedia article could be resolved for him: the bare credit leads to a disambiguation page, and this research did not establish which composer is meant, though the name was used by a well-known Hindi film composer of the period.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tawaif (1985).
recurring_themes: Not established here.
creative_style: Not established here.
historical_importance: Not established here.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and a substantial one: B. R. Chopra's Tawaif (1985), for which Rahi Masoom Raza won his second Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue, and in which Kapoor plays a man who shelters a courtesan and comes to love her. It is among the few films of his middle period that treats love as moral complication rather than courtship.
biography: The composer credited simply as Ravi on Tawaif (1985) could not be identified with confidence in this research: the single name leads only to a disambiguation page, and this workbook declines to attach a biography on the strength of a first name. The film itself is one of the more serious of Kapoor's middle period — B. R. Chopra directing Rahi Masoom Raza's script about a courtesan taken into a respectable household, which won Raza his second Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue. Single-name credits recur across the Hindi industry of the period and are among the hardest entries in this workbook to resolve. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ravindra Peepat
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Biwi-O-Biwi (1981).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside Prabhakar Tamhane.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Biwi-O-Biwi (1981), an R. K. Films production directed by Rahul Rawail with an R. D. Burman score — one of the six R. K. films in this filmography and one of the few comedies among them.
biography: Ravindra Peepat is credited as a writer on Biwi-O-Biwi (1981) and has no documented biography. The film is one of six R. K. Films productions in this filmography — the family studio that gave Kapoor his credited debut in Mera Naam Joker and his stardom in Bobby — and among the lightest: a comedy directed by Rahul Rawail with an R. D. Burman score, made while Raj Kapoor was preparing Prem Rog. It sits between the two Raj Kapoor melodramas that frame his work for the family studio. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ray Panthaki
career_background: Ray Panthaki (born 20 January 1979 in London) is a British actor, writer, director and producer. On television he is known for the BBC series EastEnders (2003–2005) and Blessed (2005), the ITV series Marcella (2016–2020), Sky Atlantic's Gangs of London and the Netflix series Away. He was nominated for Best Supporting Actor in a Play at the TMA Theatre Awards in 2006 for Gladiator Games, and for the British Independent Film Award for Best Supporting Actor in 2021 for Boiling Point.
