debut: On screen from 1999.
major_works: With Kapoor: Don't Stop Dreaming (2007). Elsewhere, EastEnders, Marcella, Gangs of London and Boiling Point.
recurring_themes: British Asian experience on screen; ensemble television drama.
creative_style: An actor who also writes, directs and produces, working mainly in British film and television.
major_awards: TMA Theatre Award nomination (2006); British Independent Film Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor (2021).
historical_importance: A significant British Asian screen actor of his generation, with a parallel career behind the camera.
relationship_with_actor: One credit: Don't Stop Dreaming (2007), one of the two English-language films in this filmography, both written and directed by Kapoor's cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor. Panthaki's involvement, along with Richard Blackwood's in the cast and Taz of Stereo Nation's score, places the film in the British Asian production world rather than the Hindi industry.
biography: Ray Panthaki is the only British screen professional with a writing credit in this filmography. A London-born actor known for EastEnders, Marcella, Gangs of London and Boiling Point — for which he received a British Independent Film Award nomination — Panthaki also writes, directs and produces. His credit here is Don't Stop Dreaming (2007), one of two English-language films Rishi Kapoor made that year for his cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor, with a soundtrack by Taz of Stereo Nation and Richard Blackwood in the cast. The film belongs to the British Asian production world rather than to Bombay, and it is among the least documented entries in this workbook.

name: Reema Rakesh Nath
career_background: Reema Rakesh Nath is an Indian film writer, director and producer, best known for scripting Saajan (1991) — a golden jubilee film and the highest-grossing Hindi release of its year — and for Aarzoo and Hum Tumhare Hain Sanam. She directed Mohabbat (1997). She is married to Rakesh Nath; her son is the actor Karan Nath, and the actors Tej Sapru and Priti Sapru are her brother and sister.
debut: Writing from the 1980s; Saajan (1991) was her biggest success.
major_works: With Kapoor: Yaraana (1995), which she wrote and produced. Elsewhere, Saajan, Aarzoo and Hum Tumhare Hain Sanam.
recurring_themes: Melodrama of sacrifice and disguise; the love triangle in which one lover conceals himself.
creative_style: A writer-producer of high melodrama with a strong instinct for the situation that sells a soundtrack.
historical_importance: The writer of Saajan, one of the defining commercial melodramas of the early 1990s, and one of the few women writing and producing at that level in the period.
relationship_with_actor: One film, which she both wrote and produced: Yaraana (1995), directed by David Dhawan with an Anu Malik score, in which Kapoor is top-billed opposite Madhuri Dixit. It is among his last leading romances, and the only one in this filmography written and produced by the same woman.
biography: Reema Rakesh Nath wrote and produced Yaraana (1995), one of Rishi Kapoor's last films as a romantic lead. Her reputation rests on Saajan (1991), the melodrama of a crippled poet who writes love letters under his friend's name — a golden jubilee film and the biggest Hindi release of its year — and she also wrote Aarzoo and Hum Tumhare Hain Sanam and directed Mohabbat. Yaraana, directed by David Dhawan with Anu Malik's songs, cast Kapoor opposite Madhuri Dixit at a point when the romantic formula he embodied was being retired. She is among the very few women in this workbook credited as both writer and producer on the same film.

name: Rensil D'Silva
career_background: Rensil D'Silva, from Mumbai, is an Indian screenwriter and film director. His article records that he wrote the screenplay for Karan Johar's Student of the Year in 2011.
debut: Screenwriting in the 2000s; he also directs.
major_works: With Kapoor: Student of the Year (2012). Elsewhere, Rang De Basanti as co-writer and Kurbaan as director.
recurring_themes: Young Indians and the institutions that shape them; the thriller with a political edge.
creative_style: A screenwriter who moved into directing, working on both youth drama and political thriller.
historical_importance: A writer on two of the more culturally visible Hindi films of his period.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Student of the Year (2012), Karan Johar's youth ensemble, in which Kapoor plays the dean of a fantasy college. The film launched three debutant actors, and his presence supplied the credibility a cast of newcomers lacked.
biography: Rensil D'Silva wrote Student of the Year, one of three Dharma Productions films that reshaped Rishi Kapoor's late career. A Mumbai screenwriter who also directs, D'Silva is credited by his own article with the screenplay of Karan Johar's 2012 film, a youth ensemble that launched Sidharth Malhotra, Alia Bhatt and Varun Dhawan and needed an established older presence to hold it together; Kapoor played the dean. In the same year Dharma's Agneepath gave him Rauf Lala. The two films together established the two registers — indulgent elder and genuine villain — that his final decade alternated between.

name: Renu Patel
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sambar Salsa (2007).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sambar Salsa (2007), one of the two English-language films in this filmography, both written and directed by Kapoor's cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor and both released that year. They are the least documented entries in the workbook.
biography: Renu Patel is credited as a producer on Sambar Salsa (2007) and has no documented biography. The film is one of two English-language pictures Rishi Kapoor made that year, both written and directed by his first cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor and both so thinly released that this workbook can record almost nothing about them: no substantial reviews, no commercial figures, and producers and banners with no documentation at all. They fall in the gap between his Yash Raj supporting roles and the Dharma films that followed. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Renuka Kunzru
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chashme Buddoor (2013).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; credited alongside Sajid–Farhad and the director David Dhawan.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chashme Buddoor (2013), David Dhawan's remake of the 1981 campus comedy, in which Kapoor appears in support. It was the fifth and last of Dhawan's films with him — more than any other director in this filmography — and came twenty-one years after their first, Bol Radha Bol.
biography: Renuka Kunzru is credited as a writer on Chashme Buddoor (2013) and has no documented biography. The film is David Dhawan's remake of Sai Paranjpye's 1981 campus comedy, and it closes the longest director relationship in this filmography: Dhawan directed Kapoor five times between 1992 and 2013, beginning with the double-role hit Bol Radha Bol when Kapoor was still a lead and ending here with him in a supporting role in a film aimed at a generation that knew him as somebody's father. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rita Rawail
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own. The name belongs to the Rawail film family.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), Rahul Rawail's comedy in which Kapoor plays Raj Khanna, a father who separates from his wife on a lie and raises one of their twin daughters alone.
biography: Rita Rawail is credited as a producer on Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001) and has no documented biography. The film matters less for her than for what it completes: Kapoor worked with three generations of the Rawail family across twenty-five years. H. S. Rawail directed him in Laila Majnu (1976), the role that fixed his tragic-romantic register, and again in Deedar-E-Yaar (1982); Rahul Rawail directed this one, by which time Kapoor was playing the father rather than the lover. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ritesh Shah
career_background: Ritesh Shah is an Indian screenwriter who works in Hindi films. Born in Anantnag, Jammu and Kashmir, into a Kashmiri family forced to migrate to Delhi during the exodus of 1990, he read English at Hindu College and took a master's in mass communication at Jamia Millia Islamia, then began as a playwright with the Act One Art Group in Delhi before moving to television in 1999 and to films after that.
debut: Television writing from 1999, including the series Kagaar; his first film as writer was Sujoy Ghosh's Home Delivery.
major_works: With Kapoor: D-Day (2013). Elsewhere, the screenplays and dialogues of Kahaani (2012), Pink (2016), Airlift (2017) and Raid (2018).
recurring_themes: Procedural thrillers and issue dramas built on investigation; ordinary people pushed against institutions.
creative_style: A dialogue specialist whose reputation rests on spare, functional speech in tense scenes rather than on flourish.
major_awards: Filmfare, Star Screen and Zee Cine awards for Best Dialogue for Pink.
historical_importance: One of the most sought-after Hindi dialogue writers of the 2010s, associated with the decade's turn towards tighter, more plot-driven commercial cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: D-Day (2013), Nikhil Advani's spy thriller, in which Kapoor plays Iqbal Seth, called Goldman, the fugitive the entire operation exists to capture. It is the most unambiguously villainous part of his late career and the role in which his charm is used as menace. Shah's own article also credits him with the dialogues of Namastey London (2007), another film in this workbook, though the Films sheet records Suresh Nair as its writer.
biography: Ritesh Shah wrote D-Day, the film that gave Rishi Kapoor the hardest role of his final decade. Born in Anantnag in 1976 and displaced to Delhi with his family in 1990, Shah came to screenwriting through Delhi theatre and the Act One Art Group, adapting Slawomir Mrozek before television took him to Mumbai in 1999. Kagaar and other serials led to his first feature, Home Delivery, and then to the run that made his name: Kahaani, Pink, Airlift and Raid, with Filmfare, Star Screen and Zee Cine awards for the dialogues of Pink. His writing favours clipped exchanges under pressure, which is what D-Day asks of Kapoor: a Dawood Ibrahim figure who is domestic and affable in one scene and lethal in the next. Kapoor had begun playing antagonists only the year before, in Agneepath; Shah's script extended that line and confirmed that the actor's late reinvention was not a single stunt.

name: Robin Bhatt
career_background: Robin Bhatt is an Indian screenwriter who works in Hindi films, the son of the director Nanabhai Bhatt and the elder half-brother of Mahesh and Mukesh Bhatt. He has worked as a writer, an assistant and an occasional actor, with around sixty-six writing credits and more than ten acting appearances.
debut: His debut as a writer was Aashiqui.
major_works: With Kapoor: Raju Chacha (2000). Elsewhere, Baazigar, Koi Mil Gaya, Krrish and Omkara.
recurring_themes: Commercial thrillers and family melodrama, much of it for Bhatt Productions.
creative_style: A career screenwriter inside a family production system, working to the demands of the star vehicle.
major_awards: An award for the screenplay of Baazigar; three further nominations, for Koi Mil Gaya, Krrish and Omkara; a lifetime achievement award at the Jaipur International Film Festival in 2019.
historical_importance: A prolific hand in the Bhatt family's 1990s output, which is one of the industry's longest-running writing operations.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Raju Chacha (2000), Anil Devgan's children's adventure, in which Kapoor plays Siddhant Rai, a wealthy widower whose three children drive off every governess he hires. It is one of the supporting-father parts that filled the gap between his years as a lead and his revival later in the decade.
biography: Robin Bhatt wrote Raju Chacha, which arrived at the lowest point of Rishi Kapoor's career. The eldest of Nanabhai Bhatt's sons and half-brother to Mahesh and Mukesh, Bhatt debuted as a writer with Aashiqui and became one of the Bhatt operation's most prolific hands, with some sixty-six credits, an award for Baazigar and nominations for Koi Mil Gaya, Krrish and Omkara. Raju Chacha was an expensive Ajay Devgn production that failed, and Kapoor's part in it, the distracted rich father, is the kind of role he took repeatedly between 1999 and 2004: the lead years were over and the Dharma and Yash Raj revival had not begun. The Jaipur International Film Festival gave Bhatt a lifetime achievement award in 2019, the year before Kapoor's death.

name: Rohan–Vinayak
career_background: A composing pair credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of their own.
major_works: With Kapoor: 102 Not Out (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: 102 Not Out (2018), Umesh Shukla's comedy about a 102-year-old father and his seventy-five-year-old son, in which Kapoor plays Babulal. It was his last completed leading role opposite Amitabh Bachchan, with whom he had worked since the 1970s.
biography: Rohan-Vinayak are credited with songs on 102 Not Out (2018) and have no documented biography. The film is the final Bachchan-Kapoor pairing and an unusual one: the two had shared the screen since Kabhi Kabhie (1976) and Amar Akbar Anthony (1977), always as contemporaries, and here play father and son, with Bachchan the parent. Kapoor was sixty-five, cast as a man of seventy-five convinced he is finished, a conceit the film treats as a correctable error. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rohena Gera
career_background: Rohena Gera is an Indian screenwriter, director and producer. She studied at Stanford University and Sarah Lawrence College, wrote for Indian television and film, and moved into documentary and then feature direction, alongside non-profit campaigning on peace and equality.
debut: Screenwriting debut on the first season of the television series Jassi Jaissi Koi Nahin in 2003.
major_works: With Kapoor: Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic (2008). Elsewhere, the documentary What's Love Got to Do with It? (2013) and the feature Sir, which premiered in Cannes' Semaine de la critique.
recurring_themes: Class and the household; marriage as a negotiated arrangement rather than a romantic conclusion.
creative_style: Observational and restrained in her own films, in contrast with the studio comedy she wrote early on.
major_awards: The Gan Foundation award in Cannes' Semaine de la critique and the grand jury and audience awards at Saint-Jean-de-Luz, all for Sir.
historical_importance: One of a small group of Indian writer-directors of her generation whose features reach European festivals on their own terms.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic (2008), Kunal Kohli's fantasy comedy, in which Kapoor appears as God, hearing four orphaned children pray and sending an angel down to them. It is the third of his four films with Kohli and the most purely decorative part of the group.
biography: Rohena Gera wrote Thoda Pyaar Thoda Magic, in which Rishi Kapoor plays God. Born in 1973 and educated at Stanford and Sarah Lawrence, Gera began in Indian television with Jassi Jaissi Koi Nahin in 2003, produced a public-service campaign against hate propaganda after the Gujarat riots, and then moved to her own work: the documentary What's Love Got to Do with It? (2013) and the feature Sir, which took the Gan Foundation award in Cannes' Semaine de la critique. Her own films examine class inside the household, which is a long way from the Yash Raj fantasy comedy she wrote for Kohli. Kapoor's cameo belongs to the stretch when he was most useful to producers as a benign presiding figure, and the credit is a reminder that writers in the Hindi industry often pass through commercial assignments some distance from the work they are later known for.

name: Rohit R. Kulkarni
career_background: A background-score composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Wedding Pullav (2015).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Wedding Pullav (2015), in which Kapoor is top-billed as Luv Kapoor but which the filmography records as a cameo. It is one of several late credits where his name carried the poster and the part ran a few minutes.
biography: Rohit R. Kulkarni composed the background score for Wedding Pullav (2015) and has no documented biography. The film shows how Kapoor's name functioned in his last years: billed first, used briefly. By 2015 he was taking three or four films a year in parts of very different weight, from the sustained lead of Kapoor & Sons the following year to single-scene appearances like Chalk N Duster, and distributors continued to put his face on the poster regardless of which kind the film was. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ronnie Screwvala
career_background: Rohinton Soli Screwvala, known as Ronnie Screwvala, is an Indian entrepreneur and film producer. He is considered a pioneer of Indian cable television and built UTV Software Communications into a media conglomerate that partnered with News Corp, 20th Century Fox, Disney and Bloomberg, divesting it to Disney in 2012 at an enterprise value of about US$1.4 billion.
debut: Cable television and then UTV; UTV Motion Pictures became a leading studio-model producer in the 2000s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Delhi-6 (2009). Elsewhere, the UTV Motion Pictures slate of the 2000s and early 2010s.
recurring_themes: The studio rather than the auteur: a slate spanning mainstream star vehicles and director-driven films.
creative_style: A corporate producer who brought studio financing, slates and overseas partnership into an industry previously run on individual proprietors.
major_awards: Named on Esquire's list of the 75 most influential people of the 21st century in 2008 and ranked in the Time 100.
historical_importance: Central to the corporatisation of Hindi film production in the 2000s, which changed who financed films and on what terms.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Delhi-6 (2009), Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra's drama, in which Kapoor plays Ali Beg, the cultivated figure of the Old Delhi lane who once loved the protagonist's mother. It is one of the roles that re-established him as a character actor worth writing for.
biography: Ronnie Screwvala produced Delhi-6 under UTV Motion Pictures, one of the films that reopened Rishi Kapoor's career. Born in 1956, Screwvala built UTV from cable television into a conglomerate with News Corp, Fox, Disney and Bloomberg as partners and sold it to Disney in 2012 for an enterprise value of about $1.4 billion, having been listed by Esquire and Time along the way; he has since worked through the Swades Foundation, UpGrad, U Sports and Unilazer Ventures. UTV's slate was exactly the kind of production environment that made Kapoor's second career possible: corporate financing allowed ensemble films where an older actor took a written part rather than a courtesy appearance. In 2009 he appeared in three such films, Delhi-6, Luck by Chance and Love Aaj Kal, after a decade of thin supporting work. Ali Beg, the neighbourhood's civilised centre with a private history, is the first of them in release order.

name: Roopvati Productions
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994), Surendra Bohra's family melodrama, in which Kapoor plays an army officer married to a woman her family has mistreated since birth and who conceals from her that another pregnancy would kill her.
biography: Roopvati Productions is credited on Saajan Ka Ghar (1994) and has no documented history. The banner belongs to the stretch of the early 1990s when Kapoor was still leading films but almost entirely in domestic melodrama: Saajan Ka Ghar, Ghar Ki Izzat and their like, built on sacrifice inside the marital household rather than on courtship. The romance in these films is settled before the plot starts, which is why his lover-boy scores drop through the period while romance centrality stays high. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Rose Movies
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Yeh Vaada Raha (1982).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Yeh Vaada Raha (1982), Kapil Kapoor's romance, in which Kapoor plays Vikram, who vows at a temple never to part from the singer Sunita and is then separated from her by a car crash and his mother's lies.
biography: Rose Movies is credited on Yeh Vaada Raha (1982) and has no documented history. The film is a pure example of the structure that dominates Kapoor's early 1980s: the lovers are aligned with each other and separated by machinery outside them, here a disfiguring accident and a mother who tells each that the other is dead. That shape is why his external-opposition average runs so far above his pair-friction average across the whole filmography. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Ruhi Rawail
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own. The name belongs to the Rawail film family.
major_works: With Kapoor: Deedar-E-Yaar (1982).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Deedar-E-Yaar (1982), H. S. Rawail's romance, in which Kapoor plays Javed, who enters Firdous's house disguised as a servant to win her and is then told by her father that his family makes the marriage impossible.
biography: Ruhi Rawail is credited as a writer on Deedar-E-Yaar (1982) and has no documented biography. The film was H. S. Rawail's second with Kapoor after Laila Majnu (1976) and an expensive failure, built on the same material as the earlier film: love declared absolutely, then broken by lineage and family prohibition. Rawail's grandson Rahul would direct Kapoor again in Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), by which time the parts had moved from the lover to the father. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: S Waris Ali
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Paraya Ghar (1989).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Paraya Ghar (1989), one of three films Kalpataru directed with Kapoor in two years. Its Wikipedia article carries only an infobox and a soundtrack listing, so nothing about the role itself can be recorded from it.
biography: S Waris Ali is credited as a producer on Paraya Ghar (1989) and has no documented biography. The film is one of twenty-eight entries in this filmography with no usable Wikipedia coverage beyond a cast list, and those gaps cluster precisely here, in the family dramas Kapoor made between 1986 and 1991 while the hits went elsewhere. Kalpataru directed him three times in this period, in Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani, Bade Ghar Ki Beti and this film, and almost nothing survives in reference sources about any of them. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: S. A. Chandrasekhar
industry: Tamil cinema, with Telugu, Kannada and Hindi films
career_background: Senapathy Albert Chandrasekaran, known as S. A. Chandrasekhar, is an Indian director, producer, screenwriter and actor who works chiefly in Tamil cinema. Born in Thangachimadam in 1945, he made his directorial debut with Aval Oru Pachai Kuzhanthai (1978) and has directed more than seventy films across four languages, many of them on social issues.
debut: Directorial debut Aval Oru Pachai Kuzhanthai (1978); breakthrough with Sattam Oru Iruttarai (1981).
major_works: With Kapoor: Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990). Elsewhere, Sattam Oru Iruttarai (1981) and a long run of Tamil vigilante and social-issue films, including those launching his son Vijay.
recurring_themes: Vigilante justice, trafficking, corruption and institutional failure, addressed directly and at speed.
creative_style: A fast, high-volume commercial director with a declamatory approach to social subjects; S. Shankar and several other directors worked as his assistants.
historical_importance: A major figure in 1980s Tamil commercial cinema and the father and early director of Vijay.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990), in which Kapoor plays Vijay, a law student who helps his classmate Bharti expose her father's trafficking of children and women. It is one of the few explicitly issue-driven films in a filmography otherwise built on romance and domestic drama, and one of the few in which Kapoor is the heroine's ally rather than her suitor.
biography: S. A. Chandrasekhar directed Azaad Desh Ke Gulam, an outlier in Rishi Kapoor's filmography. Born in Thangachimadam in 1945, Chandrasekhar debuted with Aval Oru Pachai Kuzhanthai in 1978, broke through with Sattam Oru Iruttarai in 1981 and has directed over seventy films in Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Hindi, largely on social subjects and vigilante justice; S. Shankar and Ponram were among his assistants, and his son is the actor and politician Vijay. His Hindi excursions were rare, and this is one of them, written by his wife Shoba Chandrasekhar, who appears separately in this sheet. The film gives Kapoor an unusual function: Bharti discovers her father's crimes and Vijay accompanies and supports her, which makes the female character the agent of the plot. In a filmography where women are most often the object of courtship, the role stands out more for its structure than for its quality.

name: S. D. Burman
career_background: Sachin Dev Burman was an Indian music director and singer and a member of the Tripura royal family. He composed for Hindi and Bengali films from the 1930s until his death in 1975, and sang a small number of distinctive playback songs himself.
debut: Bengali films in the 1930s, then Bombay from the 1940s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Barood (1976). Elsewhere, Sujata, Guide, Aradhana, Talaash and Prem Nagar among a very large body of work.
recurring_themes: Folk melody, particularly Bengali and north-eastern, absorbed into film song; the lyric line placed above orchestration.
creative_style: Melodic economy and an unmistakable singing voice; an influence transmitted directly to his son R. D. Burman, who composed far more of this filmography.
major_awards: National Film Award for Best Male Playback Singer for Aradhana (1970); National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Zindagi Zindagi (1974); Filmfare nominations for Sujata, Guide, Aradhana, Talaash and Prem Nagar.
historical_importance: One of the defining composers of Hindi film music's classic period, and the head of a two-generation dynasty that shaped the sound of Kapoor's own era.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Barood (1976), Pramod Chakravorty's revenge thriller, in which Kapoor plays Anup, who watches smugglers kill his father and spends twelve years preparing to kill them. Burman died on 31 October 1975, so the score reached cinemas after his death; it is the only S. D. Burman music in this filmography, while his son R. D. Burman scored a great many of Kapoor's films.
biography: S. D. Burman composed the songs for Barood, released in April 1976, some five months after his death in October 1975. Born into the Tripura royal family in 1906, Burman built one of the central bodies of work in Hindi film music, from Sujata and Guide to Aradhana and Prem Nagar, winning the National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Zindagi Zindagi and for playback singing for Aradhana. His presence in this filmography is a single late credit, and it marks a generational handover: Kapoor's career was scored overwhelmingly by R. D. Burman, his son, whose work on Khel Khel Mein, Hum Kisise Kum Naheen and Karz did more than any other music to define Kapoor's romantic image. The father's one contribution is attached instead to a revenge thriller, the genre Kapoor was least suited to and largely abandoned.

name: S. M. Abbas
career_background: S. M. Abbas, born Syed Mohammad Abbas, was an Indian film director and screenwriter active chiefly in the 1960s and 1970s. He graduated from Allahabad University, where he acted in and directed stage plays, and left for Bombay in early 1957 intending to act, instead working as an assistant and then a writer.
debut: His first film was Ek Jhalak (1957); he wrote additional dialogue on Parvarish (1958).
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Parivar (1991). Elsewhere, Shriman Satyawadi (1960), Kab? Kyoon? Aur Kahan? (1970), Hungama (1971) and Ek Hasina Do Diwane (1972).
recurring_themes: Comedy and domestic drama.
creative_style: A writer-director of the studio era working in established commercial forms.
historical_importance: A working professional of the 1960s and 1970s whose reference coverage is thin and poorly sourced.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ghar Parivar (1991), Mohanji Prasad's family drama, in which Kapoor plays Birju, billed second to Rajesh Khanna. The film's article has no plot section, so nothing about the role can be recorded from it.
biography: S. M. Abbas is credited as a writer on Ghar Parivar (1991), late in a career that belonged to the 1960s and 1970s. Born Syed Mohammad Abbas, he came to Bombay from Allahabad University in 1957 hoping to act, assisted the director Kali Das under a pseudonym and wrote additional dialogue for Raj Kapoor's Parvarish in 1958, then built a modest body of work including Shriman Satyawadi, Kab? Kyoon? Aur Kahan?, Hungama and Ek Hasina Do Diwane. His Wikipedia article is thinly referenced and reads partly as family record. The film itself is one of several in which Kapoor is second-billed to Rajesh Khanna, an arrangement that recurs through his late 1980s work and marks the period when he was no longer the industry's first choice for a lead.

name: S. Ramanathan
career_background: A director credited on one film in this filmography. No Wikipedia article under this name could be located, so nothing about his wider career can be recorded here.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rangila Ratan (1976).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rangila Ratan (1976), in which Kapoor plays a man kidnapped as a child and raised as a criminal by the man his father sent to the gallows, groomed his whole life as an instrument of revenge against his own father.
biography: S. Ramanathan directed Rangila Ratan (1976) and has no locatable Wikipedia article. The film belongs to Kapoor's second year as an adult lead, when he and his producers were still testing whether he could carry the revenge plots that were then the industry's dominant commercial form. The answer across 1975 and 1976, in Raaja, Barood, Rangila Ratan and Zinda Dil, was that he could be cast in them but was not persuasive in them, and the films that worked instead were Khel Khel Mein and Laila Majnu, one comic and one romantic. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: S.K. Jain
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989), Kalpataru's drama, in which Kapoor plays Gopal, married at his father's wish to the daughter of the family's servant, the two of them the only decent members of the household.
biography: S.K. Jain is credited as a producer on Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989) and has no documented biography. The film is one of the clearest statements of the structure that organises Kapoor's late 1980s work: a marriage arranged across a class line, a couple who behave well, and a household ranged against them. Pair friction is near zero and external opposition does all the work, which is the signature pattern of this filmography as a whole and is at its most schematic in the Kalpataru films. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: SPE Films India
career_background: A production entity credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own under this name. The credit is the Indian film arm of Sony Pictures Entertainment as it appears in the film's credits.
major_works: With Kapoor: 102 Not Out (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Part of the entry of international studios into Hindi-language production, though this particular credit is not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: 102 Not Out (2018), in which Kapoor plays Babulal opposite Amitabh Bachchan's 102-year-old father. It was his last completed leading role and the last of their many films together.
biography: SPE Films India is credited as a producer on 102 Not Out (2018) and has no documented history under that name. The credit is worth recording for what it indicates about the film's financing: by 2018 a two-hander about an elderly father and son, with no romance and no action, could be funded through an international studio's Indian arm and adapted from a Gujarati stage play. That is a different industry from the one in which Kapoor became a star, and it is the reason his last decade offered him written parts rather than ceremonial ones. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: SaarthiE Entertainment
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rajma Chawal (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rajma Chawal (2018), Leena Yadav's comedy drama, in which Kapoor plays Raj Mathur, a widower who cannot talk to his son and so steals a young woman's identity on Facebook to reach him.
biography: SaarthiE Entertainment is credited on Rajma Chawal (2018) and has no documented history. The film was released on Netflix rather than in cinemas, and it is one of the last two leading roles Kapoor completed. Raj Mathur is a part his earlier career could not have produced: the comedy depends on a father who is inept, deceitful in a small way and visibly lonely, with no romantic function at all. His final films pursue this register consistently, from Do Dooni Chaar through Sharmaji Namkeen. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Saboo Films
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), Rahul Rawail's comedy, in which Kapoor plays Raj Khanna, separated from his wife on his stepsister's lie and raising one of their twin daughters alone.
biography: Saboo Films is credited on Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001) and has no documented history. The film is a remake of The Parent Trap by way of Kabhi Kabhie's generation of stars, and it casts Kapoor as the wronged husband and father rather than as either lover. Between 1999 and 2004 almost every part he took was of this kind, and the films themselves were mostly unsuccessful; what changed after 2008 was not his willingness to play fathers but the quality of the fathers being written. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Sachin–Jigar
career_background: Sachin-Jigar are an Indian composing duo, Sachin Sanghvi and Jigar Saraiya, both from Gujarat and settled in Mumbai. Before forming the duo they were long-time assistants to Rajesh Roshan and Pritam and arranged and programmed music for composers including A. R. Rahman, Amit Trivedi, Anu Malik, Nadeem-Shravan and Sandesh Shandilya.
debut: A guest song for Life Partner (2009); their first full score followed on F.A.L.T.U, after a recommendation from Pritam.
major_works: With Kapoor: Shuddh Desi Romance (2013). Elsewhere, a large body of Hindi and Gujarati film music from 2011 onwards.
recurring_themes: Youth romance and small-town settings; songs built for situation rather than for a classical idiom.
creative_style: Programmed, rhythm-forward arrangements with folk inflections, written closely to the screenplay's needs.
historical_importance: Among the most-used composers of the 2010s, in the generation that followed Pritam in the Yash Raj and Dharma system.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Shuddh Desi Romance (2013), Maneesh Sharma's Jaipur-set comedy, in which Kapoor plays Goyal, called Tauji, who employs the hero as a rental wedding guest and presides over the film's economy of weddings that may not happen.
biography: Sachin-Jigar scored Shuddh Desi Romance, in which Rishi Kapoor plays the genial fixer at the edge of a romance about two people who keep refusing to marry. Sachin Sanghvi and Jigar Saraiya, both Gujaratis settled in Mumbai, spent years as assistants to Rajesh Roshan and Pritam and as arrangers for Rahman, Trivedi, Anu Malik and Nadeem-Shravan before Pritam's recommendation turned them into a duo in their own right from 2009. Their songs for this film are built around the hero's indecision, which is the film's subject. The casting is pointed: the actor whose own stardom was made of courtship songs appears here as the man renting out wedding crowds, in a film that treats marriage as an institution its young leads cannot commit to. It is one of four films he made with Yash Raj between 2004 and 2013.

name: Saif Ali Khan
career_background: Saif Ali Khan is an Indian actor and film producer, the son of the actress Sharmila Tagore and the cricketer Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi and titular head of the Pataudi family since 2011. He has won a National Film Award and seven Filmfare Awards and received the Padma Shri in 2010; he produced through Illuminati Films from the late 2000s.
debut: Acting debut in Parampara (1993); recognition for Dil Chahta Hai (2001) and Kal Ho Naa Ho (2003).
major_works: With Kapoor: Love Aaj Kal (2009), as producer. Elsewhere, as an actor, Dil Chahta Hai, Hum Tum, Parineeta, Omkara, Race and Sacred Games.
recurring_themes: Urban romantic comedy and, later, morally compromised men in thrillers and prestige series.
creative_style: As a producer, a star using his own name to finance director-driven projects he also leads.
major_awards: A National Film Award, seven Filmfare Awards and the Padma Shri (2010).
historical_importance: One of the central Hindi stars of the 2000s and part of the shift towards the urban, English-speaking romantic comedy.
relationship_with_actor: Two points of contact, one of them outside his roster credit. As a producer: Love Aaj Kal (2009), in which Kapoor plays the older Veer Singh Panesar, telling the story of a love he decided on at first sight, against which the film measures its modern couple. As an actor he had already played Kapoor's son in Hum Tum (2004), where Kapoor appears as Arjun Kapoor in the family scenes punctuating a romance conducted over nine years.
biography: Saif Ali Khan produced Love Aaj Kal through Illuminati Films, five years after acting as Rishi Kapoor's son in Hum Tum. Born in 1970 to Sharmila Tagore and Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi, he debuted in Parampara in 1993 and became one of the defining stars of the 2000s with Dil Chahta Hai, Kal Ho Naa Ho, Hum Tum, Parineeta and Omkara, collecting a National Film Award, seven Filmfare Awards and the Padma Shri. Love Aaj Kal is structurally the most interesting of Kapoor's late supporting roles: Imtiaz Ali gives him the older version of the film's romantic argument, a man who chose a woman at first sight and spent his life on that choice, set against Khan's modern character, who cannot. Casting Kapoor in that function used his own screen history as evidence, which is something only an actor with a thirty-five-year romantic record could supply.

name: Sajid Khan
career_background: Sajid Khan is an Indian film director and screenwriter, born in Mumbai to the stuntman-turned-director Kamran Khan and Menaka Khan. His sister is the choreographer and director Farah Khan, and Farhan and Zoya Akhtar are his maternal cousins. He was educated at Maneckji Cooper School and Mithibai College, and began as a television host before directing.
debut: A segment of the anthology Darna Zaroori Hai (2006), followed by his first full feature Heyy Babyy (2007).
major_works: With Kapoor: Housefull 2 (2012). Elsewhere, Heyy Babyy (2007), Housefull (2010), Himmatwala (2013) and Humshakals (2014).
recurring_themes: Broad ensemble farce built on mistaken identity, large star casts and deliberate vulgarity.
creative_style: High-volume slapstick with no interest in realism; the comedy is driven by configuration rather than character.
historical_importance: A principal maker of the multi-star comedy franchise that dominated Hindi box-office returns around 2010.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Housefull 2 (2012), in which Kapoor plays Chintu Kapoor, who despises his half-brother Dabboo and competes with him over whose daughter can marry the richer man. It is the broadest comedy of his late career and arrived in the same year as Agneepath, the two together marking how wide his range of late-career employment had become.
biography: Sajid Khan directed Housefull 2, in which Rishi Kapoor plays one of four feuding older men in a farce of mistaken parentage. Born in Mumbai to Kamran Khan and Menaka Khan, with Farah Khan as his sister and Farhan and Zoya Akhtar as cousins, Khan moved from television hosting to a segment of Darna Zaroori Hai in 2006 and then to Heyy Babyy, Housefull and Housefull 2, all commercially successful, before Himmatwala and Humshakals failed. The film is instructive about Kapoor's final decade: his willingness to appear in an ensemble farce, with Randhir Kapoor among the other patriarchs, sat alongside Agneepath's Rauf Lala in the same year. He treated the two assignments as equally legitimate, and that indifference to prestige is part of why he worked so steadily after 2008. His cousin Zoya Akhtar had directed Kapoor three years earlier in Luck by Chance.

name: Sajid Nadiadwala
career_background: Sajid Nadiadwala is an Indian film producer, director and screenwriter, the grandson of the producer A. K. Nadiadwala. He assisted J. P. Dutta on Ghulami at twenty-one, worked as a production assistant in his uncle's company and founded Nadiadwala Grandson Entertainment at twenty-five.
debut: Waqt Hamara Hai (1993) as producer; Kick (2014) as director.
major_works: With Kapoor: Housefull 2 (2012). Elsewhere, the Housefull and Baaghi franchises and a long run of Akshay Kumar and Salman Khan vehicles.
recurring_themes: Star-led commercial entertainment: comedy franchises, action remakes and family spectacle.
creative_style: A franchise producer who builds repeatable properties around established stars.
major_awards: A debutant director award for Kick.
historical_importance: One of the most consistently commercial Hindi producers of the past three decades and a central figure in the franchise model.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Housefull 2 (2012), in which Kapoor plays Chintu Kapoor, one of two warring half-brothers each trying to marry a daughter off to money. Nadiadwala is credited both as producer and among the writers.
biography: Sajid Nadiadwala produced and co-wrote Housefull 2, the only Nadiadwala Grandson film in this filmography. Born in 1966 and descended from the producer A. K. Nadiadwala, he began as an assistant on Ghulami, founded his own company at twenty-five and built it on Akshay Kumar and Salman Khan vehicles, from Waqt Hamara Hai and Judwaa to the Housefull and Baaghi franchises, later directing Kick himself. Housefull 2 recruited an older generation to pad its ensemble, and Kapoor took the assignment at sixty, in the same year as Agneepath and Student of the Year. Nothing in the part uses his history as a romantic star except his recognisability, which was precisely the asset the franchise model was buying. The film was among the year's larger commercial successes.

name: Salim Khan
career_background: Salim Khan is an Indian screenwriter, actor and producer, best known as one half of Salim-Javed with Javed Akhtar. Within the partnership he developed stories and characters while Akhtar concentrated on screenplay and dialogue. The pair were among the first Indian screenwriters to reach star status, and their work in the 1970s reshaped the commercial Hindi formula.
debut: Acting from the early 1960s; the Salim-Javed partnership formed in the late 1960s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zamana (1985), credited with Javed Akhtar. Elsewhere, Seeta Aur Geeta, Zanjeer, Deewaar, Sholay, Trishul, Kranti and Don.
recurring_themes: The angry young man, the divided brothers, the mother as moral centre, and the state as absent or compromised.
creative_style: Tight structural plotting around a single wounded protagonist, with dialogue built for repetition and recall.
historical_importance: Co-author of the dominant commercial template of 1970s Hindi cinema and of the archetype that made Amitabh Bachchan a star.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Zamana (1985), Ramesh Talwar's drama, credited to Salim Khan with Javed Akhtar, in which Kapoor plays Ravi, the criminal brother to Rajesh Khanna's police inspector, both of them in love with the same woman. The brother-against-brother structure is the writers' own, but by 1985 their partnership had dissolved and the formula was in decline.
biography: Salim Khan is credited, with Javed Akhtar, on Zamana (1985), the one Salim-Javed script in this filmography. Born in 1935, Khan supplied the stories and characters for the partnership that produced Zanjeer, Deewaar, Sholay, Trishul and Kranti, created the angry young man and made screenwriters visible in an industry that had treated them as staff. Zamana arrives after the split and after the template had passed its peak: two brothers divided by a murdered father neither knew, one a policeman and one a criminal, both in love with the same woman. Kapoor plays the criminal, second-billed to Rajesh Khanna, and the casting is revealing. The archetype Salim-Javed built needed an actor who could carry rage, which Kapoor could not and never pretended to; the film's structure fits Bachchan and the role fits him only approximately.

name: Sameer Dixit
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Manto (2018), Nandita Das's biographical drama, in which Kapoor appears briefly as an unnamed film producer, one of a gallery of cameos peopling the Bombay film world Saadat Hasan Manto worked in before partition.
biography: Sameer Dixit is credited as a producer on Manto (2018) and has no documented biography. Kapoor's appearance in the film is a single scene as a producer of the 1940s, and the casting is a joke the audience is expected to get: the grandson of Prithviraj Kapoor and son of Raj Kapoor, playing an anonymous functionary of the industry his family helped build, in a film about a writer it treated badly. It is one of four cameos in his last five years and the only one in a film with festival ambitions. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Sameer Uddin
career_background: A background-score composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kapoor & Sons (2016).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kapoor & Sons (2016), Shakun Batra's family drama, in which Kapoor plays the ninety-year-old Amarjeet Kapoor, whose heart attack summons his estranged grandsons home and whose stated last wish is a family photograph the film keeps failing to take.
biography: Sameer Uddin composed the background score for Kapoor & Sons (2016) and has no documented biography. The film is the best-reviewed of Kapoor's last decade and the one that required most of him physically: four hours of prosthetics daily to play a man thirty years his senior, a performance built on comic appetite rather than dignity. For a filmography organised around romantic leads, the most admired late role is a grandfather who watches pornography, forges a photograph and holds a family together by refusing to behave. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Samir Ganguly
career_background: Samir Ganguly is an Indian film director who also directed many episodes of the television serial Paying Guest. His Wikipedia article is a short stub and records almost nothing else.
major_works: With Kapoor: Anjane Mein (1978). Elsewhere, episodes of Paying Guest.
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Anjane Mein (1978), in which Kapoor and Neetu Singh take the leads as Raja and Rani, with Nirupa Roy, Ranjeet and Asha Sachdev in support. The film's article has no plot section, so the role cannot be described from it.
biography: Samir Ganguly directed Anjane Mein (1978), one of the many Rishi Kapoor and Neetu Singh pairings of that decade. His own record is almost blank: a stub noting television work on Paying Guest and nothing substantial about his films. Anjane Mein is one of eight films in this workbook marked with a major romance that has no Romances row, because the surviving documentation gives a cast list and a soundtrack and no account of the relationship at all. Kapoor and Singh made eleven films together before marrying in 1980, and several of the lesser ones are in exactly this condition: certain to have been romances, impossible to characterise.

name: Sandesh Shandilya
career_background: Sandesh Shandilya is an Indian film composer, musician and singer who has written more than twenty Hindi film soundtracks. He took his early training from the sarangi player Ustad Sultan Khan.
debut: Songs for Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham (2001); the album Piya Basanti the same year.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chalk N Duster (2016). Elsewhere, Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham (2001), Chameli (2004), Socha Na Tha (2005) and Jab We Met (2007).
recurring_themes: Melody-led romantic songs with a semi-classical inflection.
creative_style: Writes for the singing voice rather than for arrangement, often in long melodic lines; Aaoge Jab Tum is the usual example.
major_awards: International Viewers' Choice Award at the 2001 MTV Video Music Awards for Piya Basanti.
historical_importance: One of the composers who kept a melodic, semi-classical register current in the 2000s alongside more heavily programmed music.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chalk N Duster (2016), in which Kapoor appears as the host of the televised quiz that forms the film's climax, where two dismissed teachers stake their careers against five crore rupees. The part is a single sustained sequence.
biography: Sandesh Shandilya scored Chalk N Duster, in which Rishi Kapoor hosts the quiz show that decides the film. Trained under Ustad Sultan Khan, Shandilya came to notice in 2001 with songs for Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham and the album Piya Basanti, which won an International Viewers' Choice Award at that year's MTV Video Music Awards, and wrote more than twenty soundtracks including Chameli, Socha Na Tha and Jab We Met, where Aaoge Jab Tum drew the strongest notices of his career. His melodic manner has an obvious affinity with the music Kapoor lip-synced in the 1970s, but the two met only here, in a late issue film about the commercialisation of private schooling, where Kapoor plays a version of himself presiding over a game show. The role is small and the film little seen.

name: Sandow M. M. A. Chinnappa Thevar
career_background: Sandow Marudur Marudachalamurthy Ayyavoo Chinnappa Thevar was a producer of Tamil cinema from the mid-1950s through the 1970s, working under the Devar Films and Dhandayupathi Films banners. He produced sixteen films with M. G. Ramachandran and was best known for films featuring animals. The Sandow title came from the bodybuilder Eugen Sandow, in tribute to his physique.
debut: Production from the mid-1950s; national recognition with Haathi Mere Saathi (1971).
major_works: With Kapoor: Raaja (1975). Elsewhere, Haathi Mere Saathi (1971), Vellikizhamai Viratham (1974) and Aattukara Alamelu (1977).
recurring_themes: Animals as central characters, melodrama and mass-audience spectacle.
creative_style: A showman-producer who built films around a single attraction, often an elephant or other animal.
historical_importance: A dominant Tamil producer of his era and the maker of Haathi Mere Saathi, one of the most commercially successful Hindi films of the early 1970s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Raaja (1975), K. Shankar's action thriller, in which Kapoor plays twin brothers, the ordinary Raaja and the CID inspector Ram, with Rani unable to tell them apart until Ram grows a moustache for her benefit. It is Kapoor's first double role, two years before Karz and sixteen before the comic double of Bol Radha Bol.
biography: Chinnappa Thevar produced Raaja, Rishi Kapoor's first double role, in his second year as an adult lead. Born in 1915 and nicknamed Sandow after the bodybuilder Eugen Sandow, Thevar built Devar Films into one of Tamil cinema's most successful production houses, made sixteen films with M. G. Ramachandran, specialised in films with animals at their centre, and reached a national audience with Haathi Mere Saathi in 1971. He died in 1978 during the shooting of Thai Meethu Sathiyam. Raaja is a south-Indian producer's Hindi venture, directed by K. Shankar, and it tests the twin-brother device that Kapoor would use three times in his career. The pattern of his early years is visible in it: an actor whose success was romantic being cast repeatedly in action plots by producers who wanted a new young lead for an established formula.

name: Sanjay Chhel
industry: Hindi and Gujarati cinema; Gujarati theatre
career_background: Sanjay Chhel is an Indian director, writer and lyricist, born at Dwarka in Gujarat in 1967 and raised in Mumbai, the son of the art director and production designer Chhel Vayeda. He began in Gujarati theatre with one-act plays, wrote more than thirty television serials, and worked as a Hindi film lyricist and screenwriter before directing.
debut: One-act plays in Gujarati theatre, then television; his film work includes lyrics for popular Hindi songs.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017). Elsewhere, the plays Ubhi Chavi Adi Chavi and Crossword Puzzle, the serial Hum Sab Baraati, and song lyrics including Nikamma kiya is dil ne.
recurring_themes: Community comedy and the collision of regional identities; marriage as a negotiation between families.
creative_style: A theatre writer's approach to film comedy, built on verbal play and ensemble scenes.
historical_importance: A notable figure in Gujarati theatre whose Hindi film work is less prominent.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017), which he directed and in which Kapoor plays Guggi Tandon, the Punjabi half of a comedy about two fathers, one Punjabi and one Gujarati, whose children are marrying each other. His own article records the film as commercially unsuccessful.
biography: Sanjay Chhel directed Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi, one of Rishi Kapoor's last leading roles. Born at Dwarka in 1967 to the art director Chhel Vayeda and raised in Mumbai, Chhel made his name in Gujarati theatre with one-act plays, wrote over thirty television serials and worked as a Hindi lyricist and screenwriter before moving into direction. The film is a two-patriarch comedy in which Kapoor's Punjabi father faces Paresh Rawal's Gujarati one over their children's marriage, and his own article concedes it failed commercially. It belongs to the final group of films in which Kapoor is top-billed in parts organised entirely around fatherhood and community, with the romance handed to the younger cast. The structure would recur in 102 Not Out and Jhootha Kahin Ka within two years.

name: Sanjay Wandrekar
career_background: A background-score composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011), Hema Malini's film, in which Kapoor plays Altaf Zardari, the second of the men a young woman visits while searching for her biological father.
biography: Sanjay Wandrekar composed the background score for Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011) and has no documented biography. The film was Hema Malini's third as director and a comprehensive failure, and Kapoor's role is one of three possible fathers paraded before the heroine. It sits oddly in the year that also produced Patiala House, where he plays a father whose authority has wrecked his son's life. The same late-career type, the patriarch, could be written with real weight or used as a plot station, and in 2011 he took both kinds. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Sanjeev Datta
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sanam Re (2016).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sanam Re (2016), Divya Khosla Kumar's romantic drama, in which Kapoor plays Daddu, the grandfather whose prophecy organises the whole film: that his grandson will love a girl who lives five hundred steps from the studio, that they will love each other forever, and that they will never marry.
biography: Sanjeev Datta is credited as a writer on Sanam Re (2016) and has no documented biography. The part is the clearest instance of a late-career device the films use repeatedly: Kapoor as the custodian of a romantic belief the young characters have to live out. In Love Aaj Kal he supplies the old way of loving as a counter-argument; here he supplies a prophecy, and in Sanam Re the prophecy is of a love that lasts and a marriage that never happens. His own star image, built on courtship films across the 1970s, is the reason the device works with him in the chair. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Sanjeev Gupta
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The documented Sanjeev Gupta is an Indian-born British steel businessman and a different person.
major_works: With Kapoor: Besharam (2013).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Besharam (2013), Abhinav Kashyap's action comedy, in which Kapoor and Neetu Singh play Inspector Chulbul Chautala and Head Constable Bulbul Chautala, the police couple pursuing a car thief played by their son Ranbir Kapoor.
biography: Sanjeev Gupta is credited as a producer on Besharam (2013) and has no documented biography; the Wikipedia Sanjeev Gupta is a British steel magnate and unrelated. The film is the only one in which Rishi Kapoor, Neetu Singh and Ranbir Kapoor all appear, and the only one in which the couple whose romance ran through the 1970s play a married pair of police officers opposite their own son. It was mauled on release. The family reunion the production was selling is worth recording anyway: Kapoor and Singh had not acted together as a couple since the 1980s. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Sanjeev–Ajay
career_background: A composing pair credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of their own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), Smeep Kang's comedy, in which Kapoor plays Yograj Singh, a widowed father whose son has no job and no intention of returning to the family farm.
biography: Sanjeev-Ajay are credited with songs on Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019) and have no documented biography. The film was released in July 2019, nine months before Kapoor's death and after his return from cancer treatment in New York, and it is a Punjabi-comedy remake with a crowded credit list that includes several composers and lyricists for a handful of songs. It is the least regarded of his final films, and its existence alongside The Body and the posthumous Sharmaji Namkeen shows how determinedly he worked in the time he had left. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Sanjoy Chowdhury
career_background: Sanjoy Chowdhury is an Indian film score composer and the son of the composer Salil Chowdhury. He has specialised in background music rather than songs across a long list of films in several languages.
debut: The background score of the Malayalam film Ennu Swantham Janakikutty (1998), followed by John Matthew Matthan's Sarfarosh.
major_works: With Kapoor: All Is Well (2015). Elsewhere, Sarfarosh, A Wednesday! and scores in Malayalam and Bengali.
recurring_themes: Score as structural support for thrillers and social dramas.
creative_style: A specialist background-score composer working apart from the song-writing side of Hindi film music.
major_awards: Star Screen Award nomination for A Wednesday!.
historical_importance: Part of the generation that established the background score as a separate craft credit in Hindi cinema, and the carrier of his father's name into it.
relationship_with_actor: One film: All Is Well (2015), Umesh Shukla's comedy drama, in which Kapoor plays Bhajanlal Bhalla, a baker who throws his son out of the house and is then revealed to be deep in debt, with a wife suffering from Alzheimer's whom he has sent away to an ashram.
biography: Sanjoy Chowdhury scored All Is Well, the first of two films Umesh Shukla made with Rishi Kapoor. The son of Salil Chowdhury, Chowdhury debuted in 1998 on the Malayalam film Ennu Swantham Janakikutty, was brought in by John Matthew Matthan for Sarfarosh and built a career almost entirely on background music, with a Star Screen nomination for A Wednesday!. All Is Well failed, but the part it gave Kapoor is of a piece with his late work: a father whose severity is revealed to be a cover for ruin, with a wife who no longer recognises him. Three years later Shukla cast him again, in 102 Not Out, in a far better version of the same relationship, where the parent is Amitabh Bachchan and Kapoor is the son being refused permission to give up.

name: Santosh Anand
career_background: Santosh Anand is an Indian lyricist who came to prominence in the 1970s. Born in Sikandrabad in 1929, he studied library science at Aligarh Muslim University and began writing for films in 1970.
debut: Purab Aur Paschim (1970), with music by Kalyanji-Anandji.
major_works: With Kapoor: Prem Rog (1982), Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989) and Ranbhoomi (1991). Elsewhere, Ek Pyar Ka Nagma Hai from Shor (1972) and the songs of Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974).
recurring_themes: Plain-spoken moral and romantic verse, often on love as endurance rather than conquest.
creative_style: Simple diction and repeatable refrains, written to be sung slowly; a lyricist of sentiment rather than wordplay.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist twice, in 1975 and 1983; Yash Bharti Award in 2016.
historical_importance: One of the most-sung lyricists of the 1970s and early 1980s, whose second Filmfare award came for a Rishi Kapoor film.
relationship_with_actor: Three films by the Films sheet, against one in the frozen collaborator roster. He wrote the lyrics for Prem Rog (1982), Raj Kapoor's film in which Kapoor plays the servant's son who marries a widowed daughter of the house, and for Bade Ghar Ki Beti (1989), and he is credited among the writers of Ranbhoomi (1991). Prem Rog is by far the most important of the three: it is one of his defining films, and Anand's lyrics for it won him the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist in 1983.
biography: Santosh Anand wrote the lyrics of Prem Rog, which is among the two or three most important films Rishi Kapoor made. Born in Sikandrabad in 1929 and trained in library science at Aligarh, Anand began with Purab Aur Paschim in 1970 and wrote Ek Pyar Ka Nagma Hai for Shor, then the songs of Roti Kapda Aur Makaan, which brought him the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist in 1975; his second came in 1983 for Prem Rog. Raj Kapoor's film cast his son as a poor young man who loves and marries a widowed daughter of the household that raised him, against every convention the family holds, and its songs carry the argument the dialogue cannot make directly. Anand's plain, slow-moving verse suited a film built on grief and defiance rather than courtship, and it gave Kapoor his least frivolous romantic role of the period.

name: Santosh Saroj
career_background: Santosh Saroj is a Hindi-film screenwriter and dialogue writer, earlier an assistant director on films including Mausam (1975) and Raaste Ka Patthar. He worked most often with Mukul Anand and Tinu Anand and has also directed two films.
debut: Assistant direction in the mid-1970s, then writing; best known for the Amitabh Bachchan vehicles of the late 1980s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Agneepath (2012), credited among the writers of the remake. Elsewhere, Shahenshah (1988), Agneepath (1990), Khuda Gawah and Major Saab (1998).
recurring_themes: Crime melodrama and vengeance, written for a single dominant star.
creative_style: Declamatory dialogue built for star entrances and confrontation scenes.
historical_importance: A principal writer of the late-1980s Bachchan cycle, and the author of the original Agneepath, whose story credit carried into the 2012 remake.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Agneepath (2012), Karan Malhotra's remake, in which Kapoor plays Rauf Lala, the gangster whose protege destroys him. Saroj is credited among the film's writers alongside Malhotra and Ila Bedi Dutta, his claim resting on the 1990 original. The part is the hinge of Kapoor's late career: a genuine villain, played without any appeal to the audience's affection, in a year when he also appeared in Housefull 2 and Student of the Year.
biography: Santosh Saroj wrote the original Agneepath and is credited among the writers of the 2012 remake in which Rishi Kapoor plays Rauf Lala. He began as an assistant director on Mausam and Raaste Ka Patthar, then wrote the late-1980s Amitabh Bachchan films that are his best-known work, Shahenshah, Khuda Gawah and the 1990 Agneepath, as well as Major Saab in 1998, and directed two films himself. The remake's story credit is his inheritance, and the role it produced changed how the industry used Kapoor. Rauf Lala is a flesh trader with gold teeth and no redeeming warmth, and Kapoor played him at fifty-nine with evident appetite. Every antagonist he took afterwards, in Aurangzeb, D-Day, Kal Kissne Dekha and Kaanchi, follows from this one, and it is the single most consequential casting decision of his final decade.

name: Sapan–Jagmohan
career_background: A composing duo credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article located under this name.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aap Ke Deewane (1980).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Aap Ke Deewane (1980), Surendra Mohan's romance, in which Kapoor and Rakesh Roshan play inseparable friends thrown out of college on a false charge, who assume the identity of a married couple to be hired as tutors and both fall in love with the same woman.
biography: Sapan-Jagmohan are credited on Aap Ke Deewane (1980) and have no locatable Wikipedia article. The film is one of the double-hero comedies that ran through Kapoor's late 1970s and early 1980s, in which the romance is organised as a contest between two friends rather than between the couple and the world. Those films give him his highest mutuality scores and his lowest external-opposition scores, which makes them the exception in a filmography where the obstacle almost always comes from outside the pair. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Satish Bhatnagar
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tawaif (1985).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Tawaif (1985), B. R. Chopra's drama, in which Kapoor plays Dawood, forced at knifepoint to shelter a courtesan for a night and waking to find the neighbourhood has decided she is his wife.
biography: Satish Bhatnagar is credited as a writer on Tawaif (1985) and has no documented biography. The film is among the more interesting of Kapoor's mid-1980s leads and one of the few that complicates his romantic persona: Dawood resents Sultana, is courting another woman, and comes to see her worth only slowly, which inverts the instant devotion of his 1970s roles. It is a B. R. Chopra production, made in the social-problem register that studio favoured, and it gives the woman the moral initiative. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Saumya Joshi
industry: Gujarati theatre and literature; Hindi cinema
career_background: Saumya Joshi is an Indian poet, playwright, director and actor working in Gujarati literature, theatre and film. Born in Ahmedabad in 1973, he taught English literature at H. K. Arts College from 1995, founded the Fade-In Theatre in 2010 and left teaching in 2011 to work in theatre full-time.
debut: Gujarati poetry from his late teens; his plays include Welcome Zindagi and 102 Not Out.
major_works: With Kapoor: 102 Not Out (2018), adapted from his own play. Elsewhere, the poetry collection Greenroomma (2008) and his Gujarati plays.
recurring_themes: Ageing, obstinacy and family obligation treated as comedy; everyday Gujarati speech on stage.
creative_style: A playwright's structure carried into film: two or three characters, one location and an argument that runs the length of the piece.
major_awards: Chandravadan Chimanlal Mehta Award (2013), Yuva Gaurav Puraskar (2007) and Takhtasinh Parmar Prize (2008-09).
historical_importance: One of the significant contemporary Gujarati playwrights, and the author of the source play for one of the most successful Hindi films about old age.
relationship_with_actor: One film: 102 Not Out (2018), based on his Gujarati play, in which Kapoor plays Babulal, a man of seventy-five convinced he is too old and frail for anything, opposed by his 102-year-old father who intends to break a longevity record. It was Kapoor's last completed leading role and his last film with Amitabh Bachchan.
biography: Saumya Joshi wrote the play 102 Not Out and its screenplay, giving Rishi Kapoor his final completed lead. Born in Ahmedabad in 1973, Joshi taught English literature for sixteen years while building a reputation in Gujarati theatre with Welcome Zindagi and 102 Not Out, published the poetry collection Greenroomma in 2008 and won the Chandravadan Chimanlal Mehta Award in 2013. The play's premise is a father declaring his son too dull to live with, and the film keeps its two-hander shape. Casting Bachchan and Kapoor as father and son is only possible because of their shared history: they had played contemporaries and rivals since Kabhi Kabhie in 1976, and the eleven years between them is doing none of the work. Kapoor plays old age as physical caution, which is the opposite of the role he had been playing since Agneepath.

name: Seeroo Daryani
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Laila Majnu (1976).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Laila Majnu (1976), H. S. Rawail's version of the romance, in which Kapoor plays Qais, who loves Laila from childhood with a bond so literal that a blow to one draws blood from the other, kills her brother in revenge for his father, is exiled and goes mad in the desert.
biography: Seeroo Daryani is credited as a producer on Laila Majnu (1976) and has no documented biography. The film is one of the most consequential in this workbook: in his second year as a lead, it established that Kapoor could carry absolute, self-destroying love, and it fixed the tragic end of the range his comedies would otherwise have defined. The pairing with Ranjeeta was repeated, the songs became standards, and the structure, love declared as fact and destroyed entirely from outside, became the template for Yeh Vaada Raha and Deedar-E-Yaar. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Shafi Inamdar
career_background: Shafi Inamdar was an Indian actor who also directed. Educated in Ratnagiri and Mumbai, with a B.Sc. from K. C. College in 1963, he began in films with Vijeta and became a household name on television in Yeh Jo Hai Zindagi, playing, in his own description, the common man.
debut: Film debut in Vijeta; television fame with Yeh Jo Hai Zindagi in the 1980s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Hum Dono (1995), as director. Elsewhere, as an actor, Ardh Satya, Aaj Ki Awaz, Awam, Nazrana and Love 86.
recurring_themes: Middle-class domestic comedy on television; police and villain roles on film.
creative_style: An actor's director, with a background in serial television rather than in film-school technique.
historical_importance: A major television presence of the 1980s whose film direction is a footnote to his acting career.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Hum Dono (1995), which he directed, in which Kapoor plays Raju, the step-brother whose consent a will requires, forcing the man who despises him to work with him. Inamdar died the following year, aged fifty.
biography: Shafi Inamdar directed Hum Dono, one of his few credits behind the camera and one of Rishi Kapoor's last films as a co-lead. Born in 1945 and educated in Mumbai, Inamdar built his career as an actor, from Vijeta and Ardh Satya to villain and police parts in Awam and Aaj Ki Awaz, but became genuinely famous on television in Yeh Jo Hai Zindagi, whose Friday-night broadcast was said to affect cinema business. He was married to the actress Bhakti Barve and died of a heart attack in March 1996, a year after this film. Hum Dono casts Kapoor as the lower-class step-brother in an inheritance plot opposite Nana Patekar, and belongs to the mid-1990s stretch when his leads were becoming co-leads and the romance in them secondary to the mechanics of the plot.

name: Shakeel Noorani
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Shreemaan Aashique (1993).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Shreemaan Aashique (1993), Deepak Anand's romantic comedy, in which Kapoor plays Dushyant, who has promised his uncle's association of confirmed bachelors that he will never marry and is pursued by Shakuntala until he gives in.
biography: Shakeel Noorani is credited as a producer on Shreemaan Aashique (1993) and has no documented biography. The film is late evidence of a pattern unusual in this filmography and strongest in the 1990s: the woman does the pursuing. Kapoor's character refuses marriage on principle and Urmila Matondkar's heroine persists until he relents, which produces high female-agency and mutuality scores in a film of no critical standing. At forty-one he was still being cast as the reluctant object of a young woman's courtship, two years before the leads stopped coming. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Shakun Batra
career_background: Shakun Batra is an Indian filmmaker, writer and occasional actor. He entered the industry as a bit-part actor in Don: The Chase Begins Again (2006) and worked as an assistant director on Jaane Tu... Ya Jaane Na and Rock On!! before writing and directing his own films.
debut: Writing and directing debut with the romantic comedy Ek Main Aur Ekk Tu (2012).
major_works: With Kapoor: Kapoor & Sons (2016). Elsewhere, Ek Main Aur Ekk Tu (2012) and Gehraiyaan (2022).
recurring_themes: Families that cannot speak honestly to each other; affection and resentment held in the same scene.
creative_style: Overlapping dialogue, handheld camera and performances kept below the pitch of conventional Hindi melodrama; a Dharma Productions director working against the studio's house style.
major_awards: Critical recognition for Kapoor & Sons; the New York Times noted the restraint of his debut.
historical_importance: One of the directors who moved the mainstream Hindi family film away from declamation and towards naturalism in the 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kapoor & Sons (2016), in which Kapoor plays Amarjeet Kapoor, the ninety-year-old whose heart attack brings his estranged grandsons home and whose stated last wish, a family photograph captioned Kapoor and Sons since 1921, the film keeps failing to achieve. It is the best-reviewed performance of his late career and required four hours of prosthetic make-up a day.
biography: Shakun Batra directed Kapoor & Sons, which produced the finest performance of Rishi Kapoor's last decade. Born in 1983, Batra appeared in Don: The Chase Begins Again, assisted on Jaane Tu...
