Ya Jaane Na and Rock On!!, and made his writing and directing debut with Ek Main Aur Ekk Tu in 2012 before this film and Gehraiyaan. His method, overlapping talk and performances pitched well below melodrama, let Kapoor play a ninety-year-old as an appetite rather than a monument: lecherous, manipulative, funny, the only member of the family honest about what he wants. He wore prosthetics for four hours each shooting day at sixty-three. For a filmography built on romantic leads, the critical peak of the career arrives in a part with no romance in it at all, which is the sharpest single fact in this workbook.

name: Shamir Tandon
career_background: Shamir Tandon is an Indian music composer and director. Raised in a Mumbai middle-class family and orphaned early, he qualified in cost accountancy and took an MBA from Narsee Monjee, then worked as a merchant banker with Kotak Mahindra and Birla Global and as a marketing manager at Virgin EMI before composing.
debut: His debut as a music director was Stumped (2003).
major_works: With Kapoor: The Body (2019). Elsewhere, Page 3, Corporate, Traffic Signal, Mission Istaanbul and Inkaar.
recurring_themes: Urban subject films and thrillers; songs for Madhur Bhandarkar's city dramas.
creative_style: A composer from the music-business side of the industry, writing to brief; he has recorded Lata Mangeshkar, Asha Bhosle, Jagjit Singh and Manna Dey.
historical_importance: Associated with the 2000s cycle of Hindi films about urban professional life.
relationship_with_actor: One film: The Body (2019), Jeethu Joseph's thriller, in which Kapoor plays SP Jairaj Rawal, investigating the disappearance of a businesswoman's corpse from the morgue and confining her husband there until it is found. It was released in December 2019, four months before Kapoor's death.
biography: Shamir Tandon composed the songs for The Body, one of the last two films Rishi Kapoor completed. Tandon came to music from business: cost accountancy, an MBA, merchant banking at Kotak Mahindra and Birla Global, then marketing at Virgin EMI, before debuting as a composer with Stumped in 2003 and finding his place in Madhur Bhandarkar's urban dramas, Page 3, Corporate and Traffic Signal. The Body is a remake of a Spanish thriller, and it hands Kapoor the investigating officer, a part built on patience and insinuation rather than authority. It failed, as several of his last films did, but it belongs to a run of final leads in which he is the one driving the plot, which was not true of the supporting fathers he played a decade earlier.

name: Shantketan Entertainments
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), Smeep Kang's comedy, in which Kapoor plays Yograj Singh, a widowed farmer whose son avoids both work and the farm.
biography: Shantketan Entertainments is credited on Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019) and has no documented history. The film is one of three releases Kapoor had in 2018 and 2019 after returning from a year of cancer treatment in New York, and the weakest of them. It is a Punjabi-comedy remake carrying a long list of small production entities, none of them documented, which is itself characteristic: his final years mixed well-financed studio work such as 102 Not Out with films assembled from many minor investors. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Shashi Kapoor
industry: Hindi cinema; English-language Indian and British co-productions
career_background: Shashi Kapoor, born Balbir Raj Kapoor, was an Indian actor and producer and the youngest son of Prithviraj Kapoor. He began as a child actor in Raj Kapoor's Aag (1948), had his first adult role in Dharmputra (1961) and established himself in 1965 with Waqt and Jab Jab Phool Khile. Through the 1970s and early 1980s he was among the industry's most saleable stars, and he used that position to finance Film-Valas, producing art-cinema titles including Junoon, Kalyug, 36 Chowringhee Lane, Vijeta and Utsav.
debut: Child actor in Aag (1948); adult debut in Dharmputra (1961); breakthrough with Waqt and Jab Jab Phool Khile (1965).
major_works: With Kapoor: Ajooba (1991), which he directed and produced. Elsewhere, as an actor, Deewaar, Kabhi Kabhie, Trishul, Kaala Patthar, Namak Halaal and Shakespeare-Wallah; as a producer, Junoon and 36 Chowringhee Lane.
recurring_themes: As a producer, the literary and historical subject; as an actor, the urbane counterweight to Amitabh Bachchan's anger.
creative_style: Ajooba, his only film as director, is a large-scale Indo-Soviet fantasy, remote from the restrained parallel cinema he had been financing.
major_awards: Four National Film Awards and two Filmfare Awards; the Padma Bhushan in 2011 and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 2014.
historical_importance: One of the most important Hindi actors of his generation and, through Film-Valas, one of the few stars to put commercial earnings into art cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ajooba (1991), which he directed and produced, and in which his nephew plays Hassan, friend and accomplice to Amitabh Bachchan's masked rider. The two were uncle and nephew within the Kapoor family and had acted together before, notably in Kabhi Kabhie (1976); here the relationship is director and supporting actor on an expensive Indo-Soviet production that failed badly and ended Shashi Kapoor's directing career.
biography: Shashi Kapoor directed and produced Ajooba, the only film in which he directed his nephew. The youngest son of Prithviraj Kapoor, he debuted as a child in Aag in 1948, became a star with Waqt and Jab Jab Phool Khile in 1965 and spent the 1970s as the urbane half of the industry's most successful pairing, with Amitabh Bachchan, in Deewaar, Kabhi Kabhie, Trishul and Namak Halaal. He put those earnings into Film-Valas, financing Junoon, Kalyug, 36 Chowringhee Lane and Utsav, which makes Ajooba a strange final act: an Indo-Soviet fantasy adventure with a huge budget, co-directed with Gennady Vasilyev, that failed and closed his career behind the camera. Rishi Kapoor plays the hero's companion, a role of no consequence. The family connection is the point of the credit: the workbook's subject appears here inside his uncle's most expensive miscalculation.

career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography. No Wikipedia article for him could be located, so nothing about his wider career can be recorded here.

recurring_themes: Not documented.

biography: Shashi Ranjan is credited as a producer on Wedding Pullav (2015) and has no locatable Wikipedia article. The film launched two newcomers and used Kapoor's name for recognition, billing him first for a part of a few minutes. The practice was common in his last decade and makes the Films sheet's role-type column necessary: eight entries from 2008 onwards are cameos or self appearances that the posters presented as leading roles, and distinguishing them is the only way the workbook's counts of lead and supporting work mean anything. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Shibani Bathija
career_background: Shibani Bathija is an Indian screenwriter. She read English at DePauw University and studied communications at San Francisco State, worked in advertising with Sony, and entered films after showing a script to Karan Johar which Yash Raj Films accepted.
debut: Her first produced screenplays came through Karan Johar and Yash Raj Films in the mid-2000s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Fanaa (2006). Elsewhere, Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna (2006), Kidnap (2008) and My Name Is Khan (2010).
recurring_themes: Large emotional reversals inside family and marriage; romance crossed with national and religious conflict.
creative_style: Writes for scale and for the star's turning point, in the Dharma and Yash Raj register of the 2000s.
major_awards: Filmfare Award nomination for Best Screenplay for Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna, shared with Karan Johar.
historical_importance: One of the few women writing top-tier Hindi commercial screenplays in the 2000s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Fanaa (2006), Kunal Kohli's romantic thriller, in which Kapoor plays Zulfikar Ali Beg, Zooni's father, who lets his blind daughter travel to Delhi to dance at a Republic Day ceremony and years later nurses the wounded stranger she brings home, presiding over a marriage without knowing who the man is.
biography: Shibani Bathija wrote Fanaa, the second of Rishi Kapoor's four films with Kunal Kohli. She came to screenwriting from DePauw University, San Francisco State and advertising at Sony, broke in by handing a script to Karan Johar, and wrote Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna, for which she and Johar were nominated for the Filmfare screenplay award, then Kidnap and My Name Is Khan. Fanaa gave Kapoor the Kashmiri father, a part that is pure structure: he grants his daughter the freedom that sets the plot moving and later shelters the terrorist she has married. It is one of the Yash Raj supporting roles, with Hum Tum and Namastey London, that kept him employed respectably through the 2000s while the better late parts were still some years off.

name: Shoba Chandrasekhar
career_background: Shoba Chandrasekhar is an Indian playback singer, screenwriter, producer and director. She sang in light-music troupes before films, her first film song coming from Iru Malargal, and went on to write stories for more than fifty films, produce ten and direct two, Nanbargal and Innisai Mazhai. She married the director S. A. Chandrasekhar in 1973; their son is the actor and politician Vijay.
debut: Playback singing from Iru Malargal; screenwriting for her husband's films from the 1970s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990). Elsewhere, stories for a long run of Tamil films starring Vijayakanth and Vijay.
recurring_themes: Social-issue melodrama written for vigilante heroes.
creative_style: A prolific story writer inside a family production unit, working with her husband as director.
historical_importance: One of the most productive women story writers in Tamil commercial cinema, and matriarch of a film and political family.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990), written by her and directed by her husband, in which Kapoor plays Vijay, the law student who helps his classmate Bharti expose her father's trafficking of children and women.
biography: Shoba Chandrasekhar wrote Azaad Desh Ke Gulam, the Hindi film her husband S. A. Chandrasekhar directed with Rishi Kapoor in 1990. Born in 1948, she began as a light-music and playback singer, married Chandrasekhar in 1973, and became one of Tamil cinema's most prolific story writers, with credits on more than fifty films, ten as producer and two as director; their son Vijay is now chief minister of Tamil Nadu. Her usual material is the vigilante social-issue film, and this one follows the pattern, with a heroine who discovers her father's crimes and a hero who assists her investigation. The result is anomalous in this filmography: Kapoor supports a woman's plot rather than courting her, and the film records the highest female-agency reading of his 1990 work.

name: Shobha Kapoor
career_background: Shobha Kapoor is an Indian television, film and web-series producer and the managing director of Balaji Telefilms, which she runs with her daughter Ekta Kapoor. She worked as an air hostess before marriage, is married to the actor Jeetendra, and handles administration and production across the Balaji group.
debut: Balaji Telefilms from the 1990s; Balaji Motion Pictures followed in film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kucch To Hai (2003). Elsewhere, the Balaji television slate and the Balaji Motion Pictures film list.
recurring_themes: Serial melodrama and genre film aimed at the broadest domestic audience.
creative_style: An industrial producer of volume content, with her daughter supplying the creative direction.
historical_importance: Co-builder of the company that dominated Indian television drama from the late 1990s and then moved into film.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kucch To Hai (2003), in which Kapoor plays Professor Bakshi, returning to a college under the rumour that he murdered his wife and hid her body; students who break into his house find a corpse, are chased, and knock him off a cliff.
biography: Shobha Kapoor produced Kucch To Hai, made at the lowest ebb of Rishi Kapoor's career. Born in 1949 and married to Jeetendra, she built Balaji Telefilms with her daughter Ekta into the company that defined Indian television drama from the late 1990s, then extended it into film through Balaji Motion Pictures, where she manages production and administration. Kucch To Hai is a teen horror film in which Kapoor plays a professor suspected of murdering his wife, and it is the kind of work available to him between 1999 and 2004: genre pictures in which an older star supplies a red herring. Five years later the same industrial shift that built Balaji, corporate and studio financing, produced the ensemble films that gave him real parts again.

biography: Shree Shivbhakti Films is credited on Daraar (1996) and has no documented history. The film is Kapoor's last romantic lead of consequence and an unusual one: the threat to the couple is a violent husband, played by Arbaaz Khan, and Kapoor is the decent second man rather than the pursuer. By 1996 he was forty-four and the structure of his romances had changed completely from the courtship comedies of the 1970s; within three years the leads stopped. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

The film carries an unusually long writing and composing credit list for a modest comedy, which is how several of Kapoor's last productions were assembled. Its interest in this workbook is chronological rather than artistic: released in July 2019, it is the second-last film to reach cinemas in his lifetime, and the part, an exasperated father in a village comedy, is the register his final decade settled into. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

biography: Shyam Bajaj is credited as a producer on All Is Well (2015) and has no documented biography. The film was the first of two Umesh Shukla made with Kapoor and much the weaker; three years later the same director gave him 102 Not Out. Both films are about a father and a son who cannot speak to each other, and the pairing shows how narrow the margin was between a late Kapoor film that worked and one that did not. The material was the same; the execution was not. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Shyam Goel
career_background: Shyam K. Goel is an Indian screenwriter. His Wikipedia article is a short stub recording only his nomination for Best Story for Aitraaz at the 2005 IIFA awards.
debut: Not documented.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009). Elsewhere, Aitraaz (2004).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
major_awards: IIFA nomination for Best Story for Aitraaz, 2005.
historical_importance: Not independently documented beyond the Aitraaz nomination.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009), Vivek Sharma's science-fiction film, in which Kapoor plays Professor Siddharth Verma, the warden charmed by a gifted new student and revealed at the close to be the man behind the bombings the student has been trying to prevent.
biography: Shyam Goel is credited as a writer on Kal Kissne Dekha (2009), with a Wikipedia stub that records nothing but an IIFA story nomination for Aitraaz. The film is worth noting for one reason: it is the first antagonist role in this filmography, three years before Agneepath. Kapoor plays a benevolent college warden who turns out to be the bomber, which uses his likeability as misdirection in exactly the way the better villain parts would later. The film was dismissed and the performance went unnoticed, so the reinvention is usually dated to 2012; on the evidence of the Films sheet it begins here. This row is otherwise built from the film's credits.

name: Shyam-Surender

biography: Shyam-Surender are credited with the background score of Saajan Ka Ghar (1994) and have no locatable article. The film belongs to the mid-1990s group in which Kapoor plays husbands rather than lovers, and in which the plot turns on a secret he keeps for the woman's good. That device, concealment as devotion, recurs across the period and produces the workbook's lowest mutuality scores alongside high relationship-health readings, because the films present the deception as care. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Siddharth Anand
career_background: Siddharth Anand is an Indian filmmaker, grandson of the screenwriter Inder Raj Anand and son of Bittu Anand, who produced Shahenshah. He assisted Kunal Kohli on Mujhse Dosti Karoge and was promoted to associate on Hum Tum, where he was also executive producer and co-wrote the screenplay, before directing his own films.
debut: Directorial debut with Salaam Namaste (2005) for Yash Raj Films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Hum Tum (2004), as co-writer. Elsewhere, Salaam Namaste, Ta Ra Rum Pum, Bachna Ae Haseeno, Anjaana Anjaani, Bang Bang!, War and Pathaan.
recurring_themes: Urban romantic comedy in the 2000s, then large-scale action from the mid-2010s.
creative_style: A commercial technician who moved from Yash Raj's romantic register to the action spectacle that replaced it.
historical_importance: Director of two of the highest-grossing Hindi films ever made, War and Pathaan, and a central figure in the industry's turn to action franchises.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Hum Tum (2004), which he co-wrote with Kunal Kohli, and in which Kapoor plays Arjun Kapoor, father to Saif Ali Khan's Karan, appearing in the family scenes that punctuate a romance conducted over nine years and four cities.
biography: Siddharth Anand co-wrote Hum Tum, which began Rishi Kapoor's run of Yash Raj supporting roles. The grandson of the screenwriter Inder Raj Anand, he assisted Kunal Kohli on Mujhse Dosti Karoge, then served as associate, executive producer and co-writer on Hum Tum, and made his own debut with Salaam Namaste the following year; he has since directed Bang Bang!, War and Pathaan, two of the largest commercial successes in Hindi cinema. Hum Tum is a small part, the father in the domestic interludes of a nine-year romance, but it is the first of four films Kohli made with Kapoor and it put him inside the studio that would employ him repeatedly through the decade. Saif Ali Khan, his on-screen son here, would produce Love Aaj Kal five years later with Kapoor again in the older role.

name: Sidhant Madhav
career_background: A song composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), Smeep Kang's village comedy, in which Kapoor plays the widowed father Yograj Singh.
biography: Sidhant Madhav is credited with a song on Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019) and has no documented biography. He is one of four separately credited composers on the film, a division of labour that became normal in Hindi cinema after the single-composer convention broke down in the 2000s. In Kapoor's own career the contrast is stark: his 1970s films were scored almost entirely by R. D. Burman and Laxmikant-Pyarelal, each supplying a complete soundtrack, while his last films distribute three or four songs among as many composers. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Simaab Sen
career_background: A background-score composer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.

recurring_themes: Not documented.

biography: Simaab Sen composed the background score for Kaanchi: The Unbreakable (2014) and has no documented biography. The film was Subhash Ghai's last as director and a failure, and Kapoor's part is one of the second-tier antagonists that followed Agneepath. The 2012 to 2014 run, Agneepath, Aurangzeb, D-Day, Besharam and this film, shows the villain phase being worked hard by producers after the first success, with diminishing returns; what survives from it is Rauf Lala and Goldman. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Sippy Films
career_background: The production banner of the Sippy family, credited on one film in this filmography. No separate Wikipedia article for the banner was located; its principals, G. P. Sippy and Ramesh Sippy, are documented individually.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saagar (1985).
recurring_themes: Large-scale commercial production; the banner is best known for Sholay (1975).
creative_style: Not documented as a banner.
historical_importance: One of the most important production houses of 1970s Hindi cinema through Sholay, though this credit is not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Saagar (1985), Ramesh Sippy's musical romantic drama, in which Kapoor plays Ravi, returning from America to Goa and falling in love with Mona, not knowing that his friend Raja has loved her silently for years, with his grandmother opposing the match on grounds of class.
biography: Sippy Films produced Saagar, one of the better-regarded films of Rishi Kapoor's mid-1980s. The banner is the Sippy family's, known above all for Sholay, and Saagar was Ramesh Sippy's return to romance after Shakti. The film reunited Kapoor with Dimple Kapadia and gave Kamal Haasan the silently devoted friend, which makes it a triangle in which Kapoor's character is the one who wins without suffering. R. D. Burman's score is among his late best, and Kapoor's own performance drew good notices in a year when most of his films did not. This row is otherwise built from the film's credits, since no documented history of the banner itself could be located.

name: Smeep Kang
career_background: Smeep Kang is an Indian director, producer and actor working chiefly in Punjabi cinema. He graduated in chemical engineering from Punjab University and became one of the most commercially successful Punjabi comedy directors of the 2010s.
debut: Meri Vahuti Da Viyah (2007) and Chak De Phatte (2008); his breakthrough was Carry On Jatta (2012).
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019). Elsewhere, Carry On Jatta (2012), Lucky Di Unlucky Story (2013), Bhaji in Problem and Vaisakhi List (2016).
recurring_themes: Farce built on lies that multiply; family and marriage comedy in Punjabi settings.
creative_style: Broad ensemble comedy with rapid plotting, adapted from and into the Punjabi industry's house style.
historical_importance: A leading figure in the commercial revival of Punjabi cinema in the 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), which he directed, in which Kapoor plays Yograj Singh, a widowed father whose son has no job ten months after finishing his studies and no intention of helping with the farm.
biography: Smeep Kang directed Jhootha Kahin Ka, the second-last film released in Rishi Kapoor's lifetime. A chemical engineering graduate from Punjab University, Kang became the most reliable comedy director in Punjabi cinema with Chak De Phatte, Carry On Jatta and Lucky Di Unlucky Story, and brought that farce structure into Hindi here. The film is a remake and was poorly received. Its place in the filmography is as evidence of how Kapoor worked after returning from cancer treatment in 2018: he took what came, across registers and budgets, and three of his last four releases were modest comedies in which he plays an exasperated patriarch. The exception, The Body, came six months later.

The film is one of eight in this workbook whose romance is recorded as major but which has no Romances row, because its article supplies a cast list, a soundtrack and nothing about the relationship. It also marks an age gap that had become standard by then: Kapoor was forty-one and Manisha Koirala twenty-three, and the fairy-tale framing does the work of making the pairing legible. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

biography: Sonu Film International is credited on Dhartiputra (1993) and has no documented history. The film is one of the cameos scattered through Kapoor's early 1990s, when he was still taking leads but also lending his name to films that needed a known face for a reel. Those appearances are easy to miscount as supporting roles, and the Films sheet separates them: across 1985 to 1993 he made six such appearances, including three as himself, alongside more than twenty leads. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

The film is one of the multi-star ensembles that absorbed Kapoor through the mid-1980s, when his name alone no longer opened a film and producers combined three or four leads. His part is the lawyer, with the romance reduced to a subplot involving a pickpocket, and the role type in the Films sheet is ensemble lead rather than lead. The shift is measurable across the decade: romance centrality falls while his film count stays high. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

The film is one of two English-language pictures Kapoor made that year, both written and directed by his first cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor, and the pair are the least documented entries in this workbook: no reviews of substance, no commercial figures, and production entities with no record at all. They sit in the same year as Namastey London, which is to say that a Yash Raj supporting role and an undistributed British-Indian film were running in parallel. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

Kapoor's appearance is an extended musical special appearance rather than a role, in a film starring his elder brother Randhir, and it is one of the clearest examples of the credit type the Films sheet has to separate out. In the same year he carried Pyar Ke Kabil as a lead and appeared briefly in Sindoor as a singer whose partnership with the heroine causes her husband to throw her out. Three very different kinds of work in one year, all nominally billed as Rishi Kapoor films. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Subhash Kapoor

The film is a Randhir Kapoor vehicle in which Rishi Kapoor appears for a song, and it is one of three 1987 credits of entirely different weight. Treasure-hunt adventures of this kind were cheap to assemble around a cast of established names, and the guest appearance was the standard currency. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

The film is one of Mahesh Bhatt's earliest as a director, made when Kapoor was four years into his career as a lead, and it is one of the workbook's documentation gaps: romance recorded as major, no Romances row possible, because no account of the relationship survives in reference sources. 1978 was his busiest year to that point, with six releases, and the lesser ones are precisely those about which least is now recoverable. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Do Premee (1980), Raj Khosla's romance, in which Kapoor plays Chetan, who elopes with Payal after both their fathers refuse the match and is reduced to working as a driver while she works as a maid.
biography: Sudesh Issar is credited as a producer on Do Premee (1980) and has no biography of his own; the single Wikipedia reference to him is as co-director, with Suresh Issar, of Farebi in 1974. Do Premee is a pure statement of the dominant structure in this filmography: the lovers agree, both families refuse, the couple elope and are punished economically rather than emotionally. External opposition carries the entire plot and friction between the pair is almost nil, which is the pattern that separates Kapoor's romances from the quarrelling couples of his contemporaries' films.

name: Sudesh Kumar
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The documented Sudesh Kumar is an Indian Olympic wrestler and a different person.
major_works: With Kapoor: Badaltey Rishtey (1978).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Badaltey Rishtey (1978), in which Kapoor plays Manohar, who falls for the music teacher Savitri at first meeting and courts her by pretending to sell eggs at her door; she is then married off to a wealthy man under a prediction that her husband will die within forty days.
biography: Sudesh Kumar is credited as a producer on Badaltey Rishtey (1978) and has no documented biography; the Wikipedia Sudesh Kumar is an Olympic wrestler and unrelated. The film is a good example of the courtship Kapoor was built for in the late 1970s: the man invents a daily pretext to appear at the woman's door, the audience is invited to find the persistence charming, and the obstacle arrives from outside as prophecy and family calculation. Read now, the same courtship registers as pleasant rather than coercive mainly because the film grants the woman her own interest in him.

name: Sudhanshu Dube
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009), in which Kapoor plays Professor Siddharth Verma, the college warden revealed at the end to be the man behind the bombings the hero has been trying to prevent.
biography: Sudhanshu Dube is credited as a writer on Kal Kissne Dekha (2009) and has no documented biography. The film is the earliest antagonist role in this filmography and therefore more interesting than its reputation suggests: Kapoor plays an avuncular warden whose warmth is the disguise, three years before Agneepath made that trick famous. In the same year he appeared in Luck by Chance, Delhi-6 and Love Aaj Kal, so 2009 contains both halves of his late career, the respectable character parts and the genre work nobody watched. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Sudhir Mishra
career_background: The credit on this film is to a Sudhir Mishra; the documented filmmaker of that name, born in Lucknow in 1959, is a director and screenwriter whose association with this comedy is not confirmed, so the identification is uncertain. He came from a family of academics and politicians, apprenticed with Badal Sircar, and began as an assistant on Jaane Bhi Do Yaaron (1983).
debut: Assistant and co-writer on Jaane Bhi Do Yaaron (1983); directorial debut Yeh Woh Manzil To Nahin (1987), which won a National Film Award.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), if the identification holds. Elsewhere, Dharavi (1992), Hazaaron Khwaishein Aisi (2003), Chameli (2004) and Serious Men (2020).
recurring_themes: Political disillusion, the compromises of the urban middle class, and the afterlife of the 1970s.
creative_style: Realist, politically engaged filmmaking in a register remote from the family comedy credited here.
major_awards: Three national awards and the French Order of Arts and Letters.
historical_importance: One of the significant political filmmakers of post-1980s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film by the credits: Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001), Rahul Rawail's comedy in which Kapoor plays Raj Khanna, a father separated from his wife by a lie and raising one of their twin daughters alone. Given the gap between that film and the documented Mishra's work, the credit may belong to another writer of the same name.
biography: A Sudhir Mishra is credited as a writer on Kuch Khatti Kuch Meethi (2001). The documented filmmaker of that name, born in Lucknow in 1959 into a family that produced a vice-chancellor of Banaras Hindu University and a chief minister of Madhya Pradesh, apprenticed under Badal Sircar, assisted and co-wrote Jaane Bhi Do Yaaron, and directed Dharavi, Hazaaron Khwaishein Aisi, Chameli and Serious Men, winning three national awards and the French Order of Arts and Letters. That body of work has nothing in common with a Parent Trap remake, so this row flags the identification as unresolved rather than asserting it. The film itself is one of the undistinguished family comedies that filled the years between Kapoor's leading career and his revival after 2008.

name: Sujit Kumar
career_background: Sujit Kumar was an Indian actor and producer who appeared in more than 150 Hindi films from the 1960s to the 1990s and in at least twenty Bhojpuri films, in which he was often the lead. In Hindi cinema he played villains and character parts; from the late 1980s he worked mainly as a producer.
debut: Acting from the 1960s; his best-remembered appearance is in Aradhana (1969), playing the mouth organ in the jeep while Rajesh Khanna serenades Sharmila Tagore.
major_works: With Kapoor: Daraar (1996), as producer. Elsewhere, a long acting career in Hindi and Bhojpuri films and production work from the late 1980s.
recurring_themes: Commercial Hindi and Bhojpuri cinema; thrillers as a producer.
creative_style: An actor-turned-producer working within established commercial formulas.
historical_importance: A major figure in early Bhojpuri cinema and a long-serving Hindi character actor.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Daraar (1996), Abbas-Mustan's thriller, which he produced, and in which Kapoor plays Raj, who falls in love with a woman hiding from a violent husband. The Kapoor family attended Kumar's condolence meeting in 2010.
biography: Sujit Kumar produced Daraar, Rishi Kapoor's last substantial romantic lead. Born in 1934, Kumar appeared in more than 150 Hindi films and at least twenty Bhojpuri ones, leading in the latter and playing villains and character roles in the former; he is best remembered on screen for the mouth organ in Aradhana. From the late 1980s he produced, and Daraar was among his successes, an Abbas-Mustan thriller in which the obstacle to the romance is Arbaaz Khan's violent husband rather than a disapproving family. Kapoor was forty-four and, in this configuration, no longer the pursuer but the decent alternative. Kumar died of cancer in 2010; members of the Kapoor family were at his condolence meeting.

name: Sukhwant Dhadda
career_background: A director credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986), in which Kapoor plays Mangal, the one member of the household who shields his sister-in-law Rano from her drunken husband, and who is compelled by custom to marry her when the husband is murdered, though he is ten years her junior and until then her protector.
biography: Sukhwant Dhadda directed Ek Chadar Maili Si (1986) and has no documented biography. The film, adapted from Rajinder Singh Bedi's novel, gives Kapoor the most unusual relationship in this filmography: a marriage he does not want, to a woman he has protected as a brother would, imposed by custom after her husband's murder. Nothing in it is courtship, and the pairing with Hema Malini reverses the usual age arrangement of his films, since the character is explicitly the younger party. It is one of very few entries where romance is present, central and entirely without desire. This row is otherwise built from the film's credits.

name: Sumit Arora
industry: Hindi cinema; Indian television and streaming
career_background: Sumit Arora is an Indian writer and screenwriter working in Hindi films, television and web series. He began in television with dialogue for Chhoona Hai Aasmaan and Dill Mill Gayye, then wrote for streaming series and features.
debut: Television dialogue writing, then features from the mid-2010s.
major_works: With Kapoor: All Is Well (2015). Elsewhere, Stree, Ginny Weds Sunny, 83 and Jawan; the series The Family Man, Dahaad and Guns & Gulaabs.
recurring_themes: Comic dialogue in genre settings: horror comedy, crime and sport.
creative_style: A dialogue specialist whose lines are built for performance rhythm; among the most-used writers of the streaming era.
major_awards: Star Screen and Zee Cine awards for Best Dialogue for Stree.
historical_importance: One of the writers whose careers were made by the Indian streaming expansion of the late 2010s.
relationship_with_actor: One film: All Is Well (2015), Umesh Shukla's comedy drama, in which Kapoor plays Bhajanlal Bhalla, a Punjabi baker who throws his son out of the house and is revealed to be ruined by debt, with a wife suffering from Alzheimer's whom he has sent away.
biography: Sumit Arora wrote for All Is Well, early in a career that the streaming boom then accelerated. He began with television dialogue on Chhoona Hai Aasmaan and Dill Mill Gayye, won Star Screen and Zee Cine awards for the dialogue of Stree, and has since written 83, Jawan and the series The Family Man, Dahaad and Guns & Gulaabs. All Is Well failed, but Kapoor's part in it is characteristic of his late work and of the relationship the industry had settled on for him: the difficult father whose severity turns out to be shame. Umesh Shukla would rework the same father-and-son material far more successfully three years later in 102 Not Out, with Kapoor moved from the parent's chair to the child's.

name: Sunir Kheterpal
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: The Body (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: The Body (2019), Jeethu Joseph's thriller, in which Kapoor plays SP Jairaj Rawal, investigating the disappearance of a businesswoman's corpse from the morgue and confining her husband there until it is found.
biography: Sunir Kheterpal is credited as a producer on The Body (2019) and has no documented biography. The film was released in December 2019 and is the last Rishi Kapoor film to reach cinemas in his lifetime; Sharmaji Namkeen followed posthumously in 2022. It is a remake of a Spanish thriller and gives him the investigating officer, a role of patience and insinuation rather than authority, which is the register his last leads worked in. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Sunrise Pictures Pvt. Ltd.
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Halla Bol (2008).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Halla Bol (2008), Rajkumar Santoshi's drama about a street-theatre actor who becomes a superstar and loses himself, in which Kapoor appears as himself, one of several film-industry figures who appear under their own names.
biography: Sunrise Pictures is credited on Halla Bol (2008) and has no documented history. Kapoor's appearance is as himself, the fourth such credit in his filmography after Chala Murari Hero Banne, Ram Tere Kitne Nam and Akarshan. The pattern is worth noting: across thirty years, films about the film industry kept using him as a shorthand for its respectable face, and the appearances are concentrated in productions about stardom and its costs. Santoshi had directed him fifteen years earlier in Damini. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Supratik Sen
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sharmaji Namkeen (2022).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sharmaji Namkeen (2022), Hitesh Bhatia's comedy drama, in which Kapoor plays a man retired at fifty-eight against his will who finds a vocation cooking for kitty parties. It was released two years after his death, with Paresh Rawal completing the unfinished portions of the role.
biography: Supratik Sen is credited as a writer on Sharmaji Namkeen (2022) and has no documented biography. The film is the last entry in this workbook and a singular one: Kapoor died in April 2020 with the shoot incomplete, and Paresh Rawal played the remaining portions of the same character, both performances appearing in the released film. The part itself is a summary of his final decade, a man told he is finished who declines to be, and the only romance in it is implied rather than enacted. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Surani Pictures
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chalk N Duster (2016).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chalk N Duster (2016), Jayant Gilatar's social drama, in which Kapoor appears as the host of the televised quiz that forms the climax, where two dismissed teachers stake their careers against five crore rupees.
biography: Surani Pictures is credited on Chalk N Duster (2016) and has no documented history. The film came in the same year as Kapoor & Sons, and the contrast measures his range of employment at sixty-three: a prosthetic-heavy ensemble lead that drew the best reviews of his career, and a single-sequence quiz-host cameo in an issue film about private schooling. He accepted both, and the Films sheet has to separate them by role type for the workbook's counts to mean anything. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Surendra Bohra
career_background: A director and producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Saajan Ka Ghar (1994), which he directed and produced, in which Kapoor plays an army officer married to Laxmi by the father and stepmother who have mistreated her since birth, and who decides to tell nobody, including her, that another pregnancy would kill her.
biography: Surendra Bohra directed and produced Saajan Ka Ghar (1994) and has no documented biography. The film is a clear case of the mid-1990s pattern in this filmography: the marriage is settled at the start, the wife is the family's victim, and the husband's romantic function is reduced to protective concealment. Kapoor was forty-two, past the courtship roles, and the films of these years consistently score high on romance centrality and low on lover-boy, which is the divergence the workbook's two scales are designed to catch. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Suresh Bhagat
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990), S. A. Chandrasekhar's drama, in which Kapoor plays Vijay, the law student who helps his classmate Bharti expose her wealthy father's trafficking of children and women.
biography: Suresh Bhagat is credited as a producer on Azaad Desh Ke Gulam (1990) and has no documented biography. The film is one of the few in this filmography where Kapoor's character assists a woman's investigation instead of courting her, and it was made by a Tamil director and his screenwriter wife working in Hindi. Its structure gives the heroine the discovery, the documents and the decision, which produces the highest female-agency reading of his 1990 work in an otherwise unremarkable film. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Suresh K Grover
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pyar Ke Kabil (1987).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Pyar Ke Kabil (1987), Anil Ganguly's drama, in which Kapoor plays Amar Kapoor opposite Padmini Kolhapure, with Bindu, Utpal Dutt and Deven Verma in support. The article has no plot section, so the role cannot be described from it.
biography: Suresh K Grover is credited as a producer on Pyar Ke Kabil (1987) and has no documented biography. The film is one of eight in this workbook recorded as having a major romance but no Romances row, because the surviving documentation is an infobox, a cast list and a soundtrack. Padmini Kolhapure was among his more frequent co-stars of the period, after Prem Rog and Yeh Vaada Raha, and the absence of any account of this pairing is characteristic of his late-1980s films rather than exceptional. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Surinder Kapoor
career_background: Surinder Kapoor was an Indian film producer. Born in Peshawar in 1925 into a Punjabi Hindu family raised on Arya Samaj teachings, he left for Meerut after the 1947 partition and was then invited to Bombay by his cousin Prithviraj Kapoor to join the film industry. He founded S. K. International Films and served as president of the Film & Television Producers Guild of India from 1995 to 2001.
debut: His first successful Hindi production was Shehzada (1972), starring Rajesh Khanna.
major_works: With Kapoor: Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan (1978). Elsewhere, Shehzada (1972) and the S. K. International Films slate.
recurring_themes: Star-led commercial production; later, launching his own sons.
creative_style: A proprietor-producer of the old kind, running a family banner on relationships rather than on a studio structure.
historical_importance: Patriarch of the second Kapoor film family: his sons are Boney, Anil and Sanjay Kapoor, and Sridevi was his daughter-in-law.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan (1978), in which Kapoor plays Vishal Rai opposite Moushumi Chatterjee, second-billed to Ashok Kumar, with Mithun Chakraborty among his friends and Amjad Khan and Ranjeet as the antagonists. The two men were distant relatives: Surinder Kapoor was Prithviraj Kapoor's cousin, which makes this a collaboration between the two branches of the industry's Kapoor families.
biography: Surinder Kapoor produced Phool Khile Hain Gulshan Gulshan, the one film in this workbook that connects the two Kapoor dynasties. Born in Peshawar in 1925, he reached Bombay after partition at the invitation of his cousin Prithviraj Kapoor, worked his way up and founded S. K. International Films, whose first substantial success was Shehzada with Rajesh Khanna in 1972; he led the Producers Guild from 1995 to 2001 and died in 2011. His sons Boney, Anil and Sanjay became producers and an actor, and Sridevi, who never worked with Rishi Kapoor as a lead, married Boney. The film itself is minor, a 1978 drama in which Kapoor is billed below Ashok Kumar, but the credit records a family relationship that the industry's two Kapoor lines rarely put on screen together.

name: Surinder Kumar Sharma
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chala Murari Hero Banne (1977).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Chala Murari Hero Banne (1977), Asrani's satire about a cloth merchant's son who runs away to Bombay to become an actor, in which Kapoor appears as himself alongside Neetu Singh, Dharmendra, Hema Malini, Amitabh Bachchan and Ashok Kumar.
biography: Surinder Kumar Sharma is credited as a producer on Chala Murari Hero Banne (1977) and has no documented biography. The film is the first of four in which Kapoor appears as himself, and the earliest evidence that his public persona was established enough by his fourth year as a lead to be used as a cameo. Asrani directed it and cast most of the industry's leading names in walk-ons; Kapoor appears with Neetu Singh, three years before they married. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Surinder Sodhi
career_background: Surender Sodhi, often credited as Surendra Sodhi, is an Indian film score composer. He has worked almost entirely on background music rather than songs, across a long run of commercial Hindi films from the early 1990s onwards.
debut: Background scores from the early 1990s; an early credit on Vijeta (1996) appears under the name Surender Singh.
major_works: With Kapoor: Karobaar (2000). His article also credits him with the background score of Deewana (1992), which is FILM-087 in this filmography. Elsewhere, Raja Hindustani, Soldier, Baadshah, Hera Pheri and Special 26.
recurring_themes: Score for mainstream romance, action and comedy.
creative_style: A specialist background-score composer working alongside separately credited song composers, as became standard in Hindi cinema from the 1990s.
historical_importance: One of the busiest background-score composers of the 1990s and 2000s, a craft credit that reference sources record poorly.
relationship_with_actor: One film by the frozen roster, probably two in fact. Karobaar (2000), Rakesh Roshan's drama, in which Kapoor plays Amar, who marries Seema after his wealthy friend invents a pretext to stop him and later learns the pretext was a device. His own article also credits him with the background score of Deewana (1992), the Shah Rukh Khan debut in which Kapoor plays the first husband who returns; the Films sheet leaves that film's background-score field empty, so the second collaboration is recorded here in prose only.
most_important_collaboration: Deewana (1992), if his article's credit is correct; otherwise Karobaar (2000)
biography: Surinder Sodhi scored Karobaar, and by his own article also Deewana, which would make him a collaborator on one of the most commercially important films in Rishi Kapoor's career. Sodhi has built a long career in background music alone, from the early 1990s through Raja Hindustani, Soldier, Baadshah, Hera Pheri and Special 26, a craft that Hindi film reference sources document far less reliably than song composition. Deewana (1992) is the pivot of Kapoor's middle period: he plays the first husband presumed dead who returns to find his widow remarried to Shah Rukh Khan's character, and the film both succeeded hugely and signalled that the new generation had arrived. The background-score credit for it is missing from this workbook's Films sheet, so the connection is noted rather than counted.

name: Sushma Ahuja
industry: Hindi, English and Tamil cinema; Indian theatre
career_background: Sushma Ahuja is an Indian director, writer and actor who has worked in Hindi, English and Tamil films and plays. She began as a singer with All India Radio and as a dancer in her teens, worked in the Hindi theatre circuit on Hindi, Urdu and Punjabi productions, and moved to Madras in 1977, where she joined the Abhudhay theatre group and was encouraged into film direction by Singeetham Srinivasa Rao and L. V. Prasad. She apprenticed under Balu Mahendra, T. Rama Rao and Yash Chopra.
debut: Theatre and radio first; then film work as actress, writer and director.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pyaar Mein Twist (2005).
recurring_themes: Domestic relationships across generations, written from a theatre background.
creative_style: A writer who came to film through the stage and through apprenticeship rather than the industry's family networks.
historical_importance: Not widely documented; notable as a woman writing and directing across three language industries.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Pyaar Mein Twist (2005), Hriday Shetty's romantic comedy, in which Kapoor plays Yash Khurana, a widower handing his company to an insecure son and beginning an unplanned retirement, who meets Sheetal when he berates her in the street after she nearly runs him down. It is the most important film of his middle period in this workbook's terms: a central romance in which the lovers are in their fifties and the opposition comes from their adult children.
biography: Sushma Ahuja wrote Pyaar Mein Twist, which is the single most analytically interesting film in Rishi Kapoor's later career. Ahuja came to cinema from All India Radio, dance and the Hindi theatre circuit, moved to Madras in 1977, worked with the Abhudhay group and apprenticed under Balu Mahendra, T. Rama Rao and Yash Chopra before writing and directing across Hindi, English and Tamil. Her screenplay reproduces the exact structure of Bobby, the film that made Kapoor a star in 1973, with one substitution: the lovers are a widower and a widow, and the people forbidding the match are their own children rather than their parents. Kapoor plays the courtship straight, with a lover-boy score in the fifties register the 1970s films used, which is why the film anchors this workbook's argument that his romantic persona never actually declined, only changed its obstacles.

name: Sutanu Gupta
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Damini (1993).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Damini (1993), Rajkumar Santoshi's legal drama, in which Kapoor plays Shekhar, who marries Damini across a sharp class divide and then fails her: when she witnesses his younger brother and his friends raping the family's maid, he runs to stop it, arrives too late, and sides with his family's cover-up before changing course.
biography: Sutanu Gupta is credited as a writer on Damini (1993) and has no documented biography. The film is among the most important in this filmography and the most unusual in its treatment of marriage: the husband is weak rather than villainous, and the plot consists of his wife's refusal to accept his family's silence. Kapoor's role is to be insufficient, which no other film of his demands so directly, and the picture belongs to Meenakshi Seshadri and Sunny Deol. It won major awards and stands as the clearest instance of a Kapoor romance examined from the wife's point of view. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Syed Ayub
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sheshnaag (1990).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Sheshnaag (1990), K. R. Reddy's fantasy, in which Kapoor plays Bhola, who rescues a wounded shape-shifting serpent and is repaid for the rest of the film, including by her taking his sister's form after the sister is gambled away.
biography: Syed Ayub is credited as a producer on Sheshnaag (1990) and has no documented biography. The film is Kapoor's only mythological fantasy of this kind, made in the cycle of snake films that followed Nagina, and it pairs him with Rekha in a relationship that is protective and supernatural rather than romantic. It belongs to the 1990 and 1991 run, with Amiri Garibi, Azaad Desh Ke Gulam, Ghar Parivar and Ranbhoomi, in which his leads were absorbed into whatever genre was selling. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: T-Series
career_background: T-Series is the trade name of Super Cassettes Industries Private Limited, an Indian record label and film studio founded by Gulshan Kumar on 11 July 1983, the T standing for the trishula. It is chaired and managed by Bhushan Kumar, with Krishan Kumar and Neeraj Kalyan among its principals, and is the largest music record label in India, known primarily for Hindi film soundtracks.
debut: Founded in 1983 as a cassette label; later a film producer in its own right.
major_works: With Kapoor: All Is Well (2015). Elsewhere, a very large catalogue of Hindi film soundtracks and, from the 2000s, film production.
recurring_themes: Music rights first and film production second: the company's films are built around their soundtracks.
creative_style: An industrial operation in which the label's distribution power drives the production slate.
historical_importance: The dominant force in Indian recorded music for four decades, and one of the companies that changed how Hindi film music is financed, marketed and owned.
relationship_with_actor: One film: All Is Well (2015), Umesh Shukla's comedy drama, in which Kapoor plays Bhajanlal Bhalla, a baker who throws out his son and is revealed to be ruined by debt, with a wife suffering from Alzheimer's whom he has sent to an ashram.
biography: T-Series co-produced All Is Well, one of Rishi Kapoor's late supporting roles. Founded by Gulshan Kumar in July 1983 as Super Cassettes Industries, the label built itself on cheap cassettes and aggressive cover versions, became the largest record company in India, and under Bhushan Kumar moved into film production on the strength of its music rights. The chronology is pointed: T-Series arrived just as Kapoor's leading years were ending, and the soundtrack-driven economics it helped create belonged to the generation of stars who replaced him. His own hits of the 1970s had been built on R. D. Burman and Laxmikant-Pyarelal scores sold through the older gramophone trade. By the time the company produced a film he appeared in, he was the father in a failed comedy.

name: T. R. Subba Rao
career_background: Talukina Ramaswamayya Subba Rao, known as TaRaSu, was an Indian novelist and scholar of Kannada. Born in Chitradurga district in 1920 to a lawyer father, he joined the Indian freedom movement at seventeen, touring villages singing patriotic songs, and became a prolific novelist regarded as a harbinger of the Navya movement in Kannada literature.
debut: His first story, Puttana Chendu, was written to win a bet against his uncle.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zehreela Insaan (1974), adapted from his novel. Elsewhere, Durgashtamana and a large body of Kannada fiction.
recurring_themes: Historical and social Kannada fiction; rural life and the individual against convention.
creative_style: A novelist of social realism and historical reconstruction whose work was adapted repeatedly for Kannada cinema.
major_awards: Sahitya Akademi Award in 1985, posthumously, for Durgashtamana.
historical_importance: One of the significant Kannada novelists of the twentieth century; his autobiography was left unfinished at his death and completed by his wife.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Zehreela Insaan (1974), the Hindi version of Puttanna Kanagal's Kannada film Nagarahavu, adapted from his novel, in which Kapoor plays Arjun, an ill-tempered, soft-hearted young man the village reads as a bad character, obedient only to the schoolmaster who sees his qualities. It was Kapoor's first film after Bobby and his only work with a south Indian art-cinema director.
biography: T. R. Subba Rao wrote the novel behind Zehreela Insaan, the film Rishi Kapoor made immediately after Bobby. Known as TaRaSu, he was born in Chitradurga district in 1920, joined the freedom movement at seventeen, and became one of the most substantial Kannada novelists of his century, winning a posthumous Sahitya Akademi Award in 1985 for Durgashtamana. Puttanna Kanagal had filmed his novel in Kannada as Nagarahavu in 1972 and directed this Hindi version two years later. The result is the only literary adaptation of its kind in the filmography: Arjun loses one woman to a forced marriage and finds a second in his Christian classmate, and the film treats his temper as a social misreading rather than a flaw. It failed commercially, and Kapoor returned to romantic comedy.

biography: TUTU Films is credited on Amiri Garibi (1990) and has no documented history. The film gives Kapoor a supporting part in a Jeetendra vehicle, three years after Malhotra had used him for a musical guest appearance in Khazana. The arrangement is typical of 1990: he was taking leads in minor films and support in larger ones, and the role types in the Films sheet change several times a year through this period. The childhood-marriage premise also recurs, since arranged obligation rather than attraction drives most of his romances of these years. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

biography: TVM International is credited on Karobaar (2000) and has no documented history. The film was shot years before it was released, which is why it reaches cinemas in the same year as Raju Chacha with Kapoor in two quite different registers, a betrayed husband and a distracted father. Delayed releases of this kind cluster at the end of his leading career and complicate the chronology: production year and release year diverge, and the workbook follows theatrical release throughout, with the discrepancies kept in research notes. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

biography: Tanvir Ahmed directed Akarshan (1988) and has no locatable Wikipedia article; the cricketer of that name is unrelated. The film is the third of four in which Kapoor appears as himself, and the pattern they form is consistent: all four are films about the film industry, and all four use him as a recognisable fixture of it rather than as a character. In 1988 he was thirty-six, still leading films such as Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani, and already a figure the industry could cast as its own furniture. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

relationship_with_actor: One film: Sambar Salsa (2007), Aditya Raj Kapoor's English-language film, in which Kapoor plays Om Suri, the father who disapproves of his son's love for a Spanish woman, having himself married in defiance of his own elders.
biography: Thara is credited with the songs of Sambar Salsa (2007) and has no documented biography. The film is one of two English-language pictures Kapoor made that year for his first cousin Aditya Raj Kapoor, and the pair are the least documented entries in this workbook: no reviews of substance, no commercial data, and credits that cannot be traced to any documented person or company. The irony the film itself notes, a father forbidding the cross-cultural marriage he once made himself, is the only thing about it the sources support. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

biography: Tina Films International is credited on Gharana (1989) and has no documented history. The film is a good example of the economic plotting of Kapoor's late-1980s romances: the obstacle is a dowry he cannot pay, and he renounces the woman rather than being parted from her by a villain. Across the whole filmography the opposition is external in this way far more often than it is interpersonal, and in these years it is specifically financial, which is a measurable shift from the family-honour plots of the early 1980s. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

He is the suspected lover rather than an actual one.

Kapoor's part is a cameo with an unusual function: he is the imagined rival, the man whose innocent partnership with the heroine supplies her husband's jealousy. In a filmography where he is almost always the romantic subject, being cast as the suspicion itself is a rarity, and the Films sheet records the film's romance presence as none for him while the plot turns entirely on the appearance of one. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

biography: Tirupati Pictures Enterprises is credited on Deedar-E-Yaar (1982) and has no documented history. The film was an expensive failure and the second of Rawail's two with Kapoor, repeating the Laila Majnu formula of absolute love broken by lineage. 1982 is the year of his widest spread: Prem Rog for his father, Deedar-E-Yaar for Rawail, Yeh Vaada Raha for Kapil Kapoor, and the first of the films in which the romantic hero was already being written as a victim of his family rather than a suitor. This row is built from the film's credits alone.
