biography: Treetop Entertainment is credited on 102 Not Out (2018) and has no documented history. The film is Kapoor's last completed lead and his final appearance with Amitabh Bachchan, a partnership that began with Kabhi Kabhie in 1976 and ran through Amar Akbar Anthony, Naseeb and Ajooba. The two had always played contemporaries; here they play father and son, with Bachchan the parent, and the film's comedy depends on the audience knowing how long they have been on screen together. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Tushar Hiranandani
career_background: Tushar Hiranandani is an Indian screenwriter and director, born in Mumbai in 1975 into a film distribution family: his grandfather Hiranand and father Ashok Hiranandani ran the Black and White distribution company. He began as a clapper boy on Mann (1999), wrote comedies with Milap Zaveri, and is head of content development at Balaji Motion Pictures.
debut: His first film as writer was Masti (2004), directed by Indra Kumar; his directorial debut was Saand Ki Aankh (2019).
major_works: With Kapoor: Housefull 2 (2012). Elsewhere, Masti, Atithi Tum Kab Jaoge?, ABCD, Ek Villain, Main Tera Hero, Dishoom, Half Girlfriend, and as director Saand Ki Aankh, Scam 2003 and Srikanth.
recurring_themes: Broad comedy and multi-star farce as a writer; biographical underdog stories as a director.
creative_style: A franchise writer who moved into directing socially minded biopics, a sharp change of register.
historical_importance: A principal writer of the 2000s and 2010s mainstream comedy cycle.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Housefull 2 (2012), in which Kapoor plays Chintu Kapoor, one of two feuding half-brothers each trying to marry a daughter to money. Hiranandani is one of four credited writing entities on the film.
biography: Tushar Hiranandani co-wrote Housefull 2, Rishi Kapoor's broadest late comedy. Born in Mumbai in 1975 into a distribution family, he started as a clapper boy on Mann, broke through with Masti in 2004 and became one of the most-used comedy writers of his generation, on ABCD, Ek Villain, Main Tera Hero and Half Girlfriend, while heading content development at Balaji Motion Pictures. He later directed Saand Ki Aankh and Srikanth, which have nothing in common with the farces that made him. Housefull 2 required Kapoor to play a cartoon of a patriarch, with Randhir Kapoor among the other fathers, in a film whose plot is a machine for mistaken parentage. He did it in the same year as Agneepath, and the juxtaposition is the most accurate single picture of how he worked after 2008.

name: Twinkle Khanna
career_background: Twinkle Khanna is an Indian author, columnist and former actress, the daughter of the actors Dimple Kapadia and Rajesh Khanna. She acted in Hindi films from 1995 to 2001, then worked as an interior designer and newspaper columnist, published five books from Mrs Funnybones (2015) onwards, founded the digital platform Tweak India in 2019 and took a master's in fiction writing from Goldsmiths. She is married to Akshay Kumar.
debut: Acting debut in Barsaat (1995), which won her the Filmfare Award for Best Female Debut.
major_works: With Kapoor: Patiala House (2011), as producer. Elsewhere, as an actress, Jab Pyaar Kisise Hota Hai, Baadshah and Love Ke Liye Kuch Bhi Karega; as a writer, Mrs Funnybones and Pyjamas Are Forgiving.
recurring_themes: As an author, domestic comedy and women's lives; as a producer, vehicles for her husband.
creative_style: A producer by family arrangement rather than by craft background, whose own reputation now rests on writing.
major_awards: Filmfare Award for Best Female Debut for Barsaat (1995).
historical_importance: Less a film figure than a writer and columnist, and a connecting point between three film families.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Patiala House (2011), which she produced, in which Kapoor plays Gurtej Singh Kahlon, called Bauji, a Southall patriarch who forbade his gifted son from bowling for England and once threatened suicide to stop him. The family link runs deeper than the credit: her mother Dimple Kapadia made her debut opposite Kapoor in Bobby (1973) and returned to play his lover in Saagar (1985), and her father Rajesh Khanna was billed above him in Zamana and Ghar Parivar.
biography: Twinkle Khanna produced Patiala House, in which Rishi Kapoor plays the father who destroyed his son's cricket career. Born in 1973 to Dimple Kapadia and Rajesh Khanna, she won the Filmfare debut award for Barsaat in 1995, left acting in 2001, and built a second career as a columnist and author of five books, founding Tweak India in 2019. The credit sits inside a dense family history: her mother was the sixteen-year-old opposite Kapoor in Bobby, the film that made them both, and returned twelve years later in Saagar; her father spent the mid-1980s billed above him. Here her production company gives him one of the best written parts of his late career, a man whose authority has been exercised as damage, in the same year as the disposable Tell Me O Kkhuda.

name: Ulka Puri
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of her own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011), Hema Malini's film, in which Kapoor plays Altaf Zardari, the second of the men a young woman visits while searching for her biological father, living peacefully in Turkey with a wife who has no memory of losing a child.
biography: Ulka Puri is credited as a writer on Tell Me O Kkhuda (2011) and has no documented biography. The film was Hema Malini's third as director, built around her daughter Esha Deol, and it failed completely. Kapoor's part is one of three candidate fathers, a plot station rather than a character, and it came in the same year as Patiala House, where the patriarch is written with real force. The pairing is a reminder that his late revival supplied better opportunities without displacing the routine ones. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Umesh Kalbagh
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chandni (1989).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and one of the most important in the filmography: Chandni (1989), Yash Chopra's musical romance, in which Kapoor plays Rohit, who courts Chandni until she accepts him, is paralysed down one side after crashing a helicopter while showering her with rose petals, and then releases her as his family turns on her.
biography: Umesh Kalbagh is credited as a writer on Chandni (1989) and has no documented biography, which is a notable gap given the film's standing. Chandni was Yash Chopra's return to romance after a decade of action, revived the Hindi musical romance for the 1990s, and gave Kapoor his last great romantic role at thirty-seven. Its structure is the filmography's signature taken to an extreme: the lovers never quarrel, and everything that happens to them, the accident, the family's cruelty, the separation, comes from outside. The helicopter sequence that cripples Rohit is the literal image of that pattern, courtship itself becoming the catastrophe. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Usha Khanna
career_background: Usha Khanna is an Indian music director in Hindi cinema and the third woman to work as one, after Jaddan Bai and Saraswati Devi. Born in Gwalior in 1941 to the lyricist and singer Manohar Khanna, she debuted at eighteen and remained active for more than three decades, among the commercially most successful composers in a field almost entirely male.
debut: Dil Deke Dekho (1959), at the age of eighteen.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zamana (1985). Elsewhere, Shabnam, Hum Hindustani, Souten (1983) and Aap To Aise Na The.
recurring_themes: Melodic romantic songs in the mainstream idiom of the 1960s to 1980s.
creative_style: A conventional melodist of her period, writing for the playback voices of successive generations.
major_awards: Filmfare Best Music Director nomination for Souten (1983).
historical_importance: The only woman to sustain a long career as a Hindi film music director, across more than thirty years.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Zamana (1985), Ramesh Talwar's drama written by Salim Khan and Javed Akhtar, in which Kapoor plays Ravi, the criminal brother to Rajesh Khanna's police inspector, with both men in love with the same woman.
biography: Usha Khanna composed the songs for Zamana (1985), her only film in this workbook. Born in Gwalior in 1941 to the lyricist Manohar Khanna, she became the third woman music director in Hindi cinema at eighteen with Dil Deke Dekho and sustained the longest such career by far, through Shabnam, Aap To Aise Na The and Souten, for which she was nominated for the Filmfare award in 1983. The scarcity is the point: of the hundreds of composer credits across Rishi Kapoor's 160 films, one belongs to a woman. His career was scored overwhelmingly by R. D. Burman and Laxmikant-Pyarelal, and the structures of the industry that produced that concentration are the same ones that left Khanna, by some distance the most successful woman in her field, with a single appearance here.

name: Uttank Vora
industry: Hindi and Gujarati film, television and theatre
career_background: Uttank Vora is an Indian music director and composer for film, television and theatre, born in Mumbai in 1968 into a Gujarati musical family as the youngest son of Pt. Vinayakrai Vora, the classical musician who popularised the tar-shehnai as a solo instrument. He began in Gujarati musical theatre.
debut: His cinema career began with Ashutosh Gowariker's Pehla Nasha (1993).
major_works: With Kapoor: Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017). Elsewhere, the television serials Meerabai (1997), Khichdi (2002), Sarabhai vs Sarabhai (2004) and Baa Bahoo Aur Baby (2005).
recurring_themes: Comic television scoring and Gujarati theatre music.
creative_style: A composer formed by classical training and the demands of weekly television; he scored Sarabhai vs Sarabhai Take 2 with his son.
historical_importance: Composer of the themes of several of the best-known Indian television comedies.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi (2017), Sanjay Chhel's comedy, in which Kapoor plays Guggi Tandon, the Punjabi father facing a Gujarati one over their children's marriage.
biography: Uttank Vora composed the songs for Patel Ki Punjabi Shaadi, one of Rishi Kapoor's last leads. Born in Mumbai in 1968 to the classical musician Pt. Vinayakrai Vora, he worked in Gujarati musical theatre, entered cinema with Ashutosh Gowariker's Pehla Nasha in 1993, and became best known for television, scoring Khichdi, Sarabhai vs Sarabhai and Baa Bahoo Aur Baby. His presence fits the film, a Punjabi-Gujarati community comedy written by a Gujarati playwright and scored by a Gujarati television composer. Kapoor is top-billed in a part built entirely on fatherhood, with the romance given to the younger cast, which is how his final leads are consistently constructed. The film did not succeed.

name: V. D. Kalra
career_background: V. D. Kalra, also known as Vasudev Lal Kalra, was an Indian film producer. Born in Dera Ismail Khan in 1936, he came to Amritsar with his family during the 1947 partition, and he and his four brothers ran a transport goods company in Kanpur. A manager approached him in 1962 and he invested in his first film, Rut Rangili Aayi; he later left the industry and returned to the transport business.
debut: Rut Rangili Aayi, his first production, entered after a chance approach in 1962.
major_works: With Kapoor: Salaam Memsaab (1979). Elsewhere, Rut Rangili Aayi.
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented; an outside investor rather than a career producer.
historical_importance: Not independently documented. His article is unreferenced, tagged for notability, and contradicts itself on his dates.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Salaam Memsaab (1979), Asrani's comedy drama about two street singers outside the Taj Mahal hotel, in which Kapoor makes a guest appearance alongside Sunil Dutt, with no character of consequence recorded in the cast list.
biography: V. D. Kalra produced Salaam Memsaab (1979), in which Rishi Kapoor makes a guest appearance. Born in Dera Ismail Khan in 1936 and displaced to Amritsar in 1947, Kalra ran a transport goods business in Kanpur with his brothers and entered film production in 1962 after a manager approached him, financing Rut Rangili Aayi; he later returned to the transport trade. His Wikipedia article is unreferenced, tagged for notability and internally inconsistent about when he died, giving 1981, 1995 and 1996 in different places, so the dates recorded here are deliberately partial. His one appearance in this filmography is a small film for Asrani, who had directed Kapoor's self-appearance in Chala Murari Hero Banne two years earlier.

name: V.K.S. Films
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ranbhoomi (1991).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ranbhoomi (1991), Deepak Sareen's action film, in which Kapoor plays Bholanath, who comes to the city with five hundred rupees, leaves the money with a prostitute for safekeeping, and attaches himself to the gangster Roopa as a housekeeper.
biography: V.K.S. Films is credited on Ranbhoomi (1991) and has no documented history. The film places Kapoor second to Jackie Shroff's gangster in a role with almost no romantic content, which is where his co-lead parts had arrived by 1991. He had five releases that year, including Ajooba and Ghar Parivar, and in most of them he is support or half of a pair. The lover-boy readings for this period drop to their lowest point before the brief recovery of Bol Radha Bol and Deewana the following year. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vaibhav Suman
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), Smeep Kang's comedy, in which Kapoor plays Yograj Singh, a widowed father whose son has no job and no interest in the family farm.
biography: Vaibhav Suman is credited as a writer on Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019) and has no documented biography. He is one of several writers on a film with an unusually crowded credit list, and the production is the least documented of Kapoor's final releases. Its interest here is chronological: released in July 2019, between his return from cancer treatment and The Body in December, it is part of the deliberate burst of work in his last two years, when he took four films after an eighteen-month absence. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Valentin Ezhov
career_background: Valentin Ivanovich Yezhov, credited on this film as Valentin Ezhov, was a Soviet and Russian screenwriter, playwright and professor at VGIK. He began working in cinema in 1953 and became one of the most prolific screenwriters in the Soviet Union, writing or co-writing more than fifty screenplays across almost every genre, including documentaries.
debut: Film work from 1953; international recognition with Ballad of a Soldier (1959).
major_works: With Kapoor: Ajooba (1991). Elsewhere, Ballad of a Soldier (1959), co-written with Grigory Chukhray.
recurring_themes: War and its human cost, written from the experience of a veteran.
creative_style: A classically trained Soviet screenwriter and teacher, working in a tradition of structured literary scripting.
major_awards: For Ballad of a Soldier: the special jury prize at Cannes in 1960, the BAFTA Award for Best Film and the Bodil Award in 1961, and an Academy Award nomination.
historical_importance: One of the central screenwriters of post-war Soviet cinema and a teacher of several generations at VGIK.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ajooba (1991), the Indo-Soviet fantasy adventure directed by Shashi Kapoor with Gennady Vasilyev, in which Kapoor plays Hassan, friend and accomplice to Amitabh Bachchan's masked rider. Yezhov is one of two Soviet writers credited on the film, with Yu Avetikov.
biography: Valentin Yezhov co-wrote Ajooba, the Indo-Soviet co-production his uncle Shashi Kapoor directed. Born in 1921 and a veteran of the war, Yezhov entered cinema in 1953 and wrote more than fifty screenplays, the most celebrated being Ballad of a Soldier with Grigory Chukhray, which took the special jury prize at Cannes in 1960, the BAFTA for Best Film in 1961 and an Academy Award nomination; he taught for decades at VGIK. His presence on Ajooba is the most unexpected credit in this filmography, a serious Soviet screenwriter attached to an Arabian-nights adventure with flying carpets. The co-production was expensive, long-delayed and a comprehensive failure in India, and Rishi Kapoor's part in it is the hero's companion, with no romantic function at all.

name: Varun Bajaj
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: All Is Well (2015).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: All Is Well (2015), Umesh Shukla's comedy drama, in which Kapoor plays Bhajanlal Bhalla, a baker whose harshness towards his son conceals years of debt and a wife with Alzheimer's he has sent away.
biography: Varun Bajaj is credited as a producer on All Is Well (2015) and has no documented biography. The film was assembled from several production entities, including T-Series, and it failed. Its place in this workbook is as the first of Umesh Shukla's two films with Kapoor: the same father-and-son material, badly handled here and handled very well three years later in 102 Not Out, where Kapoor moves from the parent's position to the child's. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vasant Doshi
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani (1988).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani (1988), Kalpataru's drama, in which Kapoor plays Ram, the second son of the house, whose sister suggests that his wife Sita and his younger brother are having an affair, and who believes it, spies on them and keeps the suspicion alive.
biography: Vasant Doshi is credited as a producer on Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani (1988) and has no documented biography. The film is the most unusual of Kapoor's three with Kalpataru because the damage is internal: his own jealousy, planted by a sister, ruins a marriage that faces no outside threat at all. In a filmography where pair friction averages far below external opposition, this is one of the few entries that reverses the ratio, and it does so by making the husband the antagonist of his own relationship. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vashu Bhagnani
career_background: Vashu Bhagnani is an Indian film producer from Mumbai, of Sindhi descent, born in Calcutta in 1961. He left school in the sixth standard for financial reasons, sold clothes in several cities, moved to Mumbai in 1989 and worked in manufacturing before founding Puja Entertainment India in 1995.
debut: Coolie No. 1 (1995), the first film under Puja Entertainment.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009). Elsewhere, Coolie No. 1, Hero No. 1, Bade Miyan Chote Miyan, Rehnaa Hai Terre Dil Mein and Mission Raniganj.
recurring_themes: Star comedies and launches for family members; broad commercial entertainment.
creative_style: A proprietor-producer building vehicles around established comic stars and, later, around his son Jackky.
historical_importance: A durable commercial producer across three decades, notable for the Coolie No. 1 and Hero No. 1 cycle with Govinda and David Dhawan.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009), in which Kapoor plays Professor Siddharth Verma, the college warden charmed by a gifted new student and revealed at the close as the man behind the bombings the student has been trying to prevent. The film was a launch vehicle for the producer's son.
biography: Vashu Bhagnani produced Kal Kissne Dekha, which contains the first antagonist role in Rishi Kapoor's filmography. Born in Calcutta in 1961, Bhagnani left school early, sold clothes for a living, reached Mumbai in 1989 and founded Puja Entertainment in 1995, where Coolie No. 1 and Hero No. 1 made him one of the industry's reliable comedy producers; the film was built to launch his son Jackky. Its interest here is entirely in Kapoor's part: the warm, trusted warden who turns out to be the bomber, which uses his likeability as misdirection three years before Agneepath did the same thing to acclaim. The film was dismissed and the performance went unremarked, so his villain phase is usually dated to 2012. On the evidence of the Films sheet it starts here.

name: Veena Pictures
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zamana (1985).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Zamana (1985), Ramesh Talwar's drama, in which Kapoor plays Ravi, the criminal brother to Rajesh Khanna's policeman, the two divided by a misunderstanding and by a murdered father neither knew, and both in love with the same woman.
biography: Veena Pictures is credited on Zamana (1985) and has no documented history. The film is the one Salim-Javed script in this workbook and the one Usha Khanna score, which makes a minor production the point of contact with two of Hindi cinema's more significant names. It is also representative of Kapoor's mid-1980s position: second-billed to Rajesh Khanna, cast in a brother-against-brother plot designed for a different kind of star, and competing with the woman for neither sympathy nor screen time. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Veeru Devgan
career_background: Virender Harjidas Devgan, known as Veeru Devgan, was an Indian action choreographer, film director and producer. Born in Amritsar in 1934, he ran away to Bombay at thirteen, was jailed and destitute before finding work washing a cab for shelter, became a carpenter and was recruited into films by the action director Ravi Khanna, who saw him in a street fight. He contributed to more than 200 films.
debut: Action choreography from the 1960s; director of Hindustan Ki Kasam (1999).
major_works: With Kapoor: Raju Chacha (2000), as producer; his article also lists Prem Rog (FILM-037) among the films he worked on, as an action choreographer, a credit type this workbook does not track. Elsewhere, Roti Kapada Aur Makaan, Mr. Natwarlal, Kranti, Ram Teri Ganga Maili and Phool Aur Kaante.
recurring_themes: Action design for the masala cinema of the 1970s and 1980s.
creative_style: A stunt and fight designer of the pre-digital era, working in physical choreography on a very large scale.
historical_importance: One of the most prolific action directors in Hindi cinema and the father of Ajay Devgn, whose career he launched with Phool Aur Kaante.
relationship_with_actor: One film as producer: Raju Chacha (2000), Anil Devgan's expensive children's adventure, in which Kapoor plays Siddhant Rai, a wealthy widower whose three children drive off every governess he hires. His action work spans more of this filmography than the credit shows: his own article lists Prem Rog (1982) among his films, and action choreography is not a field recorded in this workbook's Films sheet.
biography: Veeru Devgan produced Raju Chacha, the Ajay Devgn vehicle that failed at the lowest point of Rishi Kapoor's career. Born in Amritsar in 1934, Devgan reached Bombay at thirteen with no ticket and no money, slept where he could and was pulled into films by an action director who saw him fighting in the street; he went on to choreograph action for more than 200 films, from Roti Kapada Aur Makaan and Kranti to Phool Aur Kaante, which launched his son. His article lists Prem Rog among his credits, so his work and Kapoor's intersected nearly twenty years before this film, in a register the workbook does not track. Raju Chacha itself gave Kapoor the distracted rich father, the part he was offered repeatedly between 1999 and 2004.

name: Venus Records & Tapes
career_background: Venus Records & Tapes, now Ishtar Music, is an Indian record label founded in 1985 by Ganesh Jain and Ratan Jain as Venus Music. It is known primarily for publishing and marketing Bollywood soundtracks and Indi-pop, and was acquired by the French company Believe Digital in 2021 and rebranded as Ishtar.
debut: Founded as Venus Music in 1985.
major_works: With Kapoor: Daraar (1996). Elsewhere, a large catalogue of Hindi film soundtracks from the late 1980s onwards.
recurring_themes: Music-led film investment: the label's productions are built around saleable soundtracks.
creative_style: A record company extending into production, in the pattern T-Series established.
historical_importance: One of the major Indian labels of the cassette and early CD era, and part of the shift that made music rights central to film financing.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Daraar (1996), Abbas-Mustan's thriller, in which Kapoor plays Raj, who falls in love with Priya in Shimla without knowing she is hiding from a husband who beat her and killed the doctor who treated her.
biography: Venus Records & Tapes backed Daraar, Rishi Kapoor's last substantial romantic lead. Founded in 1985 by Ganesh and Ratan Jain as Venus Music, the label became one of the largest in the Indian cassette era and moved into film investment on the strength of soundtrack rights, following the model T-Series had established two years earlier; Believe Digital bought it in 2021 and renamed it Ishtar. Daraar belongs to the Abbas-Mustan cycle of obsession thrillers, and it reassigns Kapoor's romantic function entirely: at forty-four he is the decent alternative rather than the pursuer, with the violent husband supplying both the plot and the danger. The film succeeded, and within three years his leading career had ended.

name: Vijay Sinha
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ranbhoomi (1991).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ranbhoomi (1991), Deepak Sareen's action film, in which Kapoor plays Bholanath, the villager who comes to the city with five hundred rupees and ends up keeping house for a gangster.
biography: Vijay Sinha is credited as a producer on Ranbhoomi (1991) and has no documented biography. The film is one of five Kapoor releases that year and one of the clearest signs of his position in the industry at the time: billed with Jackie Shroff, given a part with almost no romantic content, in an action film whose structure has no use for the qualities that made him. The pattern holds until Bol Radha Bol and Deewana in 1992 briefly restored him to the centre of his own films. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vijayashree Pictures
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Badaltey Rishtey (1978).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Badaltey Rishtey (1978), in which Kapoor plays Manohar, who falls for the music teacher Savitri at first meeting and courts her by pretending to sell eggs at her door, before she is married off to a wealthy man under a prediction that her husband will die within forty days.
biography: Vijayashree Pictures is credited on Badaltey Rishtey (1978) and has no documented history. The film is a good specimen of the courtship Kapoor was built for in the late 1970s: a daily pretext invented to appear at the woman's door, persistence presented as charm, and the obstacle arriving from outside in the form of prophecy and family calculation. Read against the modern perspective this workbook also applies, the sequence stays on the right side of coercion mainly because the film grants Savitri her own interest in him. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vikrant Batra
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Manto (2018), Nandita Das's biographical drama, in which Kapoor appears briefly as an unnamed film producer, part of a gallery of cameos peopling the Bombay film world Saadat Hasan Manto worked in before partition took him to Lahore.
biography: Vikrant Batra is credited as a producer on Manto (2018) and has no documented biography. Kapoor's single scene as an anonymous 1940s producer is the most self-aware cameo of his career: the grandson of Prithviraj Kapoor and son of Raj Kapoor, playing a functionary of the industry his family built, in a film about a writer that industry used and discarded. It is also the only festival-circuit film in his last decade, and the only one of his four late cameos with any critical standing. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vimal Kumar
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The documented Vimal Kumar is an Indian badminton player and a different person.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aap Ke Deewane (1980).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Aap Ke Deewane (1980), Surendra Mohan's romance, in which Kapoor and Rakesh Roshan play friends expelled from college on a false charge who pose as a married couple to be hired as tutors, and both fall in love with the same woman.
biography: Vimal Kumar is credited as a producer on Aap Ke Deewane (1980) and has no documented biography; the badminton player of that name is unrelated. The film belongs to the double-hero comedies that ran through Kapoor's late 1970s and early 1980s, where the romantic contest is between two friends rather than between the couple and the world. Those films produce his highest mutuality readings and his lowest external-opposition readings, which makes them the structural exception in a filmography otherwise organised around outside obstruction. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: VinR Films
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), Smeep Kang's comedy, in which Kapoor plays Yograj Singh, a widowed father exasperated by a son who will not work.
biography: VinR Films is credited on Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019) and has no documented history. The film carries an unusually long list of small production entities, writers and composers, none of them documented, which is how several of Kapoor's last projects were financed: many minor investors rather than a studio. It stands in direct contrast with 102 Not Out the year before, funded through an international studio's Indian arm, and the two together show the range of production conditions he worked in at the end. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vinay Gupta
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own. The documented Vinay Gupta is an Indian materials scientist and a different person.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), in which Kapoor plays the widowed father Yograj Singh in Smeep Kang's village comedy.
biography: Vinay Gupta is credited as a producer on Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019) and has no documented biography; the materials scientist of that name is unrelated. The film is the second-last to reach cinemas in Kapoor's lifetime and the weakest of his final four. He had returned from a year of cancer treatment in New York in late 2018 and worked steadily afterwards, across a Netflix comedy, a Punjabi-comedy remake, a thriller and the unfinished Sharmaji Namkeen, without regard to the standing of the production. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vinod Mehra
career_background: Vinod Mehra was an Indian actor in Hindi films who also produced and directed. Born in Amritsar in 1945 into a Punjabi Khatri family, he debuted as a child actor in Adl-e-Jehangir (1955), was male runner-up to Rajesh Khanna in the 1965 United Producers and Filmfare talent contest, and began his adult career with Ek Thi Reeta (1971), appearing in more than a hundred films before his death in 1990.
debut: Child actor in Adl-e-Jehangir (1955); adult debut Ek Thi Reeta (1971).
major_works: With Kapoor: Gurudev (1993), which he produced and directed. Elsewhere, a long acting career through the 1970s and 1980s.
recurring_themes: Mainstream romance and family drama as an actor; one directorial venture.
creative_style: An actor who turned to production and direction late and did not live to see the result released.
historical_importance: A durable leading and second-lead actor of the 1970s, remembered partly for his early death at forty-five.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Gurudev (1993), which he produced and directed, and in which Kapoor plays Inspector Dev, whose closest childhood friend is the son of the don he is ordered to arrest. Mehra died in October 1990; the film was released in September 1993, nearly three years later.
biography: Vinod Mehra produced and directed Gurudev, which reached cinemas three years after his death. Born in Amritsar in 1945, Mehra began as a child actor in 1955, lost the 1965 United Producers talent contest to Rajesh Khanna as male runner-up, and built a career of more than a hundred films from 1971 until he died in October 1990 at forty-five. Gurudev was his only film behind the camera and was finished and released by others in 1993, which puts it among the delayed and posthumous releases clustered through Kapoor's early 1990s. Kapoor plays a police inspector whose loyalties are divided between duty and a childhood friend, in a crowded cast with Sridevi and Anil Kapoor, and the film is remembered mainly for Mehra's absence from it.

name: Vinod Shah
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Dhan Daulat (1980).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Dhan Daulat (1980), Harish Shah's masala film, in which Kapoor plays Lucky, raised by two truck drivers who sell their truck to fund his match business, and who turns on the men who raised him after being told he was found abandoned.
biography: Vinod Shah is credited as a producer on Dhan Daulat (1980) and has no documented biography. The film is one of two Kapoor releases on 11 January 1980, the other being Do Premee, which is itself a sign of how fast he was working: five films reached cinemas that year. Dhan Daulat is a parentage melodrama in which the romance is secondary to the question of who raised him, and it belongs with Rangila Ratan and Barood among the films that cast him in plots designed for a more volatile actor. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vipin Mishra
career_background: A composer credited on one film in this filmography for both songs and background score, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aurangzeb (2013).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Aurangzeb (2013), Atul Sabharwal's crime drama, in which Kapoor plays DCP Ravikant Phogat, his honest brother's corrupt opposite and the architect of the plan to plant a young man inside the Singh household in place of his twin.
biography: Vipin Mishra wrote both the songs and the background score for Aurangzeb (2013) and has no documented biography. The film is the second of Kapoor's antagonist roles for Yash Raj and the most structurally interesting: he plays a corrupt policeman against his own honest brother, both parts in a double game, which gives him the plot's intelligence rather than only its menace. It came a year after Agneepath and in the same year as D-Day, in the concentrated villain phase that followed his reinvention at fifty-nine. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vipul Amrutlal Shah
industry: Hindi and Gujarati cinema; Gujarati theatre
career_background: Vipul Amrutlal Shah is an Indian film producer and director who began in Gujarati theatre, directing and performing in a number of well-received Gujarati plays. He moved to television with the long-running serial Ek Mahal Ho Sapno Ka, made his feature debut with the Gujarati film Dariya Chhoru, and then worked in Hindi cinema, where four of his six films starred Akshay Kumar.
debut: Gujarati theatre and the serial Ek Mahal Ho Sapno Ka; his Hindi debut was Aankhen (2002), adapted from his own Gujarati play.
major_works: With Kapoor: Namastey London (2007), which he directed and produced. Elsewhere, Aankhen (2002), Waqt: The Race Against Time (2005) and, as producer and writer, The Kerala Story.
recurring_themes: Plays adapted for the screen; family obligation, diaspora identity and national belonging.
creative_style: A theatre adapter working in mainstream Hindi cinema, latterly in explicitly political material.
historical_importance: A commercially successful director of the 2000s whose later production work turned towards propaganda.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Namastey London (2007), which he directed and produced, in which Kapoor plays Manmohan, who went to London to make his fortune and never went home, ashamed of a wife who cannot speak English and father to a daughter ashamed of India in turn.
biography: Vipul Amrutlal Shah directed Namastey London, among the best of Rishi Kapoor's supporting roles. Shah came up through Gujarati theatre, adapted his own play Aandhlo Pato into the hit Aankhen in 2002, followed it with Waqt in 2005, and made four films with Akshay Kumar; his later work includes producing and writing The Kerala Story. Namastey London gives Kapoor the Punjabi father in Southall whose own embarrassment at his wife has produced a daughter contemptuous of where she comes from, and the film takes his position seriously rather than mocking it. The part arrives in the same year as two undistributed English-language films for his cousin, which places it precisely at the turn from the thin years to the late revival.

name: Virendra Sinha
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zehreela Insaan (1974).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Zehreela Insaan (1974), Puttanna Kanagal's Hindi version of his Kannada film Nagarahavu, in which Kapoor plays Arjun, an ill-tempered, soft-hearted young man whom the village reads as a bad character and who is obedient only to the schoolmaster who sees his qualities.
biography: Virendra Sinha produced Zehreela Insaan (1974) under the Pragati Chitra International banner and has no documented biography. The film is the most interesting failure of Rishi Kapoor's early career: made immediately after Bobby, directed by a major Kannada filmmaker from a novel by the Kannada writer T. R. Subba Rao, and built around a protagonist whose anger the film treats as a social misreading rather than a flaw. It gave him two separate romances, with Aarti lost to a forced marriage and a second love in his Christian classmate, and nothing like it appears again in the filmography. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vision Universal
career_background: A production banner credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of its own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985), P. Madhavan's drama about an overweight, sensitive man who becomes a film star to win the woman he loves and returns to find her married, in which Kapoor appears as himself. The film belongs to Sanjeev Kumar.
biography: Vision Universal is credited on Ram Tere Kitne Nam (1985) and has no documented history. Kapoor's appearance as himself is the second of four such credits, and like the others it comes in a film about the film industry. 1985 was one of his busiest years, with Saagar, Tawaif and Zamana all released within months, and the self-appearance sits among them as a courtesy rather than a role. The Films sheet records its romance presence as none, which the Overview's counts depend on. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vivek Anchalia
career_background: A writer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rajma Chawal (2018).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Rajma Chawal (2018), Leena Yadav's comedy drama, in which Kapoor plays Raj Mathur, a widower who cannot talk to the son he is now alone with, joins Facebook to reach him, is blocked, and then steals a young woman's identity to become the boy's confidante.
biography: Vivek Anchalia is credited as a writer on Rajma Chawal (2018) and has no documented biography. The film went to Netflix rather than cinemas and is one of Kapoor's last two leads. The part could not have existed earlier in his career: a father who is inept, quietly dishonest and visibly lonely, with no romantic function at all, in a comedy that depends on him impersonating a young woman online. His final films pursue that register consistently, from Do Dooni Chaar through Sharmaji Namkeen. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vivek Rangachari
career_background: A producer credited on one film in this filmography, with no Wikipedia article of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: D-Day (2013).
recurring_themes: Not documented.
creative_style: Not documented.
historical_importance: Not independently documented.
relationship_with_actor: One film: D-Day (2013), Nikhil Advani's spy thriller, in which Kapoor plays Iqbal Seth, called Goldman, the fugitive a RAW agent has spent nine years undercover as a barber to track, who escapes the snatch operation and is then hunted by his own protectors.
biography: Vivek Rangachari is credited as a producer on D-Day (2013) and has no documented biography. The film gave Kapoor the hardest role of his late career, a Dawood Ibrahim figure played without charm as an exit route, and it is the second of two films Nikhil Advani made with him after Patiala House in 2011. In those two films Advani used him in opposite ways, as a father whose authority has ruined his son and as a gangster whose domesticity makes him worse, which is the clearest demonstration of how wide his late range actually was. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Vivek Sharma
career_background: Vivek Sharma is an Indian filmmaker, born in Jabalpur in 1969. He took a master's degree in physics, moved to Mumbai in 1992 and spent six years as an assistant director to Mahesh Bhatt on films including Hum Hain Rahi Pyar Ke, Naajayaz, Chaahat and Duplicate, then worked with Shah Rukh Khan and Juhi Chawla's Dreamz Unlimited on Phir Bhi Dil Hai Hindustani, Asoka and Chalte Chalte.
debut: Directorial debut with Bhoothnath (2008), for which Amitabh Bachchan agreed to lead.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009). Elsewhere, Bhoothnath (2008).
recurring_themes: Family-facing fantasy and youth cinema.
creative_style: A long-serving assistant director whose own films work in broad commercial genres.
historical_importance: Known chiefly for Bhoothnath, a commercially successful children's fantasy with Amitabh Bachchan.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Kal Kissne Dekha (2009), which he directed, in which Kapoor plays Professor Siddharth Verma, the college warden revealed at the end to be the man behind the bombings his gifted student has been trying to prevent. It is the earliest antagonist role in this filmography.
biography: Vivek Sharma directed Kal Kissne Dekha, which contains Rishi Kapoor's first villain. Born in Jabalpur in 1969 with a master's in physics, Sharma spent six years assisting Mahesh Bhatt, worked through Dreamz Unlimited on Phir Bhi Dil Hai Hindustani and Chalte Chalte, and made his debut with Bhoothnath in 2008 after persuading Amitabh Bachchan to lead it. This follow-up, a science-fiction launch vehicle for Jackky Bhagnani, failed. The role in it matters anyway: the avuncular warden whose warmth is the disguise, played three years before Agneepath made that reversal famous and earned Kapoor a second career as an antagonist. Nobody noticed at the time, which is why the Films sheet rather than the critical record is where the shift is visible.

name: Walt Disney Pictures
career_background: Walt Disney Pictures is an American film production company and a subsidiary of the Walt Disney Studios, founded on 16 October 1923 and based in Burbank, California. It became the live-action division named Walt Disney Pictures in the 1983 studio reorganisation that also created Touchstone Pictures, and its films are distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures.
debut: Live-action production from the 1950s; the Walt Disney Pictures name from 1983.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Dooni Chaar (2010). Elsewhere, a very large slate of American live-action features.
recurring_themes: Family-facing features; in India, a short-lived slate of local-language productions.
creative_style: A studio operation; in India it backed small, realistic films quite unlike its American output.
historical_importance: One of the major studios of world cinema, and for a few years around 2010 a direct investor in Hindi-language production.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Do Dooni Chaar (2010), in which Kapoor plays Santosh Duggal, a Delhi maths teacher whose family of four shares a one-bedroom flat and whose dignity is invested in a decrepit scooter called the Duggal Express, until his sister's demand that they arrive at a wedding by car sets the plot going. He played it opposite Neetu Singh, his first film with her in nearly thirty years, and it won him the National Film Award.
biography: Walt Disney Pictures financed Do Dooni Chaar, the film that confirmed Rishi Kapoor's second career. Founded in 1923 and reorganised into its present live-action form in 1983, Disney spent a few years around 2010 investing directly in Hindi-language production, and this is one of the results: a small, realistic comedy about a maths teacher who cannot afford a car, shot largely in a one-bedroom flat. It is the least glamorous film in this filmography and the best received of his leads, winning the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Hindi, and it reunited him with Neetu Singh for the first time since the 1980s, as a long-married couple rather than as lovers. The contrast with his 1970s work is the point: the romance here is domestic, exhausted and entirely credible.

name: Walt Disney Pictures India
career_background: The Indian production arm credited on this film, for which no separate Wikipedia article exists; the parent company, Walt Disney Pictures, is documented. Disney invested directly in Hindi-language production for a few years around 2010.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Dooni Chaar (2010).
recurring_themes: Small-scale, realistic Hindi features, unlike the parent studio's American slate.
creative_style: Not separately documented.
historical_importance: Part of the brief period in which Hollywood studios financed local-language Indian production directly.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Do Dooni Chaar (2010), in which Kapoor plays the Delhi maths teacher Santosh Duggal opposite Neetu Singh, and for which he won the National Film Award.
biography: Walt Disney Pictures India is credited on Do Dooni Chaar (2010) and has no documented history of its own apart from its parent company. The credit records something real about how Kapoor's late career became possible: for a few years around 2010 international studios financed small Hindi films directly, and a comedy about a schoolteacher who cannot afford a car, with no stars of the moment and no spectacle, could be made with a Disney logo on it. The film won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Hindi and reunited him with Neetu Singh after almost thirty years.

name: Yash Johar
career_background: Yash Johar was an Indian film producer and the founder of Dharma Productions. Born in Amritsar in 1929 into a Punjabi Hindu family associated with the Arya Samaj, he began in the early 1950s as a publicist and still photographer at Filmistan, joined Sunil Dutt's Ajanta Arts in 1962, and handled production for Dev Anand's Navketan Films on Guide, Jewel Thief, Prem Pujari and Hare Rama Hare Krishna before founding his own banner.
debut: Production management from the 1960s; Dharma Productions from 1976.
major_works: With Kapoor: Duniya (1984). Elsewhere, the Dharma Productions slate, including Dostana, Agneepath (1990) and Kuch Kuch Hota Hai.
recurring_themes: Lavish sets, foreign locations and an emphasis on Indian tradition and family values.
creative_style: A production man by training, whose banner's style was built on scale and sentiment.
historical_importance: Founder of one of the two or three most important production houses in modern Hindi cinema, carried on by his son Karan Johar.
relationship_with_actor: One film in his own lifetime: Duniya (1984), Ramesh Talwar's action drama, in which Kapoor plays Ravi, the lost son working for the men who framed his father. The more consequential link is institutional: Dharma, under his son Karan Johar, gave Kapoor three films in 2012 alone, including Agneepath, the remake of the 1990 film Yash Johar himself produced.
biography: Yash Johar produced Duniya, the one Dharma Productions film Rishi Kapoor made in his lifetime, and founded the company that reopened his career twenty-eight years later. Born in Amritsar in 1929, Johar learned production as a publicist at Filmistan and then with Sunil Dutt's Ajanta Arts and Dev Anand's Navketan, where he managed Guide, Jewel Thief and Hare Rama Hare Krishna, before building Dharma into a banner known for scale and sentiment; he married Yash Chopra's sister Hiroo and died in 2004. The sequence is worth stating plainly: he produced Agneepath in 1990 with Amitabh Bachchan, his son remade it in 2012 with Kapoor as Rauf Lala, and that performance, together with Student of the Year and Agneepath's reception, gave him his final decade of work.

name: Yo Yo Honey Singh
industry: Indian popular music; Hindi and Punjabi cinema
career_background: Hirdesh Singh, known as Yo Yo Honey Singh, is an Indian musician, rapper and producer. Born in Karampura, Delhi, in 1983 and educated at Guru Nanak Public School in New Delhi, he is of Punjabi origin and began in the music industry in 2006, becoming one of the most commercially dominant figures in Indian popular music in the early 2010s.
debut: The 2006 song Glassy, a collaboration with the singer Ashok Masti; his first Hindi film song was in Mastan.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019). Elsewhere, Brown Rang, High Heels and songs for Cocktail and Mastan.
recurring_themes: Punjabi pop and hip-hop built for clubs and film montages.
creative_style: Rhythm-led production with rapped hooks; the voice of the item-song economy of the 2010s.
historical_importance: The figure most associated with the Punjabi-pop takeover of Hindi film soundtracks in the early 2010s; in 2012 he set a record for the highest fee reported for a Bollywood song.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Jhootha Kahin Ka (2019), Smeep Kang's comedy, in which Kapoor plays the widowed father Yograj Singh. Singh is one of several composers credited on the film.
biography: Yo Yo Honey Singh contributed music to Jhootha Kahin Ka, one of Rishi Kapoor's last films. Born Hirdesh Singh in Delhi in 1983, he debuted in 2006 with Glassy alongside Ashok Masti, became ubiquitous in the early 2010s through college-festival touring and the YouTube success of Brown Rang and High Heels, and in 2012 reportedly commanded the highest fee ever paid for a Bollywood song, for Cocktail and Mastan. The credit marks the full distance travelled by the film song across Kapoor's career. His own stardom was built on complete soundtracks by R. D. Burman and Laxmikant-Pyarelal, picturised on him in long romantic sequences; his last films distribute a few songs among several pop producers, and he appears in them as a father watching other people dance.

biography: Yu Avetikov is one of two Soviet writers credited on Ajooba (1991) and has no locatable article. The film is the strangest entry in this filmography: an expensive Indo-Soviet co-production directed by Kapoor's uncle Shashi Kapoor with Gennady Vasilyev, written in part by the Cannes and BAFTA-winning screenwriter of Ballad of a Soldier, and released years late to comprehensive failure in India. Rishi Kapoor's role is the hero's companion, with no romance and no consequence, in what was the most costly miscalculation of his uncle's career. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

biography: Yusuf Bhatt is credited as a producer on Yaraana (1995) and has no documented biography. The film is the third of five David Dhawan made with Kapoor, the longest director relationship in this filmography, running from Bol Radha Bol in 1992 to Chashme Buddoor in 2013. Its romance follows the mid-1990s pattern in which the threat to the couple is a violent or obsessive man rather than a disapproving family, and Kapoor, at forty-three, is the refuge rather than the pursuer. Madhuri Dixit carries the film. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Zakir Hussain
industry: Hindustani classical music; international and Indian film
career_background: Ustad Zakir Hussain Qureshi was an Indian tabla player, composer, arranger, percussionist and music producer, the eldest son of the tabla master Alla Rakha. Born in Bombay in 1951, he began formal training at seven, performed from the same age and toured from twelve. George Harrison advised him against becoming a rock drummer and towards combining Eastern and Western music, and he worked across many genres, doing much to bring Indian classical music to audiences abroad.
debut: Concert performance from childhood; international collaboration from the 1970s, including the band Shakti with John McLaughlin.
major_works: With Kapoor: Manto (2018), as background-score composer. Elsewhere, a very large body of classical and cross-genre recording and performance.
recurring_themes: Rhythm as conversation; the meeting of Hindustani classical music with jazz and Western forms.
creative_style: A classical master who scored sparely for film, using percussion and acoustic texture rather than orchestral underlining.
historical_importance: One of the most celebrated Indian musicians of the past half-century; John McLaughlin called him the king of the tabla.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Manto (2018), Nandita Das's biographical drama, in which Kapoor appears briefly as an unnamed film producer in the Bombay film world Saadat Hasan Manto worked in before partition.
biography: Zakir Hussain is credited with the background score of Manto (2018), in which Rishi Kapoor has a single scene. Born in Bombay in 1951 to Alla Rakha, Hussain trained from the age of seven, performed from childhood and toured from twelve, and became the most internationally visible Indian classical musician of his generation, playing with John McLaughlin in Shakti and recording across jazz, world and classical forms until his death in San Francisco in December 2024. The identification here rests on the film's credit together with his documented composing work, so the row is graded Medium rather than High. The pairing is incidental but telling: the most distinguished musician in this entire sheet is attached to Kapoor's briefest appearance, in the only festival film of his last decade.

biography: Zoeb Springwala is credited as a producer on Patiala House (2011) and has no documented biography. The film gave Kapoor one of the strongest written parts of his late career: a Southall patriarch whose authority is exercised as sustained damage to his own son, hardened by a racist assault years earlier. It is the first of two films Nikhil Advani made with him, the second being D-Day, and together they show the two registers his last decade alternated between, the ruinous father and the genuine criminal. This row is built from the film's credits alone.

name: Zoya Akhtar
career_background: Zoya Akhtar is an Indian director, producer and screenwriter, born in 1972 to the lyricist and screenwriter Javed Akhtar and the screenwriter Honey Irani. She took a diploma in filmmaking from NYU and assisted Mira Nair, Tony Gerber and Dev Benegal before writing and directing her own films. She founded Tiger Baby Films with Reema Kagti in 2015.
debut: Directorial debut Luck by Chance (2009), which won her the Filmfare Award for Best Debut Director.
major_works: With Kapoor: Luck by Chance (2009). Elsewhere, Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara (2011), Dil Dhadakne Do (2015), Gully Boy (2019) and the series Made in Heaven and Dahaad.
recurring_themes: Ambition, privilege and the machinery of the film industry; friendship groups under pressure.
creative_style: Ensemble construction with an insider's eye for the industry's hierarchies, written and shot without melodrama.
major_awards: Four Filmfare Awards, including Best Debut Director for Luck by Chance and Best Director for Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara and Gully Boy.
historical_importance: One of the defining Hindi directors of her generation and the most incisive chronicler of the film industry's own workings.
relationship_with_actor: One film: Luck by Chance (2009), her debut, in which Kapoor plays Romy Rolly, the producer whose casting decision makes the plot possible when a portfolio reaches his studio by accident and he hands an unknown the male lead. The part is a portrait of the kind of man who had been making decisions about Kapoor's own career for thirty-five years. Sajid Khan, who directed him in Housefull 2, is her cousin.
biography: Zoya Akhtar cast Rishi Kapoor as a film producer in Luck by Chance, her debut and one of the three 2009 films that restarted his career. Born in 1972 to Javed Akhtar and Honey Irani, she trained at NYU, assisted Mira Nair and Dev Benegal, and has since made Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara, Dil Dhadakne Do and Gully Boy, winning four Filmfare Awards and founding Tiger Baby Films with Reema Kagti. Luck by Chance is the sharpest film ever made about the Hindi industry's internal workings, and Romy Rolly, vain, superstitious and casually powerful, is written from inside it. Kapoor plays him with no vanity of his own, which is the first clear sign of what his late career would be: a star who had been handled by such men for decades, willing to play one exactly.
